        "text": "\u003cp\u003eWe are halfway through the critical decade for tackling climate change, but the world is off-track to limiting global warming to 1.5°C. We are facing a triple planetary crisis of climate, biodiversity loss and pollution posing critical threats to the UK’s national interests across security, resilience, health, the economy and partnerships with other countries. That is why the UK is re-establishing itself as a climate leader on the global stage. The net zero transition is critical to both national and global security. There is no global stability without climate stability, and Britain must play its part by resetting at home and reconnecting abroad. We remain committed to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (\u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e)’s ambitions on transparency in reporting, in particular on implementing the Enhanced Transparency Framework (\u003cabbr title=\"Enhanced Transparency Framework\"\u003eETF\u003c/abbr\u003e) and stand ready to lead by example, where we can. This report covers the period of 2021-2022 and we also set out our approach going forwards.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eThe UK has made progress in cutting emissions. Between 1990 and 2022, we grew our economy by around 80% and cut our emissions by 50%\u003c/strong\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2020, the UK communicated an ambitious Nationally Determined Contribution (\u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e) target to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by at least 68% by 2030 on 1990 levels. In 2022 in response to the Glasgow Climate Pact at \u003cabbr title=\"The 26th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC\"\u003eCOP26\u003c/abbr\u003e, this target level was reconfirmed and strengthened by increasing its scope to include some crown dependencies and overseas territories and by saying more about implementation. This report sets out the progress made to meeting our 2030 \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e through policies implemented between the years 2021 and 2022 and our plans going forward.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOur Third Climate Change Risk Assessment (\u003cabbr title=\"Third Climate Change Risk Assessment\"\u003eCCRA3\u003c/abbr\u003e), published in 2022, has presented strong evidence that even under low warming scenarios the UK will be subject to a range of significant and costly impacts, including identified risks to health and productivity, the built environment, businesses, the natural environment, and to public services, unless further action is taken to adapt to climate change. Our plan to address these risks is set out in our latest National Adaptation Programme (\u003cabbr title=\"National Adaptation Programme\"\u003eNAP\u003c/abbr\u003e) published in 2023. The UK Government also submitted its first Adaptation Communication to the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e in December 2020 and updated it in 2021. The Communication set out our plans to prepare for the impacts of climate change in the UK and to support climate change adaptation overseas.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK has continued to deliver on our International Climate Finance (\u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e) commitments. We exceeded our pledge to spend £5.8bn \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e between April 2016 and March 2021. Through our \u003cabbr title=\"The 26th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC\"\u003eCOP26\u003c/abbr\u003e presidency, the UK led work on a $100bn climate finance delivery plan to provide clarity on how and when developed countries would meet their finance goal. In 2024 the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (\u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development\"\u003eOECD\u003c/abbr\u003e) reported that in 2022, this goal was achieved with $115.9bn in climate finance mobilised for developing countries.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eLooking ahead, we know we need to do more. We are committed to achieving our \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e commitments under the Paris Agreement, and net zero target by 2050.This is no small feat requiring urgent action, but there are huge opportunities. Meeting these targets requires a wide-reaching transformation of the UK economy, with consumers, businesses and government all having a role to play. That is why making Britain a clean energy superpower is one of the 5 missions of this government - delivering clean power by 2030 and accelerating to net zero across the economy. We can only deliver energy security and good jobs for todays’ generations if we deliver clean energy. And we can only deliver climate security for future generations if we show global leadership. This is why the Prime Minister announced at \u003cabbr title=\"The 29th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC\"\u003eCOP29\u003c/abbr\u003e the UK’s ambitious and credible \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e target to reduce all greenhouse gas emissions by at least 81% by 2035, compared to 1990 levels, excluding international aviation and shipping emissions. In 2025, we will publish a detailed plan, updating the policies and proposals that will enable us to meet carbon budgets 4 to 6 and our 2030 and 2035 \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contributions\"\u003eNDCs\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOn climate adaptation, we are committed to improving the evidence base and further strengthening our approach across government and local communities and will bring forward plans in due course.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOur leadership at \u003cabbr title=\"The 29th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC\"\u003eCOP29\u003c/abbr\u003e demonstrates that the UK is a global leader in the fight against climate change, and this remains a core pillar of our approach to development spending. We will continue to prioritise Climate Finance which will help vulnerable countries adapt to climate impacts and support a transition to low-carbon economies. At \u003cabbr title=\"The 29th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC\"\u003eCOP29\u003c/abbr\u003e, parties agreed that all actors should scale up financing to $1.3 trillion on the New Collective Quantified Goal (\u003cabbr title=\"New Collective Quantified Goal\"\u003eNCQG\u003c/abbr\u003e) on Climate Finance. The UK is committed to delivering climate finance to keep 1.5°C alive in line with our international commitments. This is why we are honouring the existing commitment to spend £11.6bn in International Climate Finance between April 2021 and March 2026 including at least £3bn on nature, from which £1.5bn will be dedicated to protecting and restoring forests. We will also treble our spend, from our \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e commitment, for adaptation to £1.5bn in 2025.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe look forward to our upcoming expert technical review and the Facilitative, Multilateral Consideration of Progress (\u003cabbr title=\"Facilitative Multilateral Consideration of Progress\"\u003eFMCP\u003c/abbr\u003e) to improve our practice. We encourage all Parties to come forward with their first Biennial Transparency Reports (\u003cabbr title=\"Biennial Transparency Reports\"\u003eBTRs\u003c/abbr\u003e) by the 31 December deadline.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eThe Rt Hon Ed Miliband MP, Secretary of State for Department of Energy Security and Net Zero \u0026amp; Minister Kerry McCarthy MP, Minister for Climate for Department of Energy Security and Net Zero\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e"
      }

        "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"scope\"\u003eScope\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Biennial Transparency Report (\u003cabbr title=\"Biennial Transparency Report\"\u003eBTR\u003c/abbr\u003e) is a progress report, agreed under the Enhanced Transparency Framework (\u003cabbr title=\"Enhanced Transparency Framework\"\u003eETF\u003c/abbr\u003e) under the Paris Agreement\u003csup id=\"fnref:1\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:1\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 1]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. Its purpose is to present information on mitigation, adaptation and finance in a transparent and comprehensive way that can be scrutinised by parties as well as by expert reviewers. It is submitted every 2 years.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis is the UK’s first biennial transparency report and provides detail on progress towards the UK’s 2030 Nationally Determined Contribution (\u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:2\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:2\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 2]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. This first report focuses on greenhouse gas emissions reductions between 2021 and 2022, as well as progress towards our 2030 \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e and our emission reductions projections towards 2040. It will include an overview of our adaptation plans up to 2023 and our international climate finance contributions over 2021-2022.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s 2030 \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e covers England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. It also covers the UK’s crown dependencies of the Bailiwick of Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man and the UK’s overseas territory of Gibraltar, which have all had the UK’s ratification of the Paris Agreement extended to them.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe report follows the requirements set out by the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e and therefore it does not include updates on research and systematic observation, education, training and public awareness. This will be included in our 9th National Communication to be published in 2026.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis report also reflects the recommendations made during our last Expert Review in 2023 on our 5th Biennial Report and 9th National Communication. This includes recommendations that the UK include the cost of our policies and provide clarity on the territorial scope (i.e. explain if policies applied to the devolved governments, crown dependencies and overseas territories, or England only).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe report is being submitted to the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e alongside our National Inventory Document (\u003cabbr title=\"National Inventory Document\"\u003eNID\u003c/abbr\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"structure-of-the-report\"\u003eStructure of the report\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe report is structured as follows:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca href=\"#chapter-1\"\u003eChapter 1: National Inventory Document of Anthropogenic Emissions\u003c/a\u003e presents a summary of our National Inventory Document which was submitted in December 2024.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca href=\"#chapter-2\"\u003eChapter 2: Information to track progress in achieving the UK’s Nationally Determined Contribution\u003c/a\u003e presents the UK’s mitigation actions and strategies implemented to achieve the UK’s 2030 \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e (over the period 2021-22), and projections to 2040.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca href=\"#chapter-3\"\u003eChapter 3: Information related to climate change impacts and adaptation\u003c/a\u003e presents the UK’s adaptation measures towards adaptation.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003ca href=\"#chapter-4\"\u003eChapter 4: Information on financial, technology development and transfer and capacity-building support provided and mobilised\u003c/a\u003e presents the UK’s contributions to non-annex 1 parties consistent with the requirements of the Enhanced Transparency Framework.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eAnnex 1: Support provided by the UK’s crown dependencies.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s Biennial Transparency Report submission will include our complete Common Tabular Format (\u003cabbr title=\"Common Tabular Format\"\u003eCTF\u003c/abbr\u003e) tables which can be found on the submission portal. The \u003cabbr title=\"Common Tabular Format\"\u003eCTF\u003c/abbr\u003e tables include information on:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe UK’s Greenhouse Gas Inventory\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eour financial support provided and mobilised\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eprogress made and projections\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e"

        "text": "\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s National Inventory Document (\u003cabbr title=\"National Inventory Document\"\u003eNID\u003c/abbr\u003e) is available on the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e website. This contains a full account of the UK’s \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions, their trends, the methodologies used to estimate them, and the institutional arrangements that underlie them.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEmissions estimates from the UK Greenhouse Gas Inventory are used to meet international reporting requirements under the Paris Agreement and \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e as well as domestic reporting requirements under the Climate Change Act 2008. The geographical scope of these reporting requirements differs:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eClimate Change Act scope\u003c/strong\u003e: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eParis Agreement scope\u003c/strong\u003e: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. It also includes the 3 crown dependencies (Bailiwick of Jersey, Guernsey\u003csup id=\"fnref:3\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:3\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 3]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, Isle of Man) and 1 overseas territory (Gibraltar), which to date, the UK’s ratification of the Paris Agreement has been extended to.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e scope\u003c/strong\u003e: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. It also includes those crown dependencies and overseas territories have had the UK’s ratification of the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e extended to them. These are the 3 crown dependencies (Bailiwick of Jersey, Bailiwick of Guernsey, Isle of Man) and 4 overseas territories (Gibraltar, Cayman Islands, Falkland Islands, Bermuda).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Paris Agreement scope is used for emissions estimates in the Common Reporting Tables (\u003cabbr title=\"Common Tabular         "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"national-circumstances-and-institutional-arrangements\"\u003e2.1 National circumstances and institutional arrangements\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"government-structure-brbr\"\u003e2.1.1 Government structure \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is a Party to the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e and the Paris Agreement. The UK employs a range of institutional structures – at national, sub-national and local level - to enable economy-wide emissions mitigation, as well as numerous policies and measures to underpin delivery. The UK consists of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, with aspects of government policy responsibility devolved to the democratically accountable governments within each, namely the Scottish Government, the Welsh Government and the Northern Ireland Executive. The UK Government has overall responsibility for implementation and delivery of the UK’s climate commitments under the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e, the Kyoto Protocol, and the Paris Agreement, as well as our targets for net zero by 2050, our domestic carbon budgets, and our 2030 and 2035 Nationally Determined Contributions. However, all the devolved governments play a part in this process. The approach taken by each administration will differ, drawing on the range of policies at their disposal. As explained in Chapter 1, the UK’s ratification of the Paris Agreement has to date been extended the 3 crown dependencies, and the overseas territory of Gibraltar – so these are in scope of the UK’s \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e. Climate policy is devolved to the crown dependencies and overseas territories and so they are responsible for setting their own emission reduction targets and climate policies and laws.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Climate Change Act 2008 established the world’s first legally binding framework of national emissions targets. The Act required the UK to set carbon budgets which impose legally binding limits on emissions across 5-year periods. The first 6 carbon budgets have so far been set in law. The Climate Change Committee (\u003cabbr title=\"Climate Change Committee\"\u003eCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e) is an independent, statutory body established under the Climate Change Act 2008. Their purpose is to advise the UK and devolved governments on emissions targets and to report to Parliament on progress made in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and preparing for and adapting to the impacts of climate change. More information on the Climate Change Act can be found in section 2.8.1.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK Government is split into 24 ministerial departments and 20 non-ministerial departments. Each department focuses on a different aspect of government policy, the following of which fed into this report:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eDepartment for Energy Security and Net Zero (\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e), which leads the mission to make Britain a Clean Energy Superpower, achieving clean power by 2030 and accelerating to net zero\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eDepartment for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e), the department responsible for policy and regulations on environmental, food and rural issues including domestic adaptation\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eDepartment for Education (\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Education, England\"\u003eDfE\u003c/abbr\u003e), the department responsible for children’s services and education, including early years, schools, higher and further education policy, apprenticeships and wider skills in England\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eDepartment for Transport (\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Transport\"\u003eDfT\u003c/abbr\u003e), which supports the transport network to help the UK’s businesses and get people and goods travelling around the country\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eForeign, Commonwealth and Development Office (\u003cabbr title=\"Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office\"\u003eFCDO\u003c/abbr\u003e), leads on the UK’s diplomatic, development and consular work around the world\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eDepartment for Science, Innovation and Technology (\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Science, Innovation and Technology\"\u003eDSIT\u003c/abbr\u003e), ensures that new and existing technologies are safely developed and deployed across the UK and drive forward a modern digital government for the benefit of its citizens\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eMinistry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (\u003cabbr title=\"Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local government\"\u003eMHCLG\u003c/abbr\u003e), lead on affordable homes and handing power back to communities and rebuilding local governments\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eFurther information about the UK Government can be found at GOV.UK\u003csup id=\"fnref:4\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:4\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 4]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"northern-ireland-executive-brbr\"\u003e2.1.2 Northern Ireland Executive \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn January 2020 the ‘New Decade, New Approach\u003csup id=\"fnref:5\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:5\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 5]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e’ was published, which set out a commitment to tackle climate change head-on using a coordinated and strategic approach.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOn behalf of the \u003cabbr title=\"Northern Ireland\"\u003eNI\u003c/abbr\u003e Executive the Department for Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (\u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e) has led on the development of a draft Green Growth Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:6\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:6\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 6]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, collaborating with other departments, local government and key stakeholders from across the business, voluntary and community sectors in its development.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo ensure that there is a coordinated and strategic approach to deliver a Green Growth Strategic Oversight Group, which is a group of senior officials from all 9 Northern Ireland (\u003cabbr title=\"Northern Ireland\"\u003eNI\u003c/abbr\u003e) government departments, provides overall strategic direction for the Executive’s Green Growth and climate change commitments.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"scottish-government-brbr\"\u003e2.1.3 Scottish Government \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Scottish Government has a range of responsibilities, including climate change policy and many of its constituent lever policies. The Scottish Parliament passes laws on devolved matters, which includes a statutory framework for Scotland’s approach to tackling climate change.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Scottish Government remains absolutely committed to ending Scotland’s contribution to global emissions as soon as possible, and by 2045 at the latest (through a statutory net zero target). Scotland’s emissions halved between 1990 and 2022, while our economy has grown by 67%, proving that tackling climate change and growing our economy go hand in hand.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eClimate change is embedded across the Scottish Government through a robust ministerial and corporate governance framework. Accountability for climate action is led by the Cabinet Secretary for Net Zero and Energy and supported by the Cabinet Sub-Committee for the Climate Emergency which provides cross-government leadership, assurance and coordination of efforts.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAt a corporate level, oversight and assurance of climate policy delivery is provided by the Global Climate Emergency (\u003cabbr title=\"Global Climate Emergency\"\u003eGCE\u003c/abbr\u003e) Board of senior officials, with responsibility to ensure a whole-systems approach to delivering a just transition to net zero and strengthening climate adaptation. The \u003cabbr title=\"Global Climate Emergency\"\u003eGCE\u003c/abbr\u003e Board is overseen by the Scottish Government’s Executive Team and Corporate Board. Both the \u003cabbr title=\"Global Climate Emergency\"\u003eGCE\u003c/abbr\u003e Board and Corporate Board include non-executive directors as members.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"welsh-government-brbr\"\u003e2.1.4 Welsh Government \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eWithin the Welsh Government, the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Secretary for Climate Change and Rural Affairs lead on the net zero agenda, although the Cabinet has collective responsibility for achieving Wales’ statutory emissions targets.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Climate Change Portfolio Board of senior civil servants supports Cabinet decision-making. Further support is provided by the Climate Change Committee,\u003csup id=\"fnref:7\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:7\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 7]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e which is the Welsh Government’s statutory independent advisor on climate change.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Welsh Government’s response to the climate emergency is framed by the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act (2015).\u003csup id=\"fnref:8\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:8\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 8]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e This requires the Welsh Government to take long-term policy decisions, involve people in the government decisions that affect them, and seek out opportunities to address the underlying causes of change. The Welsh Government’s Programme for government contains 10 well-being objectives, including “Embed our response to the climate and nature emergency in everything we do”.\u003csup id=\"fnref:9\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:9\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 9]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"population-profile\"\u003e2.2 Population profile\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis section discusses demographic characteristics of the UK, to provide context on the population-related drivers that affect the UK’s Greenhouse Gas (\u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e) emissions. Unless stated otherwise, the following statistics have been produced from data collected by the Office for National Statistics (\u003cabbr title=\"Office for National Statistics\"\u003eONS\u003c/abbr\u003e), who produce the official population estimates for the UK and its constituent countries.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe total population of the UK was estimated to be 67.6 million in mid-2022, which was 10.4 million more (18% more) than in mid-1990. \u003cstrong\u003eTable 4\u003c/strong\u003e shows that the population of the UK is increasing and ageing with the median age in the UK increasing from 35.8 in 1990 to 40.7 in 2022. The population aged greater than 65 years increased from 15.7% in 1990 to 18.8% in 2022.
