\u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003cp\u003eAccording to \u003cabbr title=\"Office for National Statistics\"\u003eONS\u003c/abbr\u003e projections, the UK is expected to see a continued growth in population, as shown in \u003cstrong\u003eFigure 1\u003c/strong\u003e. The population is projected to increase to 76.3 million by mid-2045, an increase equivalent to an average annual rate of growth of slightly over 0.5% between 2022 and 2045. Assumed net migration accounts for the projected increase over the next 25 years, with projected annual deaths higher than births for most of this period. \u003cabbr title=\"Office for National Statistics\"\u003eONS\u003c/abbr\u003e note that the projections do not attempt to predict the impacts of the UK leaving the EU or the lasting effects of the coronavirus pandemic.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-1\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 1: UK population estimates, mid-1996 to mid-2021, and projections to mid-2046 population projections in the UK by country, 2022-2046 (in millions)\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/678163f6153753104a921805/uk-biennial-2024-figure-1.svg\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-2\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 2: Population pyramid for the UK mid-2022 (purple and green bars) compared with mid-2011 (purple and green lines)\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/678169fc9b205eeb6cede4bc/uk-biennial-2024-figure-2.svg\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003cp\u003eEach line in \u003cstrong\u003eFigure 2\u003c/strong\u003e represents a single year of age. The length of the line relates to the number of people of that age in the population. The size and composition of the population is determined by the pattern of births, deaths and migration which have taken place in previous years. The main details illustrated by the pyramid for mid-2020 include the following:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe peaks and wide areas of the pyramid reflect the high numbers of births in the years after the Second World War and during the baby boom of the 1960s.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe sharp narrowing of the pyramid for people aged between 15 and 20 years is a consequence of low numbers of births just after the turn of the century. There followed an increase in birth rates peaking around 2008 to 2012. Since 2016, birth rates have fallen more rapidly.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eFemales outnumber males at older ages, reflecting the higher life expectancy of females, though the gap has narrowed over time.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"sex-and-youth-brbr\"\u003e2.2.1 Sex and youth \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe male to female ratio of the UK population has remained broadly steady between 1990 and 2022 at approximately 49% to 51% respectively, though within these broad percentages the gap is narrowing.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"building-stock-and-urban-structure-profile-brbr\"\u003e2.2.2 Building stock and urban structure profile \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2022, the most common types of dwellings in England were terraced houses (29%) followed by semi-detached (25%), detached (17%), purpose-built flats (17%) and all other types of dwellings (12%)\u003csup id=\"fnref:11\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:11\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 11]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"geographical-profile\"\u003e2.3 Geographical profile\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK lies between latitude 49º\u003cabbr title=\"Nitrous Oxide\"\u003eN\u003c/abbr\u003e and 61º\u003cabbr title=\"Nitrous Oxide\"\u003eN\u003c/abbr\u003e and longitude 8ºE and 2ºW, positioned in north-western Europe. There are 3 UK crown dependencies (the Bailiwick of Jersey, Bailiwick of Guernsey and the Isle of Man) and 14 overseas territories (listed below).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eAnguilla\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eBermuda\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eBritish Antarctic Territory\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eBritish Indian Ocean Territory\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eVirgin Islands (commonly known as the British Virgin Islands)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eCayman Islands\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eFalkland Islands\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eGibraltar\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eMontserrat\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ePitcairn Islands\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eSaint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eSouth Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eSovereign base areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eTurks and Caicos Islands\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"economic-profile\"\u003e2.4 Economic profile\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2022, the UK had a Gross Domestic Product (\u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e) of $3.1 trillion, making it the world’s 6th largest economy\u003csup id=\"fnref:12\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:12\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 12]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. It is the 14th largest exporter of goods ($534 billion in 2022) and second largest exporter of services ($507 billion in 2022)\u003csup id=\"fnref:13\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:13\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 13]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe level of real \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e in \u003cabbr title=\"quarter 1\"\u003eQ1\u003c/abbr\u003e of 2022 was 1.3% higher than in \u003cabbr title=\"quarter 4\"\u003eQ4\u003c/abbr\u003e of 2019\u003csup id=\"fnref:14\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:14\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 14]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, broadly in line with other \u003cabbr title=\"The Group of 7\"\u003eG7\u003c/abbr\u003e countries. Up until the Global Financial Crisis (\u003cabbr title=\"Global Financial Crisis\"\u003eGFC\u003c/abbr\u003e), the rate of growth in UK real \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e had exceeded the rate of population growth – leading to rising \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e per capita. Since then, \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e per capita growth has slowed, and fell as a result of \u003cabbr title=\"Coronavirus\"\u003eCOVID-19\u003c/abbr\u003e, mirroring the fall in \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e. As of 2022, \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e per capita was around 0.6% above 2019 (pre-\u003cabbr title=\"Coronavirus\"\u003eCOVID\u003c/abbr\u003e) levels.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAccording to the International Monetary Fund (\u003cabbr title=\"International Monetary Fund\"\u003eIMF\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:15\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:15\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 15]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e real \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e growth in the UK was 4.8% in 2022. This compares with 2.5% for the USA, 1.4% for Germany, 2.6% for France, 4.7% for Italy, and 1.2% for Japan.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe last decade has been characterised by high employment and low unemployment, and stagnant wage growth. The employment rate peaked at 76.5% in December to February 2020, which was the highest rate since comparable records began in 1971\u003csup id=\"fnref:16\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:16\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 16]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. The employment rate in 2022 was 75.1%. Similarly, the unemployment rate dropped to 3.7% in October to December 2019, the lowest since 1974, and was 3.8% in 2022\u003csup id=\"fnref:17\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:17\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 17]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. Due to the furlough scheme and other interventions the impact of the \u003cabbr title=\"Coronavirus\"\u003eCOVID-19\u003c/abbr\u003e pandemic on employment and unemployment was relatively limited. Since the start of 2010, annual real regular pay growth has averaged just 0.3%\u003csup id=\"fnref:18\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:18\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 18]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e and UK wage growth since the financial crisis has been one the slowest rates among \u003cabbr title=\"The Group of 7\"\u003eG7\u003c/abbr\u003e nations.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAs shown in \u003cstrong\u003eFigure 3\u003c/strong\u003e, the (relatively small) rise in unemployment resulting from the \u003cabbr title=\"Coronavirus\"\u003eCOVID-19\u003c/abbr\u003e pandemic has largely unwound. There has been a degree of tightness in the labour market, due to record high vacancies. Job vacancies reached 1,304,000 in the second quarter of 2022, however since then the total number of vacancies has declined by nearly 400,000\u003csup id=\"fnref:19\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:19\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 19]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-3\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 3: Unemployment rate (left hand axis) and employment rate (right hand axis), \u003cabbr title=\"Office for National Statistics\"\u003eONS\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/678531e63a9388161c5d233d/uk-biennial-2024-figure-3.svg\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003cp\u003ePrior to the \u003cabbr title=\"Coronavirus\"\u003eCOVID-19\u003c/abbr\u003e pandemic, the UK had generally enjoyed low and stable inflation, broadly in line with the Bank of England’s 2% target. Since summer 2021 however, the UK like other developed nations, experienced a rapid rise in inflation driven by mostly external factors. These include high prices for energy and other commodities, exacerbated recently due to the war in Ukraine, a mismatch of global supply and demand, as well as base effects – abnormally low inflation in 2020 due to the pandemic.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eConsumer Price Index (\u003cabbr title=\"Consumer Price Index\"\u003eCPI\u003c/abbr\u003e) inflation, see \u003cstrong\u003eFigure 4\u003c/strong\u003e, reached 11.1% in October 2022. This is the highest level of price inflation in the UK for more than 40 years. As a result, real pay growth returned to being negative for the first time since 2017. \u003cabbr title=\"Consumer Price Index\"\u003eCPI\u003c/abbr\u003e inflation returned to the target of 2% in May 2024.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-4\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 4:\u003cabbr title=\"Consumer Price Index\"\u003eCPI\u003c/abbr\u003e Annual Inflation (%)\u003csup id=\"fnref:20\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:20\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 20]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, \u003cabbr title=\"Office for National Statistics\"\u003eONS\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/678534d3c6428e0131881712/uk-biennial-2024-figure-4.svg\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK economy is dominated by the service sector, accounting for over 80% of gross value added (\u003cabbr title=\"Gross Value Added\"\u003eGVA\u003c/abbr\u003e) and employment\u003csup id=\"fnref:21\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:21\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 21]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. Prior to the \u003cabbr title=\"Coronavirus\"\u003eCOVID-19\u003c/abbr\u003e pandemic, the fastest growing sector in the economy since the global financial crisis was the information and communication sector, which grew by around 130% between \u003cabbr title=\"quarter 3\"\u003eQ3\u003c/abbr\u003e 2009 and \u003cabbr title=\"quarter 4\"\u003eQ4\u003c/abbr\u003e 2019, largely as a result of technological progress within the sector.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eLooking at more recent data, \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e grew by 0.7% in \u003cabbr title=\"quarter 1\"\u003eQ1\u003c/abbr\u003e 2022. Services grew by 0.8% on the quarter meaning it was 2.5% above pre-pandemic (\u003cabbr title=\"quarter 4\"\u003eQ4\u003c/abbr\u003e 2019) levels. Construction grew by 3.0%, and is 1.7% above pre-pandemic levels, while production fell by 1.9% and remains 5.8% below pre-pandemic levels.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eUK Government consumption and investment are the only expenditure component of \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e (the others being household consumption, business investment and net exports) that has risen since the start of the coronavirus pandemic, largely driven by health spending, and mirroring the growth seen in the health sector on the output measure. UK Government consumption has grown by 8.5% since the start of the coronavirus pandemic. Conversely, private consumption (-1.3%), business investment (5.0%) and net trade have all detracted from \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e growth since \u003cabbr title=\"quarter 4\"\u003eQ4\u003c/abbr\u003e 2019.\u003csup id=\"fnref:22\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:22\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 22]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"climate-profile\"\u003e2.5 Climate profile\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s climate is maritime, moist and temperate, with a winter mean temperature of 4.1 °C and summer mean temperature of 14.6 °C. The influence of the Atlantic Ocean means that the UK’s annual temperature range is smaller than for more continental countries at the same latitude. Average annual precipitation in the UK typically ranges from approximately 800 mm to 1400 mm, but with significant regional variations with western upland regions experiencing in excess of 2000 mm and parts of low-lying south-east England less than 600 mm. The UK climate is heavily influenced by its proximity to the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf Stream / North Atlantic Drift which brings warm water into high northern latitudes. Prevailing winds are westerly, and UK regional climates vary with distance from the Atlantic as well as with local topography. Continental influences are most strongly seen in the southeast of the country.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eVariations in the strength and position of the jet stream strongly influence UK weather. Sometimes the jet stream is directed close to or over the country, bringing extended periods of stormy, wet weather. At other times, a blocked pattern steers the jet stream away to the north or to the south, bringing generally settled, dry conditions, either warmer or colder than average. Space heating is required in most buildings throughout the winter months and the use of air conditioning in the summer months is increasing. In the UK, \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions are strongly influenced by weather conditions. In winter, cooler-than-average temperatures increase demand for space heating; and in summer, warmer-than-average temperatures increase demand for space cooling. \u003cstrong\u003eFigure 5\u003c/strong\u003e shows the average daily mean temperature for the UK by season.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-5\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 5: Average (1991-2022) daily temperature (°C) by season, UK (source: Met Office)\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/678636153ef063b15dca0f42/uk-biennial-2024-figure-5a.svg\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67863622f0528401055d2387/uk-biennial-2024-figure-5b.svg\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"uk-climate-trends23-brbr\"\u003e2.5.1 UK climate trends\u003csup id=\"fnref:23\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:23\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 23]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"temperature\"\u003e2.5.1.1 Temperature\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Central England Temperature (\u003cabbr title=\"Central England Temperature\"\u003eCET\u003c/abbr\u003e) series is the longest-compiled instrumental temperature record in the world, beginning in 1659. \u003cstrong\u003eFigure 6\u003c/strong\u003e shows that the \u003cabbr title=\"Central England Temperature\"\u003eCET\u003c/abbr\u003e for the early 21st century has been warmer than the previous 3 centuries for all seasons of the year.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-6\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 6: Seasonal Central England Temperature Anomaly series, 1659 to 2023, relative to 1991-2020 average\u003csup id=\"fnref:24\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:24\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 24]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6781224800e3d719f19217de/uk-biennial-2024-figure-6.svg\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK-wide national temperature series begins in 1884, showing an increase in temperature from the 1970s to the 2000s with the most recent decade (2014-2023) on average 0.42 °C warmer than the 1991-2020 average and 1.25 °C warmer than 1961-1990. All 10 warmest years recorded for the UK have been since 2003. Evidence from attribution science shows that the increasing trend in temperatures is overwhelmingly a result of human activities, in particular emissions of greenhouse gases.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCold years are still observed despite the warming trend, but they are less frequent and less severe than in the historical record: 2010 was the coldest year recorded since 1986 and the 22nd coldest in the UK series since 1884.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"precipitation\"\u003e2.5.1.2 Precipitation\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003ePrecipitation data for the UK show a slight increase from the 1970s onwards (\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 7\u003c/strong\u003e) that is most pronounced for Scotland. The most recent decade (2014–2023) has been on average 2% wetter than 1991-2020 and 10% wetter than 1961–1990. Five of the 10 wettest years for the UK have occurred since 2000, in a series beginning in 1836.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe largest increases in rainfall have been during the winter season, with the most recent decade (2014-2023) having winters 24% wetter than 1961-1990. This period includes the 2 wettest winters on record in 2013-2014 and 2015-2016, with winter 2019-2020 as the fifth wettest in a series from 1836. Summers of the most recent decade (2014-2023) have also been 10% wetter than 1961-1990. This changing trend in rainfall in the UK is a result of both human influence and large-scale natural variability in the climate system, which can occur over time periods of decades.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-7\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 7: Annual precipitation, UK, 1836–2023\u003csup id=\"fnref:25\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:25\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 25]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6784f0bd3ef063b15dca0ec7/uk-biennial-2024-figure-7.svg\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"sea-level\"\u003e2.5.1.3 Sea level\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eSince 1900 sea level around the UK has risen by about 18.5 cm when corrected for vertical land movement, which is comparable to the global sea level rise estimate of 20 cm. There is evidence from the observational records that the rate of sea level rise is increasing from a long-term estimate of 1.5 mm/yr, with the period 1993-2023 increasing by around 4.6 mm/year. Sea surface temperatures around the UK for the most recent decade (2014-2023) have been on average 0.3 °C warmer than the 1991-2020 average and 0.9 °C warmer than 1961-1990.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"climate-projections-brbr\"\u003e2.5.2 Climate projections \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe latest UK Climate Projections (\u003cabbr title=\"UK Climate Projections 2018\"\u003eUKCP18\u003c/abbr\u003e) provide the most up-to-date assessment of how the UK climate is projected to change in the future and includes modelling projections for 3 spatial resolutions (60km, 12km and 2.2km), probabilistic projections including extremes, and projections of sea-level rise, storm surges and waves.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOne strand of the modelling projections is \u003cabbr title=\"UK Climate Projections\"\u003eUKCP\u003c/abbr\u003e Local; the first time a climate model with a resolution similar to weather forecasting models has been used to explore national climate scenarios. This is a step forward in the ability of the climate model to simulate small-scale behaviour seen in the real atmosphere, particularly for the representation of the heavy rainfall associated with showers that affect flooding in summer. In this section, \u003cabbr title=\"UK Climate Projections\"\u003eUKCP\u003c/abbr\u003e information is used to summarise the projected effects on UK climate, both in terms of averages and extremes\u003csup id=\"fnref:26\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:26\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 26]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, followed by impact metrics. \u003cabbr title=\"UK Climate Projections\"\u003eUKCP\u003c/abbr\u003e data were used in the most recent UK Climate Change Risk Assessment (\u003cabbr title=\"UK Climate Change Risk Assessment\"\u003eUKCCRA\u003c/abbr\u003e) and are being applied by the more than 7,000 registered users to quantify and manage physical climate risks.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"uk-future-climate-overview\"\u003e2.5.2.1 UK future climate overview\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe headline findings of \u003cabbr title=\"UK Climate Projections 2018\"\u003eUKCP18\u003c/abbr\u003e state that future UK climate change will result in warmer, wetter winters and hotter, drier summers. Annual temperatures for the UK for a medium emissions scenario\u003csup id=\"fnref:27\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:27\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 27]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e from the \u003cabbr title=\"UK Climate Projections\"\u003eUKCP\u003c/abbr\u003e Probabilistic Projections suggest warming of 2.3°C (1.1°C to 3.6°C)\u003csup id=\"fnref:28\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:28\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 28]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e by the end of the century (2080- 2100) compared to the 1981-2000 baseline period. Warming is projected to be greater in summer (3°C; 1.3°C to 4.8°C) than in winter (2°C; 0.6°C to 3.5°C). UK-wide, summer precipitation decreases are expected to be -19% (-36% to -2%) while winter precipitation is projected to increase 10% (-2% to 25%) by the 2090s.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNotable UK-wide features, such as warming being greater in the summer compared to the winter are projected to occur across all regions of the UK for both low and high emissions scenarios\u003csup id=\"fnref:29\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:29\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 29]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. Similarly, the majority of UK regions are projected to experience a decrease in summer precipitation and an increase in winter precipitation. Across both seasons and emissions scenarios, regional variations are generally modest within each metric, with differences usually within 1°C or 10%, the high emissions scenario winter precipitation showing the greatest spread between regions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSea level is projected to rise around the UK compared to a 1981-2000 baseline period although the amount of sea level rise is higher in the south and increases with higher emissions scenarios. For the medium emissions scenario (RCP4.5), the \u003cabbr title=\"UK Climate Projections\"\u003eUKCP\u003c/abbr\u003e Marine Projections give rises of 0.55 m (0.40 m to 0.75 m)\u003csup id=\"fnref:30\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:30\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 30]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e in London compared to lower values of 0.33 m (0.18 m to 0.53 m) in Edinburgh in 2100. Based on exploratory results to 2300, sea levels continue to increase beyond 2100 even with large reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. For the same medium emissions scenario, sea level is projected to rise for London by 1.42 m (0.93m to 2.23 m) and 0.77 m (0.28 m to 1.6 m) for Edinburgh by 2300. However, the uncertainty around post-2100 simulations remain large due to gaps in understanding related to the role of the large ice sheets.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"uk-future-climate-extremes\"\u003e2.5.2.2 UK future climate extremes\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor day-to-day extremes, \u003cabbr title=\"UK Climate Projections 2018\"\u003eUKCP18\u003c/abbr\u003e provides extremes in terms of return periods (the average time between events) for maximum temperatures and heavy rainfall. These results project increases in both the values and range over the course of the 21st century.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe median values of high temperature and heavy rainfall expected to occur once every 50 years are projected to increase in all seasons under an illustrative high emissions scenario (RCP8.5). For example, by 2070 with a high emissions scenario, the daily maximum temperature of a 1-in-50-year event is projected to be 2.5°C (winter) and 3.7°C to 4.3°C (spring, summer, autumn) warmer than in 1990. For rainfall, the median 1-in- 50-year event is expected to have 12-19% (daily rainfall) or 11-13% (5-day accumulated rainfall) more rainfall in 2070 than in 1990 in autumn, winter or spring, with smaller increases expected in summer\u003csup id=\"fnref:31\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:31\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 31]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"UK Climate Projections\"\u003eUKCP\u003c/abbr\u003e Local models have better representation of how rainfall varies day-to-day and hour-to- hour. For hourly rainfall that is expected to occur once every 2 years, \u003cabbr title=\"UK Climate Projections\"\u003eUKCP\u003c/abbr\u003e Local projects that this will be 29% heavier in the summer under a future climate with a high emissions scenario (2060-2080, RCP8.5). Similar increases are projected for rarer events and in the autumn, with smaller increases projected in spring and winter.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"uk-climate-impact-metrics\"\u003e2.5.2.3 UK climate impact metrics\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"UK Climate Projections 2018\"\u003eUKCP18\u003c/abbr\u003e data has also been translated into metrics that quantify the expected future impacts of weather on society at different Global Warming Levels (\u003cabbr title=\"Global Warming Levels\"\u003eGWLs\u003c/abbr\u003e), ranging from 1.5°C above the pre-industrial level (consistent with a low emissions scenario by 2100) to 4°C (consistent with a high emissions scenario by 2100). Projections show increases for temperature metrics related to hot events, accompanied by reductions in metrics related to cold events.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe number of hot days (over 25°C) in the UK is projected to increase by between 5 days and 39 days per year. This could mean increased hospital admissions for those vulnerable to heat and increased transport disruption, for example from railway track buckling at higher temperatures. The projections show a 2 to 7-fold increase in an indicator of the energy demand for cooling (known as cooling degree days). Increases are also projected in an indicator of the energy available for plant growth over a year (growing degree days) of 19% to 60%. Occurrences of tropical nights, when the temperature falls no lower than 20°C, are rare in the current climate but become more frequent in a warmer climate, particularly in southeast England and in urban areas.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eConversely, the projections show a reduction in the number of frost days (below 0°C) of between 10 and 49 days per year. Decreases are also found in an indicator of energy demand for heating (known as heating degree days) of 11% to 32%, implying a decrease in the adverse effects of cold weather.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eImpacts related to rainfall include projected increases in heavy rainfall events that could cause flooding and increases in average drought severity. The projections show an increase in occurrence of high-impact levels of daily rainfall from 1 day to 8 days per year. Average drought severity is projected to increase at most \u003cabbr title=\"Global Warming Levels\"\u003eGWLs\u003c/abbr\u003e but with a small decrease possible with a low 1.5°C GWL, with changes of -3% to 19% for 12-month drought duration, and -2% to 54% for 36-month drought duration.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"sector-details\"\u003e2.6 Sector details\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"energy-brbr\"\u003e2.6.1 Energy \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK published its Net Zero Strategy in 2021, which included its commitment to decarbonise the electricity sector by 2035, subject to security of supply. This was submitted to the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e as the UK’s Long Term Low Emissions Development Strategy in 2021. Policies to support this and increase energy security were set out in this document and in the subsequent British Energy Security Strategy which was published in 2022 following Russia’s invasion of the Ukraine. The main policy focus was to increase energy efficiency and accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels through the decarbonisation of the power sector and increased electrification of heat, transport and industry.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"energy-production\"\u003e2.6.1.1 Energy production\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eTotal UK energy production increased rapidly between 1990 and 2000, mainly due to the growth of oil and gas. Production in 2000 was at record levels for natural gas, while in 1999 it was at record levels for overall energy and petroleum. Energy production has since been on a general decline, however energy production levels increased between 2014 and 2019, as new oil fields opened, combined with the growth in output from bioenergy and waste and the increased capacity of wind and solar technologies.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2022, total energy production was 110.2 million tonnes of oil equivalent, 3.1% higher than the record low level of 106.8 million tonnes of oil equivalent in 2021. Production levels for all fuels except coal, oil and bioenergy and waste are up on 2021, with oil output at a record 21st century low level. UK energy production had fallen year on year since 2018 before the rise in 2022, and energy production is now 63% below the peak recorded in 1999.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2022, coal production fell by 39% to a record low level, whilst production of oil fell by 7.6% to a record low level, with output down by 28% on pre-pandemic (2019) levels; conversely production of natural gas rose by 16% in 2022.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"energy-consumption-and-transformation\"\u003e2.6.1.2 Energy consumption and transformation\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2022\u003csup id=\"fnref:32\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:32\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 32]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e total primary energy consumption was 168.6 mega tonnes of oil equivalent (\u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Oil Equivalent\"\u003emtoe\u003c/abbr\u003e), 1.3% lower than in 2021, with record high temperatures and higher energy prices a key factor in the reduced consumption levels. The level of primary energy consumption in 2022 was 21% lower than in 1990; primary energy consumption levels peaked in 2001 and since then there has been a general downward trend. In the last 33 years, consumption of natural gas and primary electricity have risen, whilst consumption of oil and coal have fallen. However, over the past decade, the growth in consumption of bioenergy and waste has more than doubled.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2022\u003csup id=\"fnref:33\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:33\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 33]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e total final energy consumption including non-energy use was 130.9 \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Oil Equivalent\"\u003emtoe\u003c/abbr\u003e, 2.1% lower than in 2021, and 11% lower than pre-pandemic (2019) levels. The level of final energy consumption in 2022 was 17% lower than in 1990. The largest fall in final energy consumption since 1990 has occurred in the industrial sector, mainly due to structural change in the period before 2000; in the domestic sector there has been a general downward trend in consumption due to improvements in energy efficiency measures, and more recently due to the impact of higher energy prices.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"electricity\"\u003e2.6.1.3 Electricity\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eBetween 1990 and 2022 electricity supply emissions have reduced by 73%. This decrease has resulted mainly from changes in the mix of fuels being used for electricity generation, including the growth of renewables; together with greater efficiency resulting from improvements in technology. The electricity supply sector historically had the largest emissions of the sectors presented in these statistics. However, these reductions mean that since 2014 this has no longer been the case and there are now several sectors with higher emissions (the largest being transport).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSince 1990 there has been a decline in the use of coal at power stations and an increase in the use of gas, which has a lower carbon content so results in fewer emissions. Coal use in generation reduced by 97% between 1990 and 2022, making up only 3% of the fuel used for UK electricity generation in 2022 compared to 65% in 1990. Electricity supplied was 4% higher in 2022 than in 1990, having grown to a peak in 2005 and decreased since then. In 2022 the use of gas for electricity generation increased 1% from 2021 and the use of renewables and nuclear both by 5%, whereas coal saw a 16% decrease\u003csup id=\"fnref:34\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:34\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 34]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe British Energy Security Strategy published in 2022 included ambitions for up to 50 \u003cabbr title=\"Giggawatts\"\u003eGW\u003c/abbr\u003e of offshore wind by 2030, including up to 5 \u003cabbr title=\"Giggawatts\"\u003eGW\u003c/abbr\u003e of floating wind; up to 70 \u003cabbr title=\"Giggawatts\"\u003eGW\u003c/abbr\u003e of solar by 2035; up to 10 \u003cabbr title=\"Giggawatts\"\u003eGW\u003c/abbr\u003e of hydrogen by 2030, with up to 6 \u003cabbr title=\"Giggawatts\"\u003eGW\u003c/abbr\u003e from electrolytic (‘green’) hydrogen; and up to 24 \u003cabbr title=\"Giggawatts\"\u003eGW\u003c/abbr\u003e of nuclear by 2050.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe share of electricity generated from renewable sources remained stable through 2020-22.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"fuel-supply\"\u003e2.6.1.4 Fuel Supply\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eUK offshore oil and gas production started 60 years ago. This long history of oil and gas production in the UK means our offshore basin is mature and production is naturally declining. Through the North Sea Transition Deal, the oil and gas industry is committed to reducing its production emissions by 10% by 2025, 25% by 2027 and 50% by 2030, against a 2018 baseline\u003csup id=\"fnref:35\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:35\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 35]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. Transparency is also important: since 2021, the North Sea Transition Authority (\u003cabbr title=\"North Sea Transition Authority\"\u003eNSTA\u003c/abbr\u003e) has published annual Emissions Monitoring Reports, which present a wide range of data on overall greenhouse gas emissions, methane emissions, performance benchmarking and flaring and venting to track industry’s progress. The \u003cabbr title=\"North Sea Transition Authority\"\u003eNSTA\u003c/abbr\u003e’s ‘\u003cabbr title=\"Oil and Gas Authority, now the North Sea Transition Authority\"\u003eOGA\u003c/abbr\u003e Plan’ on emissions reduction, published in March 2024, sets out requirements for the oil and gas industry to decarbonise and makes it clear that for production to continue in the North Sea, it must also continue to become cleaner.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe sector’s emissions reductions will be delivered through a mixture of decreasing oil and gas production from the basin and decarbonisation measures such as ending routine flaring and venting and platform electrification. Good progress has been made in recent years - the \u003cabbr title=\"North Sea Transition Authority\"\u003eNSTA\u003c/abbr\u003e estimates that between 2018 and 2022, emissions from upstream oil and gas production decreased by approximately 23% and industry almost halved methane emissions\u003csup id=\"fnref:36\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:36\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 36]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. The UK oil and gas sector has one of the lowest upstream methane emission intensities globally, having achieved the Oil and Gas Climate Initiative’s 0.2% intensity target for 2025 early, in 2021\u003csup id=\"fnref:37\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:37\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 37]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. We continue to support the North Sea Transition Deal, including the important decarbonisation targets it set for the sector, working together to make sure the next chapter of oil and gas is also the cleanest in its history.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"transport-brbr\"\u003e2.6.2 Transport \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eDomestic transport accounted for around 28% of all UK greenhouse gas emissions in 2022, almost entirely through carbon dioxide emissions. The main source of domestic transport emissions comes from the use of petrol and diesel fuels in road transport.\nIn 2020, transport was significantly impacted by \u003cabbr title=\"Coronavirus\"\u003eCOVID-19\u003c/abbr\u003e, as people were instructed to stay at home as much as possible. This led to an annual decrease in distance travelled by cars, vans and taxis of 28% in 2020 and an 80% decrease in distance travelled by rail, both when compared with 2019. \u003cabbr title=\"Coronavirus\"\u003eCOVID-19\u003c/abbr\u003e restrictions were eased in 2021 and the last restrictions removed in 2022, resulting in consecutive years of increasing greenhouse gas emissions from domestic transport to 113.2 \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee in 2022, a 2% rise from 2021 and 12% higher than 2020, although this was still 10% lower than 2019. In 2021/22 and 2022/23, rail passenger kilometres increased incrementally, but still remained 20% below pre-pandemic levels\u003csup id=\"fnref:38\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:38\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 38]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRoad vehicles remained the most significant source of domestic transport \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions (89%), making up 25% of economy-wide domestic emissions in 2022. Cars and taxis account for the bulk of this figure at 53% of domestic transport emissions, with Heavy Goods Vehicles (\u003cabbr title=\"Heavy Goods Vehicles\"\u003eHGVs\u003c/abbr\u003e) contributing 17% and vans representing 16%\u003csup id=\"fnref:39\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:39\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 39]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-8\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 8: Passenger kilometres by mode in Great Britain, since 2012\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67853888f029f40e50881718/uk-biennial-2024-figure-8.svg\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-9\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 9: Passenger kilometres by mode (excluding cars and taxis) in Great Britain, since 2012\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67853d26f041702a11ca0f0e/uk-biennial-2024-figure-9.svg\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003cp\u003ePublic transport use was heavily impacted by \u003cabbr title=\"Coronavirus\"\u003eCOVID-19\u003c/abbr\u003e. Between 2019 and 2020, passenger kilometres travelled on buses and rail fell from 33 billion to 14 billion and 80 billion to 16 billion respectively\u003csup id=\"fnref:40\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:40\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 40]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. In contrast, active travel spiked significantly in 2020 when compared with previous years. Increases were seen in walking trips, stages and miles travelled compared to 2021, with average trips and miles above pre-pandemic levels\u003csup id=\"fnref:41\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:41\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 41]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe freight sector is vital for the UK, with 216 billion tonne-kilometres of domestic freight moved in the UK in 2022. Road freight made up the largest proportion of domestic freight being moved in the UK in 2022, accounting for 81%\u003csup id=\"fnref:42\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:42\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 42]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. Road freight has seen consistent increases from 2015 onwards. The \u003cabbr title=\"Coronavirus\"\u003eCOVID-19\u003c/abbr\u003e pandemic interrupted this trend, with an 11% decrease in road freight traffic in 2020\u003csup id=\"fnref:43\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:43\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 43]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe maritime sector remains crucial for UK transport. In total, there are 51 major seaports in the UK\u003csup id=\"fnref:44\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:44\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 44]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. In 2022, a total of 458.9 million tonnes of cargo were handled at all UK sea ports (98% at the 51 major ports); this is a 3% increase on 2021 but 5% lower than in 2019\u003csup id=\"fnref:45\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:45\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 45]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. An estimated total of 86,600 cargo vessels arrived at UK major seaports during 2022, 1.6% more than the 2021 level\u003csup id=\"fnref:46\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:46\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 46]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK aviation sector supports global travel, connectivity and trade. UK airports provide direct flights to over 100 countries and served over 195 million terminal passengers in 2022. Around 2 million commercial flights depart from or arrive at UK airports annually\u003csup id=\"fnref:47\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:47\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 47]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDomestic aviation emissions fell by more than half in 2020 compared to 2019 due to the \u003cabbr title=\"Coronavirus\"\u003eCOVID-19\u003c/abbr\u003e pandemic, the largest fall of any mode of transport, and in 2022 were still 20% lower than in 2019. Emissions from waterborne transport were 11% lower in 2022 than in 2019, having remained at a similar level to their 2020 low.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe proliferation of future green technology is advancing, supported by investment in research and development (\u003cabbr title=\"Research and development\"\u003eR\u0026amp;D\u003c/abbr\u003e), alongside incentives and other existing efficiency regulations across all modes of transport. In May 2022, £200m was announced to provide support for the rollout of zero emission \u003cabbr title=\"Heavy Goods Vehicles\"\u003eHGVs\u003c/abbr\u003e and their associated infrastructure as part of the zero emission \u003cabbr title=\"Heavy Goods Vehicle\"\u003eHGV\u003c/abbr\u003e and infrastructure demonstrator programme. In 2022, the UK committed £180m to support the development of UK sustainable aviation fuels (\u003cabbr title=\"Sustainable Aviation Fuels\"\u003eSAF\u003c/abbr\u003e) plants, building on the progress made in previous advanced fuels competitions. Additionally, the UK committed to a £206m \u003cabbr title=\"Research and development\"\u003eR\u0026amp;D\u003c/abbr\u003e programme focused on maritime decarbonisation, which is being delivered through the UK Shipping Office for Reducing Emissions (\u003cabbr title=\"Shipping Office for Reducing Emissions\"\u003eUK SHORE\u003c/abbr\u003e) between 2022 until 2025.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"industrial-processes-and-product-use-brbr\"\u003e2.6.3 Industrial processes and product use \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s industrial sector plays an important role in society, contributing £210 billion to the overall UK economy in 2022\u003csup id=\"fnref:48\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:48\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 48]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. It is a high value area of employment, directly accounting for 10%\u003csup id=\"fnref:49\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:49\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 49]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e of the UK’s total \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Value Added\"\u003eGVA\u003c/abbr\u003e in 2022 and providing 2.7 million\u003csup id=\"fnref:50\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:50\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 50]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e direct jobs across the country, rising to around 5 million jobs\u003csup id=\"fnref:51\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:51\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 51]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e if including indirect jobs across the value chain.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIndustry is also a major source of \u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e emissions, producing 17% (68.3 \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee)\u003csup id=\"fnref:52\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:52\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 52]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e of UK’s total in 2022. Roughly half of these emissions are concentrated in specific ‘clusters’\u003csup id=\"fnref:53\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:53\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 53]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e – geographical areas with large concentrations of industry. The 7 UK clusters are: Humberside, the North-West, Grangemouth in Scotland, South Wales, Teesside, Southampton and the Black Country. The remaining emissions can be found in ‘dispersed’ sites, which are industrial regions scattered around the UK. Most emissions are from energy and carbon intensive sectors including cement, chemicals, food and drink, iron and steel, non-ferrous metals, non-metallic minerals, paper and pulp and refining. Industry emissions reduced by 57% between 1990 and 2022\u003csup id=\"fnref:54\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:54\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 54]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, due mainly to the changing structure of the UK’s manufacturing and refining sector, efficiency improvements, and a shift to low carbon fuels\u003csup id=\"fnref:55\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:55\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 55]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. Refer to \u003cstrong\u003eFigures 10 and 11\u003c/strong\u003e below for an illustration of UK industrial emission and UK industrial process emission reductions from 1990 – 2022.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-10\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 10: UK industrial emissions from 1990 - 2022\u003csup id=\"fnref:56\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:56\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 56]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67854051f0528401055d2362/uk-biennial-2024-figure-10.svg\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-11\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 11: Breakdown of emissions UK industrial processes from 1990 - 2022\u003csup id=\"fnref:57\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:57\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 57]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6785451a3a9388161c5d234b/uk-biennial-2024-figure-11.svg\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"agriculture-brbr\"\u003e2.6.4 Agriculture \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2022, around 71% (17.4 million hectares) of total UK land was used for agriculture. \u003cstrong\u003eFigure 12\u003c/strong\u003e shows UK land use data for the total utilised agricultural area as of June 2022\u003csup id=\"fnref:58\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:58\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 58]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. About 4.4 million hectares of this was arable, of which around two-thirds were under cereal production and 11.4 million hectares was under grass. The remainder was common rough grazing (1.2 million hectares) and land for outdoor pigs (12,000 hectares)\u003csup id=\"fnref:59\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:59\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 59]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. Total agriculture area saw a 0.4% increase between 2016 and 2022, and total croppable area increased by 0.2%. The biggest change in agricultural land use was seen in uncropped arable land which saw an 8.4% increase since 2016.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-12\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 12: Total utilised agricultural land in the UK, 2022; \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e 2022\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/678548c0f041702a11ca0f11/uk-biennial-2024-figure-12.svg\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003cp\u003eLivestock produce greenhouse gas emissions via processes such as enteric fermentation. The total number of cattle and calves in the UK decreased by 4% between June 2016 and June 2022 to around 9.6 million. The UK’s dairy herd has decreased by 2.9%, and the UK beef herd has decreased by 8.3% over the same period. Total cattle and calf numbers in the UK during the period 2005-2023 are shown in \u003cstrong\u003eFigure 13\u003c/strong\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-13\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 13: Total cattle and calves in the UK, June 2005-June 2022\u003csup id=\"fnref:60\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:60\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 60]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67854e5bf0528401055d2369/uk-biennial-2024-figure-13.svg\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe total number of pigs in the UK in June 2022 increased by 7.3% since June 2016, to 5.2 million. Total sheep and lamb numbers in the UK during the period 2005-2023 are shown in \u003cstrong\u003eFigure 15\u003c/strong\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-15\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 15: Total sheep in the UK, 2005-2022\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67855b80f041702a11ca0f14/uk-biennial-2024-figure-15.svg\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"land-use-land-use-change-and-forestry-brbr\"\u003e2.6.5 Land use, land use change and forestry \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe area of woodland in the UK on 31 March 2022 was 3.2 million hectares. Of this total, 1.5 million hectares (46%) was in Scotland, 1.3 million hectares (41%) was in England, 0.3 million hectares (10%) was in Wales and 0.1 million hectares (4%) was in Northern Ireland. This has changed relatively little over the period 2007 to 2022 as can be seen in \u003cstrong\u003eFigure 16\u003c/strong\u003e. Publicly owned forests still account for 0.9 million hectares\u003csup id=\"fnref:61\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:61\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 61]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-16\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 16: Area of woodland, 1998-2022\u003csup id=\"fnref:62\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:62\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 62]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67852c9df0528401055d2345/uk-biennial-2024-figure-16.svg\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003cp\u003eAround 50% of the total UK woodland is made up predominantly of conifer species, the remainder being broadleaved.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe total area of new planting and restocking in the UK was 27.2 thousand hectares in 2020-21. Restocking accounted for 51% of this total. Broadleaved species accounted for 45% of the new planting area but just 18.5% of the restocked area in 2020-21\u003csup id=\"fnref:63\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:63\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 63]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\nA total of 10.0 million green tonnes of softwood was produced in the UK in 2020 and accounted for 92% of timber removals from UK woodland. UK hardwood production totalled 0.8 million green tonnes in 2020\u003csup id=\"fnref:64\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:64\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 64]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEstimated consumption of wood in the UK amounted to 48.3 million m3 wood raw material equivalent in 2022, made up of 9.8 million m3 UK production, 43.1 million m3 imports and 4.5 million m3 exports\u003csup id=\"fnref:65\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:65\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 65]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis sector can act as both a source and a sink for \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"waste-management-brbr\"\u003e2.6.6 Waste management \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2022, \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions from waste contributed around 5% of total UK emissions, representing an emissions reduction of 74% since 1990. Approximately 90% of emissions from this sector are attributable to methane\u003csup id=\"fnref:66\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:66\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 66]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK Government and the devolved governments published their individual waste strategies aiming to reduce the quantity of waste produced and to increasingly recover value from it. The strategies set out ambitions to reduce the amount of waste sent to landfill and to increase the amount of recycling or composting.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2021, households in the UK produced 27.7 million tonnes of waste, an increase of 4.6% since 2019\u003csup id=\"fnref:67\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:67\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 67]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2021, 44.6% of waste from households was recycled in the UK; this is a decrease from the peak of 46.0% achieved in 2019\u003csup id=\"fnref:68\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:68\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 68]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK commercial and industrial sectors generated 40.4 million tonnes of waste in 2020, of which 33.8 million tonnes (around 84%) was produced in England. By comparison, the 2018 UK commercial and industrial waste arisings totalled 43.9 million tonnes, of which 37.2 million tonnes was generated by England. Over two-thirds of commercial and industrial waste is generated by the commercial sector, in both the UK and England.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eLocal authorities in England recycled, composted or reused 10.8 million tonnes in 2021-22\u003csup id=\"fnref:69\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:69\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 69]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. The amount of local authority collected waste sent to landfill and incineration in 2021-22 was 2.1 million tonnes and 12.4 million tonnes, respectively. Concerning landfill, it is a reduction from 22 million tonnes sent to landfill in 2000-01.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"other-buildings-brbr\"\u003e2.6.7 Other: Buildings \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere are about 30 million buildings in the UK\u003csup id=\"fnref:70\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:70\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 70]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. In total, these buildings are responsible for around 30% of our national emissions\u003csup id=\"fnref:71\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:71\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 71]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. The vast majority of these emissions are specifically from heating: 79% of buildings emissions and about 23% of all UK emissions\u003csup id=\"fnref:72\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:72\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 72]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK has some of the oldest building stock in the world. 81% of UK homes were built before 1990 and over a third before 1945. Since 2012, the proportion of homes in \u003cabbr title=\"Energy Performance Certificate\"\u003eEPC\u003c/abbr\u003e bands A-C has risen. However, 52% of homes in England remain below \u003cabbr title=\"Energy Performance Certificate\"\u003eEPC\u003c/abbr\u003e C. The owner occupier tenure is the worst performing with around 57% of homes at \u003cabbr title=\"Energy Performance Certificate\"\u003eEPC\u003c/abbr\u003e D or below.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"national-circumstances-of-ghg-emissions-and-removals-over-time\"\u003e2.7 National circumstances of \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions and removals over time\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor full details of the UK’s emissions trends, please see the UK National Inventory Document (\u003cabbr title=\"National Inventory Document\"\u003eNID\u003c/abbr\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDespite rises in some sectors as the UK continued to recover from the coronavirus (\u003cabbr title=\"Coronavirus\"\u003eCOVID-19\u003c/abbr\u003e) pandemic, 2022 saw a fall in greenhouse gas emissions in the UK, largely due to a reduction in fuel use to heat buildings. In 2022, net territorial greenhouse gas emissions in the UK were estimated to be 407.8 million tonnes carbon dioxide equivalent (\u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee), a decrease of 3.5% from the 2021 figure of 422.7 million tonnes, and 9.3% lower when compared to 2019, the most recent pre-pandemic year. Total greenhouse gas emissions were 50.0% lower than they were in 1990. Carbon dioxide made up 80% of the 2022 total\u003csup id=\"fnref:73\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:73\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 73]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe fall in 2022 is primarily due to a reduction in gas use for heating buildings, as a result of warmer weather than in 2021. Emissions from the buildings and product uses sector fell 13.3%. Higher energy prices may have also caused people to reduce their energy use. Falls in emissions from industry and agriculture also contributed to the overall reduction.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn comparison, emissions from the domestic transport sector rose 1.6%. This follows a period of reduced domestic travel in 2020 and 2021 due to \u003cabbr title=\"Coronavirus\"\u003eCOVID-19\u003c/abbr\u003e restrictions. Domestic transport was the largest emitting sector, responsible for 28% of all greenhouse gas emissions in the UK. Emissions from electricity supply also rose by 0.6%.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"institutional-arrangements-in-place-to-track-progress-made-in-implementing-and-achieving-its-nationally-determined-contribution-ndc\"\u003e2.8 Institutional arrangements in place to track progress made in implementing and achieving its Nationally Determined Contribution (\u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"information-on-legal-institutional-administrative-and-procedural-arrangements-related-to-the-ndc-brbr\"\u003e2.8.1 Information on legal, institutional, administrative and procedural arrangements related to the \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"united-kingdom-climate-change-legislation-and-targets\"\u003e2.8.1.1 United Kingdom climate change legislation and targets\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Climate Change Act 2008 established the world’s first legally binding framework of national emissions targets.\u003csup id=\"fnref:74\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:74\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 74]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e The Act originally committed the UK to a statutory target to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to 80% lower than its 1990 baseline by 2050. In 2019, the UK amended the Act to require the net UK carbon account to be at least 100% lower than its 1990 baseline by 2050. In doing so, the UK became the first major economy to legislate for net zero emissions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s carbon budgets impose legally binding limits on emissions across 5-year periods. The first 6 carbon budgets have so far been set in law. In 2021, the UK set its Sixth Carbon Budget for the period 2033-2037 with a target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions to 965 megatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalents (\u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee), which is approximately 77% lower than 1990 levels. It will be the first carbon budget to include emissions from international aviation and shipping. Looking forward, the UK’s Seventh Carbon Budget will put into law an emissions target for 2038 and 2042 and will set out the next phase of the government’s strategy for achieving net zero emissions by 2050.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFurther information on carbon budget accounting and performance can be found in the Annual Statement of Emissions.\u003csup id=\"fnref:75\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:75\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 75]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"northern-ireland-executive\"\u003e2.8.1.2 Northern Ireland Executive\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Climate Change Act (Northern Ireland) 2022\u003csup id=\"fnref:76\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:76\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 76]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, which received Royal Assent on 6 June 2022, committed the region to net-zero greenhouse gas emissions target by 2050.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Act requires the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (\u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e) to bring forward Regulations to set specific emissions reduction targets for 2030 and 2040 and to bring forward Regulations to set the first 3 carbon budgets (2023-2027, 2028-2032 and 2033-2037).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Act places a further duty on \u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e to prepare and publish a Climate Action Plan (\u003cabbr title=\"Climate Action Plan, Northern Ireland Executive\"\u003eCAP\u003c/abbr\u003e) and to bring forward Regulations under the Act to place statutory climate change reporting duties on specified public bodies. The \u003cabbr title=\"Climate Action Plan, Northern Ireland Executive\"\u003eCAP\u003c/abbr\u003e will set out how the first carbon budget will be achieved and provide a pathway towards achieving the interim emissions reductions targets and the overall net zero target by 2050. Subsequent CAPs will be published every 5 years, in line with carbon budget periods. The Act places a duty on all Northern Ireland Executive departments to assist \u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e in preparing the \u003cabbr title=\"Climate Action Plan, Northern Ireland Executive\"\u003eCAP\u003c/abbr\u003e and to ensure that in exercising their functions they do so, in so far as it is possible to do so, in a manner which is consistent with the achievement of net zero by 2050.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"scottish-government\"\u003e2.8.1.3 Scottish Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe statutory framework for reducing greenhouse gas emissions in Scotland is set out in the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009. In 2019, the Climate Change (Emissions Reduction Targets) (Scotland) Act amended the 2009 Act and established Scotland’s target of net zero emissions by 2045. The Climate Change (Emissions Reduction Targets) (Scotland) Act 2024 amends the 2009 Act, replacing the annual emissions reduction target framework with 5-yearly carbon budgets. The target of net zero emissions in 2045 remains unchanged, and ministers are still required to produce annual reports on emissions progress. The new Act enables the levels of carbon budgets to be set once the latest advice has been received from the Climate Change Committee. Our next Climate Change Plan will cover the period 2026-2040.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Scottish Government also recognises the importance of working closely and collaboratively with the UK Government and other devolved governments to deliver a net zero that is mutually beneficial both in economic and social terms. We regularly engage with the UK Government and other devolved governments through the Net Zero, Energy and Climate Change Interministerial Group to discuss interdependencies between all 4 nations and opportunities to work collaboratively. Engagement will also remain an important part of our development of the next Climate Change Plan.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"welsh-government\"\u003e2.8.1.4 Welsh Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe statutory framework for reducing greenhouse gas emissions in Wales is set out in Part 2 of the Environment (Wales) Act (2016).\u003csup id=\"fnref:77\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:77\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 77]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e Wales has a series of 5-yearly carbon budgets and interim decadal targets to 2050. Progress is measured against a 1990 or 1995 baseline, depending on the gas in question. For each carbon budget, the Senedd Cymru (Welsh Parliament) must set a limit on the amount of international offsets that may be used.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn March 2021, the Senedd formally committed Wales to achieving net zero emissions in 2050. It also passed regulations in relation to Carbon Budgets 2 and 3, and the 2030 and 2040 interim targets, as follows:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eCarbon Budget 2 (2021-25)\u003c/strong\u003e: 37% average reduction (with no international offsets)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eCarbon Budget 3 (2026-30)\u003c/strong\u003e: 58% average reduction\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003e2030\u003c/strong\u003e: 63% reduction\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003e2040\u003c/strong\u003e: 89% reduction. Before the end of the second year after each carbon budget, the Welsh Government must publish a final statement on progress against that budget. The Climate Change Committee must then publish its own progress report, with the Welsh Government required to respond to that report in the Senedd\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"jersey\"\u003e2.8.1.5 Jersey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Carbon Neutral Roadmap\u003csup id=\"fnref:78\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:78\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 78]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e was agreed by the States of Jersey in 2022. This commits Jersey to net zero emissions by 2050 and sets out the first steps to net zero through the delivery plan which covers the period 2022-2025. The first target of a 68% reduction for 1990 levels needs to be met by 2030. Jersey’s commitment to emissions reduction is not bound by legislation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"guernsey\"\u003e2.8.1.6 Guernsey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn August 2020, Guernsey’s climate change policy, ‘Mitigating Climate Change - States of Guernsey Climate Change Policy \u0026amp; Action Plan’\u003csup id=\"fnref:79\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:79\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 79]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, received political approval. The policy sets the target to be carbon neutral by 2050, with an interim target of reducing emissions by 57% on 1990 levels by 2030. In doing so, Guernsey’s government also agreed that the climate targets should be legislated for.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"isle-of-man\"\u003e2.8.1.7 Isle of Man\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Climate Change Act 2021\u003csup id=\"fnref:80\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:80\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 80]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e contains the Isle of Man’s net zero by 2050 emissions reduction target and provides the basis of the Isle of Man’s statutory framework for climate action planning, delivery and monitoring. In addition, the Isle of Man has 2 statutory interim emissions reduction targets of 35% by 2030 and 45% by 2035\u003csup id=\"fnref:81\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:81\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 81]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (against a 2018 baseline). The Act requires a statutory climate change plan to be in place at all times, with the current plan being the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027\u003csup id=\"fnref:82\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:82\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 82]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. Prior to the current Climate Change Plan, Council of Ministers’ Climate Action Plan Phase 1\u003csup id=\"fnref:83\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:83\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 83]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e was in effect, between January 2020 and October 2022.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"gibraltar\"\u003e2.8.1.8 Gibraltar\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eGibraltar declared a climate emergency in 2019 and followed this up with the publication of the Gibraltar Climate Change Act\u003csup id=\"fnref:84\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:84\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 84]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e later that same year. The Act sets legally binding carbon emissions reduction targets against a 1990 baseline of 42% by 2030 and 100% by 2045. The Climate Change Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:85\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:85\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 85]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e published in 2021 sets out the main policies and strategies by which Gibraltar will meet these targets.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"institutional-arrangements-brbr\"\u003e2.8.2 Institutional arrangements \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"united-kingdom\"\u003e2.8.2.1 United Kingdom\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Climate Change Act 2008 is the legislative framework that holds the UK accountable for achieving our domestic climate target. The 2030 \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e falls in the same time period as the fifth carbon budget (2028-2032) but on a higher ambition.\nTo help track our progress, the Climate Change Committee publishes annual progress reports which provide an independent assessment of the government’s progress in reducing emissions, which the government responds to by the statutory date.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"northern-ireland-executive-1\"\u003e2.8.2.2 Northern Ireland Executive\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (\u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e) on an annual basis publishes the Northern Ireland Greenhouse Gas Inventory\u003csup id=\"fnref:86\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:86\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 86]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. The latest inventory covers the period 1990-2022, with the focus on ‘by source’ emissions. As part of this process \u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e also produces a set of Carbon Intensity Indicators on an annual basis. These are designed to complement the greenhouse gas inventory and allow the \u003cabbr title=\"Northern Ireland\"\u003eNI\u003c/abbr\u003e departments to track the effectiveness of their carbon reduction policies and measures.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Climate Change Act (Northern Ireland) 2022 (the Act) placed a duty on \u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e to prepare and publish a report before the end of each 5 yearly carbon budget period, setting out what progress has been made in implementing the policies and proposals contained within the associated 5 year Climate Action Plan. As part of this requirement, all \u003cabbr title=\"Northern Ireland\"\u003eNI\u003c/abbr\u003e departments have a duty to provide details of progress in implementing the policies and proposals within their areas of responsibility. Furthermore, the Act places a duty on \u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e to lay a report before the \u003cabbr title=\"Northern Ireland\"\u003eNI\u003c/abbr\u003e assembly, before the end of the second year after each carbon budget period, setting out a final statement on the total amount of \u003cabbr title=\"Northern Ireland\"\u003eNI\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions, removals and net emissions for the period. The statement must include an assessment of the extent the policies and proposals contained in the Climate Action Plan have contributed towards the achievement of the carbon budget for the given 5-year carbon budget period.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"scottish-government-1\"\u003e2.8.2.3 Scottish Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Scottish Government has put in place a National Performance Framework to achieve its purpose, and this framework sets out ‘National Outcomes’ to describe the kind of Scotland it aims to create and to help it monitor progress.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn addition to this, cross-government climate change activity is governed by the Global Climate Emergency Board through the Climate Change Programme. This programme monitors progress on a monthly basis.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Climate Change Programme consists of 3 pillars, these are The Climate Change Plan, the Scottish National Adaptation Plan 3 and Just Transition plans. Each of these plans have or will have (for those still in development) their own monitoring and evaluation frameworks. In addition to this each of these 3 pillars is required to report progress to the Scottish Parliament on an annual basis.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere are also 2 statutory nitrogen reports that the Scottish Government must update annually: the Scottish Nitrogen Balance Sheet (‘\u003cabbr title=\"Scottish Nitrogen Balance Sheet\"\u003eSNBS\u003c/abbr\u003e’) and the Nitrogen use efficiency in Scotland progress report (‘progress report’).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Scottish Nitrogen Balance Sheet\"\u003eSNBS\u003c/abbr\u003e provides a powerful new source of evidence to track how efficiently nitrogen is used in Scotland and helps to identify further opportunities to improve this. In particular, it will help support progress towards Scotland’s national climate change targets.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe progress report supports the \u003cabbr title=\"Scottish Nitrogen Balance Sheet\"\u003eSNBS\u003c/abbr\u003e.
