This reports on progress towards relevant actions to improve nitrogen use and identify opportunities for future improvements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"welsh-government-1\"\u003e2.8.2.4 Welsh Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eUnder the Environment (Wales) Act 2016, Welsh ministers must prepare and publish a plan (‘report’) for each budgetary period, setting out their policies and proposals for meeting the carbon budget. The first of these reports was published in March 2019\u003csup id=\"fnref:87\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:87\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 87]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. Throughout the delivery of its second plan (Carbon Budget 2 (\u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Budget 2\"\u003eCB2\u003c/abbr\u003e))\u003csup id=\"fnref:88\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:88\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 88]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, Welsh Government is tracking and driving forward its implementation to ensure progress is made towards targets and budgets in a fair and just way. To track progress, a comprehensive system has been developed to monitor delivery which includes the following:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eLegislation\u003c/strong\u003e – An assessment against targets and budgets every 5 years. The report\u003csup id=\"fnref:89\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:89\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 89]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, formally referred to as Statement of Progress, was published in December 2022, summarising progress for Carbon Budget 1. The next Statement of Progress (for \u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Budget 2\"\u003eCB2\u003c/abbr\u003e) is due in 2027\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eIndicators\u003c/strong\u003e – Tracking progress towards targets and budgets on an annual basis.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eA \u003cstrong\u003emonitoring and reporting system\u003c/strong\u003e, which looks more in depth at the implementation progress of Welsh policies and proposals within the Plan\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eInternal Governance\u003c/strong\u003e arrangements, such as an internal Climate Change portfolio board and cross-government Cabinet, oversee progress and drive action\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eIndependent Progress reports\u003c/strong\u003e from the Climate Change Committee. \u003cstrong\u003eScrutiny\u003c/strong\u003e from the Senedd and Senedd committees\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"jersey-1\"\u003e2.8.2.5 Jersey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe government of Jersey is made up of the Council of Ministers, comprising of the Chief Minister and 12 portfolio ministers. The Council of Ministers has the responsibility for all of Jersey’s domestic and fiscal affairs and, increasingly, the Island’s international affairs. One of the first tasks of the Council is to draw up a Common Strategic Policy (\u003cabbr title=\"Common Strategic Policy\"\u003eCSP\u003c/abbr\u003e). The \u003cabbr title=\"Common Strategic Policy\"\u003eCSP\u003c/abbr\u003e outlines the Council’s aims and objectives and gives a timetable for implementation. Once the \u003cabbr title=\"Common Strategic Policy\"\u003eCSP\u003c/abbr\u003e is approved by the States Assembly (the legislature), it is the role of the Council to make sure it is properly and efficiently delivered. The current \u003cabbr title=\"Common Strategic Policy\"\u003eCSP\u003c/abbr\u003e (2024-2026) commits to continuing to address climate change through the Carbon Neutral Roadmap, which aims to fulfil Jersey’s commitments under the Paris Agreement.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"guernsey-1\"\u003e2.8.2.6 Guernsey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe States of Guernsey is the decision-making government body for the island, which includes climate matters. It has responsibility for all island affairs, both domestic and international. The States of Guernsey has a Government Work Plan (\u003cabbr title=\"Government Work Plan\"\u003eGWP\u003c/abbr\u003e) which sets out the priorities of the government over the term. The \u003cabbr title=\"Government Work Plan\"\u003eGWP\u003c/abbr\u003e outlines the States of Guernsey’s commitment to climate change. Within the current \u003cabbr title=\"Government Work Plan\"\u003eGWP\u003c/abbr\u003e (2023-2025) there is commitment to develop a detailed plan for the mitigation of emissions and it notes the need to address the island’s exposure to the effects of climate change.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"isle-of-man-1\"\u003e2.8.2.7 Isle of Man\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eGovernmental climate action in the Isle of Man is primarily the responsibility of the Council of Ministers, with their responsibilities set out in the Climate Change Act 2021\u003csup id=\"fnref:90\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:90\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 90]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. The Climate Change Transformation Board (\u003cabbr title=\"Climate Change Transformation Board\"\u003eCCTB\u003c/abbr\u003e), supported by the Climate Change Transformation Team (\u003cabbr title=\"Climate Change Transformation Team\"\u003eCCTT\u003c/abbr\u003e), report to the Council of Ministers. The \u003cabbr title=\"Climate Change Transformation Team\"\u003eCCTT\u003c/abbr\u003e sits within the Department of Environment, Food and Agriculture (\u003cabbr title=\"Department of Environment, Food and Agriculture\"\u003eDEFA\u003c/abbr\u003e) and is responsible for the management and administration of the programme, acting as a central hub to support delivery of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027\u003csup id=\"fnref:91\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:91\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 91]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e by the government departments responsible for the individual actions, and directly delivering some cross-government actions. Key climate change related documents, including legislation, are approved by Tynwald (the Manx parliament). Annual climate change reporting by Manx public bodies to the Council of Ministers (via \u003cabbr title=\"Climate Change Transformation Team\"\u003eCCTT\u003c/abbr\u003e and \u003cabbr title=\"Climate Change Transformation Board\"\u003eCCTB\u003c/abbr\u003e) provides a framework for compliance across the Manx public sector.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"gibraltar-1\"\u003e2.8.2.8 Gibraltar\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe government of Gibraltar is made up of the Chief Minister and up to 9 other elected members of Parliament. Gibraltar is self-governing in all areas except defence and foreign policy. The government’s responsibilities in respect of climate action are set out in the 2019 Climate Change Act\u003csup id=\"fnref:92\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:92\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 92]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. In 2022 the Net Zero Delivery Body\u003csup id=\"fnref:93\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:93\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 93]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e was established. This Body is chaired by the Deputy Chief Minister and is designed to guide implementation of the Climate Change Strategy across all government bodies.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"stakeholder-engagement-related-to-the-uks-2030-nationally-determined-contribution-ndc\"\u003e2.9 Stakeholder engagement related to the UK’s 2030 Nationally Determined Contribution (\u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"cross-cutting-engagement-brbr\"\u003e2.9.1 Cross-cutting engagement \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhen setting the 2030 \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e, the UK consulted with a range of stakeholders such as businesses, civil society groups, local government and the devolved governments to capture their views on scope and target. It was also covered in correspondence with representatives of these groups and interested Parliamentarians. A copy of the UK’s updated \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e was laid in the UK’s Houses of Parliament. For more information, please see section 4a(i) of the UK’s 2030 \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003csup id=\"fnref:94\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:94\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 94]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e When the UK set its 2030 \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e, we have considered the impact of climate policy more broadly on groups protected under the 2010 Equality Act.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe are committed to ensuring that everyone has the opportunity to contribute to the transition to net zero, supporting people and communities to take action and demonstrating the benefits of the transition. We will set out the government’s approach to engaging the public in a Public Participation Strategy, to be published in 2025. This will include how we support people to adopt new technologies, as well as opportunities to ensure that public views are considered in the development of policy.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"net-zero-engagement-by-sector-england-brbr\"\u003e2.9.2 Net Zero engagement by sector (England) \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"energy\"\u003e2.9.2.1 Energy\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK works closely with industry, regulators, sector bodies, and other stakeholders to ensure that our energy system is resilient and secure, including to the impacts of climate change.\u003csup id=\"fnref:95\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:95\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 95]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo deliver production levels needed for Carbon Budget 6 (2033-2037) and net zero by 2050, the UK Government is working closely with industry and other stakeholders to overcome the barriers to growing a new low carbon energy vector for the UK.\u003csup id=\"fnref:96\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:96\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 96]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe 2021 Hydrogen Strategy, as well as underpinning policies such as the Hydrogen Production Business Model and Hydrogen Storage Business Model, have been developed through close engagement and collaboration with stakeholders across the sector.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"transport\"\u003e2.9.2.2 Transport\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhen developing the Transport Decarbonisation Plan in 2021, the UK undertook extensive stakeholder engagement including: 8 workshops with 49 local government representatives and 59 virtual policy workshops with knowledge experts, innovators, businesses, non-governmental organisations, and civil society representatives.\u003csup id=\"fnref:97\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:97\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 97]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e The Department for Transport received over 300 written submissions and evidence on measures needed to decarbonise transport. The Department for Transport also formed the Net Zero Transport Board which was a ministerial-led external advisory board providing independent, objective, and impartial advice on transport decarbonisation to the Department for Transport.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Department for Transport also engages internationally on domestic efforts including at United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change Conference of the Parties (\u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e COPs).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"industrial-processes-and-product-use\"\u003e2.9.2.3 Industrial processes and product use\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK is committed to having a thriving industrial sector aligned with our net zero target, without pushing emissions and business abroad.\u003csup id=\"fnref:98\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:98\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 98]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e The UK has successfully engaged with a wide range of stakeholders to date, including business representative organisations, think tanks and academics, industry bodies and trade associations to develop policies supporting UK industrial decarbonisation, and to develop the market for low carbon industrial products.\u003csup id=\"fnref:99\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:99\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 99]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e \u003csup id=\"fnref:100\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:100\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 100]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e This included a comprehensive programme of stakeholder engagement to support the development and launch of the Industrial Decarbonisation Strategy (2021).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"agriculture\"\u003e2.9.2.4 Agriculture\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2021-2022 the UK continued a significant reform of agricultural policy in England phasing out subsidies and expanding schemes to boost Britain’s food security and accelerate the transition to a more resilient and sustainable farming sector. The Sustainable Farming Incentive (SFI) opened in 2021 with a pilot scheme, with a wider rollout to farmers in 2022 to make their businesses more sustainable and resilient. The focus in 2022 was on moorlands, arable and horticultural soils, and improved grassland soils. In addition, in 2022 the UK launched a call for evidence exploring the potential opportunities and challenges associated with the use of methane suppressing feed products.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"land-use-land-use-change-and-forestry-lulucf\"\u003e2.9.2.5 Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry (\u003cabbr title=\"Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry\"\u003eLULUCF\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK continues to engage with stakeholders, industry bodies and landowners on a range of challenges across forestry, peatlands and other land use sectors. As part of the Environment Act 2021, we legislated for a long-term statutory tree target in England to increase tree canopy and woodland cover to 16.5% of land area in England by 2050.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"waste-management\"\u003e2.9.2.6 Waste management\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Collection and Packaging Reforms were introduced in the Environment Act 2021 Throughout the development of these reforms, the UK engaged with stakeholders through different working groups, events and forums to develop the policies further. These included the monthly Resources and Waste forums and newsletters open to all stakeholders which cover recycling collections and wider resources and waste topics.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"other-sectors\"\u003e2.9.2.7 Other sectors\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eBuildings\u003c/strong\u003e: Progress is being made to ensure secure, affordable and clean heating for UK homes and businesses.\u003csup id=\"fnref:101\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:101\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 101]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e government has taken key steps towards improving energy efficiency and deploying low-carbon heating - by engaging industry, consumers, and businesses, with targeted regulation and new market-based mechanisms, help to heat schemes, and work to increase public awareness.\u003csup id=\"fnref:102\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:102\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 102]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e Together this all helps to reduce costs for consumers and businesses, attract greater private investment and strengthen supply chain resilience – to ensure UK buildings are able to transition towards a greener future.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eGreenhouse Gas Removals\u003c/strong\u003e: In 2023, the UK set out the proposed commercial frameworks for the greenhouse gas removals (\u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas Removals\"\u003eGGR\u003c/abbr\u003e) business model and standards\u003csup id=\"fnref:103\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:103\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 103]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e following extensive engagement with industry and academia. The Carbon Capture Usage and Storage Cluster process allowed \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas Removals\"\u003eGGR\u003c/abbr\u003e and large-scale Power Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (\u003cabbr title=\"Bioenergy with Carbon Capture and Storage\"\u003eBECCS\u003c/abbr\u003e) projects to apply for access to the Hynet cluster in the North West of England as part of the Track 1 Hynet expansion process. The UK Emissions Trading Scheme Authority published a consultation seeking input on the integration of GGRs into the UK Emissions Trading Scheme.\u003csup id=\"fnref:104\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:104\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 104]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e Commercial and economic regulatory frameworks for Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage (\u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage\"\u003eCCUS\u003c/abbr\u003e) have been developed through extensive engagement and collaboration with representatives from the many sectors and industries for whom \u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage\"\u003eCCUS\u003c/abbr\u003e is critical to achieve their decarbonisation objectives.\u003csup id=\"fnref:105\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:105\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 105]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"northern-ireland-executive-brbr-1\"\u003e2.9.3 Northern Ireland Executive \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Education, England\"\u003eDfE\u003c/abbr\u003e operated a thematic approach to Stakeholder Groups in the development of the Path to Net Zero Energy Strategy. Five working groups were convened across the areas of Consumers, Energy Efficiency, Heat, Power, and Transport to provide further analysis and evidence on potential policy options, with the Transport theme led by the Department for Infrastructure. The new Strategy was published in December 2021\u003csup id=\"fnref:106\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:106\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 106]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Department for Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (\u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e) in line with the ‘New Decade, New Approach’ commitment to bring forward climate change legislation for Northern Ireland, led on the development and progression of the Climate Change Act (Northern Ireland) 2022 which received Royal Assent in June 2022\u003csup id=\"fnref:107\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:107\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 107]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. In progressing the legislation development in December 2020 \u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e provided an opportunity for stakeholder involvement through launching a public consultation ‘Discussion Document on a Climate Change Bill’\u003csup id=\"fnref:108\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:108\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 108]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. Further stakeholder engagement took place when the Northern Ireland Assembly’s Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs Committee launched a call for evidence in August 2021 seeking views from both individuals and stakeholder organisations to feed into its scrutiny process of the Bill passage. In keeping with the legislative commitment set in the Act, \u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e, in conjunction with other executive departments, commenced the development of Northern Ireland’s first Climate Action Plan (\u003cabbr title=\"Climate Action Plan, Northern Ireland Executive\"\u003eCAP\u003c/abbr\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"scottish-government-brbr-1\"\u003e2.9.4 Scottish Government \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2020, the Scottish Government published an update to the 2018 Climate Change Plan to account for the new targets set out within the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009 (as amended by the Climate Change (Emissions Reduction Targets) (Scotland) Act 2019), which includes its commitment to reaching net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2045\u003csup id=\"fnref:109\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:109\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 109]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Plan update also reflects that the 2019 Act enshrined the Scottish Government’s commitment to a just transition into law, ensuring that everyone can access the opportunities of the transition and that no one is left behind. The Plan update sets out the Scottish Government’s strategic direction, containing the policies and proposals that will put Scotland on a pathway to meet its emissions reduction targets. Collectively these policies will require societal changes, impacting how the population will travel, heat its homes and how the Scottish people consume goods and services.\nThe Scottish Government puts people, places and business at the heart of their open, transparent, and participatory approaches to policy development and government decision making. The Public Engagement Strategy is a key part of the Scottish Government’s approach to delivering upon the ambition of the updated Climate Change Plan. A broad approach to public engagement will be required in order to include people and communities in the national effort required to reach climate change goals.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Scottish Government is committed to ensuring that everyone in Scotland recognises the implications of the global climate emergency, fully understands and contributes to Scotland’s response, and embraces their role in the transition to a net zero and climate ready Scotland.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWidespread participation and engagement are essential if we are to successfully limit the effects of climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions, preparing for the impacts that are already locked in, and harnessing the opportunities to innovate during the net zero transition.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e62% of changes needed to achieve net zero can only happen with societal or individual behaviour change (Climate Change Committee) and achieving our climate targets fundamentally depends upon the involvement and support of the people of Scotland in all aspects of their lives.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Scottish Government is a member of the international Open Government Partnership. Scotland’s Open Government Action Plan commits the Scottish Government to our Open Government climate commitment, and to the values of openness, accountability, transparency, and involving people.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"welsh-government-brbr-1\"\u003e2.9.5 Welsh Government \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eFollowing a consultation held between October and December 2022 (supported by outreach engagement activity during Wales Climate Week), the Welsh Government published its public engagement strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:110\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:110\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 110]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e in July 2023. Climate Action Wales explains how the Welsh Government will work with its delivery partners to ensure that people and communities are involved in climate decision-making and supported and encouraged to make green choices in relation to home energy, travel, food and consumption. The strategy conveys a vision of a fairer society driven by improved health, wellbeing and fairness and where no-one is left behind. Its guiding principles are structured around the ‘5 ways of working’ in the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 and uses a ‘5 Es framework’ (i.e. exemplify, engage, enable, encourage and evaluate) to convey how the programme will be delivered. The Welsh Government is now focussed on ensuring delivery of the commitments within the strategy.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"jersey-brbr\"\u003e2.9.6 Jersey \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eA people-powered approach was prioritised through the development of the Carbon Neutral Roadmap. This included Jersey’s first citizens’ assembly held on climate change alongside a public campaign, the ‘Climate Conversation’ carried out in 2021.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis informed the level of ambition of the roadmap and led to the second most responded to consultation in Jersey. There is a specific climate change and sustainability engagement team within government who continue to engage with key stakeholders, industry and the public. For example, carbon literacy training has been facilitated across government and industries that are signed up to Jersey’s eco active business network.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"guernsey-brbr\"\u003e2.9.7 Guernsey \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn December 2019, an external consultancy was commissioned to facilitate a workshop with officers from across Guernsey’s government and stakeholders from local organisations. The workshop aimed to pilot and give feedback on an in-depth independent survey that was later launched in January 2020. The workshop and survey focused on heating and on-island travel, which are 2 of the biggest contributors to greenhouse gas emissions locally. Results were published online\u003csup id=\"fnref:111\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:111\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 111]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"isle-of-man-brbr\"\u003e2.9.8 Isle of Man \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eFollowing the approval of the Council of Ministers’ Climate Action Plan Phase 1\u003csup id=\"fnref:112\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:112\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 112]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, and formal acknowledgment of the climate crisis by Tynwald in 2019, development of the Climate Change Bill began. Targeted engagement with key stakeholders was held in February 2020, followed by a full public consultation\u003csup id=\"fnref:113\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:113\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 113]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e on the Bill in July 2020.\nA comprehensive public consultation was held during 2021 on the content for the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027\u003csup id=\"fnref:114\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:114\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 114]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. This ran alongside a Citizens’ Forum\u003csup id=\"fnref:115\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:115\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 115]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e and engagement with key stakeholders. The Citizens’ Forum was made up of 36 individuals who represented interest groups and wider public of the Isle of Man. The group was instrumental in the formation of the principles for the Green Living Grant\u003csup id=\"fnref:116\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:116\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 116]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. The first of regular public insight surveys relating to climate change was launched in 2021. Section E of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027 sets out actions relating to engagement and awareness, including developing awareness and educational campaigns to help ensure people understand the climate emergency, reduce climate anxiety, empower positive action and increase awareness of the Isle of Man government’s actions in addressing climate change.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"gibraltar-brbr\"\u003e2.9.9 Gibraltar \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eGibraltar consulted with non-governmental organisations as well as business representatives on the development of its climate change strategy. It also underwent internal consultation across government.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"description-of-the-uks-ndc\"\u003e2.10 Description of the UK’s \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e\n\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"scope-and-targets-brbr\"\u003e2.10.1 Scope and targets \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eParties agreed in the Paris Agreement to keep the increase in global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, and to pursue efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C. In December 2020, the UK announced its 2030 Nationally Determined Contribution (\u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e) which commits to reducing UK net greenhouse gas emissions by at least 68% by 2030 on 1990 levels. It represents a significant step forward in our ambition to tackle climate change over the next 10 years, as we accelerate towards meeting our legally binding commitment to net zero by 2050.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"identified-indicators-selected-to-track-progress-and-information-brbr\"\u003e2.10.2 Identified indicators selected to track progress and information \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eReference indicator: Net\u003csup id=\"fnref:117\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:117\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 117]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e greenhouse gas (\u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e) emissions in \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee.\nThe reference indicator (\u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee) in the reference years (1990 and 1995) will be based on the 1990-2030 UK \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e Inventory submitted to the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e in 2032. The value for the target year (2030) will be based on applying a 68% fixed percentage reduction target to the reference indicator value.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"accounting-approach-and-methodologies-brbr\"\u003e2.10.3 Accounting approach and methodologies \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis section presents information on UK \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions and the National System established to produce and quality assure the UK \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e Inventory. A fuller description of this National System can be found in the UK’s National Inventory Document (\u003cabbr title=\"National Inventory Document\"\u003eNID\u003c/abbr\u003e), submitted to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (\u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e) in 2022\u003csup id=\"fnref:118\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:118\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 118]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. The UK is obliged to produce an annual \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e inventory, containing an estimate of all anthropogenic \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions across the UK to meet its commitments under the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e and the Kyoto Protocol; it will continue to do so to meet its commitments under the Paris Agreement. Data from the \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e inventory are also used to monitor progress against Carbon Budgets under the UK Climate Change Act 2008. The methodologies used in the NIR are used across all emissions reporting in the UK to ensure consistency between estimates, only geographic scope changes.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e inventory covers the 7 direct GHGs under the Paris Agreement. These are collectively known as the ‘basket’ of GHGs and are: carbon dioxide (\u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e), methane (\u003cabbr title=\"Methane\"\u003eCH\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e4\u003c/sub\u003e), nitrous oxide (\u003cabbr title=\"Nitrous Oxide\"\u003eN\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003eO), hydrofluorocarbons (\u003cabbr title=\"Hydrofluorocarbons\"\u003eHFCs\u003c/abbr\u003e), perfluorocarbons (\u003cabbr title=\"Perfluorocarbons\"\u003ePFCs\u003c/abbr\u003e), sulphur hexafluoride (SF\u003csub\u003e6\u003c/sub\u003e) and nitrogen trifluoride (\u003cabbr title=\"Nitrogen trifluoride\"\u003eNF\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e3\u003c/sub\u003e). The last 4 gases are collectively referred to as fluorinated gases (F gases). In accordance with international reporting and carbon trading protocols, emissions from each of the gases are weighted by its global warming potential (\u003cabbr title=\"Government Work Plan\"\u003eGWP\u003c/abbr\u003e), so that total greenhouse gas emissions can be reported on a consistent basis. The \u003cabbr title=\"Government Work Plan\"\u003eGWP\u003c/abbr\u003e for each gas is defined as its warming influence in relation to that of \u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e over a 100- year period. Greenhouse gas emissions are then presented in carbon dioxide equivalent units (\u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s base year for assessing emissions of \u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e, \u003cabbr title=\"Methane\"\u003eCH\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e4\u003c/sub\u003e, and \u003cabbr title=\"Nitrous Oxide\"\u003eN\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003eO is 1990. The UK uses 1995 as the base year for emissions of the fluorinated gases: \u003cabbr title=\"Hydrofluorocarbons\"\u003eHFCs\u003c/abbr\u003e, \u003cabbr title=\"Perfluorocarbons\"\u003ePFCs\u003c/abbr\u003e, SF\u003csub\u003e6\u003c/sub\u003e and \u003cabbr title=\"Nitrogen trifluoride\"\u003eNF\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e3\u003c/sub\u003e. This is in line with most European states, and in accordance with the Paris Agreement. Land use, land-use change and forestry (\u003cabbr title=\"Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry\"\u003eLULUCF\u003c/abbr\u003e) emissions and removals are reported in the UK’s \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e inventory in accordance with the rules for reporting this sector under the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e. The \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e reporting basis includes an estimate of all anthropogenic sources minus sinks from the \u003cabbr title=\"Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry\"\u003eLULUCF\u003c/abbr\u003e sector.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK elects Cropland Management, Grazing Land Management, and Wetland Drainage and Rewetting, as \u003cabbr title=\"Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry\"\u003eLULUCF\u003c/abbr\u003e activities. The UK does not elect Revegetation, as the eligible land area for Revegetation within the UK is estimated to be very small, and therefore the associated potential sink will also be very small. In addition to the provision of a national inventory covering the whole of the UK and British crown dependencies and overseas territories, the UK also produces annual spatially disaggregated inventories to provide geographical breakdown to England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and to the 374 local authorities that make up the UK. Trends in UK \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions between 1990 and 2022, disaggregating overall emissions by gas and by source sector can be found in section \u003cstrong\u003e2.7 National circumstances of \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions and removals over time\u003c/strong\u003e. More information on UK \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions trends can be found in the Common Tabular Format tables.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"national-system-brbr\"\u003e2.10.4 National System \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eSection 1.2 of the National Inventory Document presents the full details of the UK’s institutional arrangements for inventory preparation\u003csup id=\"fnref:119\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:119\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 119]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e inventory is compiled and maintained by a consortium led by Ricardo Energy and Environment– the Inventory Agency – under contract to the Science and Innovation for Climate and Energy (\u003cabbr title=\"Science and Innovation for Climate and Energy\"\u003eSICE\u003c/abbr\u003e) Directorate in the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e). Ricardo Energy and Environment is directly responsible for producing the emissions estimates for the following categories: Energy, Industrial Processes and Product Use (\u003cabbr title=\"Industrial Processes and Product Use\"\u003eIPPU\u003c/abbr\u003e), and Waste. Ricardo Energy and Environment is also responsible for inventory planning, data collection, Quality Assurance (QA)/Quality Control (QC) and inventory management and archiving. Aether, a member within the consortium, is responsible for compiling emissions from railways and for the UK’s overseas territories and crown dependencies. Gluckman Consulting advises on fluorinated gas (F-gas) emissions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eForestry emissions and removals in the Land-Use, Land-Use Change and Forestry (\u003cabbr title=\"Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry\"\u003eLULUCF\u003c/abbr\u003e) sector are calculated by Forest Research and the remainder of the sector is calculated and compiled by the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology (\u003cabbr title=\"UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology\"\u003eUKCEH\u003c/abbr\u003e), both partners within the consortium. Agricultural sector emissions estimates are produced by Rothamsted Research, under contract to the UK Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eImprovements to the inventory are scrutinised by the UK’s National Inventory Steering Committee (\u003cabbr title=\"National Inventory Steering Committee\"\u003eNISC\u003c/abbr\u003e). The \u003cabbr title=\"National Inventory Steering Committee\"\u003eNISC\u003c/abbr\u003e is made of key stakeholders to the GHGI including representatives from the suppliers above, representatives from each of the devolved governments, and representatives from key government departments including the Department for Environment, Food, and Rural Affairs, and the Department for Transport. The \u003cabbr title=\"National Inventory Steering Committee\"\u003eNISC\u003c/abbr\u003e provides an oversight function and gives approval for any proposed changes.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"geographical-coverage-brbr\"\u003e2.10.5 Geographical Coverage \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK inventory provides data to assess progress of the UK’s commitments under the Paris Agreement Protocol, progress towards the UK’s own Carbon Budgets and to meet commitments as a Party to the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s 2030 \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e covers territorial emissions from the England, Scotland, and Northern Ireland as well as the 3 crown dependencies, Bailiwick of Jersey, Guernsey, Isle of Man and 1 overseas territory, Gibraltar.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"mitigation-policies-and-measures\"\u003e2.11 Mitigation policies and measures\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"cross-cutting-policies-and-measures-brbr\"\u003e2.11.1 Cross-cutting policies and measures \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"net-zero-strategy\"\u003e2.11.1.1 Net Zero Strategy\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Net Zero Strategy was published in 2021 to set out how we intended to keep the UK on track for our coming carbon budgets, our ambitious Nationally Determined Contribution (\u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e), and then set out our vision for a decarbonised economy in 2050.\u003csup id=\"fnref:120\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:120\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 120]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn December 2024, we published the UK Government’s annual response to the 2024 Progress Report from Climate Change Committee the independent body that advises the UK on its progress to reaching net zero.\u003csup id=\"fnref:121\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:121\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 121]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e The government’s response recognises the challenging picture outlined by the Climate Change Committee. It also sets out the urgent action that has been taken alongside further commitments to accelerate to net zero and address the Climate Change Committee’s recommendations. We will publish an updated cross-economy plan to meet carbon budgets and \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contributions\"\u003eNDCs\u003c/abbr\u003e in due course, which will set out details of policies across all sectors of the economy.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eLooking ahead, we will set Carbon Budget 7 by June 2026, in line with our statutory duties, for the period 2038 to 2042. This will set out the next phase of our pathway to net zero and policies to further decarbonise the UK economy.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"uk-emissions-trading-scheme\"\u003e2.11.1.2 UK Emissions Trading Scheme\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK Emissions Trading Scheme (\u003cabbr title=\"UK Emissions Trading Scheme\"\u003eUK ETS\u003c/abbr\u003e) is an essential part of our approach to cutting emissions and driving green investment. The scheme is run by the 4 administrations of the UK (the UK Government, Scottish Government, Welsh Government, and the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs for Northern Ireland), collectively making up the \u003cabbr title=\"UK Emissions Trading Scheme\"\u003eUK ETS\u003c/abbr\u003e Authority.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eLaunched in 2021, the \u003cabbr title=\"UK Emissions Trading Scheme\"\u003eUK ETS\u003c/abbr\u003e supports decarbonisation across aviation, power, and industry by setting a limit on emissions and creating a carbon price that incentivises businesses to reduce their emissions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2022 the \u003cabbr title=\"UK Emissions Trading Scheme\"\u003eUK ETS\u003c/abbr\u003e Authority consulted on aligning the scheme’s cap – the limit on emissions from the sectors covered – with our net zero and other climate targets. In 2023 we confirmed the implementation of this new tighter cap, aligning it with our net zero targets to ensure the sectors covered decarbonise at the pace required to contribute to achieving our climate goals.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"energy-brbr-1\"\u003e2.11.2 Energy \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"england\"\u003e2.11.2.1 England\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK Government’s energy policy through 2021-22 was to decarbonise the power sector by 2035, subject to security of supply. In November 2022, the ambition was announced to cut overall energy consumption by 15% by 2030. Energy is a devolved matter in Northern Ireland but mostly reserved in Scotland and Wales.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eThe British Energy Security Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:122\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:122\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 122]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2022)\u003c/strong\u003e: set out how government intended to improve the UK’s energy security by increasing the efficiency with which we use energy, how to increase our proportion of domestically produced energy, and how to help bring down the bills of consumers. This involved measures such a zero-rating VAT on energy efficiency and clean heat technologies.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eHydrogen Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:123\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:123\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 123]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2021)\u003c/strong\u003e: outlined a comprehensive roadmap for the development of the wider hydrogen economy over the 2020s and early 2030s, putting the UK at the forefront of the race to develop low carbon hydrogen. It laid the foundations for a hydrogen economy by 2030 that would support innovation and stimulate investment to scale up hydrogen technologies, while helping to achieve our Sixth Carbon Budget and net zero commitments and secure the economic opportunities of the transition. It also set out an aim to provide regular updates on hydrogen policy development, with the latest published in December 2023.\u003csup id=\"fnref:124\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:124\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 124]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eNorth Sea Transition Deal\u003csup id=\"fnref:125\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:125\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 125]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2021)\u003c/strong\u003e: through the North Sea Transition Deal, the offshore oil and gas industry is committed to reducing its production emissions by 10% by 2025, 25% by 2027 and 50% by 2030, against a 2018 baseline. The government continues to support the North Sea Transition Deal, including the important decarbonisation targets it set for the sector.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"northern-ireland-executive-2\"\u003e2.11.2.2 Northern Ireland Executive\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2022, the energy supply sector in Northern Ireland represented 14% of all emissions. From 1990 to 2022 the greenhouse gas emissions in the sector have reduced by 44%.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor the 12 month period January 2022 to December 2022, 51.0% of total electricity consumption in Northern Ireland was generated from renewable sources\u003csup id=\"fnref:126\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:126\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 126]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo drive forward further action to decarbonise the energy sector, in December 2021 \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Education, England\"\u003eDfE\u003c/abbr\u003e published the Northern Ireland Executive’s ‘Energy Strategy- The Path to Net Zero Energy’. Following on from which, the Climate Change Act (Northern Ireland) 2022 set a legal requirement for at least 80% of electricity consumption in Northern Ireland to be from renewable sources by 2030.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"scottish-government-2\"\u003e2.11.2.3 Scottish Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe electricity sector in Scotland is the most mature sector in terms of decarbonisation, with emissions falling by 13.0 mega tonnes carbon dioxide equivalent (\u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee) between 1990 and 2022 to 1.7 mega tonnes carbon dioxide equivalent (\u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee)– an 88.1% reduction, the largest reduction of any sector.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2022, 87.9% of electricity generated in Scotland was from zero or low carbon sources (including nuclear and pumped hydro). Specifically, 71% of electricity generated in Scotland in 2022 was from renewable sources.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"welsh-government-2\"\u003e2.11.2.4 Welsh Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Welsh Government’s policy objective is to avoid the continued extraction and consumption of fossil fuels. It expects all new development to mitigate the causes of climate change in accordance with its energy hierarchy for planning, as set out in Planning Policy Wales (2018):\u003csup id=\"fnref:127\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:127\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 127]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003col\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eReduce energy demand\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eUse energy efficiently\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eRenewable energy generation\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eMinimise carbon impact of other energy generation\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eMinimise extraction of carbon-intensive energy materials\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn the hierarchy, the extraction of minerals for the purpose of generating energy is undesirable as it is the most carbon intensive form of production. The purpose of this hierarchy is to encourage preferred generation proposals to come forward and to discourage proposals supported by the extraction of fossil fuels. In addition to Planning Policy Wales, the Welsh Government’s Coal Policy Statement (2021) is clear that it does not intend to authorise new Coal Authority mining operation licences or variations to existing licences.\u003csup id=\"fnref:128\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:128\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 128]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"jersey-2\"\u003e2.11.2.5 Jersey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThrough interconnectors to the French grid, Jersey imports most of its electricity from low carbon and certified renewable sources meaning many of the decarbonisation policies focus on electrification of on-Island heating and transport.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"guernsey-2\"\u003e2.11.2.6 Guernsey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eGuernsey’s Energy Policy\u003csup id=\"fnref:129\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:129\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 129]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e sets out a target of net zero by no later than 2050 and will transition to a low carbon Island, supported by increased use of electricity to heat homes and power on-island travel. Guernsey’s Electricity Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:130\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:130\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 130]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e outlined plans to further decarbonise the electricity sector, and how increased electrification could assist in the broader energy market underpinned by additional interconnection. The Climate Change Action Plan will explore how Guernsey can achieve this target, including more broadly across the energy sector, and how feasible it is to aim to achieve net zero before 2050. In 2019, Guernsey’s government commissioned a report entitled “Future Energy Demand and Policy Considerations for Guernsey”\u003csup id=\"fnref:131\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:131\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 131]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. The report forecasts a decline in total energy demand over time with an in increase in electricity demand up until 2050. The report identified the following as drivers to the predicted decline in energy and fuel demand: technological efficiencies, fuel efficiencies and the uptake of energy reduction measures such as loft insulation, hybrid vehicles, or newer more efficient gas boilers.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eGuernsey has an interconnector, through Jersey, with France, which provides access to the European electricity grid. Additional interconnection will provide greater electricity supply security and will allow for development of on-Island renewables and potential export opportunities.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"isle-of-man-2\"\u003e2.11.2.7 Isle of Man\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2019, the Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets (\u003cabbr title=\"Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets\"\u003eIMPACT\u003c/abbr\u003e) Report\u003csup id=\"fnref:132\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:132\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 132]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e was produced. Appendices\u003csup id=\"fnref:133\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:133\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 133]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e 13-17 and 20 relate to energy. In 2021, the Isle of Man Future Energy Scenarios\u003csup id=\"fnref:134\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:134\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 134]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e report was produced, identifying potential decarbonisation routes for the Island’s electricity supply. In 2022, the Isle of Man Renewable Heating Scenarios\u003csup id=\"fnref:135\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:135\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 135]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e report was produced, identifying potential decarbonisation routes for the Island’s building energy needs. The Phase 1 Action Plan Progress Report\u003csup id=\"fnref:136\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:136\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 136]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e details progress made against the Council of Ministers’ Climate Action Plan Phase 1\u003csup id=\"fnref:137\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:137\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 137]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e over the period 1 April 2021-31 March 2022, including actions relating to energy. Section 1 of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027\u003csup id=\"fnref:138\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:138\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 138]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e sets out the Isle of Man’s current, high-level policies relating to electricity decarbonisation. In particular, it sets a target of 2030 for full decarbonisation of the national electricity supply from fossil fuels and at least 20 \u003cabbr title=\"Megawatts\"\u003eMW\u003c/abbr\u003e locally generated renewable power by 2026. Manx Utilities, the Island’s publicly owned electricity company is delivering its Future Energy Delivery Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:139\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:139\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 139]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e which outlines the roadmap to the targets set out above.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"gibraltar-2\"\u003e2.11.2.8 Gibraltar\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Gibraltar Electricity Authority fully switched electricity generation to the North Mole Power Station in 2020. This plant runs on natural gas and represents a significant step forward for Gibraltar in terms of moving towards cleaner electricity. Although it is still a fossil fuel, it is much cleaner than the diesel oil used by the old generating stations and emissions from electricity have decreased by 37%\u003csup id=\"fnref:140\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:140\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 140]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e since 2015 despite the actual amount of electricity being consumed remaining fairly static.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2018 the government entered into a Solar Framework Agreement to promote the roll out of solar photovoltaic panels across the territory. In 2019 the first of these projects was deployed at New Harbours industrial park as part of a scheme to install over 3 \u003cabbr title=\"Megawatts\"\u003eMW\u003c/abbr\u003e of renewable energy.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Nearly Zero Energy Buildings\u003csup id=\"fnref:141\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:141\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 141]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e standards came into force in January 2021 which require all new buildings to meet very high standards of energy efficiency as well as to produce a minimum of 40% of their own energy from renewables.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"transport-brbr-1\"\u003e2.11.3 Transport \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"england-1\"\u003e2.11.3.1 England\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cstrong\u003eTransport Decarbonisation Plan\u003csup id=\"fnref:142\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:142\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 142]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2021)\u003c/strong\u003e sets out how to decarbonise the entire transport system in England, below are some of the areas that are covered:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eTechnical consultation on zero emission vehicle mandate policy design\u003csup id=\"fnref:143\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:143\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 143]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2022)\u003c/strong\u003e: Following the announcement of the UK adopting a zero emission vehicle (\u003cabbr title=\"Zero Emissions Vehicle\"\u003eZEV\u003c/abbr\u003e) mandate in the Net Zero Strategy in October 2021, the Department for Transport published a consultation seeking views on some of the design features that could be included in a car and van regulation. A summary of responses was published in 2023\u003csup id=\"fnref:144\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:144\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 144]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eNational Bus Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:145\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:145\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 145]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2021)\u003c/strong\u003e: committed to make buses more frequent, more reliable, more comprehensive, easier to understand and use, better co-ordinated and cheaper – to increase passenger numbers and reduce congestion and carbon emissions. The National Bus Strategy also re-committed to supporting the introduction of at least 4,000 zero emission buses (\u003cabbr title=\"Zero Emissions Buses\"\u003eZEBs\u003c/abbr\u003e) and achieving a zero-emission fleet.\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eJet Zero Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:146\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:146\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 146]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2022)\u003c/strong\u003e: set out its approach to achieving net zero for UK aviation by 2050. The Strategy focused on the rapid development of technologies in a way that maintains the benefits of air travel, whilst maximising the opportunities that decarbonisation brings for the UK.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eDomestic Maritime Decarbonisation\u003csup id=\"fnref:147\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:147\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 147]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2022)\u003c/strong\u003e: This consultation sought evidence on barriers and opportunities of decarbonising the maritime sector. A summary of responses was published in 2023.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eCycling and Walking Investment Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:148\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:148\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 148]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2022)\u003c/strong\u003e: sets the target that half of all journeys in towns and cities will be cycled or walked by 2030. It also includes the aim to deliver a world class cycling and walking network in England by 2040.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eRenewable Transport Fuel Obligation (\u003cabbr title=\"Renewable Transport Fuel Obligation\"\u003eRTFO\u003c/abbr\u003e) Order\u003csup id=\"fnref:149\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:149\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 149]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2007)\u003c/strong\u003e regulates renewable fuels used for transport. The \u003cabbr title=\"Renewable Transport Fuel Obligation\"\u003eRTFO\u003c/abbr\u003e was first implemented in 2008 and was the core policy measure for meeting transport targets within the EU Renewable Energy Directive. Under the \u003cabbr title=\"Renewable Transport Fuel Obligation\"\u003eRTFO\u003c/abbr\u003e, suppliers of relevant transport fuel in the UK must be able to show that a certain percentage of the fuel they supply comes from renewable and sustainable sources. Fuel suppliers that supply at least 450,000 litres of this fuel a year are obligated under the scheme.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eZero emission \u003cabbr title=\"Heavy Goods Vehicle\"\u003eHGV\u003c/abbr\u003e and infrastructure demonstrator programme\u003csup id=\"fnref:150\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:150\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 150]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e: Research and Development funding into zero emission \u003cabbr title=\"Heavy Goods Vehicle\"\u003eHGV\u003c/abbr\u003e and infrastructure demonstrators will establish new hydrogen \u003cabbr title=\"Heavy Goods Vehicle\"\u003eHGV\u003c/abbr\u003e refuelling sites and the deployment of hydrogen fuel cell \u003cabbr title=\"Heavy Goods Vehicles\"\u003eHGVs\u003c/abbr\u003e. In addition, the Tees Valley Hydrogen Transport Hub brings together hydrogen supply (refuelling infrastructure) and demand (transport applications) with the aim of demonstrating commercial viability of hydrogen in transport. Three projects, receiving £13m funding, are using hydrogen as a fuel with a fuel cell for a range of road vehicles, and through combustion for airside support vehicles. This is being supported by new publicly accessible hydrogen refuelling stations to be built in the region.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eDelivering decarbonisation through places\u003c/strong\u003e: There is no uniform approach to decarbonisation and each place in the UK has its own role to play in helping the UK to meet its legally binding target of net zero by 2050. In 2022, through an innovation grants programme, the UK provided over £550,000 to develop early-stage innovative solutions to support the decarbonisation of local transport systems.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eBetter data can provide new policy and operational insights, drive new products and services and ‘nudge’ people towards lower emission journeys. The department’s annual Transport and Environment statistical release draws together various data sources on transport’s environmental impact and provides guidance explaining the detail of estimating greenhouse gas emissions for different modes and journeys. Data consumers can use these data, without restrictions on use or disclosure, for journey planning applications, products and services enabling users to plan green journeys.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"northern-ireland-executive-3\"\u003e2.11.3.2 Northern Ireland Executive\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2022, transport was the second largest greenhouse gas emitting sector in Northern Ireland contributing 18.1% to overall emissions. The Department for Infrastructure (\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Infrastructure, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDfI\u003c/abbr\u003e) is currently developing its suite of new Transport Plans through an integrated approach with local councils Local Development Plans (\u003cabbr title=\"Local Development Plans\"\u003eLDPs\u003c/abbr\u003e). This integrated approach being undertaken between \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Infrastructure, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDfI\u003c/abbr\u003e and local councils provides a unique opportunity to make sure that the movement and accessibility of all forms, across all modes of transport, is considered as a key component in the development of areas at a local level. \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Infrastructure, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDfI\u003c/abbr\u003e has also committed investment of over £100m in hydrogen zero emissions and electric buses to support the roll out of a public transport fleet with zero emissions from engine combustion.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo support the decarbonisation of transport, \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Infrastructure, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDfI\u003c/abbr\u003e has also published an Action Plan for Electric Vehicle (\u003cabbr title=\"Electric Vehicle\"\u003eEV\u003c/abbr\u003e) Infrastructure\u003csup id=\"fnref:151\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:151\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 151]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e in November 2022. The plan was developed by the Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Task-Force which was set up in December 2021 to bring together representatives from government, consumers, energy providers, industry and \u003cabbr title=\"Electric Vehicle\"\u003eEV\u003c/abbr\u003e drivers to consider our \u003cabbr title=\"Electric Vehicle\"\u003eEV\u003c/abbr\u003e Infrastructure requirements to deliver a fit for purpose, modern \u003cabbr title=\"Electric Vehicle\"\u003eEV\u003c/abbr\u003e charging network.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"scottish-government-3\"\u003e2.11.3.3 Scottish Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eTransport is Scotland’s highest carbon emitting sector. The largest source of transport emissions is cars, which contribute almost 40% of transport emissions. This demonstrates the need to both transition to zero emission vehicles and reduce car use to combat climate change in a way that is consistent with our just transition principles.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eScottish Government and Convention of Scottish Local Authorities (\u003cabbr title=\"Convention of Scottish Local Authorities\"\u003eCOSLA\u003c/abbr\u003e) continue to work in partnership to produce the updated route map and it will be published in due course. The route map will set out the interventions to support the scale of behavioural change required and a timeline for implementing demand management.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAdditionally, Scotland has one of the most comprehensive public charging networks in the UK, with over 600 public charge points, funded through public and increasingly private sector investment. Scotland has the UK’s second highest number of electric vehicle public charge points, second only to London, and has committed to enabling the delivery of approximately 24,000 additional public \u003cabbr title=\"Electric Vehicle\"\u003eEV\u003c/abbr\u003e charge points by 2030.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThrough the Older and Disabled and Young Persons Concessionary travel schemes over £370m is spent each year to provide free bus travel for over 2 million people in Scotland, including all children and young people under 22, eligible disabled people and everyone aged 60 and over.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSince 2020 we have invested over £150 million to put more than 800 zero emission buses and coaches on the road and install supporting charging infrastructure.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOur most recent £41.7 million investment in zero emission buses has leveraged 3.2 times the amount of private sector funding, moving the transition to a sustainable financial model that ends the need for continued public subsidy.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"welsh-government-3\"\u003e2.11.3.4 Welsh Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Welsh Government has committed to using the sustainable transport hierarchy when deciding on new transport infrastructure. This gives priority to walking and cycling, public transport and ultra-low emissions vehicles over other private motor vehicles.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eTransport strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:152\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:152\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 152]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2021)\u003c/strong\u003e: identifies 3 priorities for the transport system\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eBring services to people in order to reduce the need to travel\u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eAllow people and goods to move easily from door to door by accessible, sustainable and efficient transport services and infrastructure\u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003eEncourage people to make the change to more sustainable transport\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eNational Transport Delivery Plan\u003csup id=\"fnref:153\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:153\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 153]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2022-27)\u003c/strong\u003e: sets out how the Welsh Government will deliver against these priorities, by sector and by travel mode.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eElectric Vehicle Charging Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:154\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:154\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 154]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2021)\u003c/strong\u003e: set out its vision that by 2025, all users of electric cars and vans will be confident that they can access electric vehicle charging infrastructure when and where they need it. Second generation biodiesel has also been subsidised within the bus and government fleet. The longer-term focus is on support for active travel and increased bus ridership.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"guernsey-3\"\u003e2.11.3.6 Guernsey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eGuernsey’s Integrated Transport Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:156\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:156\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 156]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, approved in 2014, sets out the strategic approach to managing the transport system on the island. Principally the Strategy takes a hierarchical approach to transport, prioritising active travel over vehicular travel, and public transport over private vehicles, which will help to reduce vehicle emissions over time.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"isle-of-man-3\"\u003e2.11.3.7 Isle of Man\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2019, the Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets (\u003cabbr title=\"Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets\"\u003eIMPACT\u003c/abbr\u003e) Report\u003csup id=\"fnref:157\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:157\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 157]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e was produced. Appendices 23-27 and 33 relate to transport\u003csup id=\"fnref:158\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:158\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 158]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. This was done after an in-depth study of the current transport network and its problems with a view to identifying solutions that encourage behavioural change and effect a modal shift towards walking, cycling and public transport.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eGibraltar has committed to ending the sale of internal combustion engine vehicles in line with EU targets. It also continues to promote active travel through the publication and implementation of its Active Travel Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:163\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:163\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 163]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e which seeks to make cycling and walking the natural choices for short journeys.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"industrial-processes-and-product-use-ippu-brbr\"\u003e2.11.4 Industrial Processes and Product Use (\u003cabbr title=\"Industrial Processes and Product Use\"\u003eIPPU\u003c/abbr\u003e) \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"england-2\"\u003e2.11.4.1 England\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn England, the \u003cabbr title=\"Industrial Processes and Product Use\"\u003eIPPU\u003c/abbr\u003e sector is being tackled through the following strategies:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eIndustrial Decarbonisation Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:164\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:164\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 164]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2021)\u003c/strong\u003e: Sets out a plan for decarbonising industry in line with net zero goals. The policy measures outlined in the \u003cabbr title=\"Industrial Decarbonisation Strategy\"\u003eIDS\u003c/abbr\u003e were: having at least 2 Carbon Capture Usage and Storage (\u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage\"\u003eCCUS\u003c/abbr\u003e) clusters in place by mid-2020s, which will increase to 4 by 2030, with the world’s first net zero cluster in place by 2040; creating a market for low carbon industrial products through measures designed to increase demand; leveraging Resource and Energy Efficiency (\u003cabbr title=\"Resource and Energy Efficiency\"\u003eREEE\u003c/abbr\u003e) measures to reduce emissions by 11 \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee per year by 2035 (including 3 \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee from Iron and Steel), and updating the UK’s Emission Trading Scheme cap in place by January 2024 to send a strong market sign to the private sector to incentivise industry to take action to decarbonise.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eNet Zero Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:165\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:165\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 165]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2021)\u003c/strong\u003e: The industry chapter of the Net Zero Strategy sets out an indicative Carbon Budget 6 pathway for industry. This pathway and updates in the Net Zero Growth Plan (\u003cabbr title=\"Net Zero Growth Plan\"\u003eNZGP\u003c/abbr\u003e) were consistent with the expectations set out in the Industrial Decarbonisation Strategy (\u003cabbr title=\"Industrial Decarbonisation Strategy\"\u003eIDS\u003c/abbr\u003e), but went further in specific areas, including increased fuel switching and Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage (\u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage\"\u003eCCUS\u003c/abbr\u003e) ambitions, and additional contributions from Resource Efficiency and Energy Efficiency (\u003cabbr title=\"Resource and Energy Efficiency\"\u003eREEE\u003c/abbr\u003e) measures.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"northern-ireland-executive-4\"\u003e2.11.4.2 Northern Ireland Executive\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eCompared to the 1990 base year, industry emissions have decreased by 3.2 \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee (61.1% reduction) and now represent 9.7% of greenhouse gas emissions in Northern Ireland. This demonstrates the significant progress made by industry so far, to embrace innovative technologies and develop more efficient processes.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eReducing industrial emissions further is central to Scotland’s net zero commitment and our economic ambitions as outlined in our Green Industrial Strategy. Scottish Government works collaboratively with the UK Government and other devolved administrations to accelerate industrial decarbonisation across our devolved and reserved competencies, including within a joint authority for the UK Emissions Trading Scheme.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEffective collaboration with the UK Government is vital on issues requiring national reform and large-scale investment including \u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage\"\u003eCCUS\u003c/abbr\u003e, electricity pricing, grid infrastructure upgrades and hydrogen business model support.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOperating since 2020, the Scottish Industrial Energy Transformation Fund (\u003cabbr title=\"Scottish Industrial Energy Transformation Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e is vital for to support the decarbonisation of industry; the Scottish Government has announced funding to accelerate a project to
