Very little heavy industry occurs on the Isle of Man. The Department for Enterprise offers a range of schemes, including the Business Energy Saving Scheme\u003csup id=\"fnref:169\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:169\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 169]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e which supports projects to improve business energy efficiency including refrigeration and air-conditioning units. The Isle of Man ratified the Montreal Protocol and made legislation\u003csup id=\"fnref:170\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:170\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 170]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e relating to the use and transfer of Ozone-Depleting Substances (\u003cabbr title=\"Ozone-Depleting Substances\"\u003eODS\u003c/abbr\u003e) and \u003cabbr title=\"Fluorinated gases\"\u003eF-gases\u003c/abbr\u003e in 2020.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"gibraltar-4\"\u003e2.11.4.8 Gibraltar\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eGibraltar does not have any heavy industry therefore emissions in this sector primarily arise from the use of refrigeration gases. In this respect, efforts are focused on improving building design to limit the need for air conditioning systems.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"agriculture-brbr-1\"\u003e2.11.5 Agriculture \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"england-3\"\u003e2.11.5.1 England\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK set out measures to support the decarbonisation of the agricultural sector. The Plan set out emissions reductions from agriculture in England through sustainable land management practices, the uptake of innovative practices and technologies, and actions to improve the productivity and profitability of the sector. Specifically, the measures set out the potential to improve farm profitability, through increases in productivity and through opportunities for diversification on low grade land. Other measures include:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eEnvironmental Land Management (\u003cabbr title=\"Environmental Land Management\"\u003eELM\u003c/abbr\u003e) schemes\u003csup id=\"fnref:171\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:171\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 171]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2022)\u003c/strong\u003e: provide a powerful vehicle for achieving net zero, and wider environmental goals, while supporting our rural economy. The scheme is split into 3 parts:\n    \u003cul\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eSustainable Farming Incentive\u003c/strong\u003e - this pays farmers and land managers for actions that protect and enhance our natural environment, support the sustainable production of food, and boost farm productivity and resilience.\u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eCountryside Stewardship\u003c/strong\u003e - this is a targeted, place-based approach that encourages sustainable farming, promotes resilience against climate change, and enhances the beauty and diversity of the countryside.\u003c/li\u003e\n      \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eLandscape Recovery\u003c/strong\u003e - this is for landowners and managers who want to take a large-scale, long-term approach to producing environmental and climate goods on their land. It will facilitate and fund ambitious projects through bespoke, 20+ year agreements.\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003c/ul\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eThe UK’s Agriculture Act\u003csup id=\"fnref:172\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:172\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 172]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2020)\u003c/strong\u003e: obligates the UK Government to produce a report on food security in the UK at least every 3 years. The UK published its first United Kingdom Food Security Report 2021\u003csup id=\"fnref:173\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:173\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 173]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e under the Agriculture Act in December 2021.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"northern-ireland-executive-5\"\u003e2.11.5.2 Northern Ireland Executive\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe latest Northern Ireland Greenhouse Gas Inventory (1990-2022) reported that the agriculture sector was the largest greenhouse gas emitting sector in Northern Ireland representing 29.1% of all emissions. To drive forward action, the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (\u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e) published the Future Agricultural Policy Decisions for Northern Ireland in March 2022\u003csup id=\"fnref:174\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:174\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 174]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. Decisions that are central to this future policy include:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eA Farm Sustainability Payment which recognises the need for continuation of an income support ‘safety net’\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eA Beef Sustainability Package comprising 2 elements; Beef Carbon Reduction Scheme and Suckler Cow Scheme\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eA Farming with Nature Package to assist farm businesses and land managers across all land types to make substantial contributions to environmental improvements and sustainability\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eFarming for Carbon measures which encourage low carbon emission farming practices\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eFurthermore, the Soil Nutrient Health Scheme\u003csup id=\"fnref:175\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:175\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 175]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e which first opened in May 2022, is a comprehensive regional soil sampling and analysis programme being funded by the department that will allow farmers to optimise crop nutrient applications, assess on-farm carbon stocks and build farm resilience through its objective to test all, or the vast majority of, the 650,000 fields used for farming in Northern Ireland to help inform their management.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"scottish-government-5\"\u003e2.11.5.3 Scottish Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Scottish Government is transforming the way we support farming and food production in Scotland to deliver our Vision for Agriculture and become a global leader in sustainable and regenerative agriculture. We want to ensure that farming across Scotland continues sustainably into the future, producing high-quality food for the nation, helping to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and delivering increased biodiversity and wider environmental benefits.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2021-22, the Scottish Government committed to bringing forward the Agriculture and Rural Communities (Scotland) Bill, which has since become an Act, to deliver that vision.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe National Test Programme was announced in October 2021 to provide funding for farmers and crofters to prepare their farms to meet the conditions of future agriculture policy and support.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulations came into force from 1 January 2022 to consolidate the Silage Surry and Agricultural Fuel Oil (Scotland) Regulations 2003 into The Water Environment (Controlled Activities) (Scotland) Regulations 2011. These included improved controls on the storage of slurry and digestate to reduce leakage, and a move to precision spreading methods to maximise the nutrient benefit and reduce emissions. This provides benefits to water quality, air quality, and climate change mitigation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"welsh-government-5\"\u003e2.11.5.4 Welsh Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eWelsh emissions for the agriculture sector decreased to 5.6 (\u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee) in 2022, this is a -3.8% change since 2021 and -7.7% from the base year (1990).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Agriculture (Wales) Act 2023 establishes Sustainable Land Management as the framework for future agriculture support.\u003csup id=\"fnref:176\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:176\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 176]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e The Welsh Government will introduce a new Sustainable Farming Scheme (\u003cabbr title=\"Sustainable Farming Scheme\"\u003eSFS\u003c/abbr\u003e) in 2026.\u003csup id=\"fnref:177\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:177\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 177]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e It will provide support for farmers to respond to the climate and nature emergencies, and to produce food in a sustainable way.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn preparation for the \u003cabbr title=\"Sustainable Farming Scheme\"\u003eSFS\u003c/abbr\u003e in 2026, the Welsh Government has introduced the Habitat Wales Scheme to increase the area of habitat land under management, along with support for Organic and Common land farmers and an extension of Farming Connect support. In addition, a new Integrated Natural Resources Scheme was launched to deliver nature-based solutions across landscapes, catchments and pan Wales. During this preparatory phase, the Welsh Government continues to support farmers and growers through a range of capital investment schemes that tackle climate change, lead to improvements in soil, air and water quality and reduce the decline in our native biodiversity.\u003csup id=\"fnref:178\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:178\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 178]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"jersey-5\"\u003e2.11.5.5 Jersey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Economic Framework for the Rural Environment\u003csup id=\"fnref:179\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:179\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 179]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e was published in 2022 and set outs emissions reduction strategies for the industry. As part of this, the revised Rural Support Scheme (\u003cabbr title=\"Rural Support Scheme\"\u003eRSS\u003c/abbr\u003e) was launched in January 2023. This provides credits to industry per Integrated Farm Management Plan. Uptake of this component of the \u003cabbr title=\"Rural Support Scheme\"\u003eRSS\u003c/abbr\u003e has been ahead of forecast with 80 local businesses now signed up to the scheme.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDuring the next 12 months, Jersey will continue to investigate the feasibility of farm-scale Anaerobic Digestion plants. The installation of this technology would reduce emissions from slurry and feed energy into the grid to accommodate peak demand.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"guernsey-5\"\u003e2.11.5.6 Guernsey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe States of Guernsey are currently reviewing their policy approach to dairy farming which is the predominant agricultural sector on the island. Northern Ireland Greenhouse Gas Inventory (1990-2022) reported that the sector represents 3.6% of all greenhouse gas emissions in Northern Ireland with waste-water handling making up 0.6% of the total emissions. From 1990 to 2022 the emissions in the sector have reduced by 61.9%. The reduction in emissions from the waste sector (1.2 \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee) is primarily due to the continued process of methane capture and oxidation systems within landfill sites. Plans are being progressed for targeted policy and legislative interventions to help tackle the remaining emissions from the sector. \u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e is exploring the feasibility of diverting biodegradable wastes from landfill and is consulting on changes to recycling and waste management to improve the quality and quantity of what is collected and to bring business into scope of mandatory recycling.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eProgress in this sector has been delivered though a number of plans and strategies over the past decade. The Northern Ireland Waste Management Strategy ‘Delivering Resource Efficiency’\u003csup id=\"fnref:206\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:206\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 206]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e was published in 2013 and set the policy framework for the management of waste in Northern Ireland to 2020. Under this Strategy Northern Ireland increased its recycling rate to over 50%. To build upon this progress a new Waste Management Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:207\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:207\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 207]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e is currently being developed by the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (\u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e) which will seek to deliver upon that at least 70% of waste being recycled target set in the Climate Change Act (Northern Ireland) 2022 and the various recycling and landfill targets set out in the Waste and Contaminated Land (Northern Ireland) Order 1997.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNorthern Ireland ‘Waste Prevention Programme -Stopping Waste in its tracks’ \u003csup id=\"fnref:208\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:208\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 208]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e which was published in 2020 set out a range of policies and actions focused on waste prevention in line with the waste hierarchy with a focus on reducing waste and supporting the principles of a circular economy. One key outcome is the continuing benefit of the carrier bag levy\u003csup id=\"fnref:209\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:209\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 209]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e which was introduced in 2013, with the proceeds generated being used, in the delivery of local projects which both enhance and improve the environment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"scottish-government-7\"\u003e2.11.7.3 Scottish Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eScotland has made strong progress in reducing greenhouse gas emissions from the waste management sector. In 2022, sector emissions stood at 1.6 \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee, 75% lower than 1990 levels. This has been driven by a reduction in the total amount of waste going to landfill in Scotland, which has dropped by nearly half over the past decade, while over 62% of waste was recycled in 2022. In the same year Scotland met its 2025 target to reduce all waste by 15% (against 2011 levels) for the second year in a row.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"welsh-government-7\"\u003e2.11.7.4 Welsh Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe latest Wales Greenhouse Gas Inventory (1990-2022) reported that the sector represents 2.8% of all greenhouse gas emissions. From 1990 to 2022 the emissions in the sector have reduced by 72%. The reduction in emissions from the waste sector is primarily due to the significant reduction in the landfilling of biodegradable waste as well as the installation of methane capture on landfill sites. There has been a significant decrease in the proportion of Local Authority collected municipal waste disposed of via landfill, falling from 42.0% in 2012-13 to 0.9% in 2023-24.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eBeyond Recycling, the Welsh Government’s strategy for making the circular economy a reality, contains 6 core themes for keeping resources in use for as long as possible and avoiding waste:\u003csup id=\"fnref:210\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:210\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 210]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eDriving innovation in materials use\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eUpscaling prevention and re-use\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eBuilding on Wales’s recycling record\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eInvesting in infrastructure\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eEnabling community and business action\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eAligning government levers\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"jersey-7\"\u003e2.11.7.5 Jersey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn Jersey, the Solid Waste Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:211\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:211\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 211]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e commits to prioritising reuse and recycling as per the waste hierarchy. Residual municipal waste is sent to an Energy Recovery Facility which generates part of our electricity. In 2022, this contributed 8% of our greenhouse gas emissions. A recent engagement campaign ‘It’s not a load of Rubbish\u003csup id=\"fnref:212\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:212\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 212]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e’, communicated the waste hierarchy of reduce, reuse recycle.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSince July 2022, the Single Use Plastics Law\u003csup id=\"fnref:213\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:213\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 213]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e came into force. This means Islanders no longer receive single use carrier bags with their purchases and are charged at least 70 pence per reusable bag.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Construction industry generates a large proportion of waste in Jersey. Working collaboratively with the industry, we have been developing a plan to reduce inert construction waste on-island.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"guernsey-7\"\u003e2.11.7.6 Guernsey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eGuernsey’s Waste Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:214\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:214\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 214]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e was approved in 2012 and is focused principally on waste reduction, with reuse and recycling prioritised over disposal. Waste has been diverted from landfill to processing as Refuse Derived Fuel – reducing emissions and increasing energy recovery.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eGuernsey’s household waste Pay-As-You-Throw scheme encourages waste reduction, and leads to increased reuse/recycling, and separation of organic waste – all of which reduce emissions in terms of processing waste/recycling. Guernsey’s Waste Management Plan\u003csup id=\"fnref:215\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:215\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 215]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, approved in 2018, outlines the implementation plan for the Waste Strategy and also encourages home composting of organic food waste and garden waste, which aims to reduce emissions from transporting organic waste to the green waste site, and from associated processing. Zero organic waste is sent to landfill, collected household and commercial food waste is processed off-island to an Anaerobic Digestion plant for energy recovery and PAS110 compliant digestate. This reduces emissions that would otherwise be created through landfill.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"isle-of-man-7\"\u003e2.11.7.7 Isle of Man\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2019, the Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets (\u003cabbr title=\"Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets\"\u003eIMPACT\u003c/abbr\u003e) Report\u003csup id=\"fnref:216\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:216\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 216]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e was produced. Appendices 13A, B and C relate to energy from waste. In 2004, the Island’s Energy from Waste Plant facility was completed which now processes all domestic and commercial residual waste, generating 10% of the Island’s electricity.\u003csup id=\"fnref:217\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:217\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 217]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e This diverts waste from landfill and has led to a significant reduction in emissions in this sector. The Phase 1 Action Plan Progress Report\u003csup id=\"fnref:218\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:218\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 218]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e details progress made against the Council of Ministers’ Climate Action Plan Phase 1\u003csup id=\"fnref:219\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:219\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 219]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e over the period 1 April 2021-31 March 2022, including actions relating to waste. Section 6 of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027\u003csup id=\"fnref:220\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:220\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 220]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e sets out the Isle of Man’s current, high-level policies relating to reducing emissions from waste, including a commitment to produce Waste Management and Circular Economy Strategies to deliver 15% sectoral emissions reduction by 2027.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"gibraltar-7\"\u003e2.11.7.8 Gibraltar\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eGibraltar’s overall objective continues to be the reduction of waste wherever possible, followed by reuse and recycling, as per the principles of the waste hierarchy and the circular economy.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eGibraltar’s overall objective continues to be the reduction of waste wherever possible, followed by reuse and recycling, as per the principles of the waste hierarchy and the circular economy. The current kerbside recycling programme was expanded in 2012 to include paper and plastic recycling as well as cooking oil and Waste from Electrical and Electronic Equipment (\u003cabbr title=\"Waste from Electrical and Electronic Equipment\"\u003eWEEE\u003c/abbr\u003e). All of Gibraltar’s waste is exported to Spain for recovery or final disposal. Current plans are focusing on the development of a Waste Management Facility in Gibraltar to maximise recovery of recyclable material prior to export. A ban on single use plastic bags\u003csup id=\"fnref:221\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:221\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 221]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e was introduced in 2019 along with a more comprehensive ban on single use plastic items.\u003csup id=\"fnref:222\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:222\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 222]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"carbon-capture-and-storage-and-greenhouse-gas-removals-brbr\"\u003e2.11.8 Carbon Capture and Storage and Greenhouse Gas Removals \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eEngland has put in place the following strategies in regards to carbon capture and storage:\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"carbon-capture-utilisation-and-storage\"\u003e2.11.8.1 Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eCarbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage (\u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage\"\u003eCCUS\u003c/abbr\u003e) is essential for industry to decarbonise. In the future net zero world, we will still need materials such as cement, steel, and chemicals. For many of these sectors, \u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage\"\u003eCCUS\u003c/abbr\u003e is currently the only viable route to decarbonise at the scale required for us to meet our targets.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eIn November 2021, the government announced the selection of the HyNet and East Coast Cluster as the first 2 industrial \u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage\"\u003eCCUS\u003c/abbr\u003e clusters to be deployed in the UK.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eIn August 2022, the government announced a shortlist of 20 projects representing a range of innovative \u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage\"\u003eCCUS\u003c/abbr\u003e technologies to be progressed to the due diligence stage for inclusion in those clusters. \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy\"\u003eBEIS\u003c/abbr\u003e (now \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e) then launched Phase-2 of the Cluster Sequencing Process to determine the projects that would make up those clusters and enter negotiations.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"greenhouse-gas-removals\"\u003e2.11.8.2 Greenhouse Gas Removals\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Net Zero Strategy (2021) set out several commitments towards the ambition of deploying at least 5 \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e/yr of engineered removals by 2030, potentially rising to 23 \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e/yr by 2035 and 75-81 \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e/yr by 2050. As outlined in the Net Zero Growth Plan and other publications, the government has taken steps to deliver on this.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n This programme was announced in 2020 and is due to complete in 2025.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"marine-and-oceans-brbr\"\u003e2.11.9 Marine and oceans \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"england-6\"\u003e2.11.9.1 England\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eEngland has several legislation and policies in place to manage and protect the marine environment:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eUK Marine and Coastal Access Act\u003csup id=\"fnref:223\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:223\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 223]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2009)\u003c/strong\u003e: makes provisions for the management of the marine environment, including providing for the designation of conservation zones.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eFisheries Act\u003csup id=\"fnref:224\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:224\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 224]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2020)\u003c/strong\u003e: sets 8 objectives, including a climate change objective, that provide the basis against which the UK Administrations will manage their fisheries.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eMarine Policy Statement\u003csup id=\"fnref:225\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:225\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 225]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2011)\u003c/strong\u003e: is the UK framework used to prepare marine plans and provides the basis for making decisions that affect the marine environment. The MPS’s high-level objectives are to promote sustainable economic development, enable the UK’s move towards a low-carbon economy, ensure a sustainable marine environment and to contribute to the societal benefits of the marine area.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eUK Marine Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:226\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:226\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 226]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2019)\u003c/strong\u003e: sets out a vision for UK waters to achieve clean, safe, healthy, biologically diverse and productive seas, which are used sustainably. The Strategy provides a legal framework, agreed with the devolved governments, for assessing and monitoring the status of UK seas and to put in place the measures needed to achieve Good Environmental Status (\u003cabbr title=\"Good Environmental Status\"\u003eGES\u003c/abbr\u003e).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"northern-ireland-executive-8\"\u003e2.11.9.2 Northern Ireland Executive\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (\u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e) as the Marine Plan Authority (\u003cabbr title=\"Marine Protected Area, Scotland\"\u003eMPA\u003c/abbr\u003e) has a duty under the Marine and Coastal Access Act 2009 and the Marine Act Northern Ireland 2013, to prepare marine plans to cover the Northern Ireland inshore and offshore regions, which facilitate the sustainable development of Northern Ireland’s marine area. The consultation on the draft Marine Plan\u003csup id=\"fnref:227\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:227\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 227]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e for Northern Ireland was launched April 2018. It set out the vision for a healthy marine area which is managed sustainably for the economic, environmental and social prosperity of present and future generations. The draft Marine Plan includes policies on climate change mitigation and will provide the framework for decision making for future use of the marine area, including for offshore renewable energy. With the public consultation responses published in April 2021, \u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e is now progressing towards adoption and publication of a Marine Plan for Northern Ireland.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2021, \u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e commenced the development of a blue carbon action plan that sets out how natural carbon stores in marine and coastal areas will be protected and restored.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"scottish-government-8\"\u003e2.11.9.3 Scottish Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Scottish Government has set out a new Blue Economy vision for the sustainable management of Scotland’s seas, establishing long term outcomes to 2045 and including a dedicated climate outcome to support ecosystem health, improved livelihoods, economic prosperity, social inclusion and wellbeing. New actions to increase protection of the marine environment include; introducing fisheries management measures across the offshore Marine Protected Area (\u003cabbr title=\"Marine Protected Area, Scotland\"\u003eMPA\u003c/abbr\u003e) network by 2025, and to consult on the inshore \u003cabbr title=\"Marine Protected Area, Scotland\"\u003eMPA\u003c/abbr\u003e network during the current programme for government. and introduction of a Scottish Wild Salmon Strategy. New evidence is also being delivered through the Scottish Blue Carbon Forum, building upon actions set out in the second Scottish Climate Change Adaptation Programme\u003csup id=\"fnref:228\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:228\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 228]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e to address Scotland’s marine climate risks.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"welsh-government-8\"\u003e2.11.9.4 Welsh Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Welsh National Marine Plan\u003csup id=\"fnref:229\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:229\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 229]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e sets out the Welsh Government’s long-term vision for Welsh seas that are clean, healthy, safe, productive and biologically diverse:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThrough an ecosystem approach, natural resources are sustainably managed and our seas are healthy and resilient, supporting a sustainable and thriving economy\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThrough access to, understanding of and enjoyment of the marine environment and maritime cultural heritage, health and well-being are improving\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThrough Blue Growth more jobs and wealth are being created and are helping coastal communities become more resilient, prosperous and equitable with a vibrant culture\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThrough the responsible deployment of low carbon technologies, the Welsh marine area is making a strong contribution to energy security and climate change emissions targets\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eWelsh Government is taking a spatial approach to implementing the Marine Plan, developing planning guidance and tools to provide greater spatial direction and to balance supporting renewable energy with protecting the marine environment. Sector Locational Guidance for wave and tidal stream energy\u003csup id=\"fnref:230\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:230\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 230]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e were published in 2022 to help understand opportunities for future sector development. In 2024, Welsh Government consulted on potential Strategic Resource Areas\u003csup id=\"fnref:231\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:231\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 231]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e to identify and safeguard key areas of resource for tidal stream energy. It is also working with stakeholders to develop planning guidance on opportunities for ecosystem enhancement and restoration.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"jersey-8\"\u003e2.11.9.5 Jersey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Carbon Neutral Roadmap sets an ambition to promote Jersey as a centre of excellence for blue carbon sequestration. In 2022, research\u003csup id=\"fnref:232\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:232\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 232]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e into Jersey’s resources was published that found that Jersey’s seabed sequesters over 10,000 tonnes of carbon annually, the equivalent combined weight of the \u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e emissions produced by the Island’s agriculture and waste management sectors. Further scientific studies are underway to better understand, protect and enhance blue carbon sequestration.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Jersey Marine Spatial Plan\u003csup id=\"fnref:233\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:233\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 233]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e has been approved. This sets out how Jersey’s territorial waters should be utilised and protected to ensure the correct balance of competing uses.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"guernsey-8\"\u003e2.11.9.6 Guernsey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eGuernsey is in the early stages of developing a marine spatial plan, with an aim for delivery by the end of 2025. It is intended that the plan will enable renewable energy developments and potential for nature, as well as managing other uses of the marine environment. As part of this work, a Blue Carbon report will be produced in the first half of 2025 which will establish the capacity of carbon storage and sequestration in Guernsey’s waters. This will then be used to advise on the climate mitigation measures that can be undertaken within Guernsey’s marine environment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Strategy for Nature\u003csup id=\"fnref:234\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:234\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 234]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, the islands national biodiversity strategy, sets out a framework to enable the long-term management of nature in Guernsey. The Strategy recognises the important role nature and nature-based solutions plays in mitigating the impacts of climate change and seeks to protect and restore habitats which play important roles in carbon sequestration and storage. It also seeks to maximise biodiversity and ensure its resilience to a changing climate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"isle-of-man-8\"\u003e2.11.9.7 Isle of Man\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2019, the Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets (\u003cabbr title=\"Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets\"\u003eIMPACT\u003c/abbr\u003e) Report\u003csup id=\"fnref:235\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:235\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 235]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e was produced. Appendix 10C relates to blue carbon. The Phase 1 Action Plan Progress Report\u003csup id=\"fnref:236\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:236\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 236]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e details progress made against the Council of Ministers’ Climate Action Plan Phase 1\u003csup id=\"fnref:237\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:237\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 237]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e over the period 1 April 2021-31 March 2022, including actions relating to blue carbon. As of 2022 10.8% of the Isle of Man’s entire territorial sea and 51.8% of the inshore (0-3 nautical mile area) were protected.\u003csup id=\"fnref:238\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:238\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 238]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e Section 4 of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027\u003csup id=\"fnref:239\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:239\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 239]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e sets out the Isle of Man’s current, high level climate policies relating to the marine environment and fisheries sector, including a commitment to work with the fishing industry to continue to reduce the carbon footprint of trawling and dredging, increase the efficiency of fishing effort and cut fuel costs. The Manx Blue Carbon Project\u003csup id=\"fnref:240\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:240\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 240]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e began in 2022, working with Bangor and Swansea Universities, as well as with the UK National Oceanography Centre to research and map blue carbon stores in the Isle of Man territorial sea. The project aims to develop a comprehensive blue carbon management plan to maximise carbon sequestration and maintain and restore related biodiversity and wider ecosystem services.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"gibraltar-8\"\u003e2.11.9.8 Gibraltar\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eUnder the Marine Strategy Framework Directive, Gibraltar updated the environmental assessment showing Good Environmental Status for British Gibraltar Territorial Waters (\u003cabbr title=\"British Gibraltar Territorial Waters\"\u003eBGTW\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:241\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:241\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 241]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. In 2021 Gibraltar published an updated monitoring programme for \u003cabbr title=\"British Gibraltar Territorial Waters\"\u003eBGTW\u003c/abbr\u003e. This programme is being implemented in collaboration with the University of Gibraltar. Gibraltar has legislated to increase the number of Marine Protected Areas and no-take zones, safeguarding the biodiversity and health of its waters. Gibraltar has also embarked on a project to increase biodiversity within the intertidal zone through the installation of vertipools on existing grey infrastructure.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"biodiversity-and-adaptation-brbr\"\u003e2.11.10 Biodiversity and Adaptation \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"england-7\"\u003e2.11.10.1 England\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eEngland has delivered the following strategies to support biodiversity and tackle adaptation:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eStrategic Framework\u003csup id=\"fnref:242\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:242\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 242]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2023)\u003c/strong\u003e: set the direction for the UK’s integrated approach to international action on nature and climate through to 2030. Its 3 overarching priorities covered: keep 1.5C alive by halving global emissions; build resilience to current and future climate impacts and; halt and reverse biodiversity loss. The framework identifies 6 global challenges to the 2030 vision and the levers available to the UK to meet those challenges. It explains the UK’s role and approach to international collaboration, drawing on our expertise, skills and leadership.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eNational Adaptation Plan (\u003cabbr title=\"National Adaptation Programme\"\u003eNAP\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:243\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:243\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 243]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2023)\u003c/strong\u003e: sets out plans to adapt to and mitigate the risks of a warming climate on the marine environment, including to protect, restore and create blue carbon habitats and manage the risks and\nopportunities to marine species, habitats, and fisheries.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eEnvironmental Improvement Plan\u003csup id=\"fnref:244\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:244\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 244]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2023)\u003c/strong\u003e: sets out the actions that must be taken to help restore nature, tackle environmental pollution, and increase prosperity. It states that \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e will lead a practical initiative to restore estuarine and coastal habitats (ReMeMaRe (Restoring Meadow, Marsh and Reef)), which will restore 15% of priority habitats along the English coast by 2043. Restored coastal wetlands such as saltmarsh and seagrass can sequester and store carbon.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"northern-ireland-executive-9\"\u003e2.11.10.2 Northern Ireland Executive\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (\u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e) has prepared the draft Northern Ireland Environmental Improvement Plan\u003csup id=\"fnref:245\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:245\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 245]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (\u003cabbr title=\"Environmental Improvement Plan\"\u003eEIP\u003c/abbr\u003e). The \u003cabbr title=\"Environmental Improvement Plan\"\u003eEIP\u003c/abbr\u003e sets out Northern Ireland’s environmental priorities for the decades ahead and will be the basis for a coherent and effective set of interventions that can deliver real improvements in the quality of the environment in Northern Ireland. The \u003cabbr title=\"Environmental Improvement Plan\"\u003eEIP\u003c/abbr\u003e will be published once it receives approval from the Northern Ireland Executive.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe draft \u003cabbr title=\"Environmental Improvement Plan\"\u003eEIP\u003c/abbr\u003e contains a commitment for \u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e to develop and publish a new Biodiversity Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:246\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:246\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 246]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e for Northern Ireland. In line with this commitment, \u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e, through a co-design process, has been leading on the development of a Nature Recovery Plan for Northern Ireland based on the 23 general targets revised and agreed at the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nations\"\u003eUN\u003c/abbr\u003e’s Convention on Biological Diversity (\u003cabbr title=\"UN’s Convention on Biological Diversity\"\u003eCBD\u003c/abbr\u003e) meeting in December 2022 (\u003cabbr title=\"The 15th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC\"\u003eCOP15\u003c/abbr\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThese targets cover the wide range of issues affecting biodiversity and, if adequately addressed, should go a long way to halt the loss of biodiversity or at least ensure many habitats and species are in a better ecological status. Target 3 of these is often viewed as the one that will have the biggest impact, if achieved. This seeks to ensure that by 2030 at least 30% of all terrestrial, inland water, and coastal and marine areas, especially areas of particular importance for biodiversity and ecosystem functions and services, are effectively conserved and managed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Nature Recovery Strategy will augment actions for promoting biodiversity in other major initiatives including the \u003cabbr title=\"Environmental Improvement Plan\"\u003eEIP\u003c/abbr\u003e and the Climate Action Plan. Once published the \u003cabbr title=\"Environmental Improvement Plan\"\u003eEIP\u003c/abbr\u003e and Nature Recovery Strategy will provide Northern Ireland commitments for environmental improvement to be included in the UK National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"scottish-government-9\"\u003e2.11.10.3 Scottish Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Scottish Government has committed to delivering improved and enduring benefits to the natural environment through the Environment Strategy for Scotland\u003csup id=\"fnref:247\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:247\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 247]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. Sitting beneath this, the Scottish Biodiversity Strategy which has now been published\u003csup id=\"fnref:248\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:248\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 248]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e takes into account the new post-2020 global biodiversity framework and targets for the Convention on Biological Diversity’s 2050 vision. The Scottish Biodiversity Programme\u003csup id=\"fnref:249\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:249\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 249]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e has been created to coordinate all activity on biodiversity including the development of a future strategic framework for biodiversity that compromises both terrestrial and marine aspects.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"welsh-government-9\"\u003e2.11.10.4 Welsh Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Nature Recovery Action Plan (2021-2022)\u003csup id=\"fnref:250\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:250\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 250]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e contains 5 themes for action:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eMaintaining and enhancing resilient ecological networks\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eIncreasing knowledge and knowledge transfer\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eRealising new investment and funding\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eUpskilling and capacity for delivery\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eMainstreaming, governance and reporting progress\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eWithin the themes, 5 immediate priorities have been identified for further action:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eAligning the responses to the climate emergency with the biodiversity crisis\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eAddressing the post-EU exit funding gap for agri-environment measures\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eProviding spatial direction for targeting action for biodiversity\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eImproving the condition of the Protected Sites Network\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eExploring new and sustainable funding mechanisms for biodiversity action\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"jersey-9\"\u003e2.11.10.5 Jersey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003ePriority is currently being given to protecting on-Island carbon sinks. This is being prioritised through the Island Plan\u003csup id=\"fnref:251\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:251\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 251]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e and our various natural area protection and enhancement programmes, such as the Jersey National Park, Ramsar sites, Biodiversity action plan, tree strategy and LEAF programme. The Climate Emergency Fund supports projects that directly address the biodiversity crisis, including those with a focus on species and habitat restoration and protection, biosecurity and the marine environment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"guernsey-9\"\u003e2.11.10.6 Guernsey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2020, Guernsey’s government published an updated Biodiversity Strategy, entitled the ‘Strategy for Nature’. The Strategy for Nature sets a framework for Guernsey’s government, the private sector and the community to strengthen Guernsey’s response to the changes facing nature from climate change and other human made pressures. It encompasses mainstreaming biodiversity and horizon scanning for pressures on nature and increasing community awareness of nature including promoting its health and wellbeing benefits. In recognition of risks to biodiversity from climate change, the Strategy for Nature includes an objective to “Reduce pressures on nature and ensure the resilience of our natural capital and assets”. This objective will be achieved by reducing threats and pressures on our natural environment and the introduction of targeted conservation action to support priority species and habitats.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eGuernsey’s government recognises the increased pressure of invasive non-native species (\u003cabbr title=\"Invasive Non-Native Species\"\u003eINNS\u003c/abbr\u003e) in light of changing climate, and also the detrimental impact of \u003cabbr title=\"Invasive Non-Native Species\"\u003eINNS\u003c/abbr\u003e on biodiversity and its resilience to the impacts of climate change. Guernsey’s \u003cabbr title=\"Invasive Non-Native Species\"\u003eINNS\u003c/abbr\u003e Action Plan aims to reduce the introduction and establishment or invasive species through enhanced biosecurity and surveillance measures. The Action Plan also seeks to manage species already present, especially those which will become more invasive with the forecast changes in climate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"isle-of-man-9\"\u003e2.11.10.7 Isle of Man\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eRatification of numerous international conventions relating to biodiversity has been extended to the Isle of Man.\u003csup id=\"fnref:252\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:252\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 252]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e The Biodiversity Strategy 2015 – 2025 is in effect\u003csup id=\"fnref:253\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:253\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 253]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. The Isle of Man became the world’s first entire island nation with Biosphere status in 2016.\u003csup id=\"fnref:254\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:254\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 254]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e In 2019, the Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets (\u003cabbr title=\"Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets\"\u003eIMPACT\u003c/abbr\u003e) Report\u003csup id=\"fnref:255\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:255\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 255]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e was produced. Appendix 10B relates to tree planting and habitat connectivity. The Phase 1 Action Plan Progress Report\u003csup id=\"fnref:256\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:256\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 256]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e details progress made against the Council of Ministers’ Climate Action Plan Phase 1\u003csup id=\"fnref:257\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:257\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 257]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e over the period 1 April 2021-31 March 2022, including actions relating to biodiversity and adaptation. The Climate Change Act 2021\u003csup id=\"fnref:258\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:258\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 258]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e contains amendments to the Town and Country Planning Act 1999, setting out 6 policy areas – including “the maximisation of carbon sequestration, maintenance and restoration of ecosystems, and biodiversity net gain” to be incorporated into national planning policy by 1 January 2025. Adaptation: \u003ca href=\"#section-3-11-2-7\"\u003eSee ‘Chapter 3, section 3.11.2.7’\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"gibraltar-9\"\u003e2.11.10.8 Gibraltar\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eOne of the main climate impacts that will be felt in Gibraltar is increased heat, with a forecast sharp increase in the number of hot days in a given year. Investing in the creation of new green areas within the city centre, such as the conversion of a concrete parking lot into Commonwealth Park\u003csup id=\"fnref:259\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:259\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 259]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e in 2014 is helping to combat the heat island effect whilst simultaneously providing new habitats and potential for increased biodiversity.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eGibraltar will also embark on an ambitious rewilding programme in the next 5 years. Notable species that will form part of the enhanced rewilding programme include, but are not limited to Lesser Kestrel ‘Falco naumanni’ (recently extinct as a nesting bird), Little Owl ‘Athene noctua’ and the Ocellated Lizard (‘Timon Lepidus’). The programme to artificially propagate and re-populate the endemic Gibraltar Campion (‘Silene tomentosa’) will be expanded with a new propagation facility created at Tovey Cottage Field Centre in addition to the Gibraltar Botanic Gardens. Other regionally important species will also be propagated and planted as part of a wider and ambitious habitat restoration programme within and outside the Gibraltar Nature Reserve.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"education-and-skills-brbr\"\u003e2.11.11 Education and skills \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"england-8\"\u003e2.11.11.1 England\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe education sector in the UK will play a critical role in positively responding to climate change and inspiring action on an international stage. The Department for Education is helping to create a sustainable future through education, developing the skills needed for a green economy, and supporting our sectors to reach net zero targets.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eStrategy for Sustainability and Climate Change\u003csup id=\"fnref:260\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:260\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 260]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2022)\u003c/strong\u003e: The department’s strategy for Sustainability and Climate Change was informed by stakeholders and young people and sets out action to 2030 on: 1) climate education; 2) green skills and careers; 3) the education estate and digital infrastructure; 4) operations and supply chains; and 5) international. The Strategy sets out initiatives including extra support for teaching about nature and climate change, a National Education Nature Park, Climate Action Award and support for education leaders to take a whole-setting approach to climate change.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eGreen apprenticeships\u003c/strong\u003e: Apprenticeships in England are a core part of the government’s skills agenda, helping grow the economy by improving the skills pipeline. Apprenticeships give employees high-quality, hands-on training to start and progress in work. There are over 680 occupations with corresponding apprenticeships, from entry-level to expert. The Institute for Apprenticeships and Technical Education (\u003cabbr title=\"Institute for Apprenticeships and Technical Education\"\u003eIfATE\u003c/abbr\u003e) has worked with employers to identify over 200 occupations which directly support the green economy.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eGreen Jobs delivery group\u003c/strong\u003e: The Green Jobs Delivery Group was the central forum for driving forwards action on green jobs and skills across government and industry. Led by ministers and business leaders, it worked to ensure workers were supported with the transition to a green economy. Through a series of deep dives, the Green Jobs Delivery Group was identifying occupations to target key skills programmes towards green sectors and occupations.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eClimate literacy across government\u003c/strong\u003e: More generally, there now exists a training offer available to all civil servants, expanded training for Fast Streamers, and embedded climate and environment objectives within the cross-cutting policy objectives and responsibilities in the Civil Service policy profession standards.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"northern-ireland-executive-10\"\u003e2.11.11.2 Northern Ireland Executive\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Department for the Economy (\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Education, England\"\u003eDfE\u003c/abbr\u003e) published the Northern Ireland Executive’s energy strategy ‘The Path to Net Zero Energy\u003csup id=\"fnref:261\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:261\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 261]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e’ December 2021, which set out the roadmap to 2030 aiming to deliver a 56% reduction in energy-related emissions, while on the pathway to net zero by 2050. To drive the strategy forward \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Education, England\"\u003eDfE\u003c/abbr\u003e will publish annual Energy Strategy Action Plans, the first of which was published January 2022\u003csup id=\"fnref:262\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:262\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 262]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e and set out a range of new initiatives such as a hydrogen centre of excellence and an energy skills audit leading to a Green Skills Action plan.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (\u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e) have been leading on the development of the Northern Ireland Executive’s Green Growth Strategy. The Strategy is the Northern Ireland Executive’s multi-decade strategy, balancing climate, environment and the economy in Northern Ireland. After extensive engagement with organisations and individuals, the draft Green Growth strategy consultation opened in October 2021\u003csup id=\"fnref:263\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:263\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 263]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, with the department hosting online public consultation sessions. Responses to the consultation have been analysed and, alongside the Climate Change Act (Northern Ireland) 2022, will inform the update of the strategy.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSkill Up is a flexible skills programme that offers a range of free training opportunities to support upskilling and reskilling, which was launched in August 2021. Funding was initially announced by \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Education, England\"\u003eDfE\u003c/abbr\u003e and the Northern Ireland Office (\u003cabbr title=\"Northern Ireland Office\"\u003eNIO\u003c/abbr\u003e) for a 3-year period, to deliver up to 10,000 training places per year in accredited qualifications.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"scottish-government-10\"\u003e2.11.11.3 Scottish Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eScotland’s National Strategy for Economic Transformation\u003csup id=\"fnref:264\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:264\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 264]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e sets out the priorities for Scotland’s economy and shows that a skilled population is fundamental to business productivity and economic prosperity. In addition, Scotland’s Purpose and Principles\u003csup id=\"fnref:265\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:265\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 265]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e sets out the framework for decision making for post-school education, skills and research to ensure that the system is fit for the future, delivering the best outcomes for learners, employers and public investment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSignificant work is progressing to reform the Scottish education and skills system so that it is more responsive to our economic, social, and environmental needs and ambitions, and the Scottish Government will continue to invest in that system and the infrastructure that supports it, including for example, schools, colleges, universities, apprenticeships and our Innovation Centres, to enable the transition to net zero.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Scottish Government’s Climate Emergency Skills Action Plan\u003csup id=\"fnref:266\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:266\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 266]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2020-2025) provided an initial framework and springboard for skills planning, development and investment across sectors of the economy known to be crucial to achieving net zero. Scotland continues to build on these strong foundations for example, through the Green Industrial Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:267\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:267\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 267]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e identifies areas of strength and opportunity for Scotland to grow globally competitive industries in the transition to net zero and outlines what government and partners will do to support stakeholders to create an enabling environment for investment and growth.In addition, Scotland’s Curriculum for Excellence incorporates an emphasis on the cross-cutting theme of Learning for Sustainability – a term that brings together sustainable development education, global citizenship and outdoor learning. A refreshed and strengthened Learning for Sustainability Action Plan was published in 2023 setting a vision (Target 2030) that by the end of this decade all 3-18 education settings will be sustainable education settings.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"welsh-government-10\"\u003e2.11.11.4 Welsh Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Curriculum for Wales, which commenced roll-out in 2022, represents the biggest change to what and how learners learn in Wales since devolution. This transformational new approach has been built by teachers and experts to prepare our learners for a changing world. One of its 4 purposes is to develop our young people as ethical, informed citizens, ready to be active citizens of Wales and the world, with building understanding of climate change and sustainability mandatory.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn Wales, 90% of schools across every local authority take part in the Eco-Schools programme.\u003csup id=\"fnref:268\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:268\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 268]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e This equates to more than 400,000 pupils – one of the highest participation rates in the world.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Welsh Government funds 100% of training costs for apprentices of any age with businesses of any size. Recipients follow an approved Welsh Apprenticeship Framework such as Energy, Engineering or Construction and must be working in Wales for 51% or more of their time. There is an employer incentive to recruit disabled apprentices as well as Supported Shared Apprenticeships.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eGreen Personal Learning Accounts provide adults in employment in Wales with a fully funded option to study part-time at an Further Education (\u003cabbr title=\"Further Education\"\u003eFE\u003c/abbr\u003e) college/with a training provider partner to up- and re-skill for the green economy including in energy, construction, engineering and manufacturing. Courses approved under this scheme are determined by an expert panel including employers to ensure a targeted approach to meeting industry demand for skills.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Welsh Government has operated a Flexible Skills Programme (\u003cabbr title=\"Flexible Skills Programme\"\u003eFSP\u003c/abbr\u003e) since 2016. The \u003cabbr title=\"Flexible Skills Programme\"\u003eFSP\u003c/abbr\u003e is a training grant, available to all employers in Wales, that wish to purchase training courses to meet upskilling objectives and potentially create and fill more green jobs. The Welsh Government will contribute 50% towards the training costs. It includes specific programmes to support skills gaps in the Engineering and Manufacturing Sector as well as the development of skills to help address Net Zero challenges such as hydrogen, amongst other areas.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Welsh Government’s Net Zero Skills Action Plan (2021)\u003csup id=\"fnref:269\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:269\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 269]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e prioritises 7 key areas of action for delivering the Welsh Government’s vision for a fairer, greener and stronger Wales:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eGain an understanding of the current skills position for each emission sector\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eBuild a shared understanding of net zero skills across Wales\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eGrow a skilled workforce to meet our net zero commitments\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eStrengthen the skills system\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ePromote opportunities for early years and young people to realise their potential\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eCross-government and partnership approach to meet our skills commitment\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eJust transition\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"jersey-10\"\u003e2.11.11.5 Jersey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eA Future Economy\u003csup id=\"fnref:270\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:270\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 270]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e work programme has set out actions to develop a more resilient supply chain and increase skills on island. This includes the green skills necessary to decarbonise and ensure a just transition.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAt \u003cabbr title=\"The 26th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC\"\u003eCOP26\u003c/abbr\u003e, the government pledged to put children first in our net zero transition. Improving climate education is vital to tackle the climate emergency. A full-time officer has been employed to improve climate education across the curriculum.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"guernsey-10\"\u003e2.11.11.6 Guernsey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eAs part of the Key Stages 1, 2 and 3 of education in Guernsey, raising awareness and learning about climate change, energy efficiency and sustainability are included in the Bailiwick of Guernsey Curriculum, published in 2017, used in Guernsey and Alderney government-maintained schools. This is achieved through subjects such as Geography and Science. Coverage is broad, focusing on, for instance: teaching and understanding how the world’s climate is changing, there being various ways to address climate change, and of the potential impacts of climate change; how sustainability is doing things in a way that ensures resources needed are not damaged or wasted and are used wisely; and about the production of carbon dioxide by human activity, the impact on the climate and greenhouse gases in the atmosphere; as well as renewable and non-renewable energy.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"isle-of-man-10\"\u003e2.11.11.7 Isle of Man\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2019, the Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets (\u003cabbr title=\"Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets\"\u003eIMPACT\u003c/abbr\u003e) Report\u003csup id=\"fnref:271\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:271\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 271]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e was produced. Appendix 9 relates to climate in the Manx curriculum. Legal requirements for new buildings to achieve a minimum SAP rating\u003csup id=\"fnref:272\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:272\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 272]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e commenced in 2020. Between 1 January 2021 and 31 December 2023 the minimum requirement was equivalent to a ‘B’ Energy Performance Certificate (\u003cabbr title=\"Energy Performance Certificate\"\u003eEPC\u003c/abbr\u003e) rating in the UK, rising to the equivalent of an ‘A’ rating in January 2024. The Phase 1 Action Plan Progress Report\u003csup id=\"fnref:273\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:273\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 273]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e details progress made against the Council of Ministers’ Climate Action Plan Phase 1\u003csup id=\"fnref:274\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:274\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 274]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e over the period 1 April 2021-31 March 2022, including actions relating to education and skills. The Isle of Man Retrofit and Low Carbon Skills Analysis\u003csup id=\"fnref:275\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:275\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 275]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e was produced in 2022. Section 2 of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027\u003csup id=\"fnref:276\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:276\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 276]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e includes a commitment to upskill the construction industry in low carbon heating technologies. In schools, training with Eco Schools\u003csup id=\"fnref:277\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:277\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 277]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e has led to 5 schools achieving Green Flag status along with the continued roll-out of Global Teacher Training.\u003csup id=\"fnref:278\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:278\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 278]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"gibraltar-10\"\u003e2.11.11.8 Gibraltar\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eGibraltar has long had an environmental education programme, carried out collaboratively between the Department of Education and the Department of the Environment and Climate Change. This has evolved to meet the changing priorities of the education sector with a greater focus on outdoor and project based learning, with a strong environmental angle. In December 2022 Gibraltar published a Bill to amend its Education and Training Act\u003csup id=\"fnref:279\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:279\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 279]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e to ensure a commitment to making learning about the environment and climate justice is a fundamental principle of education policy. This revision will also bring to bear a number of commitments which will support the prioritisation of climate emergency related workstreams including a bespoke climate change curriculum framework for sustainable schools, developing climate change INSET training for educational staff and revised career advice which includes a focus on green jobs.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"sustainability-and-behaviour-change-brbr\"\u003e2.11.12 Sustainability and Behaviour Change \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"england-9\"\u003e2.11.12.1 England\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK is working to deliver the benefits of the net zero transition to our health, our homes and our overall prosperity. Our priority is making green choices easier, clearer and more affordable, and working with industry to remove barriers. There are numerous individual actions – some one-off and some frequent – that people can take to contribute to net zero. Choices and behaviours that impact on net zero broadly fall into 3 categories: adopting new low carbon technologies; using energy, technologies, or services more efficiently; and everyday business and consumer choices.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn England, there are the following strategies in place to tackle sustainability and behaviour change:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eNational Food Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:280\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:280\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 280]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (2022)\u003c/strong\u003e: The Strategy responded to Henry Dimbleby’s independent review of the food system and set out a set of objectives to deliver “a prosperous agri-food sector”. These led to, for example, the commissioning of a review into labour shortages, establishing the Food Data Transparency Partnership, and consulting on the government Buying Standards for Food and Catering Services.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eHeat and Buildings Strategy (2021)\u003c/strong\u003e: The Strategy set out government’s overall approach to decarbonising heating, through increasing the roll out of clean heat technologies as well as the installation of energy efficiency measures. Heat pumps and heat networks were the major clean heat technologies, whilst also leaving flexibility for potential roll out of hydrogen. The strategy combined regulations to give industry certainty of technology transitions, as well as subsidies to support consumers to upgrade. These measures together built a credible path for the UK to meet its carbon budget sector effort shares for buildings.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"northern-ireland-executive-11\"\u003e2.11.12.2 Northern Ireland Executive\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Department for the Economy (\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Education, England\"\u003eDfE\u003c/abbr\u003e) have worked in collaboration across both the public and private sector, working with a cross-departmental steering group and a Circular Economy Coalition (an advisory panel established in 2021) to drive forward progress on the Circular Economy strategy. The Circularity Gap Report Northern Ireland, commissioned by \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Education, England\"\u003eDfE\u003c/abbr\u003e, was published in June 2022 and provided a snapshot of how circular Northern Ireland currently is. The report\u003csup id=\"fnref:281\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:281\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 281]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e informed much of the evidence base underpinning the development of the draft Circular Economy Strategy for Northern Ireland, which is due to be published in January 2023.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"scottish-government-11\"\u003e2.11.12.3 Scottish Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn May 2022 we launched 2 linked consultations, on a Circular Economy Bill and on a Circular Economy and Waste Route Map. The Bill establishes the legislative framework to support Scotland’s transition to a zero waste and circular economy, significantly increase reuse and recycling rates, and modernise and improve waste and recycling services. It is complemented by the Circular Economy and Waste Route Map, which sets out clear actions we need to take to progress a circular economy in Scotland by 2030. Together, they will help us achieve our sustainable resource and climate goals.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eScotland was also the first nation of the UK to implement a ban on many of the most problematic single-use plastics, with legislation coming into force in June 2022.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"welsh-government-11\"\u003e2.11.12.4 Welsh Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eClimate Action Wales\u003csup id=\"fnref:282\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:282\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 282]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e provides information and advice in relation to the following areas:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eGreen Home Energy Choices: Reducing energy consumption, Home upgrade choices\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eGreen Transport Choices: Driving less; taking up active travel and public transport, Electric vehicle adoption\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eGreen Food Choices: Reducing food waste, Healthier eating and sustainable food choices\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eGreen Consumption Choices: Shopping sustainably, using less, reusing, repairing and recycling\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Welsh Government has updated building regulations to achieve a 37% reduction in carbon emissions for new dwellings.\u003csup id=\"fnref:283\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:283\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 283]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e It intends to make further changes in 2025, raising the bar to require new homes to achieve at least a 75% reduction in emissions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Welsh Housing Quality Standard exists to improve the quality of social homes.\u003csup id=\"fnref:284\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:284\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 284]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e Social landlords are legally obliged to meet the Standard’s requirements, including those relating to energy performance and environmental impact.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"jersey-11\"\u003e2.11.12.5 Jersey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eJersey’s Carbon Neutral Roadmap\u003csup id=\"fnref:285\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:285\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 285]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e makes a commitment to behavioural change campaigns to consider and reduce all emissions associated with Islanders’ lives. Jersey-specific carbon literacy training has been developed. Officers have worked with internal colleagues, external stakeholder through the eco active business network and ministers. As an organisation the government of Jersey has the responsibility to set an example on decarbonisation and has set itself ambitious decarbonisation targets with a focus on the government estate and fleet.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"guernsey-11\"\u003e2.11.12.6 Guernsey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eGuernsey’s governmental strategy for transport has a focus on behavioural change with encouraging active travel as an alternative to vehicles forming a key part of the strategy. The island has a walking and cycling app to help navigate around the islands’ quiet lanes and Guernsey’s government has offered subsidies on electric bikes.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe island’s energy policy outlines the importance of energy efficiency measures in reducing energy related emissions and the climate change policy reaffirmed the hierarchical approaches to waste management, energy use and transport.
