This requires behavioural change to preserve resources and reduce emissions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"isle-of-man-11\"\u003e2.11.12.7 Isle of Man\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Isle of Man became the world’s first entire island nation with Biosphere status in 2016.\u003csup id=\"fnref:286\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:286\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 286]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e The Climate Change Act 2021\u003csup id=\"fnref:287\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:287\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 287]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e includes duties for Manx public bodies, which create a statutory requirement to support sustainable development and the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nations\"\u003eUN\u003c/abbr\u003e Sustainable Development goals. Each of the actions in the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027\u003csup id=\"fnref:288\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:288\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 288]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e is linked to one or more \u003cabbr title=\"United Nations\"\u003eUN\u003c/abbr\u003e Sustainable Development Goals, and the Act requires annual progress reports to include reporting on progress toward those goals.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSection C of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027 sets out how the Isle of Man government intends to ‘lead by example’ in relation to climate action, this includes commitments for climate change training across the public sector and a government-wide policy review to ensure that existing practices do not restrict our ability to meet our climate goals. Section 2 of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027 includes a commitment to a public engagement campaign promoting energy efficiency (completed in 2023\u003csup id=\"fnref:289\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:289\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 289]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"gibraltar-11\"\u003e2.11.12.8 Gibraltar\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eGibraltar has established a field centre in the Gibraltar Nature Reserve\u003csup id=\"fnref:290\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:290\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 290]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e which is serving to foster a better understanding and appreciation of local biodiversity among our young people. Tovey Cottage welcomes over 600 young people each year. Gibraltar has embarked on a process of developing Carbon Literacy training for the public sector, in collaboration with the UK Carbon Literacy Project which will help individuals to understand the carbon cost of their everyday actions and ways in which they can reduce their carbon footprint. This will result in a public sector that is engaged with the climate crisis and empowered to deliver the changes needed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eGibraltar is also committed to organising citizen’s assemblies on climate and nature to help raise further awareness and understanding and drive the behavioural changes needed at a societal level.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"health-and-air-brbr\"\u003e2.11.13 Health and air \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"england-10\"\u003e2.11.13.1 England\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eAir pollution is the biggest environmental threat to human health. Its impacts are disproportionately felt by low-income communities, exacerbating health and social inequalities. Sources that contribute to air pollution are varied; significant sources are transport, industrial processes, agriculture and home heating – specifically household burning of solid fuels. Some actions that reduce carbon also have benefits for air quality, but this is not the case for all measures, for example biomass combustion, which can have a negative impact on air quality. Government has taken action across a range of sectors.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eThe Environment Act (2021)\u003csup id=\"fnref:291\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:291\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 291]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e: required 2 targets for fine particulate matter (\u003cabbr title=\"fine particulate matter\"\u003ePM2.5\u003c/abbr\u003e) to be set in regulation. The regulations\u003csup id=\"fnref:292\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:292\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 292]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e established targets for both a maximum annual mean concentration of 10 μg m-3 by 2040 and a population exposure reduction target of 35% by 2040 compared to 2018. The dual-target approach will improve public health by tackling the highest concentrations while ensuring all areas benefit from continuous improvement. It also introduced changes to the Local Air Quality Management framework\u003csup id=\"fnref:293\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:293\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 293]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e and improvements to the enforcement of smoke control areas\u003csup id=\"fnref:294\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:294\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 294]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e which limit emissions from the burning of solid fuels in homes on appliances such as stoves and fireplaces.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eThe UK plan for tackling roadside nitrogen dioxide (NO2) concentrations (2017)\u003csup id=\"fnref:295\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:295\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 295]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e: legally obliged local authorities to reduce their NO2 exceedances in the shortest possible time. Four cities, Bath, Birmingham, Bradford and Portsmouth implemented Clean Air Zones amongst other measures in accordance with local plans.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eThe Air Quality Information Systems Review (2021)\u003csup id=\"fnref:296\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:296\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 296]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e: established to undertake a comprehensive review of how government communicates air quality information to ensure members of the public, and vulnerable groups in particular, have what they need protect themselves and understand their impact on air quality.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eGovernment’s response to the consultation on reducing ammonia emissions from solid urea fertilisers (2022)\u003csup id=\"fnref:297\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:297\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 297]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e: The response indicated support for an industry-led approach that was subsequently delivered through Red Tractor farm assurance standard\u003csup id=\"fnref:298\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:298\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 298]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e and farm advisors.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK Government, the Scottish Government, the Welsh Government, and the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs in Northern Ireland put in place a new regime for the development of ‘Best Available Techniques’\u003csup id=\"fnref:299\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:299\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 299]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e across the UK. The BAT approach ensures standards are enhanced over time by defining the techniques and technologies already in use which are the best for preventing or minimising emissions and impacts on the environment from industrial installations – this is then reflected in operator’s permits.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"northern-ireland-executive-12\"\u003e2.11.13.2 Northern Ireland Executive\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn November 2020, the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (\u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e) launched a consultation on a Discussion Document on a Clean Air Strategy for Northern Ireland\u003csup id=\"fnref:300\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:300\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 300]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e’. In June 2022, the synopsis\u003csup id=\"fnref:301\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:301\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 301]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e of that consultation was published by \u003cabbr title=\"Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland\"\u003eDAERA\u003c/abbr\u003e. Work is now ongoing to develop Northern Ireland’s first Clean Air Strategy taking into account the consultation responses.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"scottish-government-12\"\u003e2.11.13.3 Scottish Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Scottish Government published its Cleaner Air for Scotland strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:302\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:302\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 302]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e in 2015 setting out a series of actions for improving air quality across a wide range of policy areas. Following an independent review of the strategy in 2019\u003csup id=\"fnref:303\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:303\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 303]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, which made recommendations for additional action on air pollution, a new strategy - Cleaner Air for Scotland 2: Towards a Better Place for Everyone - was published in July 2021\u003csup id=\"fnref:304\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:304\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 304]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. This sets out Scotland’s air quality policy framework for the period 2021 to 2026 with a continued focus on delivery of co-benefits for air pollutant and greenhouse gas reductions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"welsh-government-12\"\u003e2.11.13.4 Welsh Government\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe aim of the Clean Air Plan for Wales: Healthy Air, Healthy Wales (2020) is to improve air quality and reduce the impacts of air pollution on human health, biodiversity, the natural environment and the economy.\u003csup id=\"fnref:305\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:305\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 305]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e The Plan sets out a 10-year pathway to achieving cleaner air is structured around 4 core themes:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003ePeople\u003c/strong\u003e: Protecting the health and well-being of current and future generations\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eEnvironment\u003c/strong\u003e: Taking action to support our natural environment, ecosystems and biodiversity\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eProsperity\u003c/strong\u003e: Working with industry to reduce emissions, supporting a cleaner and more prosperous Wales\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003ePlace\u003c/strong\u003e: Creating sustainable places through better planning, infrastructure and transport\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"jersey-12\"\u003e2.11.13.5 Jersey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eA long-term vision for Jersey was produced in 2017 through the ‘Island Outcome Indicators’\u003csup id=\"fnref:306\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:306\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 306]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. This vision includes clean air within its statement.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eJersey government are currently improving and relocating our air quality reference analysers (NOx, and Particulate Matter) to support our wider air quality monitoring programme and improve our ability to report data to Automatic Urban and Rural Network (\u003cabbr title=\"Automatic Urban and Rural Network\"\u003eAURN\u003c/abbr\u003e) standards. Jersey is developing sensor networks in partnership with external stakeholders with the aim of providing near real-time air quality data to inform the public, influence behaviour and support sustainability workstreams.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"guernsey-12\"\u003e2.11.13.6 Guernsey\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn 2019, the Environmental Pollution (Air Pollution) Ordinance\u003csup id=\"fnref:307\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:307\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 307]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e was enacted in Guernsey. This Ordinance sets local ambient air quality standards and allows greater environmental regulation of point source emitters including, but not limited to, through licensing prescribed operations, placing limits on the sulphur content of fuels and restricting burning in the open air. The limitations on burning in the open air has benefits form a climate perspective.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"isle-of-man-12\"\u003e2.11.13.7 Isle of Man\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eActions to reduce use of fossil fuels, such as the ban on fossil fuel heating systems in new buildings, created by the Climate Change Act 2021\u003csup id=\"fnref:308\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:308\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 308]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e and commencing 1 January 2025, will help to improve air quality. Other health concerns related to climate change are primarily linked with adaptation. Section A of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027\u003csup id=\"fnref:309\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:309\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 309]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e sets out actions relating to adaptation and resilience, including commitment to a Climate Change Risks and Opportunities Report for the Island, which is currently being prepared and will include risks to health.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAir quality monitoring has been increased to include NO2 and SO2 at over 60 sites around the Island, with data published monthly.\u003csup id=\"fnref:310\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:310\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 310]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"gibraltar-12\"\u003e2.11.13.8 Gibraltar\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eGibraltar has a well-established air quality monitoring network in place and results demonstrate a steady improvement in local air quality since the network started monitoring in 2005.\u003csup id=\"fnref:311\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:311\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 311]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe switch from diesel to natural gas for the generation of electricity marked a significant improvement in levels of nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter. Efforts are now focused on reducing emissions from transport and construction.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"information-on-how-actions-policies-and-measures-are-modifying-longer-term-trends-in-ghg-emissions-and-removals\"\u003e2.12 Information on how actions, policies and measures are modifying longer-term trends in \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions and removals\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo avoid duplication, please refer to the information presented in the National Inventory Report, published on \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e, under each sector for the estimated impact of actions, policies, and measures.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"information-on-the-assessment-of-economic-and-social-impacts-of-response-measures\"\u003e2.13 Information on the assessment of economic and social impacts of response measures\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe government regularly assesses the impact of existing and planned policies against its emission targets, including the \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e and Carbon Budgets. The annual Energy and Emissions Projections (\u003cabbr title=\"Energy and Emissions Projections\"\u003eEEP\u003c/abbr\u003e) take account of any policies that, as of June that year, have either been implemented or those that are planned where the level of funding has been agreed and the policy design is near final.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eUnder section 10 of the Climate Change Act 2008, the UK Government must take account of economic and social circumstances when making decisions in relation to carbon budgets. In particular, section 10 of the Act requires an appraisal of the likely impact of policies on fuel poverty, the economy, and “the competitiveness of particular sectors of the economy.”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis information is gathered by officials and presented to the \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e Secretary of State on a regular basis. A summary of the economic and social impact of the policy package is also published in reports following the setting of a carbon budgets. The most recent assessment was published in the previous UK Government’s 2023 Carbon Budget Delivery Plan.\u003csup id=\"fnref:312\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:312\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 312]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"summary-of-greenhouse-gas-emissions-and-removals\"\u003e2.14 Summary of greenhouse gas emissions and removals\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003ePlease refer to the accompanying \u003cabbr title=\"Common Tabular Format\"\u003eCTF\u003c/abbr\u003e tables submitted alongside the Biennial Transparency Report.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"projections-of-greenhouse-gas-emissions-and-removals-as-applicable\"\u003e2.15 Projections of greenhouse gas emissions and removals as applicable\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis section presents information from the most recent full update to the UK’s \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e Energy and Emissions Projections (\u003cabbr title=\"Energy and Emissions Projections\"\u003eEEP\u003c/abbr\u003e) 2023 -2050, published in December 2024\u003csup id=\"fnref:313\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:313\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 313]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. It includes estimates of future energy demand and GHGs in the UK up to 2050, and within this section we focus on projections up to 2040.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s national projections are based on a ‘With Additional Measures’ (\u003cabbr title=\"With additional measures\"\u003eWAM\u003c/abbr\u003e) scenario. This takes into account policies that, as of June 2024 have either been implemented or are planned and the level of funding has been agreed and the design of the policy is near final. These projections do not present the UK’s full package of policies, as they do not include policies that have only been announced, or are in early development or being planned by the current government. They therefore are not an assessment of the UK’s delivery position against carbon budgets or the \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e. The projections are the baseline against which new early-stage policies and proposals are assessed to monitor progress towards carbon budget targets.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor international reporting, the projections presented in this Biennial Transparency Report used the ‘With Existing Measures’ (\u003cabbr title=\"With existing measures\"\u003eWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e) policy scenario, which excludes policies that were classed as planned at the cut-off date of June 2024. Projections in this section are for the ‘With Existing Measures’ (\u003cabbr title=\"With existing measures\"\u003eWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e) scenario, unless otherwise stated.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe projection models incorporate information from the UK’s 1990-2022 \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e Inventory publication (published in 2022), and the historic statistics presented earlier this chapter are on the same basis.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eKey findings show that:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eBased on the \u003cabbr title=\"With existing measures\"\u003eWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e scenario, the projections show that by 2030, UK emissions of the basket of the 7 greenhouse gases (GHGs) covered by the Paris Agreement would be expected to be 335 \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee, approximately 479 \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee below the 1990 level (59% lower); and by 2040, the projections show equivalent figures of 505 \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee and 62% lower than 1990. These projections are not an assessment of the delivery position against carbon budgets: as policies and measures at an earlier stage of development are developed and implemented, the resulting emissions savings will be factored into future projections.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe UK projects emissions of \u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e, \u003cabbr title=\"Methane\"\u003eCH\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e4\u003c/sub\u003e and \u003cabbr title=\"Nitrous Oxide\"\u003eN\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003eO of 61%, 66% and 60% respectively below 1990 levels by 2040.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eFor the fluorinated GHGs, the UK projects that emissions of \u003cabbr title=\"Hydrofluorocarbons\"\u003eHFCs\u003c/abbr\u003e will be 74% lower than their 1990 levels by 2040. For \u003cabbr title=\"Perfluorocarbons\"\u003ePFCs\u003c/abbr\u003e, the UK projects emissions will be 90% lower, for SF\u003csub\u003e6\u003c/sub\u003e 95% lower; and for \u003cabbr title=\"Nitrogen trifluoride\"\u003eNF\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e3\u003c/sub\u003e emissions will be 42% lower than their 1990 levels by 2040.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK is committed to meeting its 2030 \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e target and will publish more detailed plans on delivery in due course, outlining the policies and proposals it has in place to meet the 2030 and 2035 \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contributions\"\u003eNDCs\u003c/abbr\u003e and carbon budgets up to 2037. The plan will include consideration of delivery risks and mitigations. The publication will also provide indicative implementation dates for policies and proposals; however these dates may change as proposals and policies develop over the coming years. When developing policies and proposals, the government considers alternative pathways and policy levers to meet its carbon targets.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"with-measures-projection-of-all-ghg-emissions-and-removals-and-with-additional-measures-projection-and-without-measures-projection-brbr\"\u003e2.15.1 ‘With measures’ projection of all \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions and removals and ‘with additional measures’ projection and ‘without measures’ projection \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe ‘with existing measures’ (\u003cabbr title=\"With existing measures\"\u003eWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e) scenario includes policies that had been implemented or adopted by June 2024 but excludes planned measures. In addition, the UK provides selected data from the ‘with additional measures’ (\u003cabbr title=\"With additional measures\"\u003eWAM\u003c/abbr\u003e) scenario, which includes planned measures as at the same policy cut-off date. Both projection scenarios exclude the use of credits from flexible mechanisms such as the Joint Implementation and Clean Development Mechanism (\u003cabbr title=\"Clean Development Mechanism\"\u003eCDM\u003c/abbr\u003e). The UK does not produce a without measures (\u003cabbr title=\"Without Measures\"\u003eWOM\u003c/abbr\u003e) scenario. Many mitigation measures were already in place when emissions projections were first produced by the UK, and there are certain policies and measures (PaMs), such as Emissions Trading Schemes (ETS), for which no past counterfactual scenario can be reliably modelled. Currently, it is not feasible to remove all these effects to produce a robust \u003cabbr title=\"Without Measures\"\u003eWOM\u003c/abbr\u003e projection. However, we are exploring options that might allow us to produce a scenario that removes those policies where we can model a suitable \u003cabbr title=\"Without Measures\"\u003eWOM\u003c/abbr\u003e counterfactual. We will implement this and incorporate it into future submissions as soon as we have identified a suitable methodology.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe figures within this National Communication include British crown dependencies and overseas territories. These territories are excluded from UK Carbon Budget’s legislation and do not appear in the \u003cabbr title=\"Energy and Emissions Projections\"\u003eEEP\u003c/abbr\u003e report. According to the UK’s 1990-2022 \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e Inventory, these regions were responsible for 0.4% of total emissions in 2022. Throughout this section, the geographical scope of the presented figures includes the UK and its crown dependencies and overseas territories as denoted by the label ‘(\u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e coverage)’ unless otherwise specified.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eUnder the \u003cabbr title=\"With existing measures\"\u003eWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e scenario, the UK projects \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions to be around 479 \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee below the 1990 level (59% lower) by 2030, and roughly 505 \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee lower by 2040. All projections include emissions from Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry (\u003cabbr title=\"Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry\"\u003eLULUCF\u003c/abbr\u003e), for consistency with Inventory Convention reporting, although the percentages are very similar if it is excluded\u003csup id=\"fnref:314\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:314\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 314]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e[Tables 5 and 6] show overall projections for each gas under \u003cabbr title=\"With existing measures\"\u003eWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e and \u003cabbr title=\"With additional measures\"\u003eWAM\u003c/abbr\u003e scenarios respectively. This shows that additional planned policies as of June 2024 are expected to mainly affect \u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e emissions, reducing them by 12 Mt more in the year 2040 than in the equivalent projection under the \u003cabbr title=\"With existing measures\"\u003eWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e scenario.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp scenario, \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ctable\u003e\n Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ctable\u003e\n  \u003cthead\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"row\"\u003e2. Industrial Processes\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e1\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e2\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e0\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e0\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd class=\"cell-text-right\"\u003e0\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"information-describing-the-methodology-used-to-develop-projections\"\u003e2.16 Information describing the methodology used to develop projections\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"projections-methods-by-sector-brbr\"\u003e2.16.1 Projections methods by sector \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK projections of emissions of \u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e and combustion-related emissions of other GHGs (\u003cabbr title=\"Methane\"\u003eCH\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e4\u003c/sub\u003e and \u003cabbr title=\"Nitrous Oxide\"\u003eN\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003eO) are based on the UK’s Energy and Emissions Projections modelling suite used for its annual publication and internal analysis.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe produce projections of energy demand and combustion-related \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions outside the power sector by applying standard statistical techniques. These project forward energy demand and emissions based on trends and relationships in past data. We adjust these projections to take account of estimated reductions in energy consumption from policies which are modelled separately using more detailed sectoral models. We then project energy-related emissions by multiplying energy demand by the relevant emissions factors\u003csup id=\"fnref:315\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:315\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 315]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe produce projections of power sector generation and associated emissions by feeding our projections of electricity demand into a model of electricity supplier behaviour.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe following table outlines a summary of the models involved in the Energy and Emissions projections:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"table-22\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTable 22: Modelling approaches for the projections\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ctable\u003e\n  \u003cthead\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\"\u003eModel\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\"\u003ePurpose\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\"\u003eNotes\u003c/th\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/thead\u003e\n  \u003ctbody\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"row\"\u003eEnergy Demand Model (\u003cabbr title=\"Energy Demand Model\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eProjecting energy demand and associated emissions\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eUses bespoke econometric analysis of past energy demand by fuel and sector as published in the UK’s annual energy statistics publication – \u003cabbr title=\"Digest of UK Energy Statistics\"\u003eDUKES\u003c/abbr\u003e (Digest of UK Energy Statistics). The resulting projection equations are combined with projections for drivers such as UK \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e growth and separately modelled policy impacts to project forward energy demand by fuel and sector. Energy demand projections are converted to emissions projections through emissions factors and calorific values.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"row\"\u003eDynamic Dispatch Model\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eProjecting energy supply and associated emissions\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eThis model is used to project emissions from the power sector. It takes projected electricity demand from the Energy Demand Model and provides a modelled generation mix that meets that level of demand under current power sector policies. It is a market-based model that simulates the operation of the electricity market and the investment decision of market participants. It is a profit-maximisation model incorporating the effect of UK policies which incentivise low-carbon generation through market mechanisms. Includes combined heat and power plants.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"row\"\u003eUK \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e Inventory Non-\u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e emissions models\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eProjecting non-combustion, non-\u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e emissions.\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eUse emissions from the 1990-2022 \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e Inventory (GHGI) as the baseline for these emissions projections. Sectoral models are used to project forward emissions from these sources.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe overall modelling approach has been consistent over time, although there have been incremental improvements to the projections which are described in the UK’s domestic \u003cabbr title=\"Energy and Emissions Projections\"\u003eEEP\u003c/abbr\u003e publications\u003csup id=\"fnref:316\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:316\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 316]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe principal source of past energy statistics is the Digest of UK Energy Statistics (\u003cabbr title=\"Digest of UK Energy Statistics\"\u003eDUKES\u003c/abbr\u003e). The UK’s model suite projects emissions using projections for fossil fuel prices, carbon prices, economic growth, temperature and demographics. Key assumptions for projections are given in \u003cabbr title=\"Common Tabular Format\"\u003eCTF\u003c/abbr\u003e Table 11.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s domestically published projections include variant scenarios for high and low fossil fuel price assumptions, high and low \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e growth rates. More detail on this is provided later in this section.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"transport-2\"\u003e2.16.1.1 Transport\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e road transport model is an econometric response surface model integrated into the economy-wide Energy Demand Model (\u003cabbr title=\"Energy Demand Model\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e) and calibrated against the Department for Transport’s (\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Transport\"\u003eDfT\u003c/abbr\u003e’s) National Transport Model (\u003cabbr title=\"National Transport Model\"\u003eNTM\u003c/abbr\u003e). The econometric model is multi-modal as it includes cars, light good vehicles (LGVs), heavy goods vehicles (\u003cabbr title=\"Heavy Goods Vehicles\"\u003eHGVs\u003c/abbr\u003e), and public service vehicles (PSVs). Car demand has a link to population, and \u003cabbr title=\"Heavy Goods Vehicle\"\u003eHGV\u003c/abbr\u003e demand is linked to projections for manufacturing Gross Value added (\u003cabbr title=\"Gross Value Added\"\u003eGVA\u003c/abbr\u003e). Other factors which affect transport demand are the oil price, motor spirit/diesel engine share, and fuel efficiency and biofuel substitution effects.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eMost energy efficiency improvements are policy-driven, such as by new car emissions intensity targets and complementary measures such as lower rolling resistance tyres for \u003cabbr title=\"Heavy Goods Vehicles\"\u003eHGVs\u003c/abbr\u003e. Unlike for other demand sectors, impacts of policies and measures on road transport fuel demand are modelled within the \u003cabbr title=\"Energy and Emissions Projections\"\u003eEEP\u003c/abbr\u003e modelling suite. Road vehicle efficiencies, motor spirit/diesel engine shares, and biofuel use under different policy scenarios are used to calculate mitigation impacts from differences in demand between scenarios.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eElectricity demand from electric cars and LGVs is passed to the Dynamic Dispatch Model (\u003cabbr title=\"Dynamic Dispatch Model\"\u003eDDM\u003c/abbr\u003e) which takes this additional demand into account when calculating power sector generation. The activity data (vehicle distances travelled) is projected using the latest \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Transport\"\u003eDfT\u003c/abbr\u003e traffic forecasts.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Transport\"\u003eDfT\u003c/abbr\u003e’s projected traffic growth, the planned electrification of existing track, and the construction of new lines such as Crossrail and High Speed 2 underpin the rail transport model.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eProjections for UK commercial aviation involve estimates of future UK \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e, consumer expenditure, population, and oil prices. The Fleet Mix Model captures efficiency improvements, for example the model assumes increasing use of biofuels. \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Transport\"\u003eDfT\u003c/abbr\u003e provides more detailed information about methodology and assumptions with its aviation forecast. The modelling has extrapolated trends in the \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e Inventory to extend aviation emissions projections to \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e coverage.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK projects that national navigation will remain largely static.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"energy-supply\"\u003e2.16.1.2 Energy supply\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK uses the \u003cabbr title=\"Dynamic Dispatch Model\"\u003eDDM\u003c/abbr\u003e to project investment and generation in the electricity supply sector. The \u003cabbr title=\"Dynamic Dispatch Model\"\u003eDDM\u003c/abbr\u003e is a market-based model that simulates the operation of the electricity market and the investment decision of the market participants in detail. It is a profit-maximisation model incorporating the effect of government policies such as Contracts for Difference which incentivise low-carbon generation through market mechanisms.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Dynamic Dispatch Model\"\u003eDDM\u003c/abbr\u003e also models investment in the supply of heat and electricity from Combined Heat and Power plants, mostly in industry.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"industrial-and-commercial-sector-emissions\"\u003e2.16.1.3 Industrial and Commercial sector emissions\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor emissions projections, the UK breaks manufacturing down into sectors using the Standard Industrial Classification (\u003cabbr title=\"Standard Industrial Classification\"\u003eSIC\u003c/abbr\u003e). The manufacturing sectors in the \u003cabbr title=\"Energy Demand Model\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e are:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eChemicals\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eConstruction\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eEngineering and vehicles\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eFood, drink and tobacco\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eIron and steel\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eNon-ferrous metals\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eNon-metallic mineral products\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ePulp, paper and printing\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eTextile products; and\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eManufacturing not elsewhere classified\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK projects Gross Value Added (\u003cabbr title=\"Gross Value Added\"\u003eGVA\u003c/abbr\u003e) for each of these sectors using \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e, interest rates, and, in some cases, terms of trade (the relative prices of imports and exports). The UK projects total energy demand for each sector from \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Value Added\"\u003eGVA\u003c/abbr\u003e and energy prices. Except for iron and steel, the model splits total energy demand into different fuels using historical fuel demands and projections of relative fuel prices. In iron and steel, the UK estimates energy demand using sector \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Value Added\"\u003eGVA\u003c/abbr\u003e and the tonnages of steel produced using electricity or by the Basic Oxygen Steel (\u003cabbr title=\"Basic Oxygen Steel\"\u003eBOS\u003c/abbr\u003e) process.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEnergy demand is projected by commercial services from sector \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Value Added\"\u003eGVA\u003c/abbr\u003e, and temperature based on econometric analysis of past consumption, \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Value Added\"\u003eGVA\u003c/abbr\u003e and temperature.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"residential\"\u003e2.16.1.4 Residential\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK projects the residential emissions from gas, oil and solid fuels use separately. The estimates depend on assumptions about the percentage of households using each fuel as their main heating source. The primary drivers of residential energy demand are household numbers, fuel prices, temperature and income.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eResidential demand for electricity is projected using the same drivers and passed to the \u003cabbr title=\"Dynamic Dispatch Model\"\u003eDDM\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"agriculture-2\"\u003e2.16.1.5 Agriculture\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eUK agriculture uses a relatively small amount of energy. Therefore, projections of its combustion emissions come from simple trend models.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK uses Food and Agricultural Policy Research Institute (\u003cabbr title=\"Food and Agricultural Policy Research Institute\"\u003eFAPRI\u003c/abbr\u003e) methodology\u003csup id=\"fnref:317\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:317\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 317]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e to provide projections of activity, such as livestock numbers, crop production, fertiliser nitrogen use, and non-\u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e emissions to 2030. Projections for later years are held constant. The \u003cabbr title=\"Food and Agricultural Policy Research Institute\"\u003eFAPRI\u003c/abbr\u003e projections come from an economic model that assumes a specific set of international prices for agricultural commodities and a path for the sterling exchange rate. Together, these factors are important determinants of the returns to farmers and hence of total agricultural production. The UK converts these \u003cabbr title=\"Food and Agricultural Policy Research Institute\"\u003eFAPRI\u003c/abbr\u003e activity projections to emissions using the latest agriculture model in the UK’s \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e Inventory.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"waste-management-1\"\u003e2.16.1.6 Waste management\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eProjections of \u003cabbr title=\"Methane\"\u003eCH\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e4\u003c/sub\u003e from landfill depend on UK projections of tonnages of municipal waste going to landfill and on figures for commercial and industrial waste. Waste composition is projected from knowledge of changes to BWT processes and from projections of waste arising.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThese projections of waste going to landfill are then run through MELMod, the landfill emissions calculation model. The MELMod model is based on the \u003cabbr title=\"Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change\"\u003eIPCC\u003c/abbr\u003e’s first-order decay methodology, which the 2014 \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e Inventory report summarises. UK population projections underpin predictions of emissions of \u003cabbr title=\"Methane\"\u003eCH\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e4\u003c/sub\u003e and \u003cabbr title=\"Nitrous Oxide\"\u003eN\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003eO from domestic wastewater and sewage/sludge decomposition. Industrial wastewater emissions are predicted to stay constant. BWT emissions from multiple sources are combined. Some are projected to be constant, and some are extrapolated from the latest year of historical data using sector experts’ estimates of future BWT capacity.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"industrial-processes-1\"\u003e2.16.1.7 Industrial processes\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eManufacturing sub-sector \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Value Added\"\u003eGVA\u003c/abbr\u003e projections or energy demand projections are used to project \u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e emissions from industrial processes where there is evidence of correlation. Other \u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e emissions are projected to remain constant at the last actual value from the UK’s \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e Inventory (published 2022).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eMany methods are used for projections of non-\u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e emissions from industrial processes. Some sources use manufacturing sector GVAs while others use more detailed assumptions about future activity. Annex \u003cabbr title=\"Nitrous Oxide\"\u003eN\u003c/abbr\u003e of the UK’s domestic \u003cabbr title=\"Energy and Emissions Projections\"\u003eEEP\u003c/abbr\u003e publication\u003csup id=\"fnref:318\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:318\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 318]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e provides more information on non-\u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e emissions projection methods.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"public-sector\"\u003e2.16.1.8 Public sector\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eSector employment levels are used as the main driver in modelling non-electricity energy demand from public services. The projections assume that the historical trend of improving energy efficiency per employee will continue. Temperature also affects public sector demand. The models break non-electricity energy demand into fuels using the same proportions as in latest historical data.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"land-use-land-use-change-and-forestry-lulucf-2\"\u003e2.16.1.9 Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry (\u003cabbr title=\"Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry\"\u003eLULUCF\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Centre for Ecology and Hydrology and Forest Research model \u003cabbr title=\"Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry\"\u003eLULUCF\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions using approaches that are consistent with the current inventory methodology. They produce 4 scenarios – Baseline, Central, High and Low – for future emissions. Each makes assumptions about afforestation, wildfires, peat extraction, land use change and deforestation. They developed these scenarios with a policy maker stakeholder group and updated them in 2016 following discussions with UK devolved governments. Broadly, their central scenario is a continuation of current policies and activity rates. This is the scenario used in generating emissions projections for this report.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"estimation-of-emissions-in-crown-dependencies-and-overseas-territories-brbr\"\u003e2.16.2 Estimation of emissions in crown dependencies and overseas territories \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s crown dependencies and overseas territories are not included in the projections which the UK produces annually to monitor progress against its own carbon budgets. The projections in this report supplement the UK annual figures with forecasts for areas that are consistent with the UK’s 1990-2022 \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e Inventory. Emissions in these territories are only a small proportion of UK emissions, making up 0.4% of the UK’s \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e coverage emissions in 2022. Two different approaches are used for projecting these territories:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eFor most sectors (excluding 1. Energy and memo items), emissions for crown dependencies and overseas territories are projected based on simple linear trends of the emissions in each National Communication sector based on observations from the previous 9 years;\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eHowever due to the significant impact of \u003cabbr title=\"Coronavirus\"\u003eCOVID-19\u003c/abbr\u003e on transport sectors (particularly 1. Energy, and memo item rows), we used a different methodology. For these sectors, we projected emissions for crown dependencies and overseas territories with the same trajectory as the UK emissions for the equivalent sector.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"strengths-of-the-projection-methodology-brbr\"\u003e2.16.3 Strengths of the projection methodology \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s modelling methodology has the following strengths:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe initial starting point for the UK’s Energy and Emissions Projections is the latest historical data from the \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e Inventory and \u003cabbr title=\"Digest of UK Energy Statistics\"\u003eDUKES\u003c/abbr\u003e. In the case of \u003cabbr title=\"Energy and Emissions Projections\"\u003eEEP\u003c/abbr\u003e 2023, this was based on the UK’s \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e Inventory 1990-2022 and 2022 energy statistics (both of these with latest actuals 2022). These are well established sources of information;\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe main Energy Demand Model (\u003cabbr title=\"Energy Demand Model\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e) uses econometric methods that capture long-run relationships between economic activity, energy consumption and emissions;\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe detailed model of electricity generation captures both short-run fuel switching and long-term investment strategies;\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe UK updates its projections regularly as part of the monitoring of UK national carbon budgets;\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eModels use authoritative national and international sources for socio-economic projections;\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThere is a rolling programme of review and update for the projection methodologies and econometric models, and modelling performance is tested by back-casting to see how well the model predicts what happened in the recent past;\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe projections distinguish between business as usual emissions and the emission reductions due to mitigating policies and measures; and\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe modelling estimates the mitigation impacts of policies using a common cross-government methodology.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"weaknesses-of-the-projection-methodology-brbr\"\u003e2.16.4 Weaknesses of the projection methodology \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s modelling has the following weaknesses:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe modelling generally assumes that historical relationships will continue in the future, which can fail to capture structural changes and new technologies where these fall outside the scope of included policies and measures;\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eIt hasn’t been possible to update uncertainty analysis, so uncertainty ranges quoted are still based on analysis from 2019. Similarly, analysis assumed that the drivers of uncertainty were similar to previous years;\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThere is considerable recognised uncertainty in economic and demographic projections from external sources;\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe UK cannot provide separate quantified impacts for some types of policy due to modelling limitations. Policies which operate fully or partly through a price impact such as the Climate Change Levy (an environmental tax on the\nenergy that businesses use) cannot be quantified due to limitations with our modelling approach. These are taken into account in the modelling (through their impact on energy demand), but we do not have estimates of the individual impacts; and\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eAs with all econometric modelling, this is subject to estimation errors.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"key-assumptions-brbr\"\u003e2.16.5 Key assumptions \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eA set of key assumptions about UK economic growth, demographic changes and future fuel price trajectories underpin the UK’s projections. The main sources of projected assumptions are the forecasts made by the UK’s Office for Budget Responsibility (\u003cabbr title=\"Office for Budget Responsibility\"\u003eOBR\u003c/abbr\u003e) and Office for National Statistics (\u003cabbr title=\"Office for National Statistics\"\u003eONS\u003c/abbr\u003e), and supplemented by International Monetary Fund projections of world growth. Fuel prices are produced by the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e). \u003cabbr title=\"Common Tabular Format\"\u003eCTF\u003c/abbr\u003e Table 11 documents key parameters and assumptions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK released \u003cabbr title=\"Energy and Emissions Projections\"\u003eEEP\u003c/abbr\u003e 2023 -2050 in December 2024. UK \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e forecasts to 2023 were from the March 2024 Economic and Fiscal Outlook publication. Beyond 2023, \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e growth projections came from the March 2024 Long-term economic determinants forecast. The UK’s Office for National Statistics (\u003cabbr title=\"Office for National Statistics\"\u003eONS\u003c/abbr\u003e) produced 2021-based population projections in January 2024. The household projections are also from \u003cabbr title=\"Office for National Statistics\"\u003eONS\u003c/abbr\u003e and are 2018-based (but including a projection update by the Welsh Government in August 2020). \u003cstrong\u003eTable 23\u003c/strong\u003e shows updated socio-economic growth assumptions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"table-23\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTable 23: UK growth \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"quality-assurance-and-quality-controls-brbr\"\u003e2.16.6 Quality assurance and quality controls \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eQuality assurance of modelling is a high priority within UK Government, and analysis for the \u003cabbr title=\"Energy and Emissions Projections\"\u003eEEP\u003c/abbr\u003e follows the \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e quality assurance guidelines.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA small group of \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e analysts produces the energy and emission projections, and owns, maintains and updates the Energy Demand Model (known as the \u003cabbr title=\"Energy Demand Model\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e) which underpins the projections. The \u003cabbr title=\"Energy and Emissions Projections\"\u003eEEP\u003c/abbr\u003e team liaises with other modelling teams, both inside and outside \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e, to quality assure and compile the data which go into the overall projections.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFigures relating to electricity come from iteratively solving 2 specialised models with the \u003cabbr title=\"Energy Demand Model\"\u003eEDM\u003c/abbr\u003e. These are the Dynamic Dispatch Model (\u003cabbr title=\"Dynamic Dispatch Model\"\u003eDDM\u003c/abbr\u003e) and the Prices and Bills Model of retail electricity prices. This cycling ensures that electricity demand is in equilibrium with prices. The co-ordinators of these models also assure projections results. Projections for non-energy non-\u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e emissions are produced by the \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e Science division.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Centre for Ecology and Hydrology produces the UK’s \u003cabbr title=\"Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry\"\u003eLULUCF\u003c/abbr\u003e projections under contract; this is overseen by the \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e Science and Innovation for Climate and Energy Directorate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e bases transport sector modelling on, and calibrates it against, the detailed models for road, rail and air used by the Department for Transport (\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Transport\"\u003eDfT\u003c/abbr\u003e). These latter are in turn subject to \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Transport\"\u003eDfT\u003c/abbr\u003e’s quality assurance.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAnalytical teams in the relevant areas prepare estimates of the emissions or energy savings due to UK Government policies. Analysts prepare these policy savings estimates according to central guidance, which ensures that energy use and \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions are valued consistently across UK Government.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAnalysts send the policy savings in a standard template and the \u003cabbr title=\"Energy and Emissions Projections\"\u003eEEP\u003c/abbr\u003e team checks them to look for any unaccounted overlaps and to ensure internal consistency between energy and emissions savings. The team confirms the model savings with the submitting analysts and departments. The UK updates its \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e projections to inform progress against national carbon budgets and publishes each set of projections. The \u003cabbr title=\"Energy and Emissions Projections\"\u003eEEP\u003c/abbr\u003e team improves and adapts the core Energy Demand Model incrementally, quality assuring each change to confirm validity and robustness. (The team responsible for the \u003cabbr title=\"Dynamic Dispatch Model\"\u003eDDM\u003c/abbr\u003e quality assures any change relating to electricity generation). The \u003cabbr title=\"Energy and Emissions Projections\"\u003eEEP\u003c/abbr\u003e team presents interim and final results to a Steering Group which oversees the process, and stakeholders review draft \u003cabbr title=\"Energy and Emissions Projections\"\u003eEEP\u003c/abbr\u003e reports before publication. The UK’s independent Climate Change Committee reviews the projections after their release.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"uncertainty-brbr\"\u003e2.16.7 Uncertainty \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn December 2024 the UK published annexes of data to accompany its domestic projections. These included low and high fossil fuel prices and low and high UK \u003cabbr title=\"Gross Domestic Product\"\u003eGDP\u003c/abbr\u003e rates as variant scenarios and sensitivities.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"table-26\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTable 26: Prices in fossil fuel variant scenarios, 2023 prices (various scenarios, UK \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"overall-uncertainty-brbr\"\u003e2.16.9 Overall uncertainty \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eFuture values of key variables such as fossil fuel prices, the impacts of policy and demographic/economic growth cannot be known with certainty. However, these variables underpin the UK projections. Understanding the impact of this uncertainty is important in the context of the UK’s aim to reduce emissions through policy intervention, and so it is regularly investigated in \u003cabbr title=\"Energy and Emissions Projections\"\u003eEEP\u003c/abbr\u003e publications. Uncertainty analysis presented here is based on the most influential drivers of energy use and emissions, previously identified through sensitivity analysis. The \u003cabbr title=\"Energy and Emissions Projections\"\u003eEEP\u003c/abbr\u003e team carries out a Monte Carlo simulation to vary the values of these drivers, firstly obtaining historical distributions of input values then running the projections model on samples from these distributions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe uncertainty ranges presented in this section are still derived from the uncertainty analysis from the estimates published in \u003cabbr title=\"Energy and Emissions Projections\"\u003eEEP\u003c/abbr\u003e 2018, due to time constraints at the time of analysis.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis method underpins the 95% confidence interval estimates presented in Figure 5.3 and \u003cstrong\u003eTable 29\u003c/strong\u003e. The upper and lower boundaries represent the projected emissions corresponding to the lower 2.5% and upper 97.5% percentiles of the Monte Carlo simulations respectively. Although the high/low emissions projections in \u003cstrong\u003eFigure 20\u003c/strong\u003e show UK coverage (excluding \u003cabbr title=\"crown dependencies and overseas territories\"\u003eCDOTs\u003c/abbr\u003e), they do indicate the scale of uncertainty in the projections reported in this section, as CDOT emissions were only 0.4% of the overall total in 2022.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis analysis excludes the electricity supply industry and possible ‘structural breaks’ in society or the economy which might significantly affect emissions. For example, societal and behavioural step changes or breakthrough technologies like improved storage could have profound impacts on the UK’s energy mix and emissions but are hard to anticipate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-20\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 20: Uncertainty in UK projected emissions, \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003ee (\u003cabbr title=\"With additional measures\"\u003eWAM\u003c/abbr\u003e scenario, UK coverage)\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg coverage)\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ctable\u003e\n  \u003cthead\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\" uncertainty in historical inputs or emission estimates, such as those before 2022.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eBy 2030, the UK \u003cabbr title=\"With additional measures\"\u003eWAM\u003c/abbr\u003e scenario projects \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e emissions will be between 17% and 21% below 2022 levels. By 2039, the range is slightly wider with emissions projected between 23% and 29% below 2022 levels. The higher uncertainty for later years reflects the reduced confidence in modelled projections further into the future.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"projections-for-precursor-gases-brbr\"\u003e2.16.10 Projections for precursor gases \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eProjections for emissions from precursor gases in the UK are not included within this analysis but are produced by the National Atmospheric Emissions Inventory (\u003cabbr title=\"National Atmospheric Emissions Inventory\"\u003eNAEI\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:320\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:320\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 320]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. The projections are produced at 5-year intervals out to 2050 and contains the pollutants regulated under the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nations\"\u003eUN\u003c/abbr\u003e Gothenburg protocol.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"projections-of-key-indicators-to-determine-progress-towards-ndc\"\u003e2.17 Projections of key indicators to determine progress towards \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e\n\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"With existing measures\"\u003eWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e scenario projections in this section include the impact of the UK’s implemented and adopted policies and measures at the policy cut-off point of June 2024. They are the baseline or counterfactual projection showing what the UK would expect to happen if no policies at an earlier stage of development were implemented.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe name, sector, \u003cabbr title=\"Greenhouse Gas\"\u003eGHG\u003c/abbr\u003e(s) and activity affected, and descriptions of these policies and measures can be found in \u003cabbr title=\"Common Tabular Format\"\u003eCTF\u003c/abbr\u003e Table 5. The \u003cabbr title=\"With existing measures\"\u003eWEM\u003c/abbr\u003e scenario within this section does not include planned policies, but those are included within domestic reporting and are therefore shown in \u003cabbr title=\"Common Tabular Format\"\u003eCTF\u003c/abbr\u003e Table 5.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK has continued to update its analysis of policies and measures expected to help meet both Nationally Determined Contributions and the targets for Carbon Budgets set under the UK Climate Change Act (2008). Over time, the UK’s projections will include newer or more recently announced policies as they progress to the impact assessment stage. Within this section, we also include the total of territorial and international aviation and shipping (\u003cabbr title=\"International Aviation and Shipping\"\u003eIAS\u003c/abbr\u003e) policy savings.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTable 5.3.1 and Figure 5.4 show the projected impact of demand-side policies only. Power supply markets are highly interconnected, meaning it is not possible to robustly disaggregate the impacts of individual supply-side policies. We are reviewing the method for calculating savings from overall power interventions, but for now the tables in this section and in \u003cabbr title=\"Common Tabular Format\"\u003eCTF\u003c/abbr\u003e Table 5 exclude the aggregated emissions savings from power supply policies.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"table-30\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTable 30: Projected impact of policies (excluding power sector         "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"national-circumstances-institutional-arrangements-and-legal-frameworks\"\u003e3.1 National circumstances, institutional arrangements and legal frameworks\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe devolved governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland contribute to the UK’s overall climate objectives and have their own adaptation targets; unless stated otherwise, the information below outlines England’s approach. The devolved government has provided information on their strategies in section 3.10.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"biogeophysical-characteristics\"\u003e3.2 Biogeophysical characteristics\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe are already seeing climate impacts across the globe, with observed increases in the frequency and intensity of heatwaves, flooding, drought and wildfires. According to the World Meteorological Organization\u003csup id=\"fnref:321\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:321\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 321]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, long-term global warming is currently around 1.3°C compared to the 1850-1900 baseline, whilst in the UK, the 10 warmest years on record have all occurred since 2003\u003csup id=\"fnref:322\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:322\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 322]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. Human-induced warming is increasing at around 0.25⁰C\u003csup id=\"fnref:323\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:323\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 323]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e per decade, leading to further increases in global and UK climate hazards into the future.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe latest State of the UK Climate report,\u003csup id=\"fnref:324\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:324\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 324]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e highlighted a year of extremes. 2022 was shown to be the warmest year in the UK series from 1884, 0.9 °C above the 1991–2020 average, and for the first time 40 °C was recorded in the UK. The period January–August 2022 was also the driest across England and Wales since 1976, with drought status declared across parts of England and all of Wales. Rising sea levels have continued to be observed in the UK and have risen by 18.5cm since 1900’s. The rate of sea level rise has also accelerated, with over 60% of the observed sea level rise (11.4cm) occurring over the past 30 years.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eMore recently, Met Office\u003csup id=\"fnref:325\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:325\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 325]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e observations show that 2023 was the second warmest year for the UK according to mean temperature. Both Wales and Northern Ireland experienced their warmest years on record in 2023. Changes in rainfall extremes has also begun to be observed in the UK. In 2023, the UK saw 11% more rain than average with a provisional figure of 1289.8mm falling.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"economy\"\u003e3.3 Economy\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe economic losses from flooding in England between November 2019 and March 2020 are estimated to be about £333 million and would have been significantly larger in the absence of flood defences\u003csup id=\"fnref:326\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:326\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 326]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. The ‘Monetary Valuation of Risks and Opportunities in the third Climate Change Risk Assessment(\u003cabbr title=\"Third Climate Change Risk Assessment\"\u003eCCRA3\u003c/abbr\u003e)’\u003csup id=\"fnref:327\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:327\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 327]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e report found that around a quarter of the 61 climate risks and opportunities it identified each have the potential to result in economic impacts higher than £1 billion per year by 2050.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDisruption from climate change has the potential to reduce government revenues and increase government expenditure, reduce external performance (exports), damage infrastructure assets, increase social costs thereby increasing vulnerability for some population groups, and reduce economic growth (source: World Bank Group, 2020; Inclusive Futures, 2020). However, early adaptation action can help to reduce future costs and many adaptation actions represent good value for money. The ‘Monetary Valuation of Risks and Opportunities in \u003cabbr title=\"Third Climate Change Risk Assessment\"\u003eCCRA3\u003c/abbr\u003e’\u003csup id=\"fnref:328\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:328\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 328]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e report found that, for a range of early interventions, benefit-cost ratios typically range from 2:1 to 10:1. This means that every £1 invested in these adaptation actions could result in £2 to £10 in net economic benefit.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"infrastructure\"\u003e3.4 Infrastructure\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eRecent events such as Storm Arwen in 2021 and the heatwaves of 2022 demonstrate the kinds of impacts climate risks can lead to, from power outages to buckling train tracks. The evidence suggests these impacts will get more intense and frequent under any emissions scenario to 2050.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo help manage climate risks to infrastructure sectors:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eEnsuring that the regulatory framework is delivering adaptation outcomes\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ePutting the necessary investment in place\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eEngaging with infrastructure operators and regulators to improve understanding of and approaches to identifying and managing climate risk\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK has a robust system to ensure that public investment in infrastructure appropriately considers climate risk, which the \u003cabbr title=\"International Monetary Fund\"\u003eIMF\u003c/abbr\u003e’s Public Investment Management Assessment\u003csup id=\"fnref:329\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:329\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 329]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (\u003cabbr title=\"IMF’s Public Investment Management Assessment\"\u003ePIMA\u003c/abbr\u003e) found to be relatively well-designed. The Green Book is guidance issued by \u003cabbr title=\"His Majesty\"\u003eHM\u003c/abbr\u003e Treasury on how to appraise policies, programmes and projects. It also provides guidance on the design and use of monitoring and evaluation before, during and after implementation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe following levers are used to manage climate risks in infrastructure.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eNational Infrastructure Strategy\u003csup id=\"fnref:330\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:330\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 330]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eUK Government Resilience Framework\u003csup id=\"fnref:331\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:331\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 331]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eAdaptation Reporting Power (\u003cabbr title=\"Adaptation Reporting Power\"\u003eARP\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:332\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:332\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 332]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eCritical National Infrastructure (\u003cabbr title=\"Critical National Infrastructure\"\u003eCNI\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:333\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:333\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 333]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e policy\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ePlanning policy\u003csup id=\"fnref:334\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:334\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 334]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eInstitutional framework: strengthening our understanding of climate risk to infrastructure, through the National Infrastructure Commission (\u003cabbr title=\"National Infrastructure Commission\"\u003eNIC\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:335\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:335\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 335]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, the Infrastructure and Projects Authority’s (\u003cabbr title=\"Infrastructure and Projects Authority\"\u003eIPA\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:336\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:336\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 336]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e and the National Wealth Fund (formerly the UK Infrastructure Bank)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eMajor public investment in infrastructure is subject to an additional level of scrutiny through the UK Government’s Infrastructure and Projects Authority, which provides an assurance function to support the successful delivery of projects within the UK Government’s Major Projects Portfolio (\u003cabbr title=\"Government’s Major Projects Portfolio\"\u003eGMPP\u003c/abbr\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Infrastructure and Projects Authority’s (\u003cabbr title=\"Infrastructure and Projects Authority\"\u003eIPA\u003c/abbr\u003e) Gate Review process is designed to provide a realistic view on a programme and project’s ability to deliver agreed outcomes against time, cost, benefits and quality, and these Gate Reviews include tests to ensure infrastructure projects have considered climate risk and adaptation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"global-goal-on-adaptation-gga-thematic-target-5---climate-resilient-infrastructure-brbr\"\u003e3.4.1 Global Goal on Adaptation (\u003cabbr title=\"Global Goal for Adaptation\"\u003eGGA\u003c/abbr\u003e) Thematic target 5 - Climate-resilient Infrastructure \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eAdaptation is embedded through the planning system for major infrastructure projects. National Policy Statements (\u003cabbr title=\"National Policy Statements\"\u003eNPSs\u003c/abbr\u003e) are a key part of the system for managing Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects (\u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects\"\u003eNSIPs\u003c/abbr\u003e) and are important in ensuring that government policy is implemented effectively through the planning system. Infrastructure \u003cabbr title=\"National Policy Statements\"\u003eNPSs\u003c/abbr\u003e include requirements for planning applicants to demonstrate how they have considered the risks posed by the changing climate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ePlans for reforms to the NSIP\u003csup id=\"fnref:337\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:337\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 337]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e regime that will ensure the system can support our future infrastructure needs by making the system better, faster, greener, fairer and more resilient.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK Government Resilience Framework\u003csup id=\"fnref:338\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:338\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 338]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, sets out how the government will work with industry and regulators to improve the security and resilience of UK \u003cabbr title=\"Critical National Infrastructure\"\u003eCNI\u003c/abbr\u003e for example by using common but flexible resilience standards across \u003cabbr title=\"Critical National Infrastructure\"\u003eCNI\u003c/abbr\u003e, and by reviewing existing regulatory regimes on resilience to ensure they are fit for purpose.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"global-goal-on-adaptation-gga-thematic-target-1---water\"\u003e3.4.2 Global Goal on Adaptation (\u003cabbr title=\"Global Goal for Adaptation\"\u003eGGA\u003c/abbr\u003e) Thematic target 1 - Water\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003ePrivate investment in national infrastructure is often also subject to sector-specific regulation ensuring appropriate consideration of climate risk.
