It will explore options to establish appropriate governance arrangements so that the UK Environment Act 2021 biodiversity targets are delivered in a way that considers a changing climate\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e‘Local Nature Recovery Strategies’\u003csup id=\"fnref:388\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:388\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 388]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (\u003cabbr title=\"Local Nature Recovery Strategies\"\u003eLNRS\u003c/abbr\u003e) are measures set out in the Environment Act (2021) and will support public, private and voluntary sector organisations to work together on identifying collective priorities for restoring nature and improving climate resilience\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe government and external partners will integrate water management by delivering catchment action plans backed up with new funding to improve all water bodies in England. This will target actions where they will deliver the greatest impact for water quality, drought and flood management, and nature recovery.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"monitoring-and-evaluation-of-adaptation-actions-and-processes\"\u003e3.18 Monitoring and evaluation of adaptation actions and processes\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"achievements-impacts-resilience-review-effectiveness-and-results-brbr\"\u003e3.18.1 Achievements, impacts, resilience, review, effectiveness and results \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eEffective monitoring and evaluation (\u003cabbr title=\"Monitoring and Evaluation\"\u003eM\u0026amp;E\u003c/abbr\u003e) is important for informing future decision making on adaptation. The Climate Change Committee’s Technical Report for the \u003cabbr title=\"Third Climate Change Risk Assessment\"\u003eCCRA3\u003c/abbr\u003e Independent Assessment outlines that for many of the risks and opportunities, adaptation actions can often take a long time to take effect. In particular, the complexity of how systems respond to adaptation measures while also responding to other environmental and socio-economic pressures is not easily untangled.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Monitoring and Evaluation\"\u003eM\u0026amp;E\u003c/abbr\u003e can help assess the effectiveness of actions taken, inform resource allocation decisions and reassess goals based on their feasibility or relative importance. When developing policy responses for climate risks, policy officials will also identify accompanying process and outcome indicators. Such indicators will help us assess whether: a) actions are being delivered b) actions are efficient 8 c) progress is being made on the declared outcomes.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAt present, gaps exist in our ability to monitor our adaptation efforts. This is due to the complexity of adaptation and the associated challenges of identifying and developing appropriate indicators. As outlined in the \u003cabbr title=\"Monitoring and Evaluation\"\u003eM\u0026amp;E\u003c/abbr\u003e annex\u003csup id=\"fnref:389\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:389\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 389]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e to \u003cabbr title=\"The third National Adaptation Programme\"\u003eNAP3\u003c/abbr\u003e, some of the common challenges included:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eProving cause and effect for adaptation actions in a complex system with multiple drivers of change.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eTracking progress to a moving target in a system with interacting and cascading climate and socioeconomic risks.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe mismatch between short evaluation cycles and the time needed to effect change, especially for the natural environment.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eAccess to high quality, affordable and trustworthy data.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThese challenges are consistent with the findings of the Climate Change Committee in its 2021 progress report to Parliament. Adaptation process indicators (such as the number of plans adopted, or buildings retrofitted) are relatively simple to measure. Indicators that measure adaptation outcomes (such as climate-sensitive sectors of the economy being better adapted) are rarer as they are harder to measure. Work is ongoing to identify a suite of existing and potential indicators to evaluate the success of the \u003cabbr title=\"The third National Adaptation Programme\"\u003eNAP3\u003c/abbr\u003e programme. In many cases, indicators will be researched or developed as part of an action.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAs committed to in \u003cabbr title=\"The third National Adaptation Programme\"\u003eNAP3\u003c/abbr\u003e, the UK Government is developing an Monitoring Evaluation and Learning framework, expected in 2025.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"global-goal-on-adaptation-gga-process-target-4---monitoring-evaluation-and-learning-mel-brbr\"\u003e3.18.2 Global Goal on Adaptation (\u003cabbr title=\"Global Goal for Adaptation\"\u003eGGA\u003c/abbr\u003e) process target 4 - Monitoring, evaluation and learning (\u003cabbr title=\"Monitoring, evaluation and learning\"\u003eMEL\u003c/abbr\u003e) \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eAdapting to a changing climate is a dynamic problem involving complex environmental and socioeconomic systems, such as our food or energy systems.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDue to the complexity of this challenge, \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e is using a theory of change approach applying the logic of interventions from action to impact to developing adaptation policy. As described in the ‘Magenta Book’,\u003csup id=\"fnref:390\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:390\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 390]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e which sets out guidance on evaluation in government, a theory of change captures the reasoning behind how an intervention is expected to work. The main steps involved in achieving the desired outcomes will be explicitly outlined (see \u003cstrong\u003eFigure 22\u003c/strong\u003e). Equally importantly, policymakers will clearly define any assumptions made, the quality and strength of the evidence supporting those assumptions, and wider contextual factors. Monitoring, evaluation and learning are fundamental components of this approach and will be used to challenge the assumptions made and support continuous improvement.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ePlease see below schematic for the recommended process for developing plans to adapt to climate change. Initially, the impacts of climate change and the adaptation options available will be considered. The logical steps of the theory of change approach will then be followed to design an intervention. First, the impact desired will be clearly stated and then the necessary outcomes, outputs, activities and resources required to achieve it. Continuous feedback loops to monitor, evaluate, report and finally revise plans are needed throughout each stage.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-22\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 22: Schematic of the recommended process for developing plans to adapt to climate change through a theory of change approach\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv the theory of change define:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eWhat assumptions have been made?\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eWhat is the strength of the evidence base and how can it be improved?\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eWhat wider contextual factors exist?\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003chr\u003e\u003cp\u003eMonitoring, evaluation and learning fosters a culture of sharing and learning from experiences and bringing risk owning teams from across departments together into outcome-based groupings, to more easily identify synergies and interdependencies and ensure we are working together efficiently.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"approaches-and-systems-used-and-their-outputs-brbr\"\u003e3.18.3 Approaches and systems used, and their outputs \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThroughout the \u003cabbr title=\"The third National Adaptation Programme\"\u003eNAP3\u003c/abbr\u003e period, \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e will continue to support risk owning departments across UK Government to further develop and implement their adaptation plans.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Climate Change Committee’s latest progress report in 2023 introduced a new framework which assesses 13 sectors structured around social outcomes or systems impacted by climate change, known as ‘monitoring maps’. These most notably increase the focus on tangible changes in the economy, society and the environment by identifying a set of outcomes and actions necessary to deliver climate resilience within each sector (Climate Change Committee, 2023). It also expands on the enabling conditions required to achieve the outcomes, and the role of public policy in bringing them about.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Climate Change Committee (\u003cabbr title=\"Climate Change Committee\"\u003eCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e) is looking to share learnings from the UK experience and to learn from others\u003csup id=\"fnref:391\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:391\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 391]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e about theirs. The \u003cabbr title=\"Climate Change Committee\"\u003eCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e developed a set of briefings detailing the approaches, reflections and lessons learned by the \u003cabbr title=\"Climate Change Committee\"\u003eCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e in 12 years of advising the UK on emissions reductions and adapting\u003csup id=\"fnref:392\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:392\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 392]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e to climate change.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEngland will continue to champion action to advance adaptation alongside mitigation internationally, helping to build global resilience, drive action to protect those who are most vulnerable to climate change, and learn from others as per the CCCs advice. ‘The 2030 Strategic Framework for International Climate and Nature Action\u003csup id=\"fnref:393\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:393\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 393]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e’ was the first strategy to integrate our approach to climate mitigation, adaptation, and other environmental policies, to maximise co-benefits and minimise trade-offs, seeking to advance global adaptation and resilience as an international priority, including through co-beneficial mitigation and nature actions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"how-support-programmes-meet-specific-vulnerabilities-and-adaptation-needs-brbr\"\u003e3.18.4 How support programmes meet specific vulnerabilities and adaptation needs \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eClimate risks to the UK resulting from high temperatures, changes to air quality, and flooding can impact people’s health and wellbeing as well as on the delivery of health and social care services. These risks also impact on food safety, water quality and water supplies, and an increased likelihood of vector-borne disease in the UK. Such risks are more likely to negatively impact on some members of the population, including people with disabilities and older people. Of the UK population, 38% of disabled people are 65 and older (source: UK Disability Survey research report, June 2021). In addition, overseas climate change impacts can increase the presence of diseases within the UK.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"how-adaptation-actions-influence-other-development-goals\"\u003e3.19 How adaptation actions influence other development goals\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eSustainable development has been considered and integrated into actions across all critical sectors identified in \u003cabbr title=\"Third Climate Change Risk Assessment\"\u003eCCRA3\u003c/abbr\u003e, including education, health, the natural environment, and infrastructure. In addition to the actions, we are taking domestically, sustainable development is at the core of the UK’s Official Development Assistance, enabling adaptation and resilience overseas. This not only enhances the resilience of the UK to climate risk but helps support the sustainable development needs of other countries.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s International Climate Finance considers gender equality, disability inclusion and other sustainable development goals, with key performance indicators evaluating the success of UK International Climate Finance, including measurements of sustainable development objectives. More on this in chapter 4.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAdaptation and resilience of people and our natural environment contributes to many of the Sustainable Development Goals (\u003cabbr title=\"Sustainable Development Goals\"\u003eSDGs\u003c/abbr\u003e). For marine ecosystems, \u003cabbr title=\"Sustainable Development Goal 13 to take urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts\"\u003eSDG13\u003c/abbr\u003e and \u003cabbr title=\"Sustainable Development Goal 14 to conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources for sustainable development\"\u003eSDG14\u003c/abbr\u003e on Climate Action and Life Below Water are the most relevant for ocean-climate policy, and adaptation actions contribute to the UK’s progress against the targets. The UK’s Voluntary National Review of Progress against the \u003cabbr title=\"Sustainable Development Goals\"\u003eSDGs\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csup id=\"fnref:394\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:394\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 394]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e highlights strong progress against \u003cabbr title=\"Sustainable Development Goal 14 to conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources for sustainable development\"\u003eSDG14\u003c/abbr\u003e targets. The North East Atlantic Ocean Acidification Hub has been established in the UK. The Hub will act as the European regional centre for conducting monitoring and research into ocean acidification, primarily within the Northeast Atlantic region, including the submission of data to the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nations\"\u003eUN\u003c/abbr\u003e for \u003cabbr title=\"Sustainable Development Goal\"\u003eSDG\u003c/abbr\u003e 14.3 on ocean acidity.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"global-goal-on-adaptation-gga-thematic-target-3--health-brbr\"\u003e3.19.1 Global Goal on Adaptation (\u003cabbr title=\"Global Goal for Adaptation\"\u003eGGA\u003c/abbr\u003e) Thematic target 3 – Health \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eSince 2022, the climate-heath nexus has gained increasing attention, as countries recognise the importance of strengthening comprehensive policies to prevent the health impacts of climate change, building resilient and sustainable health systems, improving their ability to anticipate and implement adaptation interventions against climate-sensitive disease and health risks, bolstering climate-health information services, surveillance, early warning and response systems and a climate-ready health workforce. Subsequently, at \u003cabbr title=\"The 28th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC\"\u003eCOP28\u003c/abbr\u003e the UK announced the UK’s flagship Climate Resilient and Sustainable Health Systems Programme.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe government set out its plans to support vulnerable communities through:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cabbr title=\"Flood and Coastal Erosion Risk Management\"\u003eFCERM\u003c/abbr\u003e research and development projects\u003csup id=\"fnref:395\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:395\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 395]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, providing a critical assessment of the links between flooding and social vulnerability, social deprivation and inequalities and in the UK.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eImplementing the Approved document O\u003csup id=\"fnref:396\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:396\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 396]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e of the Building Regulations, in June 2022, to limit excess heat and solar gains across all new residential buildings. It will use recommendations from the Housing Health and Safety Rating System review to support the effective enforcement of quality and safety standards in all tenures of residential accommodation, including standards related to excess heat by 2030.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eMonitoring the occurrence of vector-borne diseases (\u003cabbr title=\"Vector-borne diseases\"\u003eVBDs\u003c/abbr\u003e); with the assistance of its specialised agencies, it will enhance surveillance and monitoring of overseas health risks as well as update the risk assessments of the Human Animal Infections Risk Surveillance (\u003cabbr title=\"Human Animal Infections Risk Surveillance\"\u003eHAIRS\u003c/abbr\u003e) group, to provide a cross-government risk assessment defining the risk of \u003cabbr title=\"Vector-borne diseases\"\u003eVBDs\u003c/abbr\u003e in the UK.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eBuilding the capacity and capability of those working in the sector and those travelling overseas to recognise cases of suspected \u003cabbr title=\"Vector-borne diseases\"\u003eVBDs\u003c/abbr\u003e to increase detection of cases, limit spread and improve patient outcomes.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eIn collaboration with its specialised agencies, making access to the Air Quality and Health Information and government Web Services available to the public and vulnerable groups.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"cooperation-good-practices-experience-and-lessons-learned\"\u003e3.20 Cooperation, good practices, experience and lessons learned\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"efforts-to-share-information-good-practices-experience-and-lessons-learned-including-as-they-relate-to-brbr\"\u003e3.20.1 Efforts to share information, good practices, experience and lessons learned, including as they relate to: \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"science-planning-and-policies-relevant-to-adaptation\"\u003e3.20.1.1 Science, planning and policies relevant to adaptation\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e is supporting teams to learn from each other by facilitating communities of practice, working groups and expert panels. These range across areas such as specific sector-based risks, monitoring and evaluation and economic appraisal.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAs part of the 2024-27 Met Office Hadley Centre Climate Programme (\u003cabbr title=\"Met Office Hadley Centre Climate Programme\"\u003eMOHCCP\u003c/abbr\u003e), government is working with the Met Office, academic partners and users of \u003cabbr title=\"UK Climate Projections\"\u003eUKCP\u003c/abbr\u003e to develop further climate science capability to support adaptation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA Climate Adaptation Research and Innovation Board (\u003cabbr title=\"Climate Adaptation Research and Innovation Board\"\u003eCARIB\u003c/abbr\u003e) has been convened to ensure that adaptation research and innovation efforts are targeted to support \u003cabbr title=\"The third National Adaptation Programme\"\u003eNAP3\u003c/abbr\u003e delivery over the plan period (2023-28). \u003cabbr title=\"Climate Adaptation Research and Innovation Board\"\u003eCARIB\u003c/abbr\u003e brings together senior representatives from government departments, non-departmental public bodies and non-ministerial departments with major climate adaptation research and innovation (\u003cabbr title=\"Research and innovation\"\u003eR\u0026amp;I\u003c/abbr\u003e) budgets or responsibilities under \u003cabbr title=\"The third National Adaptation Programme\"\u003eNAP3\u003c/abbr\u003e. This will be achieved through the development of a Climate Adaptation Research and Innovation Framework (\u003cabbr title=\"Climate Adaptation Research and Innovation Framework\"\u003eCARIF\u003c/abbr\u003e) to provide strategic direction and influence spending decisions on climate adaptation across departments and UK Research and Innovation (\u003cabbr title=\"UK Research and Innovation\"\u003eUKRI\u003c/abbr\u003e) programmes.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"integration-of-adaptation-actions-into-planning-at-different-levels\"\u003e3.20.1.2 Integration of adaptation actions into planning at different levels\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe government is improving its understanding of the distributional impacts of climate change and adaptation action through research programmes for the Independent Assessment of the fourth Climate Change Risk Assessment (\u003cabbr title=\"Fourth Climate Change Risk Assessment\"\u003eCCRA4\u003c/abbr\u003e) and the \u003cabbr title=\"UK Research and Innovation\"\u003eUKRI\u003c/abbr\u003e-\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e funded ‘Maximising UK Adaptation to Climate Change’\u003csup id=\"fnref:397\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:397\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 397]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (\u003cabbr title=\"Maximising UK Adaptation to Climate Change\"\u003eMACC\u003c/abbr\u003e) Programme.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"helping-developing-countries-to-identify-effective-adaptation-practices-needs-priorities-and-challenges-and-gaps-in-a-way-that-is-consistent-with-encouraging-good-practices\"\u003e3.21 Helping developing countries to identify effective adaptation practices, needs, priorities, and challenges and gaps in a way that is consistent with encouraging good practices\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eSince 2011, the UK has supported over 110 million people adapt to the effects of climate change. To achieve this, the UK funds a range of bilateral, regional multilateral programmes to increase adaptation action in priority sectors and assist countries with their national adaptation plans and processes.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis includes helping improve accessible early warning systems and preparations as well as developing the capacity to act on the risks identified and strengthening the delivery mechanisms that enable effective early action to reach those who need it most. The UK is the sole funder of the Risk-informed Early Action Partnership (\u003cabbr title=\"Risk-informed Early Action Partnership\"\u003eREAP\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:398\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:398\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 398]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, an initiative launched in 2019 that brings together relevant actors from the development, humanitarian and climate communities on the Early Warning Early Action (\u003cabbr title=\"Early Warning Early Action\"\u003eEWEA\u003c/abbr\u003e) agenda. \u003cabbr title=\"Risk-informed Early Action Partnership\"\u003eREAP\u003c/abbr\u003e provides international analysis, evidence, learning, coordination, and debate, to integrate and expand a systemic shift towards acting earlier to reduce the impacts of disasters, with the target of making 1 billion people safer from disasters by 2025.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK recognises that \u003cabbr title=\"Small Island Developing States\"\u003eSIDS\u003c/abbr\u003e are on the frontline of climate change and are uniquely climate and economically vulnerable. The UK’s Small Island Developing State Capacity and Resilience (\u003cabbr title=\"Small Island Developing States Capacity and Resilience Programme\"\u003eSIDAR\u003c/abbr\u003e) programme, and the Sustainable Blue Economies programme, both launched in 2022, will support access to climate finance and the development of prosperous ocean-based economies.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK supports Least Developed Countries (\u003cabbr title=\"Least Developed Countries\"\u003eLDCs\u003c/abbr\u003e) by:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eChairing the Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems Initiative (\u003cabbr title=\"Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems Initiative\"\u003eCREWS\u003c/abbr\u003e),\u003csup id=\"fnref:399\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:399\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 399]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eSupporting the Least Developed Countries Initiative for Effective Adaptation and Resilience (\u003cabbr title=\"Least Developed Countries Initiative for Effective Adaptation and Resilience\"\u003eLIFE-AR\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:400\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:400\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 400]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e programme since 2020.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe government is also assisting in building resilience locally, the Weather and Climate Information Services (\u003cabbr title=\"Weather and Climate Information Services\"\u003eWISER\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:401\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:401\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 401]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e programme enables communities and governments to better anticipate and prepare for climate shocks and stresses, reducing their impact and protecting lives, homes and livelihoods. To date, \u003cabbr title=\"Weather and Climate Information Services\"\u003eWISER\u003c/abbr\u003e has helped to avoid over £200 million worth of losses in East Africa through application of climate information and helped to improve the resilience of over 8 million people who use \u003cabbr title=\"Weather and Climate Information Services\"\u003eWISER\u003c/abbr\u003e services. Additionally, \u003cabbr title=\"Weather and Climate Information Services\"\u003eWISER\u003c/abbr\u003e in the Middle East and North Africa aims to deliver transformation in the generation and use of co-produced weather and climate services to support decision making at local, national, and regional levels.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"global-goal-on-adaptation-gga-thematic-target-6---livelihoods-brbr\"\u003e3.21.1 Global Goal on Adaptation (\u003cabbr title=\"Global Goal for Adaptation\"\u003eGGA\u003c/abbr\u003e) Thematic target 6 - Livelihoods \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK has been a leading supporter and contributor to several climate finance programmes internationally that have embedded gender inclusion within their design and combine both gender mainstreaming and gender focussed programming. For example:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK has been the leading supporter to date of the United Nations Development Programme (\u003cabbr title=\"United Nations Development Programme\"\u003eUNDP\u003c/abbr\u003e)’s Climate Finance Network (\u003cabbr title=\"Climate Finance Network\"\u003eCFN\u003c/abbr\u003e), which has a dedicated workstream on Gender and Social Inclusion and Climate Change Finance and supports the network’s countries in integrating gender and social inclusion into climate change planning and budgeting processes.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK has also worked to build women’s and girl’s climate resilience through investment in more inclusive core and shock-responsive social protection. Through the Better Assistance in Crisis (\u003cabbr title=\"Better Assistance in Crisis\"\u003eBASIC\u003c/abbr\u003e) and Gender-responsive Social Protection (\u003cabbr title=\"Gender-responsive social protection\"\u003eGSP\u003c/abbr\u003e) programmes we are providing technical assistance and expertise to support partners on how to ensure social protection systems and interventions can respond to climate risks and the differential needs of women and girls, in the \u003cabbr title=\"Coronavirus\"\u003eCOVID-19\u003c/abbr\u003e response and recovery.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"strengthening-scientific-research-and-knowledge-related-to-i-climate-including-research-and-systematic-observation-and-early-warning-systems-to-inform-climate-services-and-decision-making-ii-vulnerability-and-adaptation-iii-monitoring-and-evaluation\"\u003e3.22 Strengthening scientific research and knowledge related to: (i) Climate, including research and systematic observation and early warning systems, to inform climate services and decision-making; (ii) Vulnerability and adaptation; (iii) Monitoring and evaluation\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eResearch and information sharing are integral to building capability. Increased awareness of climate risks will improve risk management plans and enable the public, businesses and other organisations to make more informed decisions. This is why the government is supporting and funding several innovative research programmes.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eUnder the UK’s \u003cabbr title=\"The 26th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC\"\u003eCOP26\u003c/abbr\u003e Presidency, we launched the Adaptation Research Alliance (\u003cabbr title=\"Adaptation Research Alliance\"\u003eARA\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:402\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:402\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 402]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, a global coalition of over 180 organisations across the spectrum – from research to action – from 60 economies. The \u003cabbr title=\"Adaptation Research Alliance\"\u003eARA\u003c/abbr\u003e supports action-oriented research that informs adaptation solutions and reduces risks from climate change at the scale and urgency demanded by the science. The Climate Adaptation and Resilience (\u003cabbr title=\"Climate Adaptation and Resilience\"\u003eCLARE\u003c/abbr\u003e) programme\u003csup id=\"fnref:403\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:403\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 403]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e is a UK-Canada framework research programme on climate adaptation and resilience, aiming to enable socially inclusive and sustainable action to build resilience to climate change and natural hazards in Africa and Asia-Pacific. Bridging critical gaps between science and action, \u003cabbr title=\"Climate Adaptation and Resilience\"\u003eCLARE\u003c/abbr\u003e develops new tools and supports partner governments, communities, and the private sector to use evidence and innovation to drive effective solutions to the climate challenge, whilst building the capacity of both those carrying out the research and those using the resulting evidence.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"policy-innovation-and-pilot-projects-brbr\"\u003e3.22.1 Policy innovation and pilot projects \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe government has committed to support world-leading science and evidence, such as the UK Climate Projections and jointly fund a £15 million UK Research and Innovation/\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e programme to support the research and innovation needed to deliver adaptation action.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAs part of UK Research and Innovation’s ‘building a secure and resilient world’ and ‘building a green future’ strategic themes, the Maximising UK Adaptation to Climate Change (\u003cabbr title=\"Maximising UK Adaptation to Climate Change\"\u003eMACC\u003c/abbr\u003e) programme will identify the skills, standards and data provision needed to increase adaptation capability across government and wider society.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Maximising UK Adaptation to Climate Change\"\u003eMACC\u003c/abbr\u003e programme will build capacity, knowledge, and skills that will offer practical and scalable solutions to meet the UK’s challenges in the face of a changing climate and put the UK at the forefront of climate adaptation strategies at both the local and national level. The programme will also fund transdisciplinary research to collaborate and facilitate two-way transfer of knowledge between research, policy and other end users to drive transformation, helping the UK to adapt to climate change, focusing on 4 themes:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003etheme 1\u003c/strong\u003e: societies’ exposure and vulnerability to extreme climate hazards\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003etheme 2\u003c/strong\u003e: adaptation solutions\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003etheme 3\u003c/strong\u003e: future resilience and decision making\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003etheme 4\u003c/strong\u003e: enablers of adaptation\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eUK Government investment in climate services helps to provide information for the public and businesses. Evidence from a range of studies suggests that weather and climate services, including early warning systems, can lead to economic benefit-cost ratios of around 9:1, arising from the information used to improve decision making.\u003csup id=\"fnref:404\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:404\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 404]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e Supported by this investment, the Met Office Hadley Centre delivers world-leading evidence on climate variability to better inform decision-making, including the UK Climate Projections. As part of the 2024-27 Met Office Hadley Centre Climate Programme (\u003cabbr title=\"Met Office Hadley Centre Climate Programme\"\u003eMOHCCP\u003c/abbr\u003e), the UK Government is working with the Met Office, academic partners and users of \u003cabbr title=\"UK Climate Projections\"\u003eUKCP\u003c/abbr\u003e to develop further climate science capability to support adaptation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK is also the current chair and board member of the Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems Initiative (\u003cabbr title=\"Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems Initiative\"\u003eCREWS\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:405\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:405\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 405]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, a specialised financing mechanism launched in 2015 that responds to the urgent need to address climate related risks and their impacts on vulnerable communities – specifically \u003cabbr title=\"Least Developed Countries\"\u003eLDCs\u003c/abbr\u003e and \u003cabbr title=\"Small Island Developing States\"\u003eSIDS\u003c/abbr\u003e, whilst empowering the leadership of women.\u003c/p\u003e"

        "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"information-on-national-circumstances\"\u003e4.1 Information on national circumstances\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"description-of-the-systems-used-to-track-and-report-on-support-provided-and-mobilised-brbr\"\u003e4.1.1 Description of the systems used to track and report on support provided and mobilised \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK has committed to spend £11.6 billion of International Climate Finance (\u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e) between financial years 2021/22 to 2025/26. This is new and additional climate finance support from the UK’s previous \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e commitment of £5.8 billion between 2016/17 and 2020/21. The UK spent £5.98 billion within this previous commitment period.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK aims to achieve a balance between mitigation and adaptation support through its £11.6 billion \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e commitment. We have made the following further key sub-commitments:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e£1.5bn adaptation spend in 2025;\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eAt least £3bn on development solutions that protect and restore nature and biodiversity, including £1.5bn on forests, and\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eUp to £1bn on clean energy research and demonstration programmes through the Ayrton Fund\u003csup id=\"fnref:406\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:406\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 406]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eUK \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e targets strong outcomes for climate mitigation and adaptation, nature and biodiversity. We use our \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e to reduce poverty through supporting resilience and accelerating the global shift to net zero by giving developing countries access to more, better and faster finance and helping to mobilise finance from the private sector to meet climate and nature goals.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK balances our \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e spend between support for mitigation and adaptation. We invest in mitigation where there are opportunities for green-growth, where emissions are growing rapidly and in nature-rich countries that play a role as major carbon sinks to reduce future climate impacts.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOur \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e programmes support the most vulnerable, helping build the capacity of people and communities to adapt and become more resilient to the impacts of climate change, supporting transformation of systems, and helping countries and communities deal with impacts when they occur. There is more detail about our adaptation support for developing countries in chapter 3.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eUK \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e supports accelerating the clean energy transition in both energy-producing and energy-consuming sectors to help countries provide access to affordable, reliable, and clean energy for all. This transition will reduce or avoid high emissions pathways, making use of innovation, different technologies, and carbon pricing and addressing social and gender barriers to clean energy access.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn line with the recommendations from the Dasgupta Review\u003csup id=\"fnref:407\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:407\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 407]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e and the commitments set out in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework\u003csup id=\"fnref:408\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:408\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 408]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, we use \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e to protect, sustainably manage and restore nature, reviving natural and degraded terrestrial and marine ecosystems. We help the transition to nature positive economies by supporting governments, central banks, businesses, and financial institutions to integrate the value of nature into their decision-making.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e is part of the UK’s Official Development Assistance (\u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e) budget. The UK met our commitment to ensure that all new bilateral UK aligned with the Paris Agreement in 2023. In addition to \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e from the \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e budget, from 2021 onwards the UK has also reported climate eligible outflows from British International Investments (\u003cabbr title=\"British International Investment\"\u003eBII\u003c/abbr\u003e). The UK also puts \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e into \u003cabbr title=\"British International Investment\"\u003eBII\u003c/abbr\u003e; to avoid double counting, \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e inflow amounts are deducted from climate eligible outflows for reporting.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e is spent through these government departments: the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (\u003cabbr title=\"Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office\"\u003eFCDO\u003c/abbr\u003e), the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e), the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e), and the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Science, Innovation and Technology\"\u003eDSIT\u003c/abbr\u003e). \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e is allocated to these departments via a wider process called a Spending Review, where budgets are allocated to departments over a set period. The most recent Spending Review completed at end of October 2024 allocated funding for UK financial years 2024/25 to 2025/26 (i.e. April 2025 to March 2026). For UK \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e, this means budgets have been allocated to cover the full £11.6bn commitment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDepartments are responsible for their \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e expenditure but draw on shared guidance and methodologies where possible. An example of where methodologies are being improved is in \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Science, Innovation and Technology\"\u003eDSIT\u003c/abbr\u003e. \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Science, Innovation and Technology\"\u003eDSIT\u003c/abbr\u003e is developing a methodology to categorise, and attribute spend to \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e eligible projects with the view of providing a full project list with updated \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e spend during the course of 2025. The figure below outlines how \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e expenditure is identified as programmes are developed:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-23\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 23: Identification of \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image embedded\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"img\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6784f99af041702a11ca0ed3/uk-biennial-2024-figure-23.svg\" alt=\"\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003chr\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDescription of figure 23\u003c/strong\u003e:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA flowchart showing  how \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e expenditure is identified.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eInternal guidance supports processes. of \u003cstrong\u003eKey Performance Indicators\u003c/strong\u003e\u003csup id=\"fnref:410\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:410\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote id=\"fnref:417\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:417\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 417]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (\u003cabbr title=\"Creditor Reporter title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e. This includes 2 years of programme level \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e data and a narrative chapter.\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eReported via The UK’s 5th Biennial Report\u003csup id=\"fnref:418\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:418\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 418]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"description-of-challenges-and-limitations-brbr\"\u003e4.1.2 Description of challenges and limitations \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"impact-of-external-global-events\"\u003eImpact of external global events\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe previous UK Government temporarily reduced the UK’s annual \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e target from 0.7% of Gross National Income (\u003cabbr title=\"Gross National Income\"\u003eGNI\u003c/abbr\u003e) to 0.5%. We will remain one of the most generous donors amongst the \u003cabbr title=\"The Group of 7\"\u003eG7\u003c/abbr\u003e, and our \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e offer will continue to grow in line with \u003cabbr title=\"Gross National Income\"\u003eGNI\u003c/abbr\u003e. We will restore \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e spending to 0.7% of \u003cabbr title=\"Gross National Income\"\u003eGNI\u003c/abbr\u003e as soon as fiscal circumstances allow. Despite these challenges we remain committed to meeting our commitments to climate finance.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"granular-data-tracking\"\u003eGranular data tracking\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eOur programme level data tables contain several hundred individual programmes. Each programme is likely to involve several delivery partners from the original recipient of UK funding right through to the recipient of support on the ground. Each stage in the delivery chain could be at a different geographical level and be mobilising other sources of finance.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt is therefore challenging to track \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e at a granular level. It requires capacity and capability to manage this and overall internal resources to deliver the \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e are not unlimited. It also requires data and information from external sources.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"finance-mobilised-from-technical-assistance\"\u003eFinance mobilised from Technical Assistance\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eAs part of the set of Key Performance Indicators (\u003cabbr title=\"Key Performance Indicators\"\u003eKPIs\u003c/abbr\u003e) developed to monitor and track outcomes and impacts from across UK \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e programmes, there are indicators for measuring private and public finance mobilised for climate action. However, these build on the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development (\u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development\"\u003eOECD\u003c/abbr\u003e) methodologies for mobilised finance, so do not capture the widest extent of finance catalysed by \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e interventions, or mobilised through technical assistance.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK welcomes the scrutiny of other organisations on our \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e to provide external assurance and identify areas of improvement. An example of this is from the Independent Commission for Aid Impact’s (\u003cabbr title=\"Independent Commission for Aid Impact\"\u003eICAI\u003c/abbr\u003e) rapid review of the \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e that was published in February 2024\u003csup id=\"fnref:419\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:419\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 419]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. The government response to this report was published\u003csup id=\"fnref:420\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:420\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 420]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e in December 2024.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"information-on-experience-and-good-practices-to-incentivise-further-private-climate-financing-and-investment-brbr\"\u003e4.1.3 Information on experience and good practices to incentivise further private climate financing and investment \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"incentivising-private-climate-financing\"\u003eIncentivising private climate financing\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eA key focus of the UK’s \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e is mobilising private finance to support the transition to low-carbon and climate-resilient development pathways in developing countries. Our latest cumulative \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e results show that our \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e spend has mobilised £7.8bn in private finance to support climate change. The annual amounts reported for 2021 and 2022 in our \u003cabbr title=\"Common Tabular Format\"\u003eCTF\u003c/abbr\u003e tables are £2.085bn and £1.28bn.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK uses a variety of financial instruments, including grants, concessional loans, returnable loans, performance-based incentives, guarantees, and insurance, to mobilize private finance. These instruments are designed to reduce the perceived risks associated with low-carbon investments, making them more attractive to private investors. An example is the Renewable Energy Performance Platform (\u003cabbr title=\"Renewable Energy Performance Platform\"\u003eREPP\u003c/abbr\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"desnzfcdo-case-study-repp\"\u003e\n\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e/\u003cabbr title=\"Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office\"\u003eFCDO\u003c/abbr\u003e case study: \u003cabbr title=\"Renewable Energy Performance Platform\"\u003eREPP\u003c/abbr\u003e\n\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Renewable Energy Performance Platform\"\u003eREPP\u003c/abbr\u003e provided technical and financial support to private sector developers of small-scale renewable energy projects in sub-Saharan Africa. \u003cabbr title=\"Renewable Energy Performance Platform\"\u003eREPP\u003c/abbr\u003e provided tailored support and funding required in individual project finance deals to enable developers to overcome barriers to investment. These barriers include a lack of early-stage funding, costly risk mitigation instruments, underdeveloped capital markets and weak or immature policy and regulatory frameworks. To overcome these barriers, \u003cabbr title=\"Renewable Energy Performance Platform\"\u003eREPP\u003c/abbr\u003e provided project development capital to support work such as feasibility studies. It also provided viability gap finance using a range of financial instruments and structures.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSome examples of \u003cabbr title=\"Renewable Energy Performance Platform\"\u003eREPP\u003c/abbr\u003e results are a US$1m development loan to construction of Mpanda 10.2 \u003cabbr title=\"Megawatts\"\u003eMW\u003c/abbr\u003e run-of-river hydropower plant in Burundi, US$1.2m mezzanine loan to Tanzania’s first ever wind farm, which began operations in July 2020, providing much-needed energy security to a growing rural population and US$2.9m to Bboxx data-driven platform that provides access to innovative products and services like plug-and-play solar home systems (\u003cabbr title=\"Plug and Play solar home systems\"\u003eSHS\u003c/abbr\u003e), solar-powered water pumps and e-mobility solutions to cash-loan funding. Bboxx is making good progress in transforming the utility sector through its increased presence in West Africa.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK is also using its \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e to mobilise private finance by providing technical assistance to support regulatory reforms and build the capacity of key institutions in developing countries. This helps create a stable and predictable investment environment that encourages private sector participation in climate projects.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK funds research, development, and demonstration projects to accelerate the commercialization of innovative clean energy technologies. This includes supporting early-stage testing and scaling of new technologies and business models. Some examples of this can be seen further on in this chapter.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"supporting-policy-change\"\u003eSupporting policy change\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe third Portfolio Evaluation of UK \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e, Support for Policy Change\u003csup id=\"fnref:421\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:421\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 421]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, found evidence that \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e had supported some aspects of policy change, and that the UK’s approach was valued by most policymakers and other donors. We welcomed the findings of this evaluation and published a Management Response\u003csup id=\"fnref:422\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:422\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 422]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. Key findings were:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e works in a collaborative, non-prescriptive style in partner countries, to support the types of policy changes beneficial to climate and the environment. This collaborative approach creates a sense of ownership by partner governments which increases the likelihood of policy change occurring, and it being effective and sustainable.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e has been effective in supporting changes to forestry and land-use policy in Colombia and Indonesia, and renewable energy policy in Uganda.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eFour types of intervention were successful in supporting policy change in national and sub-national government:\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003col\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eGenerating and brokering evidence to convince people to change policy\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eExploiting opportunities to convince a critical mass of decision makers to change\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eEmpowering others to advocate for or deliver policy change through capacity-building, and\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eProviding resources to deliver policy change.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eFive types of intervention were successful in supporting policy change in global institutions:\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003col\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eFinancial leverage\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eCreating momentum through coalitions of support\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eBuilding confidence through UK expertise\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eLeadership, and\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eBuilding capability through experience\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"example\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eCase study: \u003cabbr title=\"Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation\"\u003eREDD+\u003c/abbr\u003e Early Movers (\u003cabbr title=\"REDD+ Early Movers Programme\"\u003eREM\u003c/abbr\u003e) Programme\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e has supported the \u003cabbr title=\"REDD+ Early Movers Programme\"\u003eREM\u003c/abbr\u003e programme, which aims to reward countries or jurisdictions considered as pioneers in forest protection and climate mitigation. One of the areas the \u003cabbr title=\"REDD+ Early Movers Programme\"\u003eREM\u003c/abbr\u003e programme operates in is Mato Grosso in Brazil, where the programme has delivered a project called Muxirum Quilombola. The main objectives of the Muxirum Quilombola project were to ensure communities could be empowered politically, socially, culturally and economically, with a focus on Quilombolo women and youth. Muxirum Quilombola has benefitted more than 500 Quilombola families, promoting sustainable management, environmental preservation and income generation.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"example\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eCase Study: Nationally Determined Contributions Partnership\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e has supported the \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution Partnership\"\u003eNDCP\u003c/abbr\u003e (Nationally Determined Contributions Partnership), which is a partnership of over 120 countries and almost 100 institutions, formed after the signing of the Paris Agreement, to help countries effectively implement their commitments and access finance, supporting ambitious climate action whilst enhancing sustainable development.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eThrough the \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution Partnership\"\u003eNDCP\u003c/abbr\u003e, the UK supports developing countries to turn their \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contributions\"\u003eNDCs\u003c/abbr\u003e and other relevant climate plans into specific strategies and measures, support their implementation, as well as coordinating major climate donors to more effectively meet the needs identified.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eAn example of the impact of the \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution Partnership\"\u003eNDCP\u003c/abbr\u003e is in Colombia. Here, the Colombian government requested the support of the \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution Partnership\"\u003eNDCP\u003c/abbr\u003e to improve the quality and ambition of their \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e, and mobilise financial resources for \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e investment projects. The British Embassy in Colombia was able to support this process, using their strong relationship with the Colombian government facilitated by the UK-Colombia Partnership for Sustainable Growth\u003csup id=\"fnref:423\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:423\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 423]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. Five embedded advisor roles, including in-country facilitators and a climate finance advisor, were recruited by the \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution Partnership\"\u003eNDCP\u003c/abbr\u003e Support Unit, utilising funds from the UK Country Engagement Fund. These roles were dispersed across the Colombian Ministries of Environment and Sustainable Development, National Planning, Finance, and Agriculture.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eThe support from the \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution Partnership\"\u003eNDCP\u003c/abbr\u003e helped the Colombian government to agree a revised \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e in 2020 that included a more ambitious mitigation target of not emitting more than 169.4 \u003cabbr title=\"Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents\"\u003eMtCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003eeq by 2030, equivalent to a 51% reduction in emissions from a revised 2030 reference scenario, as compared to a 20% reduction in their first \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eThus far the Climate Finance Broker Facility (established via the \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution Partnership\"\u003eNDCP\u003c/abbr\u003e facilitator in the Colombian Ministry of National Planning) has supported 7 projects with over US$1m of funding from institutional members such as the Global Green Growth Institute (\u003cabbr title=\"Global Green Growth Institute\"\u003eGGGI\u003c/abbr\u003e), the United States Agency for International Development (\u003cabbr title=\"United States Agency for International Development\"\u003eUSAID\u003c/abbr\u003e), the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (\u003cabbr title=\"United Nations Department for Economic and Social Affairs\"\u003eUNDESA\u003c/abbr\u003e) and the World Wildlife Fund (\u003cabbr title=\"World Wildlife Fund\"\u003eWWF\u003c/abbr\u003e). Coordination across these members would not be possible without \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e Partnership support.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"efforts-taken-to-enhance-comparability-and-accuracy-of-information-reported-brbr\"\u003e4.1.4 Efforts taken to enhance comparability and accuracy of information reported \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo ensure the UK’s \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e information is accurate and comparable to other sources of climate finance, we work through several mechanisms. We engage closely through the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e transparency process, not only in reports such as this, but in the Facilitative Multilateral Consideration of Progress and through the in-donor peer review process, where we participate both as an assessee and an assessor.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe also work closely with the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee (\u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee\"\u003eOECD-DAC\u003c/abbr\u003e) and member countries. For example, we attend regular meetings of \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development\"\u003eOECD\u003c/abbr\u003e \u003cabbr title=\"Development Assistance Committee\"\u003eDAC\u003c/abbr\u003e’s Working Party on Development Finance Statistics (\u003cabbr title=\"Working Party on Development Finance Statistics\"\u003eWP-STAT\u003c/abbr\u003e) to discuss technical issues related to \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e reporting. A significant amount of recent work has been on harmonising \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development\"\u003eOECD\u003c/abbr\u003e and \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e climate finance reporting practices and aligning key guidance such as the Rio Marker handbook with the Paris Agreement.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK, through its \u003cabbr title=\"The 26th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC\"\u003eCOP26\u003c/abbr\u003e presidency, led on the development of the $100bn climate finance delivery plan\u003csup id=\"fnref:424\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:424\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 424]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e and has been closely involved in subsequent work with the \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development\"\u003eOECD\u003c/abbr\u003e and donors to publish follow up reports on progress towards the $100bn goal. The most recent of these was published in May 2024\u003csup id=\"fnref:425\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:425\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 425]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, reporting that in 2022 a total of $115.9bn of climate finance was mobilised for developing countries, the first year that the $100bn goal has been exceeded.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK Government is committed to supporting the greater use of International Aid Transparency Initiative (\u003cabbr title=\"International Aid Transparency Initiative\"\u003eIATI\u003c/abbr\u003e) data and other aid information across all recipient countries of \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e and works closely with other donors in country to support development outcomes.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK Government is actively engaged in efforts to fortify international aid transparency standards. This is achieved through collaboration with \u003cabbr title=\"International Aid Transparency Initiative\"\u003eIATI\u003c/abbr\u003e, Civil Society Organisations, implementing partners, and other donor countries by advocating for higher aid transparency standards. The UK encourages our implementing partners to publish data on UK-funded activities in accordance with the \u003cabbr title=\"International Aid Transparency Initiative\"\u003eIATI\u003c/abbr\u003e standard and provides them with the necessary guidance to do so. In line with this, information on \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e programming managed by UK Government departments is available on the \u003cabbr title=\"International Aid Transparency Initiative\"\u003eIATI\u003c/abbr\u003e Datastore\u003csup id=\"fnref:426\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:426\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 426]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e and the UK’s Development Tracker website (\u003cabbr title=\"Development Tracker\"\u003eDevTracker\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:427\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:427\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 427]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. Our commitment to this cause remains steadfast as we continue to work towards enhancing transparency in international aid.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe ensure the accuracy of our financial information by having all payments go through an internal approval process involving a programme team, a financial team and finally senior management. In the case of \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e, a third party provides finance services such as payment processing, meaning additional checks will be carried out. Once payments are made, they are recorded on the finance journal, which also goes through an internal checking process. \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e teams will use the journal data to record the payment in internal data systems, which in turn are used for external reporting. Data for external reporting will also be quality assured to check for accuracy. For example, the \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e programme level data was originally collated for the UK’s annual provisional \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e publication and then collated again for the UK’s final \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e publication. It has also been compiled and provided to the \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee\"\u003eOECD-DAC\u003c/abbr\u003e to support their work on reporting on progress towards $100bn.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor reporting mobilised finance, the UK developed a Key Performance Indicator (KPI 12)\u003csup id=\"fnref:428\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:428\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 428]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e for applicable \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e programmes to report against. To ensure comparability, the methodology for this KPI is aligned with \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development\"\u003eOECD\u003c/abbr\u003e \u003cabbr title=\"Development Assistance Committee\"\u003eDAC\u003c/abbr\u003e methodologies for measuring the amounts mobilised from the private sector by official development finance interventions. Accuracy is ensured through a robust quality assurance process: each \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e programme reports results, these are quality assured by an analyst working closely with the programme lead. The results are then aggregated up by department and quality assured as a whole, then \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e results are signed off by the Head of \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e Portfolio and Strategy and the Head of International Climate and Energy Analysis. Results are then aggregated across \u003cabbr title=\"Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office\"\u003eFCDO\u003c/abbr\u003e, \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e and \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs\"\u003eDefra\u003c/abbr\u003e and quality assured again, then assembled into an annual statistics publication and signed off again by Senior staff in each department before publication\u003csup id=\"fnref:429\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:429\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 429]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e will continue to place a strong focus on Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (\u003cabbr title=\"Monitoring, evaluation and learning\"\u003eMEL\u003c/abbr\u003e) to improve the effectiveness of our investments and those of our partners. This will be achieved through strengthening the evidence base and facilitating learning about sustainable approaches to reduce poverty and tackle climate change and environmental degradation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe intended impact is to deliver transformational climate change programmes. We will build on our robust cross-government results framework and will continue to publish results annually, to allow the public to track progress against our Key Performance Indicators (\u003cabbr title=\"Key Performance Indicators\"\u003eKPIs\u003c/abbr\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAll \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e programmes are required to collect and report on relevant \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e \u003cabbr title=\"Key Performance Indicators\"\u003eKPIs\u003c/abbr\u003e, disaggregated by gender, age, and disability where possible, alongside other programme-specific indicators. Where the UK co-funds a programme with other donors, only ‘UK-attributed’ \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e results are included, in proportion to the UK’s donor share.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor each key performance indicator, results are added together across all relevant programmes and over time, to give cumulative results across the whole \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e portfolio. We use \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e \u003cabbr title=\"Key Performance Indicators\"\u003eKPIs\u003c/abbr\u003e alongside a broad range of evidence to evaluate the success of our \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e programmes and inform funding decisions to maximise value for money and the successful delivery of our strategic climate, nature and sustainable development objectives. We will continue to review the \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e \u003cabbr title=\"Key Performance Indicators\"\u003eKPIs\u003c/abbr\u003e and the way we use them to inform our decision-making, to ensure that we are achieving climate, and nature impacts in line with our priorities and the needs of developing countries.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp id=\"figure-24\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFigure 24: \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e results achieved from April 2011 to March
