greenhouse gas emissions supported by TA\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003chr\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Independent Committee for Aid Impact (\u003cabbr title=\"Independent Commission for Aid Impact\"\u003eICAI\u003c/abbr\u003e) regularly undertakes external assessments of the \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e performance – 2 reviews focused on low-carbon and forestry \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e programmes have rated different aspects of operation as ‘Green-Amber’. \u003cabbr title=\"Independent Commission for Aid Impact\"\u003eICAI\u003c/abbr\u003e recommendations as well as evidence generated through monitoring and evaluation are actively fed back into strategy, programme development and implementation. For the current phase of delivery, \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e analysts are working across government to update our approach to portfolio monitoring and evaluation, building on lessons learnt from \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e to date.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"information-on-institutional-arrangements-for-the-provision-of-technology-development-and-transfer-and-capacity-building-support\"\u003e4.2 Information on institutional arrangements for the provision of technology development and transfer and capacity-building support\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK Government departments responsible for delivering our \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e commitment work together in several ways for the provision of technology development and transfer and capacity building support. There is more detail on technology development and transfer later in this chapter. Drawing on each department’s expertise, \u003cabbr title=\"Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office\"\u003eFCDO\u003c/abbr\u003e, \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e and \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Science, Innovation and Technology\"\u003eDSIT\u003c/abbr\u003e work together on the Ayrton Fund. \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Science, Innovation and Technology\"\u003eDSIT\u003c/abbr\u003e have key research organisations such as UK Research and Innovation (\u003cabbr title=\"UK Research and Innovation\"\u003eUKRI\u003c/abbr\u003e) as some of their arms-lengths bodies and deliver many of their \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e projects through UK universities. \u003cabbr title=\"Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office\"\u003eFCDO\u003c/abbr\u003e draw on their overseas network and use this to ensure support can be country specific. Whilst \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e are responsible for much of the domestic policy on areas such as energy transition and draw on this expertise in a developing country context.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis complementary approach across departments is also used for the provision of capacity building support. We have used some case studies below to demonstrate this.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"example\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eCase study: \u003cabbr title=\"Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office\"\u003eFCDO\u003c/abbr\u003e overseas network engagement with UK-based teams\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office\"\u003eFCDO\u003c/abbr\u003e has a large network of individuals with significant skills and experience in international delivery of \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e programmes. \u003cabbr title=\"Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office\"\u003eFCDO\u003c/abbr\u003e’s people, presence, instruments and systems allow us to deliver catalytic global leadership, multilateral and private sector leverage, and significant direct, real-world, bilateral results and impact. The \u003cabbr title=\"Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office\"\u003eFCDO\u003c/abbr\u003e has a strong Climate and Environment Cadre based overseas and in the UK. Additional Cadres such as the Food and Agriculture and Urban and Infrastructure are deeply engaged in delivery of our international climate finance. Programme Managers are a key element of the strong expertise that exists across \u003cabbr title=\"Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office\"\u003eFCDO\u003c/abbr\u003e for \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e delivery, overseeing spend and tracking results and will work closely with advisors.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"example\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eCase study: Sustainable Cooling and Cold Chain Solutions (\u003cabbr title=\"Sustainable Cooling and Cold Chain Solutions programme\"\u003eSCCCS\u003c/abbr\u003e) programme\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eSustainable Cooling and Cold Chain Solutions (\u003cabbr title=\"Sustainable Cooling and Cold Chain Solutions programme\"\u003eSCCCS\u003c/abbr\u003e) works with United Nations Environment Programme (\u003cabbr title=\"United Nations Environment Programme\"\u003eUNEP\u003c/abbr\u003e) in partnership with the University of Birmingham to influence the uptake of cooling and cold-chains solutions across Africa and India. \u003cabbr title=\"Sustainable Cooling and Cold Chain Solutions programme\"\u003eSCCCS\u003c/abbr\u003e uses a ‘hub and spoke’ model; setting up regional hubs and developing \u003cabbr title=\"Specialised Outreach and Knowledge Establishments\"\u003eSPOKES\u003c/abbr\u003e (Specialised Outreach and Knowledge Establishments) to share research, innovation and knowledge on cooling and cold-chains for both food and vaccine supply chains. There are additional workstreams supporting the development of modelling, policies and tools that implement global best practice and provide technical assistance for policy makers. Since its establishment in 2019 the programme has influenced the uptake of cooling and cold-chains solutions in 51 developing countries and supported over 1,600 people to adapt to the effects of climate change by improving food and vaccine preservation.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"example\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eCase study: \u003cabbr title=\"UK Partnering for Accelerated Climate Transitions\"\u003eUK PACT\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eUK Partnering for Accelerated Climate Transitions (\u003cabbr title=\"UK Partnering for Accelerated Climate Transitions\"\u003eUK PACT\u003c/abbr\u003e) supports \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e-eligible countries with high mitigation potential to increase their climate ambitions and implement that ambition more rapidly, more effectively, and more equitably. \u003cabbr title=\"UK Partnering for Accelerated Climate Transitions\"\u003eUK PACT\u003c/abbr\u003e is jointly funded and governed by the \u003cabbr title=\"Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office\"\u003eFCDO\u003c/abbr\u003e and \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy \u0026amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)\"\u003eDESNZ\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eKey features of \u003cabbr title=\"UK Partnering for Accelerated Climate Transitions\"\u003eUK PACT\u003c/abbr\u003e are that it aims to respond explicitly to partner government demand for capacity building interventions, and that it shares UK expertise (for example in areas such as climate legislation, green finance, and smart energy). \u003cabbr title=\"UK Partnering for Accelerated Climate Transitions\"\u003eUK PACT\u003c/abbr\u003e operates through a ‘hybrid’ model of dedicated programme funded teams of \u003cabbr title=\"Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office\"\u003eFCDO\u003c/abbr\u003e Officials based overseas providing local context to programme strategy and implementation in-country, and UK based officials providing global programme strategy and delivery.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eBetween April 2021 and March 2022, \u003cabbr title=\"UK Partnering for Accelerated Climate Transitions\"\u003eUK PACT\u003c/abbr\u003e delivered 114 mitigation technical assistance projects across 16 partner countries.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003e30 skill-shares and 7 secondments were delivered, with 6,265 people receiving training, with training beneficiaries rating the trainings as 4.5/5 in terms of usefulness.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eThe programme delivered full scale country programmes in Colombia, Mexico, South Africa, China, and extensions were agreed to extend 44 projects from the first funding rounds to provide multi-year delivery.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"example\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eCase study: Small Island Developing States Capacity and Resilience Programme (\u003cabbr title=\"Small Island Developing States Capacity and Resilience Programme\"\u003eSIDAR\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eAnnounced at \u003cabbr title=\"The 26th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC\"\u003eCOP26\u003c/abbr\u003e in Glasgow, the \u003cabbr title=\"Small Island Developing States Capacity and Resilience Programme\"\u003eSIDAR\u003c/abbr\u003e programme aims to raise £40m over 5 years to \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e-eligible Small Island Developing States (\u003cabbr title=\"Small Island Developing States\"\u003eSIDS\u003c/abbr\u003e) to increase capacity and improve international funding and policy frameworks. This will enable \u003cabbr title=\"Small Island Developing States\"\u003eSIDS\u003c/abbr\u003e governments to better access and utilise climate finance available to them.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cp\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Small Island Developing States Capacity and Resilience Programme\"\u003eSIDAR\u003c/abbr\u003e programme has delivered some important outcomes. These include:\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cul\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003eSupporting the Resilient and Sustainable Islands initiative (\u003cabbr title=\"Resilient and Sustainable Islands Initiative\"\u003eRESI\u003c/abbr\u003e) to launch the Resilient monthly podcast series;\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003eHosting the first public engagement and high-level technical discussions on the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nations\"\u003eUN\u003c/abbr\u003e’s Multidimensional Vulnerability Index (\u003cabbr title=\"Multidimensional Vulnerability Index\"\u003eMVI\u003c/abbr\u003e);\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003ePutting in place 2 regional agreements supporting the Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre and Global Green Growth Institute in the Pacific;\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003eSupporting 2 events that considered how to address financing and economic issues facing \u003cabbr title=\"Small Island Developing States\"\u003eSIDS\u003c/abbr\u003e, and;\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003eTaking forward a new partnership for sustainability and resilience through \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development\"\u003eOECD\u003c/abbr\u003e Development Assistance Committee and the Alliance of Small Island States (\u003cabbr title=\"Alliance of Small Island States\"\u003eAOSIS\u003c/abbr\u003e) Taskforce\u003csup id=\"fnref:430\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:430\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 430]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"underlying-assumptions-definitions-and-methodologies\"\u003e4.3 Underlying assumptions, definitions and methodologies\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s climate finance reporting methodology is set out below:\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"reporting-year-brbr\"\u003e4.3.1 Reporting Year \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eCalendar year. We have reported spend for 2021 and 2022 in our data tables referenced in section 3. The £11.6bn \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e commitment starts in the UK fiscal year 21/22, which runs from April to March. So, 2021 calendar year figures will include some spend from the previous \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e commitment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"exchange-rate-brbr\"\u003e4.3.2 Exchange Rate \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe report in pound sterling and convert to United States dollars using the \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development\"\u003eOECD\u003c/abbr\u003e annual exchange rate\u003csup id=\"fnref:431\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:431\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 431]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e for the relevant year.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"funding-status-brbr\"\u003e4.3.3 Funding Status \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe use the ‘committed’ status for our reported spend. This reflects that the money has been accounted as spent from government budgets and the figures we report are the same as how we are tracking the budget internally. We do not report political pledges that have not yet been followed up with actual funding being provided. For some programmes, such as our contributions to multilateral funds, we use a funding instrument called a Promissory Note. This commits a level of funding to the named recipient of the note, who is then able to request cash drawdowns from the note, which the government (as the note issuer) provides. For accounting purposes (and therefore our reporting methodology) we report the spend at the point the Promissory Note is formally issued and not the subsequent cash drawdowns.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"channel-brbr\"\u003e4.3.4 Channel \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe report the channel as multilateral for those funds and core contributions to organisations already pre-named on the multilateral tab\u003csup id=\"fnref:432\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:432\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 432]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e In addition if we have reported the spend as multilateral for our wider \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e reporting to the \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee\"\u003eOECD-DAC\u003c/abbr\u003e, we will also use this channel.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAll other spend will be reported under the bilateral channel. We will use the multi-bilateral channel for specific programmes via multilateral organisations. We don’t use the regional channel.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"funding-source-brbr\"\u003e4.3.5 Funding Source \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eMost of our reported climate finance comes from the UK’s \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e budget. The only exception are climate eligible outflows from the British International Investments (see section 1.1 for further information).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"financial-instrument-brbr\"\u003e4.3.6 Financial Instrument \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe report most of our spend as grant as this finance is provided with no requirement for return of funds back to us (except where funding is unused once a programme has finished or in cases where funding has been misused). We do report some spend as equity as this relates to programmes where we invest in vehicles that will purchase assets where we have a legal right to returns made on these assets. There is also a programme that uses a combination of grant and equity finance.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"concessional-finance-brbr\"\u003e4.3.7 Concessional finance \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eAs most of our climate finance comes from the UK’s \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e budget it must comply with the \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee\"\u003eOECD-DAC\u003c/abbr\u003e rules on \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e eligibility as well as spending requirements set out in the UK’s International Development Act\u003csup id=\"fnref:433\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:433\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 433]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e. We use \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee\"\u003eOECD-DAC\u003c/abbr\u003e PSI (Private Sector Instrument) rules for our equity spend which includes assessments both as the institutional level (the entity that receives our funding) and at the instrument level (the downstream investment made by that entity) to ensure the finance is concessional and the value reported reflects the development effort made. Returns from these instruments that come back to UK Government count as negative \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e and will count against \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e targets unless re-spent.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"type-of-support-brbr\"\u003e4.3.8 Type of support \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe assess whether our support is mitigation or adaptation as part of the overall process set out in figure 1, where we use the \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development\"\u003eOECD\u003c/abbr\u003e Rio Marker guidance. We only report spend as cross-cutting where we are not able to split the amounts for example subscription payments to the \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"sectorsub-sector-brbr\"\u003e4.3.9 Sector/sub-sector \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor the sector classification, we assess the programme to see which of the drop-down sectors is the best fit (Energy, Transport, Industry, Agriculture, Forestry, Water and Sanitation, Cross-Cutting or Other). We will use ‘Other’ where the other main sector choices don’t seem a good match and will include a more specific sector, typically this will be the sub-sector choice.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor sub-sector classification we report the same \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee\"\u003eOECD-DAC\u003c/abbr\u003e 5-digit sector code as used for the same programme when reporting the spend to the \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee\"\u003eOECD-DAC\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"capacity-building-andor-technology-development-and-transfer-objectives-brbr\"\u003e4.3.10 Capacity building and/or technology development and transfer objectives \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eMany of the programmes we support with our \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e will be contributing to these objectives. For example, capacity building and other types of technical assistance are often an essential element to ensuring the other objectives of the programme can be achieved. In our reporting we select a set of examples that showcase how our \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e is supporting these objectives rather than attempting to report every programme that is contributing.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe use our knowledge of the programme to identify which programmes to tag and will draw on other sources of information e.g. the summary description of the programme on \u003cabbr title=\"Development Tracker\"\u003eDevTracker\u003c/abbr\u003e (see footnote 4) or if the programme (for tagging as capacity building) has been marked with the ‘Free-Standing Technical Co-operation’ marker under our \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee\"\u003eOECD-DAC\u003c/abbr\u003e reporting.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe’ve recently developed an additional 4 Key Performance Indicators to monitor \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e technical assistance programmes – covering countries supported, individuals and organisations supported, climate policies informed, and emissions reduced or avoided supported by \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e technical assistance\u003csup id=\"fnref:434\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:434\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 434]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"climate-specific-support-brbr\"\u003e4.3.11 Climate specific support \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003ePlease see figure 1 for an overview of the process used to identify if our programmes are climate specific and the level of climate finance we should report. Again, the Rio Marker guidance is used to support this assessment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"avoiding-double-counting-brbr\"\u003e4.3.12 Avoiding double counting \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe report our climate finance spend at the point the money leaves government; this means we do not double count contributions made by other donors. For example, our contribution to a multi-donor trust fund such as the Green Climate Fund (\u003cabbr title=\"Green Climate Fund\"\u003eGCF\u003c/abbr\u003e) is done when we make contributions to the \u003cabbr title=\"Green Climate Fund\"\u003eGCF\u003c/abbr\u003e itself rather than when the \u003cabbr title=\"Green Climate Fund\"\u003eGCF\u003c/abbr\u003e makes downstream payments into specific projects, at which point all the donor contributions will be mixed increasing the risk of double-counting.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor private finance reporting, where possible we use project level information to make sure that there is no double-counting. The data we report to the \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development\"\u003eOECD\u003c/abbr\u003e is also used in their climate finance provided and mobilised report, after the \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development\"\u003eOECD\u003c/abbr\u003e has done additional checks to make sure there’s no double-counting across donors. By using the \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development\"\u003eOECD\u003c/abbr\u003e \u003cabbr title=\"Development Assistance Committee\"\u003eDAC\u003c/abbr\u003e methodologies for measuring the amounts mobilised from the private sector by official development finance interventions we are minimising the likelihood of double counting occurring.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWe don’t use \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e to purchase carbon credits for compliance with our own domestic climate targets, so we avoid double-counting in this type of support under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eUnless we are the sole funder or there is clear country specific agreement associated with our funding, we don’t attribute our spend to specific individual countries. If a programme is benefitting multiple countries (and the selection is specific enough to mean that a less granular geographic level e.g. global or regional is not more appropriate) then we will list those countries for that programme reporting line in our data tables under section 3. But we won’t report a specific spend amount per country.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAs covered under section 1.1 we avoid double counting the climate finance spend through \u003cabbr title=\"British International Investment\"\u003eBII\u003c/abbr\u003e by deducting the \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e inflow amount from the climate eligible outflows we report.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"private-finance-brbr\"\u003e4.3.13 Private finance \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eFunding is only classified as ‘mobilised private climate finance’ if it meets 3 definitional tests:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ePrivate finance test: Is the finance provided by a private organisation?\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFinance is classified as public or private based on the type of organisation providing the finance. In general, organisations are defined as public if they are government agencies, or if governments own more than 50% of equity/shares in an organisation with multiple shareholders (for example, a bank with both public and private shareholders). In all other cases, they are classified as private organisations.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn some cases, this ownership-based approach may not accurately reflect the character of financial transactions made by organisations that are publicly owned but operate according to market-oriented commercial or private principles. In these cases, programmes may classify reporting based on who exercises control of investment decisions or based on the principles used to make investment decisions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eClimate finance test: Is the finance intended for climate change adaptation or mitigation purposes?\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFinance is categorised as climate finance if the purpose of the project/programme includes support to meet climate change mitigation and/or adaptation goals, based on \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development\"\u003eOECD\u003c/abbr\u003e Statistical Reporting Directives. Climate financing is not determined based on whether the source of the finance is nominally drawn from a climate change fund/window/etc.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf finance also provides support to other (non-climate) goals, only the portion of the funding directed towards climate goals is counted as climate finance.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eMobilised finance test: Has the finance been mobilised by the \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e, i.e. is it additional and causally linked to \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e funding or support?\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eMobilised finance is funding from another actor that has been directed to an objective, project or programme that would otherwise not have benefitted from these funds and is a direct result of the original mobilising actor’s efforts.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis doesn’t include finance that would have occurred anyway without the initial \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e. This definition requires funds to be additional, in that they would not otherwise have been allocated to a climate objective or activity, and that the \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e programme can identify a causal link between its funding or actions and the mobilised finance.\nMobilised resources need to be estimated based on boundaries to define the scope and account for the total private finance that could be associated with different public interventions. We aim to establish these boundaries at project-level, according to different instruments:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eProject-level boundaries for grants, loans and syndicated loans. In these cases, mobilised financing might include upfront project level financing (i.e. resources committed to the project from the private sector at the time of project approval) or subsequent financing following UK investment (i.e. resources mobilised after the project has been operating, such as when commercial banks or venture capital funds finance a project part-designed or financed by the UK Government).\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eFor other types of financial instruments, such as guarantees and Collective Investment Vehicles, the precise boundaries will vary according to the level and quality of available data, as well as causality considerations based on conservative approaches.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eWe follow the guidance in the \u003cabbr title=\"Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development\"\u003eOECD\u003c/abbr\u003e \u003cabbr title=\"Development Assistance Committee\"\u003eDAC\u003c/abbr\u003e methodologies on reporting for specific instruments, including on setting appropriate boundaries at the instrument level.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eMobilised private finance is reported based on the year in which the finance is legally committed by the organisation/actor. To note in our private finance mobilised data set submitted as part of this \u003cabbr title=\"Biennial Transparency Report\"\u003eBTR\u003c/abbr\u003e - The amount mobilised reported by the UK represents the private finance mobilised that can be attributed to the UK within the given year only (i.e. 2022 only) whilst the amount of resources used to mobilise the support represents the total UK commitment to the programme and not the amount committed in the given year. This means the 2 figures cannot be directly compared across programmes as the amount mobilised is an in-year value whilst the amount of resources is a cumulative figure.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"ensuring-support-addresses-needs-and-priorities-of-developing-countries-brbr\"\u003e4.3.14 Ensuring support addresses needs and priorities of developing countries \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK uses a variety of approaches to ensure that its climate finance support is addressing the needs and priorities of developing countries. The UK’s work on aligning all \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e with the Paris Agreement includes a requirement that the spend must be aligned, and where possible elevate, to countries \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e’s and adaptation plans. Individual programme business cases (which are publicly available via the \u003cabbr title=\"Development Tracker\"\u003eDevTracker\u003c/abbr\u003e website) will set out in more detail how this requirement is being met.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK provides support for programmes that developing countries can bid into, where the application and assessment process will require that the funding proposals are aligned with a country’s climate action plans. For example, the Mitigation Action Facility\u003csup id=\"fnref:435\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:435\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 435]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e or the Green Climate Fund\u003csup id=\"fnref:436\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:436\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 436]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e where a funding proposal must be supported by a letter from the recipient country government.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK also supports programmes that facilitate wider access to climate finance for countries climate action plans. These include the UK setting up the Taskforce on Access to Climate Finance and supporting programmes such as the \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e Partnership\u003csup id=\"fnref:437\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:437\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 437]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e and the Climate Finance Accelerator\u003csup id=\"fnref:438\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:438\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 438]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"how-support-is-in-line-with-the-long-term-goals-of-the-paris-agreement-brbr\"\u003e4.3.15 How support is in line with the long-term goals of the Paris Agreement \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eAs referenced elsewhere in this chapter, the UK has committed to align its bilateral \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e spend with the Paris Agreement and delivered on this from 2023. The UK will continue to engage with our multilateral partners to ensure our multilateral \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e can also be aligned. The UK is implementing this commitment by:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eUndertaking climate risk assessments for \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e programming\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eUsing carbon pricing in \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e programme appraisals\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eEnsuring \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e programming is line with the UK Government’s fossil fuel policy\u003csup id=\"fnref:439\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:439\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 439]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eEnsuring that \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e programming is aligned to, and where possible elevate, countries \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contributions\"\u003eNDCs\u003c/abbr\u003e and adaptation plans.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"new-and-additional-finance-brbr\"\u003e4.3.16 New and additional finance \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK determines that its climate finance is new and additional as our £11.6bn commitment is completely new climate finance from our previous £5.8bn commitment. Also, the finance reported under section 3 has not been reported in previous \u003cabbr title=\"United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change\"\u003eUNFCCC\u003c/abbr\u003e biennial reports.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"how-the-information-provided-represents-a-progression-from-previous-levels-of-finance-under-the-paris-agreement-brbr\"\u003e4.3.17 How the information provided represents a progression from previous levels of finance under the Paris Agreement \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK’s current 5 year £11.6bn \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e commitment is a doubling of its previous 5-year commitment of £5.8bn. Within the £11.6bn, the UK has a target to spend £1.5bn on adaptation in 2025, which is a doubling of the adaptation the UK spent in 2019.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere will be annual fluctuations in the UK’s level of climate finance based on the budget allocations made in the Spending Review process and these in turn can be impacted by in-year pressures (see section 4.2 for examples of these). But the overall volumes of climate finance the UK is providing are increasing.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"multilateral-finance-brbr\"\u003e4.3.18 Multilateral finance \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK uses a combination of in-flow and outflow approaches to determine the level of multilateral finance reported. Where the UK has deemed that a multilateral is providing 100% climate finance e.g. Climate Investment Funds, then our full in-flow contribution is reported as climate specific. Where a multilateral fund or programme is deemed as providing less than 100% climate finance e.g. Global Environment Facility, then the UK splits the level of its inflow contribution as general and climate specific. The assessment on the level of climate finance is estimated by the scope of the fund/programmes activities to determine what amount is climate specific.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor the years covered under this \u003cabbr title=\"Biennial Transparency Report\"\u003eBTR\u003c/abbr\u003e report (2021 and 2022) the UK is not reporting as climate finance its core contributions to multilateral banks e.g. World Bank. However as set out in the UK’s written ministerial statement (see footnote 7) in future years, the methodology will change and climate specific shares from multilateral bank core contributions will be reported.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"information-on-financial-support-provided-and-mobilized-under-article-9-of-the-paris-agreement\"\u003e4.4 Information on financial support provided and mobilized under Article 9 of the Paris Agreement\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"united-kingdom-brbr\"\u003e4.4.1 United Kingdom \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK has included the relevant information and data in the climate finance reporting tables.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"jersey-brbr-3\"\u003e4.4.2 Jersey \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eJersey Overseas Aid (\u003cabbr title=\"Jersey Overseas Aid\"\u003eJOA\u003c/abbr\u003e) is the Island’s independent, publicly funded relief and development agency. Its annual budget is distributed through development and humanitarian funding streams. \u003cabbr title=\"Jersey Overseas Aid\"\u003eJOA\u003c/abbr\u003e allocates its funding through bilateral partnerships with pre-approved international non-governmental organisations (\u003cabbr title=\"Non-Governmental Organisations\"\u003eNGOs\u003c/abbr\u003e), multilateral organisations and \u003cabbr title=\"United Nations\"\u003eUN\u003c/abbr\u003e Agencies.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eBetween 2018-2022, \u003cabbr title=\"Jersey Overseas Aid\"\u003eJOA\u003c/abbr\u003e streamlined its development programme – operating in 6 countries across 3 thematic areas: Dairy for Development, Financial Inclusion and Conservation Livelihoods. Each of the themes contain cross-cutting components that indirectly contribute to Article 9 of the Paris Agreement. In particular, the Conservation, Lives and Livelihoods portfolio contributes to climate resilience and conservation efforts with a strategic focus on ‘the link between human development and environmental protection.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn addition, \u003cabbr title=\"Jersey Overseas Aid\"\u003eJOA\u003c/abbr\u003e’s humanitarian funding stream includes direct response to the effects of climate change globally.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"guernsey-brbr-3\"\u003e4.4.3 Guernsey \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Guernsey Overseas Aid and Development Commission (\u003cabbr title=\"Gurnsey Overseas Aid \u0026amp; Development Commission\"\u003eGOA\u0026amp;DC\u003c/abbr\u003e) is part of the Guernsey government and is mandated to distribute funds for aid and development overseas by making contributions to charity programmes and to disaster and emergency relief. The \u003cabbr title=\"Gurnsey Overseas Aid \u0026amp; Development Commission\"\u003eGOA\u0026amp;DC\u003c/abbr\u003e does not provide bilateral funding. Its overall budget for 2022 was £3.225 million. This increased to £4.397million by 2024. The majority of its budget is spent on 4 workstreams. The Single Year Project Grant Aid Awards are grants of up to £55,000 (£50,000 in 2022) each for projects being undertaken by charities registered in the United Kingdom, Guernsey or Jersey. Many of these projects, but not all, relate to or include elements that help to mitigate the impact of climate change. The 2022 Budget for this workstream was £2.354 million. The Multi Year Project Grant Aid Awards are similar to the above except they are grants of up to £165,000 (£150,000 in 2022) each for projects over a 3 year period. In addition, the \u003cabbr title=\"Gurnsey Overseas Aid \u0026amp; Development Commission\"\u003eGOA\u0026amp;DC\u003c/abbr\u003e considers Multi Year Awards which demonstrate a particular focus on mitigating the impact of climate change or ‘reaching the further first’ (e.g. on the grounds of disability, ethnicity, displacement, etc.). The 2022 Budget for this workstream was £300,000. The third main workstream is Disaster and Emergency Relied Awards. Applications are welcomed from Charities already known to the Commission, or donations are made to the Disasters Emergency Committee (\u003cabbr title=\"Disasters Emergency Committee\"\u003eDEC\u003c/abbr\u003e) Live Appeals. These often are for climate related emergencies. The 2022 Budget for this workstream was £360,000. The final main workstream is Community Partnerships which encourages Guernsey community groups to raise funds for international development through this match funding scheme. The 2022 Budget for this workstream was £125,000.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Table only shows Awards made in 2021 and 2022 which fully or partially relate to mitigating climate change.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"isle-of-man-brbr-3\"\u003e4.4.4 Isle of Man \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Isle of Man International Development annual budget is distributed via 5 funding streams, which in 2018 – 2019 included an increase of £100,000, raising the budget from £2.4 million to £2.5 million. Emergency funding is reserved for the Disasters Emergency Committee (\u003cabbr title=\"Disasters Emergency Committee\"\u003eDEC\u003c/abbr\u003e) Live Appeals, which is allocated where necessary and focused on specific disaster situations, including climate related emergencies such as flooding and cyclones. The largest funding stream, International Development Partnerships, is a 2-year funding cycle worth £1.2 million per year and which is open to application by charities registered in the UK or Isle of Man. Since 2020 and remaining for 2024-2026, Climate Change is 1 of 2 designated themes for this funding stream, inviting applications for projects specifically tackling the causes and impacts of climate change globally. More locally, the Small Grants funding stream is open only to Isle of Man registered charities for up to £100,000 each per funding round, to carry out an International Development project of their design. This stream similarly welcomes applications which address the effects of climate change. All Isle of Man government funding streams are open to application by registered organisations except for Disaster and Emergency Relief, which is allocated to be mobilised at short notice.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e*Exchange rate calculated using historical exchange rates on the given payment date from Exchange Rates website\u003csup id=\"fnref:440\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:440\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 440]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ePlease see [annex 1]: Support provided by crown dependencies.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"information-on-support-for-technology-development-and-transfer-provided-under-article-10-of-the-paris-agreement\"\u003e4.5 Information on support for technology development and transfer provided under Article 10 of the Paris Agreement\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"strategies-employed-to-support-technology-development-and-transfer-including-case-studies-brbr\"\u003e4.5.1 Strategies employed to support technology development and transfer, including case studies \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eUK development assistance is actively supporting the development of new and improved technologies and business models which help tackle climate change, while also reaching the poorest; providing life changing services, creating green jobs, building resilience and boosting local and national economies.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe UK uses international climate finance (\u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e) and other levers to support technology-driven innovation that will help developing countries decarbonise high-emission sectors and move towards clean energy systems.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe UK is committed to a comprehensive, long-term and co-ordinated UK capability-building offer on clean energy access and transition for emerging and developing countries, enhancing their implementation of nationally determined contributions (\u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contributions\"\u003eNDCs\u003c/abbr\u003e).\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThis includes accelerating and scaling up the transition to clean and affordable technology in sectors such as energy and mobility, working through programmes and partnerships, such as the \u003cabbr title=\"The 26th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC\"\u003eCOP26\u003c/abbr\u003e Breakthrough Agenda, the Energy Transition Council, and others, as well as investing and working with partners to increase global funding for decarbonisation through multilateral initiatives such as the international Climate Investment Funds, Mitigation Action Facility, \u003cabbr title=\"Energy Sector Management Assistance Programme\"\u003eESMAP\u003c/abbr\u003e, and the global \u003cabbr title=\"Nationally Determined Contribution\"\u003eNDC\u003c/abbr\u003e Partnership.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe Ayrton Fund\u003csup id=\"fnref:441\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:441\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 441]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e is a UK International Climate Finance (\u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e) commitment of up to £1 billion on clean energy innovation. It is part of the wider £11.6 billion of \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e and provides Official Development Assistance (\u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e) for the Research, Development, and Demonstration (\u003cabbr title=\"Research, Development and Demonstration\"\u003eRD\u0026amp;D\u003c/abbr\u003e) of innovative, clean energy technologies and business models for developing countries over the 5-year period between April 2021 and March 2026.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe Ayrton Fund focuses on a series of high priority Ayrton Challenge technology areas, which are critical but off-track for delivery of \u003cabbr title=\"United Nations\"\u003eUN\u003c/abbr\u003e Sustainable Development Goals 7 and 13, and where the UK is well-placed to support. These include areas such as energy storage, next generation solar, sustainable cooling, clean hydrogen, smart energy systems and more.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eBy the end of Year 3 of the Ayrton Fund (FY 23/24), UK innovation-focused \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e reached 27m people in developing countries with improved access to clean energy, leveraged over \u003cstrong\u003e£1.8 billion\u003c/strong\u003e in private and public finance, reduced \u003cstrong\u003e4.1m\u003c/strong\u003e tonnes of \u003cabbr title=\"Carbon Dioxide\"\u003eCO\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003csub\u003e2\u003c/sub\u003e (equivalent to the annual carbon footprint of over 700,000 people in the UK\u003csup id=\"fnref:442\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:442\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 442]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e), and created and supported 169,000 green jobs.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eUnder the Breakthrough Agenda\u003csup id=\"fnref:443\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:443\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 443]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e launched by World Leaders at \u003cabbr title=\"The 26th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC\"\u003eCOP26\u003c/abbr\u003e, we are building coalitions, partnerships and platforms with the ambition that developing countries have ready access to aggregated, coordinated and impactful assistance in each sector of the economy.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"example\"\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eCase Studies\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\n  \u003cul\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003eUK support to the Energy Sector Management Assistance Programme (\u003cabbr title=\"Energy Sector Management Assistance Programme\"\u003eESMAP\u003c/abbr\u003e) assists low and middle-income countries to reduce poverty and boost growth through environmentally sustainable energy solutions. They work to accelerate the energy transition required to achieve \u003cabbr title=\"United Nations\"\u003eUN\u003c/abbr\u003e Sustainable Development Goal 7 to ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable, and modern energy for all.\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Energy Sector Management Assistance Programme\"\u003eESMAP\u003c/abbr\u003e-IFC Offshore Wind Development Program supported by the UK enables sharing of expertise for countries developing their own offshore wind roadmaps. It received the Collaboration Award at the Global Offshore Wind Awards 2023, recognising the Program’s efforts to accelerate deployment of offshore wind in emerging markets.\u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli\u003eA further example is, SunCulture, a Nairobi-based solar irrigation start-up supported by the \u003cabbr title=\"Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office\"\u003eFCDO\u003c/abbr\u003e and partners since 2018, has recently raised investment from British International Investments and also $27m\u003csup id=\"fnref:444\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:444\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 444]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e in Series B funding including from the Private Infrastructure Development Group (PIDG) to expand delivery of its ‘pay-as-you-pump’ solar water pumping equipment which has already reached more than 40,000 farmers in East Africa, tripling typical yields and actually reducing overall water use with more efficient irrigation approaches – boosting livelihoods and helping people adapt to more variable rainfall.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"support-provided-at-different-stages-of-the-technology-cycle-brbr\"\u003e4.5.2 Support provided at different stages of the technology cycle \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK provides support at different stages of the technology cycle and across different technology readiness levels.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor example, the Ayrton Fund covers a range of UK \u003cabbr title=\"Official Development Assistance\"\u003eODA\u003c/abbr\u003e-funded clean energy Research, Development and Demonstration (\u003cabbr title=\"Research, Development and Demonstration\"\u003eRD\u0026amp;D\u003c/abbr\u003e) support, focused on delivering real change across 3 interconnected themes which describe the whole energy system and its applications, and link with the 3 pillars of supply, demand, and delivery, while supporting the Global Net Zero agenda. access\u003csup id=\"fnref:445\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:445\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 445]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, energy system models\u003csup id=\"fnref:446\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:446\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 446]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, low carbon development\u003csup id=\"fnref:447\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:447\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 447]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, modern cooking\u003csup id=\"fnref:448\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:448\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 448]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, efficient appliances\u003csup id=\"fnref:449\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:449\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 449]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, etc.); targeted training, job placements and businesses; new clean energy master’s courses and modules\u003csup id=\"fnref:451\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:451\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote in the South. Ayrton Fund activities under this intervention have benefited 67 countries in Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and the Indo-Pacific. For example, the UK’s Clean Climate Growth (\u003cabbr title=\"Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth\"\u003eCCG\u003c/abbr\u003e) programme’s tools and training supported the development of Uganda’s Energy Transition Plan\u003csup id=\"fnref:453\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:453\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 453]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (\u003cabbr title=\"Uganda’s Energy Transition Plan\"\u003eETP\u003c/abbr\u003e). The \u003cabbr title=\"Uganda’s Energy Transition Plan\"\u003eETP\u003c/abbr\u003e sets Uganda’s pathway to achieve universal access to modern energy and sustainably power the country’s economic transformation. The \u003cabbr title=\"Uganda’s Energy Transition Plan\"\u003eETP\u003c/abbr\u003e was developed by Uganda’s Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development, with support from the International Energy Agency (\u003cabbr title=\"International Energy Agency\"\u003eIEA\u003c/abbr\u003e) in partnership with \u003cabbr title=\"Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth\"\u003eCCG\u003c/abbr\u003e. \u003cabbr title=\"Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth\"\u003eCCG\u003c/abbr\u003e provided training to Ugandan government officials in the use of \u003cabbr title=\"Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth\"\u003eCCG\u003c/abbr\u003e open-source modelling tools and supported them in the creation of energy systems models. The resulting analysis provided an input in the development of the \u003cabbr title=\"Uganda’s Energy Transition Plan\"\u003eETP\u003c/abbr\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"open-calls-brbr\"\u003e4.5.4 Open Calls \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe UK is stimulating a pipeline of new ideas and innovations in clean energy technologies and business models that have the potential to be commercialised and scaled-up in developing countries, particularly through UK-international joint ventures. The UK is achieving this by supporting open funding competitions through Energy Catalyst, which is funded through the Transforming Energy Access (\u003cabbr title=\"Transforming Energy Access\"\u003eTEA\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:454\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:454\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 454]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e platform and the Global Challenges Research Fund (\u003cabbr title=\"Global Challenges Research Fund\"\u003eGCRF\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:455\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:455\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 455]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e and has provided financial and technical support to over 90 UK-led \u003cabbr title=\"Research and development\"\u003eR\u0026amp;D\u003c/abbr\u003e projects in Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and the Indo-Pacific, across the full spectrum of Ayrton thematic challenges. So far, new demonstrators have been agreed in Tanzania and Uganda to scale-up and demonstrate eCooking from April 2024.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 Since 2011 UK \u003cabbr title=\"International Climate Finance\"\u003eICF\u003c/abbr\u003e has leveraged £7.8 billion of private finance for climate change. Examples of UK efforts to encourage private sector activity through Ayrton Fund programming:\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"transforming-energy-access-tea-platform\"\u003e4.5.10.1 Transforming Energy Access (\u003cabbr title=\"Transforming Energy Access\"\u003eTEA\u003c/abbr\u003e) platform\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eBetween 2016 and 2024, the £265m \u003cabbr title=\"Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office\"\u003eFCDO\u003c/abbr\u003e Transforming Energy Access\u003csup id=\"fnref:483\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:483\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 483]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e (\u003cabbr title=\"Transforming Energy Access\"\u003eTEA\u003c/abbr\u003e) platform, which invests in early-stage testing and scale-up of new clean energy technologies and business models for developing countries, leveraged £1.5 billion in additional investment into clean energy research, innovation and scale-up from both public and private sources.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cabbr title=\"Transforming Energy Access\"\u003eTEA\u003c/abbr\u003e-supported innovators have gone on to raise significant investment capital, including for example Sheffield-based Mobile Power\u003csup id=\"fnref:484\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:484\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 484]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e who developed an innovative battery swapping and distribution system in use in Sierra Leone, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Liberia, Uganda, Zambia, Gambia and Nigeria and have raised over £5m in follow on investment. Mobile Power have rented their portable batteries over 16 million times to date and have 55,000 active customers who use these batteries to power electric motorbikes, for phone charging, lightening, and for powering small DC appliances such as TVs and fans.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eAnother example of a \u003cabbr title=\"Transforming Energy Access\"\u003eTEA\u003c/abbr\u003e-supported innovator is Wales-based SureChill\u003csup id=\"fnref:485\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:485\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 485]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e who developed a unique cooling technology approved by the World Health Organisation that ensures a refrigerator remains perfectly cool during any power outage, and who raised over £7 million in follow on investment. SureChill refrigerators are used in several countries in Sub-Saharan Africa including Kenya, Senegal, Nigeria, Zambia, and Mali.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"africa-clean-energy-programme-ace\"\u003e4.5.10.2 Africa Clean Energy Programme (\u003cabbr title=\"Africa Clean Energy Programme\"\u003eACE\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eThe Africa Clean Energy Programme (\u003cabbr title=\"Africa Clean Energy Programme\"\u003eACE\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/strong\u003e is a regional programme including a Challenge Fund supporting start-ups or expansion of household solar energy businesses in 9 countries in Sub-Saharan Africa and supporting the deployment of mini grids through the African Development Bank.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eDuring the Ayrton Fund period, the programme leveraged £2.8 million in private finance in support of programme activities and is estimated to have provided 0.67 \u003cabbr title=\"Megawatts\"\u003eMW\u003c/abbr\u003e of installed off-grid clean energy capacity.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"global-facility-to-decarbonise-transport-gfdt\"\u003e4.5.10.3 Global Facility to Decarbonise Transport (\u003cabbr title=\"Global Facility to Decarbonise Transport\"\u003eGFDT\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe \u003cstrong\u003e\u003cabbr title=\"Global Facility to Decarbonise Transport\"\u003eGFDT\u003c/abbr\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e is a new, first of its kind World Bank Trust Fund\u003csup id=\"fnref:486\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:486\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 486]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e that provides financial and technical assistance to support transport decarbonisation in low and middle-income countries. Its mission is to accelerate innovation and investment in climate-smart mobility solutions, with the goal of achieving net zero in the global transport sector by 2050. GFTD funding and project preparation helps move big transport decarbonisation projects that otherwise would not go forward. In doing so, the Fund empowers low and middle-income countries to build transport systems that not only reduce emissions, but are also safe, modern, inclusive, and resilient.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThree \u003cabbr title=\"Global Facility to Decarbonise Transport\"\u003eGFDT\u003c/abbr\u003e innovation-focused projects have been badged as Ayrton to date, including in India (developing a new business model to help unlock commercial financing at scale for e-buses, e-motorcycles and electric 3-wheelers).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"efforts-to-accelerate-encourage-and-enable-innovation-including-research-development-and-deployment-efforts-and-collaborative-approaches-to-research-and-development-brbr\"\u003e4.5.11 Efforts to accelerate, encourage and enable innovation, including research, development and deployment efforts, and collaborative approaches to research and development \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eExamples of Ayrton Fund activities accelerating innovation include:\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"international-science-partnership-fund-ispf\"\u003e4.5.11.1 International Science Partnership Fund (\u003cabbr title=\"International Science Partnership Fund\"\u003eISPF\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eInternational Science Partnership Fund (\u003cabbr title=\"International Science Partnership Fund\"\u003eISPF\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003csup id=\"fnref:487\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:487\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 487]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e will facilitate participation of world-class UK academic researchers and their international partners in cutting-edge research. This is an existing fund that supports world-class research in cutting-edge science and innovation to tackle the major themes of our time: Planet, Health, Tech, and Talent.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eUnder the theme of ‘Resilient Planet’, \u003cabbr title=\"International Science Partnership Fund\"\u003eISPF\u003c/abbr\u003e will give researchers and innovators access to global talent, large-scale facilities, research ecosystems and markets to swiftly move forward ideas to greater maturity, applicability, and commercialisation.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe programme will build on \u003cabbr title=\"Department for Science, Innovation and Technology\"\u003eDSIT\u003c/abbr\u003e’s small portfolio of energy research and ensure a strong strategic direction of the work and coherence with other government departments. It will comprise a combination of scaling-up of existing activities, such as Innovate UK’s Energy Catalyst and EPSRC’s energy access projects, and new thematic projects in areas such as solar/biofuels, whole systems, heating/refrigeration, sustainable transport, and industrial energy.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe fund launched in December 2022 with an initial £119 million. A further £218 million was announced in November 2023 for research and innovation partnerships with low and middle-income countries to support sustainable development.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eResearch partnerships that bring together multiple countries and both university and private sector expertise, produce game-changing technologies, innovations and evidence, benefiting hundreds of millions of people in lower-income countries. The UK’s International Science Partnerships Fund is an example of how we can foster prosperity by solving shared global research and innovation challenges. Genuine partnerships are essential to achieve the ambitions set out in the UK’s Science and Technology Framework and the International Technology Strategy.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTransforming Energy Access (\u003cabbr title=\"Transforming Energy Access\"\u003eTEA\u003c/abbr\u003e) countries.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eBetween 2016 and 2024, through effective partnerships and collaborative approaches with the private sector, academia, \u003cabbr title=\"Non-Governmental Organisations\"\u003eNGOs\u003c/abbr\u003e and international organisations, \u003cabbr title=\"Transforming Energy Access\"\u003eTEA\u003c/abbr\u003e has stimulated UK-led research and development of \u003cstrong\u003e662 new clean energy technologies and business models\u003c/strong\u003e in areas such as energy storage\u003csup id=\"fnref:489\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:489\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 489]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, sustainable cooling, electric pressure cookers, remote network management, energy access crowdfunding\u003csup id=\"fnref:490\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:490\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 490]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e, improving clean energy access for \u003cstrong\u003e27 million people\u003c/strong\u003e in developing countries (including 13 million women).\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eIt has also \u003cstrong\u003eleveraged £1.5 billion\u003c/strong\u003e of additional investment into clean energy technology research, innovation and scale-up from both private and public sources; created and supported \u003cstrong\u003e125,000 sustainable long-term jobs\u003c/strong\u003e (including 27,000 jobs for women); supported \u003cstrong\u003e759 young Africans\u003c/strong\u003e with job placements and \u003cstrong\u003e1,135 managers\u003c/strong\u003e with specialist training in clean energy access businesses; and led to the \u003cstrong\u003eavoidance of 2.7 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions\u003c/strong\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch5 id=\"clean-energy-innovation-facility-ceif\"\u003e4.5.12 Clean Energy Innovation Facility (\u003cabbr title=\"Clean Energy Innovation Facility\"\u003eCEIF\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/h5\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe \u003cabbr title=\"Clean Energy Innovation Facility\"\u003eCEIF\u003c/abbr\u003e 1.0 programme, under the umbrella \u003cabbr title=\"Clean Energy Innovation Facility\"\u003eCEIF\u003c/abbr\u003e platform, aims to accelerate the commercialisation of innovative clean energy technologies in developing countries along key themes such as industrial decarbonisation, sustainable cooling, smart energy, and energy storage. A programme extension of up to £55m (\u003cabbr title=\"Clean Energy Innovation Facility\"\u003eCEIF\u003c/abbr\u003e 2.0) has been approved and started in March 2024. The \u003cabbr title=\"Clean Energy Innovation Facility\"\u003eCEIF\u003c/abbr\u003e 2.0 programme will focus on piloting and demonstrating innovative technologies across 3 key themes - industrial decarbonisation, sustainable cooling, and smart energy.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eUp to 2023/24, \u003cabbr title=\"Clean Energy Innovation Facility\"\u003eCEIF\u003c/abbr\u003e 1.0 supported 55 sustainable cooling technologies with 62 pilots in Colombia, Mexico, Nigeria, Kenya, Rwanda, India, and Bangladesh. The pilots focused on key themes, namely cooling in cities, cold chains, temperature-controlled logistics, space cooling, and cooling-as-a-service (\u003cabbr title=\"Cooling-as-a-service\"\u003eCaaS\u003c/abbr\u003e) business models. Alongside this, the International Finance Corporation (IFC) - delivery partner for \u003cabbr title=\"Clean Energy Innovation Facility\"\u003eCEIF\u003c/abbr\u003e - launched the India Cooling Innovation Lab\u003csup id=\"fnref:491\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:491\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 491]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e in December 2023 bringing together technology innovators and local companies to pilot innovative smart energy technologies.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eUnder the Industrial Decarbonisation theme, in 2023 \u003cabbr title=\"Clean Energy Innovation Facility\"\u003eCEIF\u003c/abbr\u003e supported 17 ongoing projects in Morocco, Mexico, Dominican Republic, Colombia, Türkiye, Pakistan, India, Vietnam, Bangladesh, as well as regional activities in East Asia and Pacific and those with a global reach. Under the Smart Energy theme, \u003cabbr title=\"Clean Energy Innovation Facility\"\u003eCEIF\u003c/abbr\u003e redefined the fund based on lessons learnt over the past 4 years and planned a strong pipeline of projects showcasing the impact of these changes.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"knowledge-generated-brbr\"\u003e4.5.13 Knowledge generated \u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eThe \u003cstrong\u003eUK’s Climate Compatible Growth (\u003cabbr title=\"Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth\"\u003eCCG\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/strong\u003e programme has produced knowledge products which are being used in teaching and research within 7 universities or research institutes in Low and Middle-Income Countries.\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eFurther to attending \u003cabbr title=\"Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth\"\u003eCCG\u003c/abbr\u003e training courses, academics within these 7 universities are either teaching \u003cabbr title=\"Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth\"\u003eCCG\u003c/abbr\u003e tools in their courses or using \u003cabbr title=\"Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth\"\u003eCCG\u003c/abbr\u003e tools in their research. Examples include: at Strathmore University\u003csup id=\"fnref:492\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:492\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 492]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e in Nairobi, Kenya, the \u003cabbr title=\"Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth\"\u003eCCG\u003c/abbr\u003e energy systems modelling tool OSeMOSYS\u003csup id=\"fnref:493\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:493\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 493]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e is being taught as part of the Masters of Science in Sustainable Energy Transitions; at the Addis Ababa Institute of Technology for Research Advancement\u003csup id=\"fnref:494\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:494\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 494]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e \u003cabbr title=\"Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth\"\u003eCCG\u003c/abbr\u003e tools are being used to assess the potential impact of climate change on hydropower supply in Ethiopia; at Makerere University\u003csup id=\"fnref:495\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:495\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 495]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e in Kampala, Uganda \u003cabbr title=\"Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth\"\u003eCCG\u003c/abbr\u003e tools including Model for Analysis of the Energy Demand (\u003cabbr title=\"Model for Analysis of the Energy Demand\"\u003eMAED\u003c/abbr\u003e) and OSeMOSYS\u003csup id=\"fnref:496\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:496\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 496]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e are being taught in the ‘Master of Energy Economics and Governance’ course.\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n\u003cstrong\u003eThe Accelerating Smart Power and Renewable Energy in India (\u003cabbr title=\"Accelerating Smart Power and Renewable Energy in India\"\u003eASPIRE\u003c/abbr\u003e)\u003c/strong\u003e seeks to leverage carbon financing to provide market-driven solar-powered induction cooking solutions to target households in India that are below the poverty line and use firewood as their primary cooking fuel. In 2023/24, the programme facilitated 17 strategic engagements between Indian and UK organisations, disseminated 50 technical study reports enriching knowledge exchange, and empowered 1,800 senior level stakeholders through capacity building workshops.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"footnotes\" role=\"doc-endnotes\"\u003e\n  \u003col\u003e\n    \u003cli id=\"fn:1\"\u003e\n      \u003cp\u003eBiennial Transparency reports are submitted under article 13 of the Paris Agreement in compliance with the obligations according to Decision 18/CMA.11 and following the Modalities, Procedures and Guidelines (MPGs). \u003ca href=\"#fnref:1\" class=\"reversefootnote\" role=\"doc-backlink\" aria-label=\"go to where this is referenced\"\u003e↩\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n    \u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli id=\"fn:2\"\u003e\n      \u003cp\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-uks-nationally-determined-contribution-communication-to-the-unfccc\"\u003eUK’s 2030 Nationally Determined Contribution\u003c/a\u003e \u003ca href=\"#fnref:2\" class=\"reversefootnote\" role=\"doc-backlink\" aria-label=\"go to where this is referenced\"\u003e↩\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n    \u003c/li\u003e\n    \u003cli id=\"fn:3\"\u003e\n      \u003cp\u003eThe UK’s ratification of the Paris Agreement was extended to Guernsey in 2023 at their request but has not yet been extended to the whole Bailiwick of Guernsey which includes the islands of Alderney and Sark.
