        <div class="govspeak"><h2 id="ministerial-foreword">Ministerial foreword</h2>

<p>We are halfway through the critical decade for tackling climate change, but the world is off-track to limiting global warming to 1.5°C. We are facing a triple planetary crisis of climate, biodiversity loss and pollution posing critical threats to the UK’s national interests across security, resilience, health, the economy and partnerships with other countries. That is why the UK is re-establishing itself as a climate leader on the global stage. The net zero transition is critical to both national and global security. There is no global stability without climate stability, and Britain must play its part by resetting at home and reconnecting abroad. We remain committed to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (<abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr>)’s ambitions on transparency in reporting, in particular on implementing the Enhanced Transparency Framework (<abbr title="Enhanced Transparency Framework">ETF</abbr>) and stand ready to lead by example, where we can. This report covers the period of 2021-2022 and we also set out our approach going forwards.</p>

<p><strong>The UK has made progress in cutting emissions. Between 1990 and 2022, we grew our economy by around 80% and cut our emissions by 50%</strong>.</p>

<p>In 2020, the UK communicated an ambitious Nationally Determined Contribution (<abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr>) target to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by at least 68% by 2030 on 1990 levels. In 2022 in response to the Glasgow Climate Pact at <abbr title="The 26th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC">COP26</abbr>, this target level was reconfirmed and strengthened by increasing its scope to include some crown dependencies and overseas territories and by saying more about implementation. This report sets out the progress made to meeting our 2030 <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr> through policies implemented between the years 2021 and 2022 and our plans going forward.</p>

<p>Our Third Climate Change Risk Assessment (<abbr title="Third Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA3</abbr>), published in 2022, has presented strong evidence that even under low warming scenarios the UK will be subject to a range of significant and costly impacts, including identified risks to health and productivity, the built environment, businesses, the natural environment, and to public services, unless further action is taken to adapt to climate change. Our plan to address these risks is set out in our latest National Adaptation Programme (<abbr title="National Adaptation Programme">NAP</abbr>) published in 2023. The UK Government also submitted its first Adaptation Communication to the <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> in December 2020 and updated it in 2021. The Communication set out our plans to prepare for the impacts of climate change in the UK and to support climate change adaptation overseas.</p>

<p>The UK has continued to deliver on our International Climate Finance (<abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr>) commitments. We exceeded our pledge to spend £5.8bn <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> between April 2016 and March 2021. Through our <abbr title="The 26th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC">COP26</abbr> presidency, the UK led work on a $100bn climate finance delivery plan to provide clarity on how and when developed countries would meet their finance goal. In 2024 the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (<abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development">OECD</abbr>) reported that in 2022, this goal was achieved with $115.9bn in climate finance mobilised for developing countries.</p>

<p>Looking ahead, we know we need to do more. We are committed to achieving our <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr> commitments under the Paris Agreement, and net zero target by 2050.This is no small feat requiring urgent action, but there are huge opportunities. Meeting these targets requires a wide-reaching transformation of the UK economy, with consumers, businesses and government all having a role to play. That is why making Britain a clean energy superpower is one of the 5 missions of this government - delivering clean power by 2030 and accelerating to net zero across the economy. We can only deliver energy security and good jobs for todays’ generations if we deliver clean energy. And we can only deliver climate security for future generations if we show global leadership. This is why the Prime Minister announced at <abbr title="The 29th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC">COP29</abbr> the UK’s ambitious and credible <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr> target to reduce all greenhouse gas emissions by at least 81% by 2035, compared to 1990 levels, excluding international aviation and shipping emissions. In 2025, we will publish a detailed plan, updating the policies and proposals that will enable us to meet carbon budgets 4 to 6 and our 2030 and 2035 <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contributions">NDCs</abbr>.</p>

<p>On climate adaptation, we are committed to improving the evidence base and further strengthening our approach across government and local communities and will bring forward plans in due course.</p>

<p>Our leadership at <abbr title="The 29th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC">COP29</abbr> demonstrates that the UK is a global leader in the fight against climate change, and this remains a core pillar of our approach to development spending. We will continue to prioritise Climate Finance which will help vulnerable countries adapt to climate impacts and support a transition to low-carbon economies. At <abbr title="The 29th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC">COP29</abbr>, parties agreed that all actors should scale up financing to $1.3 trillion on the New Collective Quantified Goal (<abbr title="New Collective Quantified Goal">NCQG</abbr>) on Climate Finance. The UK is committed to delivering climate finance to keep 1.5°C alive in line with our international commitments. This is why we are honouring the existing commitment to spend £11.6bn in International Climate Finance between April 2021 and March 2026 including at least £3bn on nature, from which £1.5bn will be dedicated to protecting and restoring forests. We will also treble our spend, from our <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> commitment, for adaptation to £1.5bn in 2025.</p>

<p>We look forward to our upcoming expert technical review and the Facilitative, Multilateral Consideration of Progress (<abbr title="Facilitative Multilateral Consideration of Progress">FMCP</abbr>) to improve our practice. We encourage all Parties to come forward with their first Biennial Transparency Reports (<abbr title="Biennial Transparency Reports">BTRs</abbr>) by the 31 December deadline.</p>

<p><strong>The Rt Hon Ed Miliband MP, Secretary of State for Department of Energy Security and Net Zero &amp; Minister Kerry McCarthy MP, Minister for Climate for Department of Energy Security and Net Zero</strong></p>

<h2 id="introduction">Introduction</h2>

<h3 id="scope">Scope</h3>

<p>The Biennial Transparency Report (<abbr title="Biennial Transparency Report">BTR</abbr>) is a progress report, agreed under the Enhanced Transparency Framework (<abbr title="Enhanced Transparency Framework">ETF</abbr>) under the Paris Agreement<sup id="fnref:1"><a href="#fn:1" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 1]</a></sup>. Its purpose is to present information on mitigation, adaptation and finance in a transparent and comprehensive way that can be scrutinised by parties as well as by expert reviewers. It is submitted every 2 years.</p>

<p>This is the UK’s first biennial transparency report and provides detail on progress towards the UK’s 2030 Nationally Determined Contribution (<abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:2"><a href="#fn:2" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 2]</a></sup>. This first report focuses on greenhouse gas emissions reductions between 2021 and 2022, as well as progress towards our 2030 <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr> and our emission reductions projections towards 2040. It will include an overview of our adaptation plans up to 2023 and our international climate finance contributions over 2021-2022.</p>

<p>The UK’s 2030 <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr> covers England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. It also covers the UK’s crown dependencies of the Bailiwick of Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man and the UK’s overseas territory of Gibraltar, which have all had the UK’s ratification of the Paris Agreement extended to them.</p>

<p>The report follows the requirements set out by the <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> and therefore it does not include updates on research and systematic observation, education, training and public awareness. This will be included in our 9th National Communication to be published in 2026.</p>

<p>This report also reflects the recommendations made during our last Expert Review in 2023 on our 5th Biennial Report and 9th National Communication. This includes recommendations that the UK include the cost of our policies and provide clarity on the territorial scope (i.e. explain if policies applied to the devolved governments, crown dependencies and overseas territories, or England only).</p>

<p>The report is being submitted to the <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> alongside our National Inventory Document (<abbr title="National Inventory Document">NID</abbr>).</p>

<h3 id="structure-of-the-report">Structure of the report</h3>

<p>The report is structured as follows:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<a href="#chapter-1">Chapter 1: National Inventory Document of Anthropogenic Emissions</a> presents a summary of our National Inventory Document which was submitted in December 2024.</li>
  <li>
<a href="#chapter-2">Chapter 2: Information to track progress in achieving the UK’s Nationally Determined Contribution</a> presents the UK’s mitigation actions and strategies implemented to achieve the UK’s 2030 <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr> (over the period 2021-22), and projections to 2040.</li>
  <li>
<a href="#chapter-3">Chapter 3: Information related to climate change impacts and adaptation</a> presents the UK’s adaptation measures towards adaptation.</li>
  <li>
<a href="#chapter-4">Chapter 4: Information on financial, technology development and transfer and capacity-building support provided and mobilised</a> presents the UK’s contributions to non-annex 1 parties consistent with the requirements of the Enhanced Transparency Framework.</li>
  <li>Annex 1: Support provided by the UK’s crown dependencies.</li>
</ul>

<p>The UK’s Biennial Transparency Report submission will include our complete Common Tabular Format (<abbr title="Common Tabular Format">CTF</abbr>) tables which can be found on the submission portal. The <abbr title="Common Tabular Format">CTF</abbr> tables include information on:</p>

<ul>
  <li>the UK’s Greenhouse Gas Inventory</li>
  <li>our financial support provided and mobilised</li>
  <li>progress made and projections</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="chapter-1">Chapter 1: National Inventory Document of Anthropogenic Emissions</h2>

<p>The UK’s National Inventory Document (<abbr title="National Inventory Document">NID</abbr>) is available on the <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> website. This contains a full account of the UK’s <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> emissions, their trends, the methodologies used to estimate them, and the institutional arrangements that underlie them.</p>

<p>Emissions estimates from the UK Greenhouse Gas Inventory are used to meet international reporting requirements under the Paris Agreement and <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> as well as domestic reporting requirements under the Climate Change Act 2008. The geographical scope of these reporting requirements differs:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>Climate Change Act scope</strong>: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Paris Agreement scope</strong>: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. It also includes the 3 crown dependencies (Bailiwick of Jersey, Guernsey<sup id="fnref:3"><a href="#fn:3" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 3]</a></sup>, Isle of Man) and 1 overseas territory (Gibraltar), which to date, the UK’s ratification of the Paris Agreement has been extended to.</li>
  <li>
<strong><abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> scope</strong>: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. It also includes those crown dependencies and overseas territories have had the UK’s ratification of the <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> extended to them. These are the 3 crown dependencies (Bailiwick of Jersey, Bailiwick of Guernsey, Isle of Man) and 4 overseas territories (Gibraltar, Cayman Islands, Falkland Islands, Bermuda).</li>
</ul>

<p>The Paris Agreement scope is used for emissions estimates in the Common Reporting Tables (<abbr title="Common Tabular Format">CTF</abbr>) accompanying this submission.</p>

<p id="table-1"><strong>Table 1: UK greenhouse gas emissions by geographic scope, <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e</strong></p>

<table>
  <thead>

<p><strong>Total UK greenhouse gas emissions in 2022 (Paris Agreement scope) are estimated to be 407.8 million tonnes <abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> equivalent (<abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e), a decrease of 50% from 817.1 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e in 1990</strong>. The breakdown of gases in 2022 is as follows:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> contributed 80%</li>
  <li>
<abbr title="Methane">CH</abbr><sub>4</sub> contributed 14%</li>
  <li>
<abbr title="Nitrous Oxide">N</abbr><sub>2</sub>O contributed 4%; and</li>
  <li>Fluorinated gases (<abbr title="Fluorinated gases">F-gases</abbr>) contributed 2%</li>
</ul>

<p>The sectoral breakdown in 2022 is:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Non-transport emissions from the energy sector contributed 51% to the total net emissions
    <ul>
      <li>
<abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> is the dominant gas consisting of 97% of emissions</li>
      <li>Since 1990, emissions have declined by 56%</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>Transport emissions from the energy sector contributed 28%
    <ul>
      <li>
<abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> is the dominant gas consisting of 99% of emissions</li>
      <li>Since 1990, emissions have declined by 11%</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>The agricultural sector contributed 12%
    <ul>
      <li>
<abbr title="Methane">CH</abbr><sub>4</sub> and <abbr title="Nitrous Oxide">N</abbr><sub>2</sub>O contributed 67% and 30% respectively, with the remainder made up by <abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub>
</li>
      <li>Since 1990, emissions from this sector have declined by 17%</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>Industrial processes and product use contributed 7%
    <ul>
      <li>
<abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> and <abbr title="Fluorinated gases">F-gases</abbr> contributed 68% and 29% respectively, with the remainder made up by <abbr title="Methane">CH</abbr><sub>4</sub> and <abbr title="Nitrous Oxide">N</abbr><sub>2</sub>O</li>
      <li>Since 1990, emissions have declined by 66%</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>The waste sector contributed 5%
    <ul>
      <li>
<abbr title="Methane">CH</abbr><sub>4</sub> is the dominant gas consisting of 90% of all emissions</li>
      <li>Since 1990, emissions have declined by 74%</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>The Land-Use, Land-Use Change, and Forestry (<abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr>) sector contains sinks as well as sources of <abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> emissions. <abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr> was a net source in both 1990 and 2022, and in 2022, contributed less than 0.2% to total net emissions
    <ul>
      <li>Emissions from this sector occur for <abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub>, <abbr title="Nitrous Oxide">N</abbr><sub>2</sub>O and <abbr title="Methane">CH</abbr><sub>4</sub>
</li>
      <li>Since 1990, net emissions from this sector have declined by 94%</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<h2 id="chapter-2">Chapter 2: Information necessary to track progress made in implementing and achieving <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contributions">NDCs</abbr>
</h2>

<h3 id="national-circumstances-and-institutional-arrangements">2.1 National circumstances and institutional arrangements</h3>

<h4 id="government-structure-brbr">2.1.1 Government structure <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is a Party to the <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> and the Paris Agreement. The UK employs a range of institutional structures – at national, sub-national and local level - to enable economy-wide emissions mitigation, as well as numerous policies and measures to underpin delivery. The UK consists of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, with aspects of government policy responsibility devolved to the democratically accountable governments within each, namely the Scottish Government, the Welsh Government and the Northern Ireland Executive. The UK Government has overall responsibility for implementation and delivery of the UK’s climate commitments under the <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr>, the Kyoto Protocol, and the Paris Agreement, as well as our targets for net zero by 2050, our domestic carbon budgets, and our 2030 and 2035 Nationally Determined Contributions. However, all the devolved governments play a part in this process. The approach taken by each administration will differ, drawing on the range of policies at their disposal. As explained in Chapter 1, the UK’s ratification of the Paris Agreement has to date been extended the 3 crown dependencies, and the overseas territory of Gibraltar – so these are in scope of the UK’s <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr>. Climate policy is devolved to the crown dependencies and overseas territories and so they are responsible for setting their own emission reduction targets and climate policies and laws.</p>

<p>The Climate Change Act 2008 established the world’s first legally binding framework of national emissions targets. The Act required the UK to set carbon budgets which impose legally binding limits on emissions across 5-year periods. The first 6 carbon budgets have so far been set in law. The Climate Change Committee (<abbr title="Climate Change Committee">CCC</abbr>) is an independent, statutory body established under the Climate Change Act 2008. Their purpose is to advise the UK and devolved governments on emissions targets and to report to Parliament on progress made in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and preparing for and adapting to the impacts of climate change. More information on the Climate Change Act can be found in section 2.8.1.</p>

<p>The UK Government is split into 24 ministerial departments and 20 non-ministerial departments. Each department focuses on a different aspect of government policy, the following of which fed into this report:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (<abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr>), which leads the mission to make Britain a Clean Energy Superpower, achieving clean power by 2030 and accelerating to net zero</li>
  <li>Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (<abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr>), the department responsible for policy and regulations on environmental, food and rural issues including domestic adaptation</li>
  <li>Department for Education (<abbr title="Department for Education, England">DfE</abbr>), the department responsible for children’s services and education, including early years, schools, higher and further education policy, apprenticeships and wider skills in England</li>
  <li>Department for Transport (<abbr title="Department for Transport">DfT</abbr>), which supports the transport network to help the UK’s businesses and get people and goods travelling around the country</li>
  <li>Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (<abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr>), leads on the UK’s diplomatic, development and consular work around the world</li>
  <li>Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (<abbr title="Department for Science, Innovation and Technology">DSIT</abbr>), ensures that new and existing technologies are safely developed and deployed across the UK and drive forward a modern digital government for the benefit of its citizens</li>
  <li>Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (<abbr title="Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local government">MHCLG</abbr>), lead on affordable homes and handing power back to communities and rebuilding local governments</li>
</ul>

<p>Further information about the UK Government can be found at GOV.UK<sup id="fnref:4"><a href="#fn:4" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 4]</a></sup></p>

<h4 id="northern-ireland-executive-brbr">2.1.2 Northern Ireland Executive <br><br>
</h4>

<p>In January 2020 the ‘New Decade, New Approach<sup id="fnref:5"><a href="#fn:5" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 5]</a></sup>’ was published, which set out a commitment to tackle climate change head-on using a coordinated and strategic approach.</p>

<p>On behalf of the <abbr title="Northern Ireland">NI</abbr> Executive the Department for Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (<abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr>) has led on the development of a draft Green Growth Strategy<sup id="fnref:6"><a href="#fn:6" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 6]</a></sup>, collaborating with other departments, local government and key stakeholders from across the business, voluntary and community sectors in its development.</p>

<p>To ensure that there is a coordinated and strategic approach to deliver a Green Growth Strategic Oversight Group, which is a group of senior officials from all 9 Northern Ireland (<abbr title="Northern Ireland">NI</abbr>) government departments, provides overall strategic direction for the Executive’s Green Growth and climate change commitments.</p>

<h4 id="scottish-government-brbr">2.1.3 Scottish Government <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The Scottish Government has a range of responsibilities, including climate change policy and many of its constituent lever policies. The Scottish Parliament passes laws on devolved matters, which includes a statutory framework for Scotland’s approach to tackling climate change.</p>

<p>The Scottish Government remains absolutely committed to ending Scotland’s contribution to global emissions as soon as possible, and by 2045 at the latest (through a statutory net zero target). Scotland’s emissions halved between 1990 and 2022, while our economy has grown by 67%, proving that tackling climate change and growing our economy go hand in hand.</p>

<p>Climate change is embedded across the Scottish Government through a robust ministerial and corporate governance framework. Accountability for climate action is led by the Cabinet Secretary for Net Zero and Energy and supported by the Cabinet Sub-Committee for the Climate Emergency which provides cross-government leadership, assurance and coordination of efforts.</p>

<p>At a corporate level, oversight and assurance of climate policy delivery is provided by the Global Climate Emergency (<abbr title="Global Climate Emergency">GCE</abbr>) Board of senior officials, with responsibility to ensure a whole-systems approach to delivering a just transition to net zero and strengthening climate adaptation. The <abbr title="Global Climate Emergency">GCE</abbr> Board is overseen by the Scottish Government’s Executive Team and Corporate Board. Both the <abbr title="Global Climate Emergency">GCE</abbr> Board and Corporate Board include non-executive directors as members.</p>

<h4 id="welsh-government-brbr">2.1.4 Welsh Government <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Within the Welsh Government, the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Secretary for Climate Change and Rural Affairs lead on the net zero agenda, although the Cabinet has collective responsibility for achieving Wales’ statutory emissions targets.</p>

<p>The Climate Change Portfolio Board of senior civil servants supports Cabinet decision-making. Further support is provided by the Climate Change Committee,<sup id="fnref:7"><a href="#fn:7" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 7]</a></sup> which is the Welsh Government’s statutory independent advisor on climate change.</p>

<p>The Welsh Government’s response to the climate emergency is framed by the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act (2015).<sup id="fnref:8"><a href="#fn:8" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 8]</a></sup> This requires the Welsh Government to take long-term policy decisions, involve people in the government decisions that affect them, and seek out opportunities to address the underlying causes of change. The Welsh Government’s Programme for government contains 10 well-being objectives, including “Embed our response to the climate and nature emergency in everything we do”.<sup id="fnref:9"><a href="#fn:9" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 9]</a></sup></p>

<h3 id="population-profile">2.2 Population profile</h3>

<p>This section discusses demographic characteristics of the UK, to provide context on the population-related drivers that affect the UK’s Greenhouse Gas (<abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr>) emissions. Unless stated otherwise, the following statistics have been produced from data collected by the Office for National Statistics (<abbr title="Office for National Statistics">ONS</abbr>), who produce the official population estimates for the UK and its constituent countries.</p>

<p>The total population of the UK was estimated to be 67.6 million in mid-2022, which was 10.4 million more (18% more) than in mid-1990. <strong>Table 4</strong> shows that the population of the UK is increasing and ageing with the median age in the UK increasing from 35.8 in 1990 to 40.7 in 2022. The population aged greater than 65 years increased from 15.7% in 1990 to 18.8% in 2022. The male to female ratio of the UK population has remained broadly steady between 1990 and 2022 at approximately 49% to 51%, though within these broad percentages the gap is narrowing<sup id="fnref:10"><a href="#fn:10" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 10]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>According to <abbr title="Office for National Statistics">ONS</abbr> projections, the UK is expected to see a continued growth in population, as shown in <strong>Figure 1</strong>. The population is projected to increase to 76.3 million by mid-2045, an increase equivalent to an average annual rate of growth of slightly over 0.5% between 2022 and 2045. Assumed net migration accounts for the projected increase over the next 25 years, with projected annual deaths higher than births for most of this period. <abbr title="Office for National Statistics">ONS</abbr> note that the projections do not attempt to predict the impacts of the UK leaving the EU or the lasting effects of the coronavirus pandemic.</p>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/678163f6153753104a921805/uk-biennial-2024-figure-1.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<p id="figure-2"><strong>Figure 2: Population pyramid for the UK mid-2022 (purple and green bars) compared with mid-2011 (purple and green lines)</strong></p>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/678169fc9b205eeb6cede4bc/uk-biennial-2024-figure-2.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<p>Each line in <strong>Figure 2</strong> represents a single year of age. The length of the line relates to the number of people of that age in the population. The size and composition of the population is determined by the pattern of births, deaths and migration which have taken place in previous years. The main details illustrated by the pyramid for mid-2020 include the following:</p>

<ul>
  <li>The peaks and wide areas of the pyramid reflect the high numbers of births in the years after the Second World War and during the baby boom of the 1960s.</li>
  <li>The sharp narrowing of the pyramid for people aged between 15 and 20 years is a consequence of low numbers of births just after the turn of the century. There followed an increase in birth rates peaking around 2008 to 2012. Since 2016, birth rates have fallen more rapidly.</li>
  <li>Females outnumber males at older ages, reflecting the higher life expectancy of females, though the gap has narrowed over time.</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="sex-and-youth-brbr">2.2.1 Sex and youth <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The male to female ratio of the UK population has remained broadly steady between 1990 and 2022 at approximately 49% to 51% respectively, though within these broad percentages the gap is narrowing.</p>

<h4 id="building-stock-and-urban-structure-profile-brbr">2.2.2 Building stock and urban structure profile <br><br>
</h4>

<p>In 2022, the most common types of dwellings in England were terraced houses (29%) followed by semi-detached (25%), detached (17%), purpose-built flats (17%) and all other types of dwellings (12%)<sup id="fnref:11"><a href="#fn:11" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 11]</a></sup>.</p>

<h3 id="geographical-profile">2.3 Geographical profile</h3>

<p>The UK lies between latitude 49º<abbr title="Nitrous Oxide">N</abbr> and 61º<abbr title="Nitrous Oxide">N</abbr> and longitude 8ºE and 2ºW, positioned in north-western Europe. There are 3 UK crown dependencies (the Bailiwick of Jersey, Bailiwick of Guernsey and the Isle of Man) and 14 overseas territories (listed below).</p>

<ul>
  <li>Anguilla</li>
  <li>Bermuda</li>
  <li>British Antarctic Territory</li>
  <li>British Indian Ocean Territory</li>
  <li>Virgin Islands (commonly known as the British Virgin Islands)</li>
  <li>Cayman Islands</li>
  <li>Falkland Islands</li>
  <li>Gibraltar</li>
  <li>Montserrat</li>
  <li>Pitcairn Islands</li>
  <li>Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha</li>
  <li>South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands</li>
  <li>Sovereign base areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia</li>
  <li>Turks and Caicos Islands</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="economic-profile">2.4 Economic profile</h3>

<p>In 2022, the UK had a Gross Domestic Product (<abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr>) of $3.1 trillion, making it the world’s 6th largest economy<sup id="fnref:12"><a href="#fn:12" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 12]</a></sup>. It is the 14th largest exporter of goods ($534 billion in 2022) and second largest exporter of services ($507 billion in 2022)<sup id="fnref:13"><a href="#fn:13" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 13]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>The level of real <abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr> in <abbr title="quarter 1">Q1</abbr> of 2022 was 1.3% higher than in <abbr title="quarter 4">Q4</abbr> of 2019<sup id="fnref:14"><a href="#fn:14" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 14]</a></sup>, broadly in line with other <abbr title="The Group of 7">G7</abbr> countries. Up until the Global Financial Crisis (<abbr title="Global Financial Crisis">GFC</abbr>), the rate of growth in UK real <abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr> had exceeded the rate of population growth – leading to rising <abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr> per capita. Since then, <abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr> per capita growth has slowed, and fell as a result of <abbr title="Coronavirus">COVID-19</abbr>, mirroring the fall in <abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr>. As of 2022, <abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr> per capita was around 0.6% above 2019 (pre-<abbr title="Coronavirus">COVID</abbr>) levels.</p>

<p>According to the International Monetary Fund (<abbr title="International Monetary Fund">IMF</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:15"><a href="#fn:15" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 15]</a></sup> real <abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr> growth in the UK was 4.8% in 2022. This compares with 2.5% for the USA, 1.4% for Germany, 2.6% for France, 4.7% for Italy, and 1.2% for Japan.</p>

<p>The last decade has been characterised by high employment and low unemployment, and stagnant wage growth. The employment rate peaked at 76.5% in December to February 2020, which was the highest rate since comparable records began in 1971<sup id="fnref:16"><a href="#fn:16" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 16]</a></sup>. The employment rate in 2022 was 75.1%. Similarly, the unemployment rate dropped to 3.7% in October to December 2019, the lowest since 1974, and was 3.8% in 2022<sup id="fnref:17"><a href="#fn:17" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 17]</a></sup>. Due to the furlough scheme and other interventions the impact of the <abbr title="Coronavirus">COVID-19</abbr> pandemic on employment and unemployment was relatively limited. Since the start of 2010, annual real regular pay growth has averaged just 0.3%<sup id="fnref:18"><a href="#fn:18" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 18]</a></sup> and UK wage growth since the financial crisis has been one the slowest rates among <abbr title="The Group of 7">G7</abbr> nations.</p>

<p>As shown in <strong>Figure 3</strong>, the (relatively small) rise in unemployment resulting from the <abbr title="Coronavirus">COVID-19</abbr> pandemic has largely unwound. There has been a degree of tightness in the labour market, due to record high vacancies. Job vacancies reached 1,304,000 in the second quarter of 2022, however since then the total number of vacancies has declined by nearly 400,000<sup id="fnref:19"><a href="#fn:19" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 19]</a></sup>.</p>

<p id="figure-3"><strong>Figure 3: Unemployment rate (left hand axis) and employment rate (right hand axis), <abbr title="Office for National Statistics">ONS</abbr></strong></p>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/678531e63a9388161c5d233d/uk-biennial-2024-figure-3.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<p>Prior to the <abbr title="Coronavirus">COVID-19</abbr> pandemic, the UK had generally enjoyed low and stable inflation, broadly in line with the Bank of England’s 2% target. Since summer 2021 however, the UK like other developed nations, experienced a rapid rise in inflation driven by mostly external factors. These include high prices for energy and other commodities, exacerbated recently due to the war in Ukraine, a mismatch of global supply and demand, as well as base effects – abnormally low inflation in 2020 due to the pandemic.</p>

<p>Consumer Price Index (<abbr title="Consumer Price Index">CPI</abbr>) inflation, see <strong>Figure 4</strong>, reached 11.1% in October 2022. This is the highest level of price inflation in the UK for more than 40 years. As a result, real pay growth returned to being negative for the first time since 2017. <abbr title="Consumer Price Index">CPI</abbr> inflation returned to the target of 2% in May 2024.</p>

<p id="figure-4"><strong>Figure 4:<abbr title="Consumer Price Index">CPI</abbr> Annual Inflation (%)<sup id="fnref:20"><a href="#fn:20" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 20]</a></sup>, <abbr title="Office for National Statistics">ONS</abbr></strong></p>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/678534d3c6428e0131881712/uk-biennial-2024-figure-4.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<p>The UK economy is dominated by the service sector, accounting for over 80% of gross value added (<abbr title="Gross Value Added">GVA</abbr>) and employment<sup id="fnref:21"><a href="#fn:21" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 21]</a></sup>. Prior to the <abbr title="Coronavirus">COVID-19</abbr> pandemic, the fastest growing sector in the economy since the global financial crisis was the information and communication sector, which grew by around 130% between <abbr title="quarter 3">Q3</abbr> 2009 and <abbr title="quarter 4">Q4</abbr> 2019, largely as a result of technological progress within the sector.</p>

<p>Looking at more recent data, <abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr> grew by 0.7% in <abbr title="quarter 1">Q1</abbr> 2022. Services grew by 0.8% on the quarter meaning it was 2.5% above pre-pandemic (<abbr title="quarter 4">Q4</abbr> 2019) levels. Construction grew by 3.0%, and is 1.7% above pre-pandemic levels, while production fell by 1.9% and remains 5.8% below pre-pandemic levels.</p>

<p>UK Government consumption and investment are the only expenditure component of <abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr> (the others being household consumption, business investment and net exports) that has risen since the start of the coronavirus pandemic, largely driven by health spending, and mirroring the growth seen in the health sector on the output measure. UK Government consumption has grown by 8.5% since the start of the coronavirus pandemic. Conversely, private consumption (-1.3%), business investment (5.0%) and net trade have all detracted from <abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr> growth since <abbr title="quarter 4">Q4</abbr> 2019.<sup id="fnref:22"><a href="#fn:22" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 22]</a></sup></p>

<h3 id="climate-profile">2.5 Climate profile</h3>

<p>The UK’s climate is maritime, moist and temperate, with a winter mean temperature of 4.1 °C and summer mean temperature of 14.6 °C. The influence of the Atlantic Ocean means that the UK’s annual temperature range is smaller than for more continental countries at the same latitude. Average annual precipitation in the UK typically ranges from approximately 800 mm to 1400 mm, but with significant regional variations with western upland regions experiencing in excess of 2000 mm and parts of low-lying south-east England less than 600 mm. The UK climate is heavily influenced by its proximity to the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf Stream / North Atlantic Drift which brings warm water into high northern latitudes. Prevailing winds are westerly, and UK regional climates vary with distance from the Atlantic as well as with local topography. Continental influences are most strongly seen in the southeast of the country.</p>

<p>Variations in the strength and position of the jet stream strongly influence UK weather. Sometimes the jet stream is directed close to or over the country, bringing extended periods of stormy, wet weather. At other times, a blocked pattern steers the jet stream away to the north or to the south, bringing generally settled, dry conditions, either warmer or colder than average. Space heating is required in most buildings throughout the winter months and the use of air conditioning in the summer months is increasing. In the UK, <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> emissions are strongly influenced by weather conditions. In winter, cooler-than-average temperatures increase demand for space heating; and in summer, warmer-than-average temperatures increase demand for space cooling. <strong>Figure 5</strong> shows the average daily mean temperature for the UK by season.</p>

<p id="figure-5"><strong>Figure 5: Average (1991-2022) daily temperature (°C) by season, UK (source: Met Office)</strong></p>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/678636153ef063b15dca0f42/uk-biennial-2024-figure-5a.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67863622f0528401055d2387/uk-biennial-2024-figure-5b.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<h4 id="uk-climate-trends23-brbr">2.5.1 UK climate trends<sup id="fnref:23"><a href="#fn:23" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 23]</a></sup> <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="temperature">2.5.1.1 Temperature</h5>

<p>The Central England Temperature (<abbr title="Central England Temperature">CET</abbr>) series is the longest-compiled instrumental temperature record in the world, beginning in 1659. <strong>Figure 6</strong> shows that the <abbr title="Central England Temperature">CET</abbr> for the early 21st century has been warmer than the previous 3 centuries for all seasons of the year.</p>

<p id="figure-6"><strong>Figure 6: Seasonal Central England Temperature Anomaly series, 1659 to 2023, relative to 1991-2020 average<sup id="fnref:24"><a href="#fn:24" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 24]</a></sup></strong></p>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6781224800e3d719f19217de/uk-biennial-2024-figure-6.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<p>The UK-wide national temperature series begins in 1884, showing an increase in temperature from the 1970s to the 2000s with the most recent decade (2014-2023) on average 0.42 °C warmer than the 1991-2020 average and 1.25 °C warmer than 1961-1990. All 10 warmest years recorded for the UK have been since 2003. Evidence from attribution science shows that the increasing trend in temperatures is overwhelmingly a result of human activities, in particular emissions of greenhouse gases.</p>

<p>Cold years are still observed despite the warming trend, but they are less frequent and less severe than in the historical record: 2010 was the coldest year recorded since 1986 and the 22nd coldest in the UK series since 1884.</p>

<h5 id="precipitation">2.5.1.2 Precipitation</h5>

<p>Precipitation data for the UK show a slight increase from the 1970s onwards (<strong>Figure 7</strong>) that is most pronounced for Scotland. The most recent decade (2014–2023) has been on average 2% wetter than 1991-2020 and 10% wetter than 1961–1990. Five of the 10 wettest years for the UK have occurred since 2000, in a series beginning in 1836.</p>

<p>The largest increases in rainfall have been during the winter season, with the most recent decade (2014-2023) having winters 24% wetter than 1961-1990. This period includes the 2 wettest winters on record in 2013-2014 and 2015-2016, with winter 2019-2020 as the fifth wettest in a series from 1836. Summers of the most recent decade (2014-2023) have also been 10% wetter than 1961-1990. This changing trend in rainfall in the UK is a result of both human influence and large-scale natural variability in the climate system, which can occur over time periods of decades.</p>

<p id="figure-7"><strong>Figure 7: Annual precipitation, UK, 1836–2023<sup id="fnref:25"><a href="#fn:25" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 25]</a></sup></strong></p>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6784f0bd3ef063b15dca0ec7/uk-biennial-2024-figure-7.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<h5 id="sea-level">2.5.1.3 Sea level</h5>

<p>Since 1900 sea level around the UK has risen by about 18.5 cm when corrected for vertical land movement, which is comparable to the global sea level rise estimate of 20 cm. There is evidence from the observational records that the rate of sea level rise is increasing from a long-term estimate of 1.5 mm/yr, with the period 1993-2023 increasing by around 4.6 mm/year. Sea surface temperatures around the UK for the most recent decade (2014-2023) have been on average 0.3 °C warmer than the 1991-2020 average and 0.9 °C warmer than 1961-1990.</p>

<h4 id="climate-projections-brbr">2.5.2 Climate projections <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The latest UK Climate Projections (<abbr title="UK Climate Projections 2018">UKCP18</abbr>) provide the most up-to-date assessment of how the UK climate is projected to change in the future and includes modelling projections for 3 spatial resolutions (60km, 12km and 2.2km), probabilistic projections including extremes, and projections of sea-level rise, storm surges and waves.</p>

<p>One strand of the modelling projections is <abbr title="UK Climate Projections">UKCP</abbr> Local; the first time a climate model with a resolution similar to weather forecasting models has been used to explore national climate scenarios. This is a step forward in the ability of the climate model to simulate small-scale behaviour seen in the real atmosphere, particularly for the representation of the heavy rainfall associated with showers that affect flooding in summer. In this section, <abbr title="UK Climate Projections">UKCP</abbr> information is used to summarise the projected effects on UK climate, both in terms of averages and extremes<sup id="fnref:26"><a href="#fn:26" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 26]</a></sup>, followed by impact metrics. <abbr title="UK Climate Projections">UKCP</abbr> data were used in the most recent UK Climate Change Risk Assessment (<abbr title="UK Climate Change Risk Assessment">UKCCRA</abbr>) and are being applied by the more than 7,000 registered users to quantify and manage physical climate risks.</p>

<h5 id="uk-future-climate-overview">2.5.2.1 UK future climate overview</h5>

<p>The headline findings of <abbr title="UK Climate Projections 2018">UKCP18</abbr> state that future UK climate change will result in warmer, wetter winters and hotter, drier summers. Annual temperatures for the UK for a medium emissions scenario<sup id="fnref:27"><a href="#fn:27" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 27]</a></sup> from the <abbr title="UK Climate Projections">UKCP</abbr> Probabilistic Projections suggest warming of 2.3°C (1.1°C to 3.6°C)<sup id="fnref:28"><a href="#fn:28" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 28]</a></sup> by the end of the century (2080- 2100) compared to the 1981-2000 baseline period. Warming is projected to be greater in summer (3°C; 1.3°C to 4.8°C) than in winter (2°C; 0.6°C to 3.5°C). UK-wide, summer precipitation decreases are expected to be -19% (-36% to -2%) while winter precipitation is projected to increase 10% (-2% to 25%) by the 2090s.</p>

<p>Notable UK-wide features, such as warming being greater in the summer compared to the winter are projected to occur across all regions of the UK for both low and high emissions scenarios<sup id="fnref:29"><a href="#fn:29" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 29]</a></sup>. Similarly, the majority of UK regions are projected to experience a decrease in summer precipitation and an increase in winter precipitation. Across both seasons and emissions scenarios, regional variations are generally modest within each metric, with differences usually within 1°C or 10%, the high emissions scenario winter precipitation showing the greatest spread between regions.</p>

<p>Sea level is projected to rise around the UK compared to a 1981-2000 baseline period although the amount of sea level rise is higher in the south and increases with higher emissions scenarios. For the medium emissions scenario (RCP4.5), the <abbr title="UK Climate Projections">UKCP</abbr> Marine Projections give rises of 0.55 m (0.40 m to 0.75 m)<sup id="fnref:30"><a href="#fn:30" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 30]</a></sup> in London compared to lower values of 0.33 m (0.18 m to 0.53 m) in Edinburgh in 2100. Based on exploratory results to 2300, sea levels continue to increase beyond 2100 even with large reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. For the same medium emissions scenario, sea level is projected to rise for London by 1.42 m (0.93m to 2.23 m) and 0.77 m (0.28 m to 1.6 m) for Edinburgh by 2300. However, the uncertainty around post-2100 simulations remain large due to gaps in understanding related to the role of the large ice sheets.</p>

<h5 id="uk-future-climate-extremes">2.5.2.2 UK future climate extremes</h5>

<p>For day-to-day extremes, <abbr title="UK Climate Projections 2018">UKCP18</abbr> provides extremes in terms of return periods (the average time between events) for maximum temperatures and heavy rainfall. These results project increases in both the values and range over the course of the 21st century.</p>

<p>The median values of high temperature and heavy rainfall expected to occur once every 50 years are projected to increase in all seasons under an illustrative high emissions scenario (RCP8.5). For example, by 2070 with a high emissions scenario, the daily maximum temperature of a 1-in-50-year event is projected to be 2.5°C (winter) and 3.7°C to 4.3°C (spring, summer, autumn) warmer than in 1990. For rainfall, the median 1-in- 50-year event is expected to have 12-19% (daily rainfall) or 11-13% (5-day accumulated rainfall) more rainfall in 2070 than in 1990 in autumn, winter or spring, with smaller increases expected in summer<sup id="fnref:31"><a href="#fn:31" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 31]</a></sup>.</p>

<p><abbr title="UK Climate Projections">UKCP</abbr> Local models have better representation of how rainfall varies day-to-day and hour-to- hour. For hourly rainfall that is expected to occur once every 2 years, <abbr title="UK Climate Projections">UKCP</abbr> Local projects that this will be 29% heavier in the summer under a future climate with a high emissions scenario (2060-2080, RCP8.5). Similar increases are projected for rarer events and in the autumn, with smaller increases projected in spring and winter.</p>

<h5 id="uk-climate-impact-metrics">2.5.2.3 UK climate impact metrics</h5>

<p><abbr title="UK Climate Projections 2018">UKCP18</abbr> data has also been translated into metrics that quantify the expected future impacts of weather on society at different Global Warming Levels (<abbr title="Global Warming Levels">GWLs</abbr>), ranging from 1.5°C above the pre-industrial level (consistent with a low emissions scenario by 2100) to 4°C (consistent with a high emissions scenario by 2100). Projections show increases for temperature metrics related to hot events, accompanied by reductions in metrics related to cold events.</p>

<p>The number of hot days (over 25°C) in the UK is projected to increase by between 5 days and 39 days per year. This could mean increased hospital admissions for those vulnerable to heat and increased transport disruption, for example from railway track buckling at higher temperatures. The projections show a 2 to 7-fold increase in an indicator of the energy demand for cooling (known as cooling degree days). Increases are also projected in an indicator of the energy available for plant growth over a year (growing degree days) of 19% to 60%. Occurrences of tropical nights, when the temperature falls no lower than 20°C, are rare in the current climate but become more frequent in a warmer climate, particularly in southeast England and in urban areas.</p>

<p>Conversely, the projections show a reduction in the number of frost days (below 0°C) of between 10 and 49 days per year. Decreases are also found in an indicator of energy demand for heating (known as heating degree days) of 11% to 32%, implying a decrease in the adverse effects of cold weather.</p>

<p>Impacts related to rainfall include projected increases in heavy rainfall events that could cause flooding and increases in average drought severity. The projections show an increase in occurrence of high-impact levels of daily rainfall from 1 day to 8 days per year. Average drought severity is projected to increase at most <abbr title="Global Warming Levels">GWLs</abbr> but with a small decrease possible with a low 1.5°C GWL, with changes of -3% to 19% for 12-month drought duration, and -2% to 54% for 36-month drought duration.</p>

<h3 id="sector-details">2.6 Sector details</h3>

<h4 id="energy-brbr">2.6.1 Energy <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK published its Net Zero Strategy in 2021, which included its commitment to decarbonise the electricity sector by 2035, subject to security of supply. This was submitted to the <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> as the UK’s Long Term Low Emissions Development Strategy in 2021. Policies to support this and increase energy security were set out in this document and in the subsequent British Energy Security Strategy which was published in 2022 following Russia’s invasion of the Ukraine. The main policy focus was to increase energy efficiency and accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels through the decarbonisation of the power sector and increased electrification of heat, transport and industry.</p>

<h5 id="energy-production">2.6.1.1 Energy production</h5>

<p>Total UK energy production increased rapidly between 1990 and 2000, mainly due to the growth of oil and gas. Production in 2000 was at record levels for natural gas, while in 1999 it was at record levels for overall energy and petroleum. Energy production has since been on a general decline, however energy production levels increased between 2014 and 2019, as new oil fields opened, combined with the growth in output from bioenergy and waste and the increased capacity of wind and solar technologies.</p>

<p>In 2022, total energy production was 110.2 million tonnes of oil equivalent, 3.1% higher than the record low level of 106.8 million tonnes of oil equivalent in 2021. Production levels for all fuels except coal, oil and bioenergy and waste are up on 2021, with oil output at a record 21st century low level. UK energy production had fallen year on year since 2018 before the rise in 2022, and energy production is now 63% below the peak recorded in 1999.</p>

<p>In 2022, coal production fell by 39% to a record low level, whilst production of oil fell by 7.6% to a record low level, with output down by 28% on pre-pandemic (2019) levels; conversely production of natural gas rose by 16% in 2022.</p>

<h5 id="energy-consumption-and-transformation">2.6.1.2 Energy consumption and transformation</h5>

<p>In 2022<sup id="fnref:32"><a href="#fn:32" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 32]</a></sup> total primary energy consumption was 168.6 mega tonnes of oil equivalent (<abbr title="Megatonnes of Oil Equivalent">mtoe</abbr>), 1.3% lower than in 2021, with record high temperatures and higher energy prices a key factor in the reduced consumption levels. The level of primary energy consumption in 2022 was 21% lower than in 1990; primary energy consumption levels peaked in 2001 and since then there has been a general downward trend. In the last 33 years, consumption of natural gas and primary electricity have risen, whilst consumption of oil and coal have fallen. However, over the past decade, the growth in consumption of bioenergy and waste has more than doubled.</p>

<p>In 2022<sup id="fnref:33"><a href="#fn:33" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 33]</a></sup> total final energy consumption including non-energy use was 130.9 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Oil Equivalent">mtoe</abbr>, 2.1% lower than in 2021, and 11% lower than pre-pandemic (2019) levels. The level of final energy consumption in 2022 was 17% lower than in 1990. The largest fall in final energy consumption since 1990 has occurred in the industrial sector, mainly due to structural change in the period before 2000; in the domestic sector there has been a general downward trend in consumption due to improvements in energy efficiency measures, and more recently due to the impact of higher energy prices.</p>

<h5 id="electricity">2.6.1.3 Electricity</h5>

<p>Between 1990 and 2022 electricity supply emissions have reduced by 73%. This decrease has resulted mainly from changes in the mix of fuels being used for electricity generation, including the growth of renewables; together with greater efficiency resulting from improvements in technology. The electricity supply sector historically had the largest emissions of the sectors presented in these statistics. However, these reductions mean that since 2014 this has no longer been the case and there are now several sectors with higher emissions (the largest being transport).</p>

<p>Since 1990 there has been a decline in the use of coal at power stations and an increase in the use of gas, which has a lower carbon content so results in fewer emissions. Coal use in generation reduced by 97% between 1990 and 2022, making up only 3% of the fuel used for UK electricity generation in 2022 compared to 65% in 1990. Electricity supplied was 4% higher in 2022 than in 1990, having grown to a peak in 2005 and decreased since then. In 2022 the use of gas for electricity generation increased 1% from 2021 and the use of renewables and nuclear both by 5%, whereas coal saw a 16% decrease<sup id="fnref:34"><a href="#fn:34" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 34]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>The British Energy Security Strategy published in 2022 included ambitions for up to 50 <abbr title="Giggawatts">GW</abbr> of offshore wind by 2030, including up to 5 <abbr title="Giggawatts">GW</abbr> of floating wind; up to 70 <abbr title="Giggawatts">GW</abbr> of solar by 2035; up to 10 <abbr title="Giggawatts">GW</abbr> of hydrogen by 2030, with up to 6 <abbr title="Giggawatts">GW</abbr> from electrolytic (‘green’) hydrogen; and up to 24 <abbr title="Giggawatts">GW</abbr> of nuclear by 2050.</p>

<p>The share of electricity generated from renewable sources remained stable through 2020-22.</p>

<h5 id="fuel-supply">2.6.1.4 Fuel Supply</h5>

<p>UK offshore oil and gas production started 60 years ago. This long history of oil and gas production in the UK means our offshore basin is mature and production is naturally declining. Through the North Sea Transition Deal, the oil and gas industry is committed to reducing its production emissions by 10% by 2025, 25% by 2027 and 50% by 2030, against a 2018 baseline<sup id="fnref:35"><a href="#fn:35" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 35]</a></sup>. Transparency is also important: since 2021, the North Sea Transition Authority (<abbr title="North Sea Transition Authority">NSTA</abbr>) has published annual Emissions Monitoring Reports, which present a wide range of data on overall greenhouse gas emissions, methane emissions, performance benchmarking and flaring and venting to track industry’s progress. The <abbr title="North Sea Transition Authority">NSTA</abbr>’s ‘<abbr title="Oil and Gas Authority, now the North Sea Transition Authority">OGA</abbr> Plan’ on emissions reduction, published in March 2024, sets out requirements for the oil and gas industry to decarbonise and makes it clear that for production to continue in the North Sea, it must also continue to become cleaner.</p>

<p>The sector’s emissions reductions will be delivered through a mixture of decreasing oil and gas production from the basin and decarbonisation measures such as ending routine flaring and venting and platform electrification. Good progress has been made in recent years - the <abbr title="North Sea Transition Authority">NSTA</abbr> estimates that between 2018 and 2022, emissions from upstream oil and gas production decreased by approximately 23% and industry almost halved methane emissions<sup id="fnref:36"><a href="#fn:36" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 36]</a></sup>. The UK oil and gas sector has one of the lowest upstream methane emission intensities globally, having achieved the Oil and Gas Climate Initiative’s 0.2% intensity target for 2025 early, in 2021<sup id="fnref:37"><a href="#fn:37" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 37]</a></sup>. We continue to support the North Sea Transition Deal, including the important decarbonisation targets it set for the sector, working together to make sure the next chapter of oil and gas is also the cleanest in its history.</p>

<h4 id="transport-brbr">2.6.2 Transport <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Domestic transport accounted for around 28% of all UK greenhouse gas emissions in 2022, almost entirely through carbon dioxide emissions. The main source of domestic transport emissions comes from the use of petrol and diesel fuels in road transport.
In 2020, transport was significantly impacted by <abbr title="Coronavirus">COVID-19</abbr>, as people were instructed to stay at home as much as possible. This led to an annual decrease in distance travelled by cars, vans and taxis of 28% in 2020 and an 80% decrease in distance travelled by rail, both when compared with 2019. <abbr title="Coronavirus">COVID-19</abbr> restrictions were eased in 2021 and the last restrictions removed in 2022, resulting in consecutive years of increasing greenhouse gas emissions from domestic transport to 113.2 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e in 2022, a 2% rise from 2021 and 12% higher than 2020, although this was still 10% lower than 2019. In 2021/22 and 2022/23, rail passenger kilometres increased incrementally, but still remained 20% below pre-pandemic levels<sup id="fnref:38"><a href="#fn:38" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 38]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>Road vehicles remained the most significant source of domestic transport <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> emissions (89%), making up 25% of economy-wide domestic emissions in 2022. Cars and taxis account for the bulk of this figure at 53% of domestic transport emissions, with Heavy Goods Vehicles (<abbr title="Heavy Goods Vehicles">HGVs</abbr>) contributing 17% and vans representing 16%<sup id="fnref:39"><a href="#fn:39" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 39]</a></sup>.</p>

<p id="figure-8"><strong>Figure 8: Passenger kilometres by mode in Great Britain, since 2012</strong></p>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67853888f029f40e50881718/uk-biennial-2024-figure-8.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<p id="figure-9"><strong>Figure 9: Passenger kilometres by mode (excluding cars and taxis) in Great Britain, since 2012</strong></p>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67853d26f041702a11ca0f0e/uk-biennial-2024-figure-9.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<p>Public transport use was heavily impacted by <abbr title="Coronavirus">COVID-19</abbr>. Between 2019 and 2020, passenger kilometres travelled on buses and rail fell from 33 billion to 14 billion and 80 billion to 16 billion respectively<sup id="fnref:40"><a href="#fn:40" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 40]</a></sup>. In contrast, active travel spiked significantly in 2020 when compared with previous years. Increases were seen in walking trips, stages and miles travelled compared to 2021, with average trips and miles above pre-pandemic levels<sup id="fnref:41"><a href="#fn:41" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 41]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>The freight sector is vital for the UK, with 216 billion tonne-kilometres of domestic freight moved in the UK in 2022. Road freight made up the largest proportion of domestic freight being moved in the UK in 2022, accounting for 81%<sup id="fnref:42"><a href="#fn:42" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 42]</a></sup>. Road freight has seen consistent increases from 2015 onwards. The <abbr title="Coronavirus">COVID-19</abbr> pandemic interrupted this trend, with an 11% decrease in road freight traffic in 2020<sup id="fnref:43"><a href="#fn:43" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 43]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>The maritime sector remains crucial for UK transport. In total, there are 51 major seaports in the UK<sup id="fnref:44"><a href="#fn:44" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 44]</a></sup>. In 2022, a total of 458.9 million tonnes of cargo were handled at all UK sea ports (98% at the 51 major ports); this is a 3% increase on 2021 but 5% lower than in 2019<sup id="fnref:45"><a href="#fn:45" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 45]</a></sup>. An estimated total of 86,600 cargo vessels arrived at UK major seaports during 2022, 1.6% more than the 2021 level<sup id="fnref:46"><a href="#fn:46" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 46]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>The UK aviation sector supports global travel, connectivity and trade. UK airports provide direct flights to over 100 countries and served over 195 million terminal passengers in 2022. Around 2 million commercial flights depart from or arrive at UK airports annually<sup id="fnref:47"><a href="#fn:47" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 47]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>Domestic aviation emissions fell by more than half in 2020 compared to 2019 due to the <abbr title="Coronavirus">COVID-19</abbr> pandemic, the largest fall of any mode of transport, and in 2022 were still 20% lower than in 2019. Emissions from waterborne transport were 11% lower in 2022 than in 2019, having remained at a similar level to their 2020 low.</p>

<p>The proliferation of future green technology is advancing, supported by investment in research and development (<abbr title="Research and development">R&amp;D</abbr>), alongside incentives and other existing efficiency regulations across all modes of transport. In May 2022, £200m was announced to provide support for the rollout of zero emission <abbr title="Heavy Goods Vehicles">HGVs</abbr> and their associated infrastructure as part of the zero emission <abbr title="Heavy Goods Vehicle">HGV</abbr> and infrastructure demonstrator programme. In 2022, the UK committed £180m to support the development of UK sustainable aviation fuels (<abbr title="Sustainable Aviation Fuels">SAF</abbr>) plants, building on the progress made in previous advanced fuels competitions. Additionally, the UK committed to a £206m <abbr title="Research and development">R&amp;D</abbr> programme focused on maritime decarbonisation, which is being delivered through the UK Shipping Office for Reducing Emissions (<abbr title="Shipping Office for Reducing Emissions">UK SHORE</abbr>) between 2022 until 2025.</p>

<h4 id="industrial-processes-and-product-use-brbr">2.6.3 Industrial processes and product use <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK’s industrial sector plays an important role in society, contributing £210 billion to the overall UK economy in 2022<sup id="fnref:48"><a href="#fn:48" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 48]</a></sup>. It is a high value area of employment, directly accounting for 10%<sup id="fnref:49"><a href="#fn:49" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 49]</a></sup> of the UK’s total <abbr title="Gross Value Added">GVA</abbr> in 2022 and providing 2.7 million<sup id="fnref:50"><a href="#fn:50" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 50]</a></sup> direct jobs across the country, rising to around 5 million jobs<sup id="fnref:51"><a href="#fn:51" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 51]</a></sup> if including indirect jobs across the value chain.</p>

<p>Industry is also a major source of <abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> emissions, producing 17% (68.3 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e)<sup id="fnref:52"><a href="#fn:52" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 52]</a></sup> of UK’s total in 2022. Roughly half of these emissions are concentrated in specific ‘clusters’<sup id="fnref:53"><a href="#fn:53" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 53]</a></sup> – geographical areas with large concentrations of industry. The 7 UK clusters are: Humberside, the North-West, Grangemouth in Scotland, South Wales, Teesside, Southampton and the Black Country. The remaining emissions can be found in ‘dispersed’ sites, which are industrial regions scattered around the UK. Most emissions are from energy and carbon intensive sectors including cement, chemicals, food and drink, iron and steel, non-ferrous metals, non-metallic minerals, paper and pulp and refining. Industry emissions reduced by 57% between 1990 and 2022<sup id="fnref:54"><a href="#fn:54" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 54]</a></sup>, due mainly to the changing structure of the UK’s manufacturing and refining sector, efficiency improvements, and a shift to low carbon fuels<sup id="fnref:55"><a href="#fn:55" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 55]</a></sup>. Refer to <strong>Figures 10 and 11</strong> below for an illustration of UK industrial emission and UK industrial process emission reductions from 1990 – 2022.</p>

<p id="figure-10"><strong>Figure 10: UK industrial emissions from 1990 - 2022<sup id="fnref:56"><a href="#fn:56" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 56]</a></sup></strong></p>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67854051f0528401055d2362/uk-biennial-2024-figure-10.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<p id="figure-11"><strong>Figure 11: Breakdown of emissions UK industrial processes from 1990 - 2022<sup id="fnref:57"><a href="#fn:57" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 57]</a></sup></strong></p>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6785451a3a9388161c5d234b/uk-biennial-2024-figure-11.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<h4 id="agriculture-brbr">2.6.4 Agriculture <br><br>
</h4>

<p>In 2022, around 71% (17.4 million hectares) of total UK land was used for agriculture. <strong>Figure 12</strong> shows UK land use data for the total utilised agricultural area as of June 2022<sup id="fnref:58"><a href="#fn:58" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 58]</a></sup>. About 4.4 million hectares of this was arable, of which around two-thirds were under cereal production and 11.4 million hectares was under grass. The remainder was common rough grazing (1.2 million hectares) and land for outdoor pigs (12,000 hectares)<sup id="fnref:59"><a href="#fn:59" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 59]</a></sup>. Total agriculture area saw a 0.4% increase between 2016 and 2022, and total croppable area increased by 0.2%. The biggest change in agricultural land use was seen in uncropped arable land which saw an 8.4% increase since 2016.</p>

<p id="figure-12"><strong>Figure 12: Total utilised agricultural land in the UK, 2022; <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> 2022</strong></p>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/678548c0f041702a11ca0f11/uk-biennial-2024-figure-12.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<p>Livestock produce greenhouse gas emissions via processes such as enteric fermentation. The total number of cattle and calves in the UK decreased by 4% between June 2016 and June 2022 to around 9.6 million. The UK’s dairy herd has decreased by 2.9%, and the UK beef herd has decreased by 8.3% over the same period. Total cattle and calf numbers in the UK during the period 2005-2023 are shown in <strong>Figure 13</strong>.</p>

<p id="figure-13"><strong>Figure 13: Total cattle and calves in the UK, June 2005-June 2022<sup id="fnref:60"><a href="#fn:60" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 60]</a></sup></strong></p>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67854e5bf0528401055d2369/uk-biennial-2024-figure-13.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<p>The total number of pigs in the UK in June 2022 increased by 7.3% since June 2016, to 5.2 million. There was a 16% decrease in the total number of breeding pigs in the UK over the same period. This decrease was a reaction to the large backlog of pigs on farm in England at the end of 2021 and start of 2022. Total pig numbers in the UK during the period 1996-2022 are shown in <strong>Figure 14</strong>.</p>

<p id="figure-14"><strong>Figure 14: Total pigs in the UK</strong></p>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67855778c6428e0131881729/uk-biennial-2024-figure-14.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<p>The total number of sheep and lambs in the UK decreased by 2.3% between June 2016 and June 2022, to 33.2 million. The UK’s female breeding flock decreased by 2.93% to 15.8 million over the same period. Decreases were also seen in other sheep and lambs for the UK falling 1.6%. Total sheep and lamb numbers in the UK during the period 2005-2023 are shown in <strong>Figure 15</strong>.</p>

<p id="figure-15"><strong>Figure 15: Total sheep in the UK, 2005-2022</strong></p>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67855b80f041702a11ca0f14/uk-biennial-2024-figure-15.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<h4 id="land-use-land-use-change-and-forestry-brbr">2.6.5 Land use, land use change and forestry <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The area of woodland in the UK on 31 March 2022 was 3.2 million hectares. Of this total, 1.5 million hectares (46%) was in Scotland, 1.3 million hectares (41%) was in England, 0.3 million hectares (10%) was in Wales and 0.1 million hectares (4%) was in Northern Ireland. This has changed relatively little over the period 2007 to 2022 as can be seen in <strong>Figure 16</strong>. Publicly owned forests still account for 0.9 million hectares<sup id="fnref:61"><a href="#fn:61" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 61]</a></sup>.</p>

<p id="figure-16"><strong>Figure 16: Area of woodland, 1998-2022<sup id="fnref:62"><a href="#fn:62" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 62]</a></sup></strong></p>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67852c9df0528401055d2345/uk-biennial-2024-figure-16.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<p>Around 50% of the total UK woodland is made up predominantly of conifer species, the remainder being broadleaved.</p>

<p>The total area of new planting and restocking in the UK was 27.2 thousand hectares in 2020-21. Restocking accounted for 51% of this total. Broadleaved species accounted for 45% of the new planting area but just 18.5% of the restocked area in 2020-21<sup id="fnref:63"><a href="#fn:63" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 63]</a></sup>.
A total of 10.0 million green tonnes of softwood was produced in the UK in 2020 and accounted for 92% of timber removals from UK woodland. UK hardwood production totalled 0.8 million green tonnes in 2020<sup id="fnref:64"><a href="#fn:64" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 64]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>Estimated consumption of wood in the UK amounted to 48.3 million m3 wood raw material equivalent in 2022, made up of 9.8 million m3 UK production, 43.1 million m3 imports and 4.5 million m3 exports<sup id="fnref:65"><a href="#fn:65" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 65]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>This sector can act as both a source and a sink for <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> emissions.</p>

<h4 id="waste-management-brbr">2.6.6 Waste management <br><br>
</h4>

<p>In 2022, <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> emissions from waste contributed around 5% of total UK emissions, representing an emissions reduction of 74% since 1990. Approximately 90% of emissions from this sector are attributable to methane<sup id="fnref:66"><a href="#fn:66" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 66]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>The UK Government and the devolved governments published their individual waste strategies aiming to reduce the quantity of waste produced and to increasingly recover value from it. The strategies set out ambitions to reduce the amount of waste sent to landfill and to increase the amount of recycling or composting.</p>

<p>In 2021, households in the UK produced 27.7 million tonnes of waste, an increase of 4.6% since 2019<sup id="fnref:67"><a href="#fn:67" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 67]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>In 2021, 44.6% of waste from households was recycled in the UK; this is a decrease from the peak of 46.0% achieved in 2019<sup id="fnref:68"><a href="#fn:68" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 68]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>The UK commercial and industrial sectors generated 40.4 million tonnes of waste in 2020, of which 33.8 million tonnes (around 84%) was produced in England. By comparison, the 2018 UK commercial and industrial waste arisings totalled 43.9 million tonnes, of which 37.2 million tonnes was generated by England. Over two-thirds of commercial and industrial waste is generated by the commercial sector, in both the UK and England.</p>

<p>Local authorities in England recycled, composted or reused 10.8 million tonnes in 2021-22<sup id="fnref:69"><a href="#fn:69" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 69]</a></sup>. The amount of local authority collected waste sent to landfill and incineration in 2021-22 was 2.1 million tonnes and 12.4 million tonnes, respectively. Concerning landfill, it is a reduction from 22 million tonnes sent to landfill in 2000-01.</p>

<h4 id="other-buildings-brbr">2.6.7 Other: Buildings <br><br>
</h4>

<p>There are about 30 million buildings in the UK<sup id="fnref:70"><a href="#fn:70" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 70]</a></sup>. In total, these buildings are responsible for around 30% of our national emissions<sup id="fnref:71"><a href="#fn:71" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 71]</a></sup>. The vast majority of these emissions are specifically from heating: 79% of buildings emissions and about 23% of all UK emissions<sup id="fnref:72"><a href="#fn:72" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 72]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>The UK has some of the oldest building stock in the world. 81% of UK homes were built before 1990 and over a third before 1945. Since 2012, the proportion of homes in <abbr title="Energy Performance Certificate">EPC</abbr> bands A-C has risen. However, 52% of homes in England remain below <abbr title="Energy Performance Certificate">EPC</abbr> C.
