The owner occupier tenure is the worst performing with around 57% of homes at <abbr title="Energy Performance Certificate">EPC</abbr> D or below.</p>

<h3 id="national-circumstances-of-ghg-emissions-and-removals-over-time">2.7 National circumstances of <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> emissions and removals over time</h3>

<p>For full details of the UK’s emissions trends, please see the UK National Inventory Document (<abbr title="National Inventory Document">NID</abbr>).</p>

<p>Despite rises in some sectors as the UK continued to recover from the coronavirus (<abbr title="Coronavirus">COVID-19</abbr>) pandemic, 2022 saw a fall in greenhouse gas emissions in the UK, largely due to a reduction in fuel use to heat buildings. In 2022, net territorial greenhouse gas emissions in the UK were estimated to be 407.8 million tonnes carbon dioxide equivalent (<abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e), a decrease of 3.5% from the 2021 figure of 422.7 million tonnes, and 9.3% lower when compared to 2019, the most recent pre-pandemic year. Total greenhouse gas emissions were 50.0% lower than they were in 1990. Carbon dioxide made up 80% of the 2022 total<sup id="fnref:73"><a href="#fn:73" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 73]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>The fall in 2022 is primarily due to a reduction in gas use for heating buildings, as a result of warmer weather than in 2021. Emissions from the buildings and product uses sector fell 13.3%. Higher energy prices may have also caused people to reduce their energy use. Falls in emissions from industry and agriculture also contributed to the overall reduction.</p>

<p>In comparison, emissions from the domestic transport sector rose 1.6%. This follows a period of reduced domestic travel in 2020 and 2021 due to <abbr title="Coronavirus">COVID-19</abbr> restrictions. Domestic transport was the largest emitting sector, responsible for 28% of all greenhouse gas emissions in the UK. Emissions from electricity supply also rose by 0.6%.</p>

<h3 id="institutional-arrangements-in-place-to-track-progress-made-in-implementing-and-achieving-its-nationally-determined-contribution-ndc">2.8 Institutional arrangements in place to track progress made in implementing and achieving its Nationally Determined Contribution (<abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr>)</h3>

<h4 id="information-on-legal-institutional-administrative-and-procedural-arrangements-related-to-the-ndc-brbr">2.8.1 Information on legal, institutional, administrative and procedural arrangements related to the <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr> <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="united-kingdom-climate-change-legislation-and-targets">2.8.1.1 United Kingdom climate change legislation and targets</h5>

<p>The Climate Change Act 2008 established the world’s first legally binding framework of national emissions targets.<sup id="fnref:74"><a href="#fn:74" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 74]</a></sup> The Act originally committed the UK to a statutory target to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to 80% lower than its 1990 baseline by 2050. In 2019, the UK amended the Act to require the net UK carbon account to be at least 100% lower than its 1990 baseline by 2050. In doing so, the UK became the first major economy to legislate for net zero emissions.</p>

<p>The UK’s carbon budgets impose legally binding limits on emissions across 5-year periods. The first 6 carbon budgets have so far been set in law. In 2021, the UK set its Sixth Carbon Budget for the period 2033-2037 with a target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions to 965 megatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalents (<abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e), which is approximately 77% lower than 1990 levels. It will be the first carbon budget to include emissions from international aviation and shipping. Looking forward, the UK’s Seventh Carbon Budget will put into law an emissions target for 2038 and 2042 and will set out the next phase of the government’s strategy for achieving net zero emissions by 2050.</p>

<p>Further information on carbon budget accounting and performance can be found in the Annual Statement of Emissions.<sup id="fnref:75"><a href="#fn:75" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 75]</a></sup></p>

<h5 id="northern-ireland-executive">2.8.1.2 Northern Ireland Executive</h5>

<p>The Climate Change Act (Northern Ireland) 2022<sup id="fnref:76"><a href="#fn:76" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 76]</a></sup>, which received Royal Assent on 6 June 2022, committed the region to net-zero greenhouse gas emissions target by 2050.</p>

<p>The Act requires the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (<abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr>) to bring forward Regulations to set specific emissions reduction targets for 2030 and 2040 and to bring forward Regulations to set the first 3 carbon budgets (2023-2027, 2028-2032 and 2033-2037).</p>

<p>The Act places a further duty on <abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr> to prepare and publish a Climate Action Plan (<abbr title="Climate Action Plan, Northern Ireland Executive">CAP</abbr>) and to bring forward Regulations under the Act to place statutory climate change reporting duties on specified public bodies. The <abbr title="Climate Action Plan, Northern Ireland Executive">CAP</abbr> will set out how the first carbon budget will be achieved and provide a pathway towards achieving the interim emissions reductions targets and the overall net zero target by 2050. Subsequent CAPs will be published every 5 years, in line with carbon budget periods. The Act places a duty on all Northern Ireland Executive departments to assist <abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr> in preparing the <abbr title="Climate Action Plan, Northern Ireland Executive">CAP</abbr> and to ensure that in exercising their functions they do so, in so far as it is possible to do so, in a manner which is consistent with the achievement of net zero by 2050.</p>

<h5 id="scottish-government">2.8.1.3 Scottish Government</h5>

<p>The statutory framework for reducing greenhouse gas emissions in Scotland is set out in the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009. In 2019, the Climate Change (Emissions Reduction Targets) (Scotland) Act amended the 2009 Act and established Scotland’s target of net zero emissions by 2045. The Climate Change (Emissions Reduction Targets) (Scotland) Act 2024 amends the 2009 Act, replacing the annual emissions reduction target framework with 5-yearly carbon budgets. The target of net zero emissions in 2045 remains unchanged, and ministers are still required to produce annual reports on emissions progress. The new Act enables the levels of carbon budgets to be set once the latest advice has been received from the Climate Change Committee. Our next Climate Change Plan will cover the period 2026-2040.</p>

<p>The Scottish Government also recognises the importance of working closely and collaboratively with the UK Government and other devolved governments to deliver a net zero that is mutually beneficial both in economic and social terms. We regularly engage with the UK Government and other devolved governments through the Net Zero, Energy and Climate Change Interministerial Group to discuss interdependencies between all 4 nations and opportunities to work collaboratively. Engagement will also remain an important part of our development of the next Climate Change Plan.</p>

<h5 id="welsh-government">2.8.1.4 Welsh Government</h5>

<p>The statutory framework for reducing greenhouse gas emissions in Wales is set out in Part 2 of the Environment (Wales) Act (2016).<sup id="fnref:77"><a href="#fn:77" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 77]</a></sup> Wales has a series of 5-yearly carbon budgets and interim decadal targets to 2050. Progress is measured against a 1990 or 1995 baseline, depending on the gas in question. For each carbon budget, the Senedd Cymru (Welsh Parliament) must set a limit on the amount of international offsets that may be used.</p>

<p>In March 2021, the Senedd formally committed Wales to achieving net zero emissions in 2050. It also passed regulations in relation to Carbon Budgets 2 and 3, and the 2030 and 2040 interim targets, as follows:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>Carbon Budget 2 (2021-25)</strong>: 37% average reduction (with no international offsets)</li>
  <li>
<strong>Carbon Budget 3 (2026-30)</strong>: 58% average reduction</li>
  <li>
<strong>2030</strong>: 63% reduction</li>
  <li>
<strong>2040</strong>: 89% reduction. Before the end of the second year after each carbon budget, the Welsh Government must publish a final statement on progress against that budget. The Climate Change Committee must then publish its own progress report, with the Welsh Government required to respond to that report in the Senedd</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="jersey">2.8.1.5 Jersey</h5>

<p>The Carbon Neutral Roadmap<sup id="fnref:78"><a href="#fn:78" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 78]</a></sup> was agreed by the States of Jersey in 2022. This commits Jersey to net zero emissions by 2050 and sets out the first steps to net zero through the delivery plan which covers the period 2022-2025. The first target of a 68% reduction for 1990 levels needs to be met by 2030. Jersey’s commitment to emissions reduction is not bound by legislation.</p>

<h5 id="guernsey">2.8.1.6 Guernsey</h5>

<p>In August 2020, Guernsey’s climate change policy, ‘Mitigating Climate Change - States of Guernsey Climate Change Policy &amp; Action Plan’<sup id="fnref:79"><a href="#fn:79" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 79]</a></sup>, received political approval. The policy sets the target to be carbon neutral by 2050, with an interim target of reducing emissions by 57% on 1990 levels by 2030. In doing so, Guernsey’s government also agreed that the climate targets should be legislated for.</p>

<h5 id="isle-of-man">2.8.1.7 Isle of Man</h5>

<p>The Climate Change Act 2021<sup id="fnref:80"><a href="#fn:80" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 80]</a></sup> contains the Isle of Man’s net zero by 2050 emissions reduction target and provides the basis of the Isle of Man’s statutory framework for climate action planning, delivery and monitoring. In addition, the Isle of Man has 2 statutory interim emissions reduction targets of 35% by 2030 and 45% by 2035<sup id="fnref:81"><a href="#fn:81" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 81]</a></sup> (against a 2018 baseline). The Act requires a statutory climate change plan to be in place at all times, with the current plan being the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027<sup id="fnref:82"><a href="#fn:82" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 82]</a></sup>. Prior to the current Climate Change Plan, Council of Ministers’ Climate Action Plan Phase 1<sup id="fnref:83"><a href="#fn:83" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 83]</a></sup> was in effect, between January 2020 and October 2022.</p>

<h5 id="gibraltar">2.8.1.8 Gibraltar</h5>

<p>Gibraltar declared a climate emergency in 2019 and followed this up with the publication of the Gibraltar Climate Change Act<sup id="fnref:84"><a href="#fn:84" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 84]</a></sup> later that same year. The Act sets legally binding carbon emissions reduction targets against a 1990 baseline of 42% by 2030 and 100% by 2045. The Climate Change Strategy<sup id="fnref:85"><a href="#fn:85" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 85]</a></sup> published in 2021 sets out the main policies and strategies by which Gibraltar will meet these targets.</p>

<h4 id="institutional-arrangements-brbr">2.8.2 Institutional arrangements <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="united-kingdom">2.8.2.1 United Kingdom</h5>

<p>The Climate Change Act 2008 is the legislative framework that holds the UK accountable for achieving our domestic climate target. The 2030 <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr> falls in the same time period as the fifth carbon budget (2028-2032) but on a higher ambition.
To help track our progress, the Climate Change Committee publishes annual progress reports which provide an independent assessment of the government’s progress in reducing emissions, which the government responds to by the statutory date.</p>

<h5 id="northern-ireland-executive-1">2.8.2.2 Northern Ireland Executive</h5>

<p>The Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (<abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr>) on an annual basis publishes the Northern Ireland Greenhouse Gas Inventory<sup id="fnref:86"><a href="#fn:86" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 86]</a></sup>. The latest inventory covers the period 1990-2022, with the focus on ‘by source’ emissions. As part of this process <abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr> also produces a set of Carbon Intensity Indicators on an annual basis. These are designed to complement the greenhouse gas inventory and allow the <abbr title="Northern Ireland">NI</abbr> departments to track the effectiveness of their carbon reduction policies and measures.</p>

<p>The Climate Change Act (Northern Ireland) 2022 (the Act) placed a duty on <abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr> to prepare and publish a report before the end of each 5 yearly carbon budget period, setting out what progress has been made in implementing the policies and proposals contained within the associated 5 year Climate Action Plan. As part of this requirement, all <abbr title="Northern Ireland">NI</abbr> departments have a duty to provide details of progress in implementing the policies and proposals within their areas of responsibility. Furthermore, the Act places a duty on <abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr> to lay a report before the <abbr title="Northern Ireland">NI</abbr> assembly, before the end of the second year after each carbon budget period, setting out a final statement on the total amount of <abbr title="Northern Ireland">NI</abbr> emissions, removals and net emissions for the period. The statement must include an assessment of the extent the policies and proposals contained in the Climate Action Plan have contributed towards the achievement of the carbon budget for the given 5-year carbon budget period.</p>

<h5 id="scottish-government-1">2.8.2.3 Scottish Government</h5>

<p>The Scottish Government has put in place a National Performance Framework to achieve its purpose, and this framework sets out ‘National Outcomes’ to describe the kind of Scotland it aims to create and to help it monitor progress.</p>

<p>In addition to this, cross-government climate change activity is governed by the Global Climate Emergency Board through the Climate Change Programme. This programme monitors progress on a monthly basis.</p>

<p>The Climate Change Programme consists of 3 pillars, these are The Climate Change Plan, the Scottish National Adaptation Plan 3 and Just Transition plans. Each of these plans have or will have (for those still in development) their own monitoring and evaluation frameworks. In addition to this each of these 3 pillars is required to report progress to the Scottish Parliament on an annual basis.</p>

<p>There are also 2 statutory nitrogen reports that the Scottish Government must update annually: the Scottish Nitrogen Balance Sheet (‘<abbr title="Scottish Nitrogen Balance Sheet">SNBS</abbr>’) and the Nitrogen use efficiency in Scotland progress report (‘progress report’).</p>

<p>The <abbr title="Scottish Nitrogen Balance Sheet">SNBS</abbr> provides a powerful new source of evidence to track how efficiently nitrogen is used in Scotland and helps to identify further opportunities to improve this. In particular, it will help support progress towards Scotland’s national climate change targets.</p>

<p>The progress report supports the <abbr title="Scottish Nitrogen Balance Sheet">SNBS</abbr>. This reports on progress towards relevant actions to improve nitrogen use and identify opportunities for future improvements.</p>

<h5 id="welsh-government-1">2.8.2.4 Welsh Government</h5>

<p>Under the Environment (Wales) Act 2016, Welsh ministers must prepare and publish a plan (‘report’) for each budgetary period, setting out their policies and proposals for meeting the carbon budget. The first of these reports was published in March 2019<sup id="fnref:87"><a href="#fn:87" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 87]</a></sup>. Throughout the delivery of its second plan (Carbon Budget 2 (<abbr title="Carbon Budget 2">CB2</abbr>))<sup id="fnref:88"><a href="#fn:88" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 88]</a></sup>, Welsh Government is tracking and driving forward its implementation to ensure progress is made towards targets and budgets in a fair and just way. To track progress, a comprehensive system has been developed to monitor delivery which includes the following:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>Legislation</strong> – An assessment against targets and budgets every 5 years. The report<sup id="fnref:89"><a href="#fn:89" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 89]</a></sup>, formally referred to as Statement of Progress, was published in December 2022, summarising progress for Carbon Budget 1. The next Statement of Progress (for <abbr title="Carbon Budget 2">CB2</abbr>) is due in 2027</li>
  <li>
<strong>Indicators</strong> – Tracking progress towards targets and budgets on an annual basis.</li>
  <li>A <strong>monitoring and reporting system</strong>, which looks more in depth at the implementation progress of Welsh policies and proposals within the Plan</li>
  <li>
<strong>Internal Governance</strong> arrangements, such as an internal Climate Change portfolio board and cross-government Cabinet, oversee progress and drive action</li>
  <li>
<strong>Independent Progress reports</strong> from the Climate Change Committee. <strong>Scrutiny</strong> from the Senedd and Senedd committees</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="jersey-1">2.8.2.5 Jersey</h5>

<p>The government of Jersey is made up of the Council of Ministers, comprising of the Chief Minister and 12 portfolio ministers. The Council of Ministers has the responsibility for all of Jersey’s domestic and fiscal affairs and, increasingly, the Island’s international affairs. One of the first tasks of the Council is to draw up a Common Strategic Policy (<abbr title="Common Strategic Policy">CSP</abbr>). The <abbr title="Common Strategic Policy">CSP</abbr> outlines the Council’s aims and objectives and gives a timetable for implementation. Once the <abbr title="Common Strategic Policy">CSP</abbr> is approved by the States Assembly (the legislature), it is the role of the Council to make sure it is properly and efficiently delivered. The current <abbr title="Common Strategic Policy">CSP</abbr> (2024-2026) commits to continuing to address climate change through the Carbon Neutral Roadmap, which aims to fulfil Jersey’s commitments under the Paris Agreement.</p>

<h5 id="guernsey-1">2.8.2.6 Guernsey</h5>

<p>The States of Guernsey is the decision-making government body for the island, which includes climate matters. It has responsibility for all island affairs, both domestic and international. The States of Guernsey has a Government Work Plan (<abbr title="Government Work Plan">GWP</abbr>) which sets out the priorities of the government over the term. The <abbr title="Government Work Plan">GWP</abbr> outlines the States of Guernsey’s commitment to climate change. Within the current <abbr title="Government Work Plan">GWP</abbr> (2023-2025) there is commitment to develop a detailed plan for the mitigation of emissions and it notes the need to address the island’s exposure to the effects of climate change.</p>

<h5 id="isle-of-man-1">2.8.2.7 Isle of Man</h5>

<p>Governmental climate action in the Isle of Man is primarily the responsibility of the Council of Ministers, with their responsibilities set out in the Climate Change Act 2021<sup id="fnref:90"><a href="#fn:90" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 90]</a></sup>. The Climate Change Transformation Board (<abbr title="Climate Change Transformation Board">CCTB</abbr>), supported by the Climate Change Transformation Team (<abbr title="Climate Change Transformation Team">CCTT</abbr>), report to the Council of Ministers. The <abbr title="Climate Change Transformation Team">CCTT</abbr> sits within the Department of Environment, Food and Agriculture (<abbr title="Department of Environment, Food and Agriculture">DEFA</abbr>) and is responsible for the management and administration of the programme, acting as a central hub to support delivery of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027<sup id="fnref:91"><a href="#fn:91" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 91]</a></sup> by the government departments responsible for the individual actions, and directly delivering some cross-government actions. Key climate change related documents, including legislation, are approved by Tynwald (the Manx parliament). Annual climate change reporting by Manx public bodies to the Council of Ministers (via <abbr title="Climate Change Transformation Team">CCTT</abbr> and <abbr title="Climate Change Transformation Board">CCTB</abbr>) provides a framework for compliance across the Manx public sector.</p>

<h5 id="gibraltar-1">2.8.2.8 Gibraltar</h5>

<p>The government of Gibraltar is made up of the Chief Minister and up to 9 other elected members of Parliament. Gibraltar is self-governing in all areas except defence and foreign policy. The government’s responsibilities in respect of climate action are set out in the 2019 Climate Change Act<sup id="fnref:92"><a href="#fn:92" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 92]</a></sup>. In 2022 the Net Zero Delivery Body<sup id="fnref:93"><a href="#fn:93" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 93]</a></sup> was established. This Body is chaired by the Deputy Chief Minister and is designed to guide implementation of the Climate Change Strategy across all government bodies.</p>

<h3 id="stakeholder-engagement-related-to-the-uks-2030-nationally-determined-contribution-ndc">2.9 Stakeholder engagement related to the UK’s 2030 Nationally Determined Contribution (<abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr>)</h3>

<h4 id="cross-cutting-engagement-brbr">2.9.1 Cross-cutting engagement <br><br>
</h4>

<p>When setting the 2030 <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr>, the UK consulted with a range of stakeholders such as businesses, civil society groups, local government and the devolved governments to capture their views on scope and target. It was also covered in correspondence with representatives of these groups and interested Parliamentarians. A copy of the UK’s updated <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr> was laid in the UK’s Houses of Parliament. For more information, please see section 4a(i) of the UK’s 2030 <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr>.<sup id="fnref:94"><a href="#fn:94" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 94]</a></sup> When the UK set its 2030 <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr>, we have considered the impact of climate policy more broadly on groups protected under the 2010 Equality Act.</p>

<p>We are committed to ensuring that everyone has the opportunity to contribute to the transition to net zero, supporting people and communities to take action and demonstrating the benefits of the transition. We will set out the government’s approach to engaging the public in a Public Participation Strategy, to be published in 2025. This will include how we support people to adopt new technologies, as well as opportunities to ensure that public views are considered in the development of policy.</p>

<h4 id="net-zero-engagement-by-sector-england-brbr">2.9.2 Net Zero engagement by sector (England) <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="energy">2.9.2.1 Energy</h5>

<p>The UK works closely with industry, regulators, sector bodies, and other stakeholders to ensure that our energy system is resilient and secure, including to the impacts of climate change.<sup id="fnref:95"><a href="#fn:95" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 95]</a></sup></p>

<p>To deliver production levels needed for Carbon Budget 6 (2033-2037) and net zero by 2050, the UK Government is working closely with industry and other stakeholders to overcome the barriers to growing a new low carbon energy vector for the UK.<sup id="fnref:96"><a href="#fn:96" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 96]</a></sup></p>

<p>The 2021 Hydrogen Strategy, as well as underpinning policies such as the Hydrogen Production Business Model and Hydrogen Storage Business Model, have been developed through close engagement and collaboration with stakeholders across the sector.</p>

<h5 id="transport">2.9.2.2 Transport</h5>

<p>When developing the Transport Decarbonisation Plan in 2021, the UK undertook extensive stakeholder engagement including: 8 workshops with 49 local government representatives and 59 virtual policy workshops with knowledge experts, innovators, businesses, non-governmental organisations, and civil society representatives.<sup id="fnref:97"><a href="#fn:97" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 97]</a></sup> The Department for Transport received over 300 written submissions and evidence on measures needed to decarbonise transport. The Department for Transport also formed the Net Zero Transport Board which was a ministerial-led external advisory board providing independent, objective, and impartial advice on transport decarbonisation to the Department for Transport.</p>

<p>The Department for Transport also engages internationally on domestic efforts including at United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change Conference of the Parties (<abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> COPs).</p>

<h5 id="industrial-processes-and-product-use">2.9.2.3 Industrial processes and product use</h5>

<p>The UK is committed to having a thriving industrial sector aligned with our net zero target, without pushing emissions and business abroad.<sup id="fnref:98"><a href="#fn:98" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 98]</a></sup> The UK has successfully engaged with a wide range of stakeholders to date, including business representative organisations, think tanks and academics, industry bodies and trade associations to develop policies supporting UK industrial decarbonisation, and to develop the market for low carbon industrial products.<sup id="fnref:99"><a href="#fn:99" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 99]</a></sup> <sup id="fnref:100"><a href="#fn:100" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 100]</a></sup> This included a comprehensive programme of stakeholder engagement to support the development and launch of the Industrial Decarbonisation Strategy (2021).</p>

<h5 id="agriculture">2.9.2.4 Agriculture</h5>

<p>In 2021-2022 the UK continued a significant reform of agricultural policy in England phasing out subsidies and expanding schemes to boost Britain’s food security and accelerate the transition to a more resilient and sustainable farming sector. The Sustainable Farming Incentive (SFI) opened in 2021 with a pilot scheme, with a wider rollout to farmers in 2022 to make their businesses more sustainable and resilient. The focus in 2022 was on moorlands, arable and horticultural soils, and improved grassland soils. In addition, in 2022 the UK launched a call for evidence exploring the potential opportunities and challenges associated with the use of methane suppressing feed products.</p>

<h5 id="land-use-land-use-change-and-forestry-lulucf">2.9.2.5 Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry (<abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr>)</h5>

<p>The UK continues to engage with stakeholders, industry bodies and landowners on a range of challenges across forestry, peatlands and other land use sectors. As part of the Environment Act 2021, we legislated for a long-term statutory tree target in England to increase tree canopy and woodland cover to 16.5% of land area in England by 2050.</p>

<h5 id="waste-management">2.9.2.6 Waste management</h5>

<p>The Collection and Packaging Reforms were introduced in the Environment Act 2021 Throughout the development of these reforms, the UK engaged with stakeholders through different working groups, events and forums to develop the policies further. These included the monthly Resources and Waste forums and newsletters open to all stakeholders which cover recycling collections and wider resources and waste topics.</p>

<h5 id="other-sectors">2.9.2.7 Other sectors</h5>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>Buildings</strong>: Progress is being made to ensure secure, affordable and clean heating for UK homes and businesses.<sup id="fnref:101"><a href="#fn:101" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 101]</a></sup> government has taken key steps towards improving energy efficiency and deploying low-carbon heating - by engaging industry, consumers, and businesses, with targeted regulation and new market-based mechanisms, help to heat schemes, and work to increase public awareness.<sup id="fnref:102"><a href="#fn:102" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 102]</a></sup> Together this all helps to reduce costs for consumers and businesses, attract greater private investment and strengthen supply chain resilience – to ensure UK buildings are able to transition towards a greener future.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Greenhouse Gas Removals</strong>: In 2023, the UK set out the proposed commercial frameworks for the greenhouse gas removals (<abbr title="Greenhouse Gas Removals">GGR</abbr>) business model and standards<sup id="fnref:103"><a href="#fn:103" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 103]</a></sup> following extensive engagement with industry and academia. The Carbon Capture Usage and Storage Cluster process allowed <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas Removals">GGR</abbr> and large-scale Power Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (<abbr title="Bioenergy with Carbon Capture and Storage">BECCS</abbr>) projects to apply for access to the Hynet cluster in the North West of England as part of the Track 1 Hynet expansion process. The UK Emissions Trading Scheme Authority published a consultation seeking input on the integration of GGRs into the UK Emissions Trading Scheme.<sup id="fnref:104"><a href="#fn:104" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 104]</a></sup> Commercial and economic regulatory frameworks for Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage (<abbr title="Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage">CCUS</abbr>) have been developed through extensive engagement and collaboration with representatives from the many sectors and industries for whom <abbr title="Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage">CCUS</abbr> is critical to achieve their decarbonisation objectives.<sup id="fnref:105"><a href="#fn:105" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 105]</a></sup>
</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="northern-ireland-executive-brbr-1">2.9.3 Northern Ireland Executive <br><br>
</h4>

<p><abbr title="Department for Education, England">DfE</abbr> operated a thematic approach to Stakeholder Groups in the development of the Path to Net Zero Energy Strategy. Five working groups were convened across the areas of Consumers, Energy Efficiency, Heat, Power, and Transport to provide further analysis and evidence on potential policy options, with the Transport theme led by the Department for Infrastructure. The new Strategy was published in December 2021<sup id="fnref:106"><a href="#fn:106" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 106]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>The Department for Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (<abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr>) in line with the ‘New Decade, New Approach’ commitment to bring forward climate change legislation for Northern Ireland, led on the development and progression of the Climate Change Act (Northern Ireland) 2022 which received Royal Assent in June 2022<sup id="fnref:107"><a href="#fn:107" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 107]</a></sup>. In progressing the legislation development in December 2020 <abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr> provided an opportunity for stakeholder involvement through launching a public consultation ‘Discussion Document on a Climate Change Bill’<sup id="fnref:108"><a href="#fn:108" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 108]</a></sup>. Further stakeholder engagement took place when the Northern Ireland Assembly’s Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs Committee launched a call for evidence in August 2021 seeking views from both individuals and stakeholder organisations to feed into its scrutiny process of the Bill passage. In keeping with the legislative commitment set in the Act, <abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr>, in conjunction with other executive departments, commenced the development of Northern Ireland’s first Climate Action Plan (<abbr title="Climate Action Plan, Northern Ireland Executive">CAP</abbr>).</p>

<h4 id="scottish-government-brbr-1">2.9.4 Scottish Government <br><br>
</h4>

<p>In 2020, the Scottish Government published an update to the 2018 Climate Change Plan to account for the new targets set out within the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009 (as amended by the Climate Change (Emissions Reduction Targets) (Scotland) Act 2019), which includes its commitment to reaching net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2045<sup id="fnref:109"><a href="#fn:109" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 109]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>The Plan update also reflects that the 2019 Act enshrined the Scottish Government’s commitment to a just transition into law, ensuring that everyone can access the opportunities of the transition and that no one is left behind. The Plan update sets out the Scottish Government’s strategic direction, containing the policies and proposals that will put Scotland on a pathway to meet its emissions reduction targets. Collectively these policies will require societal changes, impacting how the population will travel, heat its homes and how the Scottish people consume goods and services.
The Scottish Government puts people, places and business at the heart of their open, transparent, and participatory approaches to policy development and government decision making. The Public Engagement Strategy is a key part of the Scottish Government’s approach to delivering upon the ambition of the updated Climate Change Plan. A broad approach to public engagement will be required in order to include people and communities in the national effort required to reach climate change goals.</p>

<p>The Scottish Government is committed to ensuring that everyone in Scotland recognises the implications of the global climate emergency, fully understands and contributes to Scotland’s response, and embraces their role in the transition to a net zero and climate ready Scotland.</p>

<p>Widespread participation and engagement are essential if we are to successfully limit the effects of climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions, preparing for the impacts that are already locked in, and harnessing the opportunities to innovate during the net zero transition.</p>

<p>62% of changes needed to achieve net zero can only happen with societal or individual behaviour change (Climate Change Committee) and achieving our climate targets fundamentally depends upon the involvement and support of the people of Scotland in all aspects of their lives.</p>

<p>The Scottish Government is a member of the international Open Government Partnership. Scotland’s Open Government Action Plan commits the Scottish Government to our Open Government climate commitment, and to the values of openness, accountability, transparency, and involving people.</p>

<h4 id="welsh-government-brbr-1">2.9.5 Welsh Government <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Following a consultation held between October and December 2022 (supported by outreach engagement activity during Wales Climate Week), the Welsh Government published its public engagement strategy<sup id="fnref:110"><a href="#fn:110" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 110]</a></sup> in July 2023. Climate Action Wales explains how the Welsh Government will work with its delivery partners to ensure that people and communities are involved in climate decision-making and supported and encouraged to make green choices in relation to home energy, travel, food and consumption. The strategy conveys a vision of a fairer society driven by improved health, wellbeing and fairness and where no-one is left behind. Its guiding principles are structured around the ‘5 ways of working’ in the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 and uses a ‘5 Es framework’ (i.e. exemplify, engage, enable, encourage and evaluate) to convey how the programme will be delivered. The Welsh Government is now focussed on ensuring delivery of the commitments within the strategy.</p>

<h4 id="jersey-brbr">2.9.6 Jersey <br><br>
</h4>

<p>A people-powered approach was prioritised through the development of the Carbon Neutral Roadmap. This included Jersey’s first citizens’ assembly held on climate change alongside a public campaign, the ‘Climate Conversation’ carried out in 2021.</p>

<p>This informed the level of ambition of the roadmap and led to the second most responded to consultation in Jersey. There is a specific climate change and sustainability engagement team within government who continue to engage with key stakeholders, industry and the public. For example, carbon literacy training has been facilitated across government and industries that are signed up to Jersey’s eco active business network.</p>

<h4 id="guernsey-brbr">2.9.7 Guernsey <br><br>
</h4>

<p>In December 2019, an external consultancy was commissioned to facilitate a workshop with officers from across Guernsey’s government and stakeholders from local organisations. The workshop aimed to pilot and give feedback on an in-depth independent survey that was later launched in January 2020. The workshop and survey focused on heating and on-island travel, which are 2 of the biggest contributors to greenhouse gas emissions locally. Results were published online<sup id="fnref:111"><a href="#fn:111" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 111]</a></sup>.</p>

<h4 id="isle-of-man-brbr">2.9.8 Isle of Man <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Following the approval of the Council of Ministers’ Climate Action Plan Phase 1<sup id="fnref:112"><a href="#fn:112" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 112]</a></sup>, and formal acknowledgment of the climate crisis by Tynwald in 2019, development of the Climate Change Bill began. Targeted engagement with key stakeholders was held in February 2020, followed by a full public consultation<sup id="fnref:113"><a href="#fn:113" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 113]</a></sup> on the Bill in July 2020.
A comprehensive public consultation was held during 2021 on the content for the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027<sup id="fnref:114"><a href="#fn:114" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 114]</a></sup>. This ran alongside a Citizens’ Forum<sup id="fnref:115"><a href="#fn:115" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 115]</a></sup> and engagement with key stakeholders. The Citizens’ Forum was made up of 36 individuals who represented interest groups and wider public of the Isle of Man. The group was instrumental in the formation of the principles for the Green Living Grant<sup id="fnref:116"><a href="#fn:116" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 116]</a></sup>. The first of regular public insight surveys relating to climate change was launched in 2021. Section E of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027 sets out actions relating to engagement and awareness, including developing awareness and educational campaigns to help ensure people understand the climate emergency, reduce climate anxiety, empower positive action and increase awareness of the Isle of Man government’s actions in addressing climate change.</p>

<h4 id="gibraltar-brbr">2.9.9 Gibraltar <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Gibraltar consulted with non-governmental organisations as well as business representatives on the development of its climate change strategy. It also underwent internal consultation across government.</p>

<h3 id="description-of-the-uks-ndc">2.10 Description of the UK’s <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr>
</h3>

<h4 id="scope-and-targets-brbr">2.10.1 Scope and targets <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Parties agreed in the Paris Agreement to keep the increase in global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, and to pursue efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C. In December 2020, the UK announced its 2030 Nationally Determined Contribution (<abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr>) which commits to reducing UK net greenhouse gas emissions by at least 68% by 2030 on 1990 levels. It represents a significant step forward in our ambition to tackle climate change over the next 10 years, as we accelerate towards meeting our legally binding commitment to net zero by 2050.</p>

<h4 id="identified-indicators-selected-to-track-progress-and-information-brbr">2.10.2 Identified indicators selected to track progress and information <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Reference indicator: Net<sup id="fnref:117"><a href="#fn:117" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 117]</a></sup> greenhouse gas (<abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr>) emissions in <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e.
The reference indicator (<abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e) in the reference years (1990 and 1995) will be based on the 1990-2030 UK <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> Inventory submitted to the <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> in 2032. The value for the target year (2030) will be based on applying a 68% fixed percentage reduction target to the reference indicator value.</p>

<h4 id="accounting-approach-and-methodologies-brbr">2.10.3 Accounting approach and methodologies <br><br>
</h4>

<p>This section presents information on UK <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> emissions and the National System established to produce and quality assure the UK <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> Inventory. A fuller description of this National System can be found in the UK’s National Inventory Document (<abbr title="National Inventory Document">NID</abbr>), submitted to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (<abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr>) in 2022<sup id="fnref:118"><a href="#fn:118" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 118]</a></sup>. The UK is obliged to produce an annual <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> inventory, containing an estimate of all anthropogenic <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> emissions across the UK to meet its commitments under the <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> and the Kyoto Protocol; it will continue to do so to meet its commitments under the Paris Agreement. Data from the <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> inventory are also used to monitor progress against Carbon Budgets under the UK Climate Change Act 2008. The methodologies used in the NIR are used across all emissions reporting in the UK to ensure consistency between estimates, only geographic scope changes.</p>

<p>The <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> inventory covers the 7 direct GHGs under the Paris Agreement. These are collectively known as the ‘basket’ of GHGs and are: carbon dioxide (<abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub>), methane (<abbr title="Methane">CH</abbr><sub>4</sub>), nitrous oxide (<abbr title="Nitrous Oxide">N</abbr><sub>2</sub>O), hydrofluorocarbons (<abbr title="Hydrofluorocarbons">HFCs</abbr>), perfluorocarbons (<abbr title="Perfluorocarbons">PFCs</abbr>), sulphur hexafluoride (SF<sub>6</sub>) and nitrogen trifluoride (<abbr title="Nitrogen trifluoride">NF</abbr><sub>3</sub>). The last 4 gases are collectively referred to as fluorinated gases (F gases). In accordance with international reporting and carbon trading protocols, emissions from each of the gases are weighted by its global warming potential (<abbr title="Government Work Plan">GWP</abbr>), so that total greenhouse gas emissions can be reported on a consistent basis. The <abbr title="Government Work Plan">GWP</abbr> for each gas is defined as its warming influence in relation to that of <abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> over a 100- year period. Greenhouse gas emissions are then presented in carbon dioxide equivalent units (<abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e).</p>

<p>The UK’s base year for assessing emissions of <abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub>, <abbr title="Methane">CH</abbr><sub>4</sub>, and <abbr title="Nitrous Oxide">N</abbr><sub>2</sub>O is 1990. The UK uses 1995 as the base year for emissions of the fluorinated gases: <abbr title="Hydrofluorocarbons">HFCs</abbr>, <abbr title="Perfluorocarbons">PFCs</abbr>, SF<sub>6</sub> and <abbr title="Nitrogen trifluoride">NF</abbr><sub>3</sub>. This is in line with most European states, and in accordance with the Paris Agreement. Land use, land-use change and forestry (<abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr>) emissions and removals are reported in the UK’s <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> inventory in accordance with the rules for reporting this sector under the <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr>. The <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> reporting basis includes an estimate of all anthropogenic sources minus sinks from the <abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr> sector.</p>

<p>The UK elects Cropland Management, Grazing Land Management, and Wetland Drainage and Rewetting, as <abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr> activities. The UK does not elect Revegetation, as the eligible land area for Revegetation within the UK is estimated to be very small, and therefore the associated potential sink will also be very small. In addition to the provision of a national inventory covering the whole of the UK and British crown dependencies and overseas territories, the UK also produces annual spatially disaggregated inventories to provide geographical breakdown to England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and to the 374 local authorities that make up the UK. Trends in UK <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> emissions between 1990 and 2022, disaggregating overall emissions by gas and by source sector can be found in section <strong>2.7 National circumstances of <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> emissions and removals over time</strong>. More information on UK <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> emissions trends can be found in the Common Tabular Format tables.</p>

<h4 id="national-system-brbr">2.10.4 National System <br><br>
</h4>
<p>Section 1.2 of the National Inventory Document presents the full details of the UK’s institutional arrangements for inventory preparation<sup id="fnref:119"><a href="#fn:119" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 119]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>The UK’s <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> inventory is compiled and maintained by a consortium led by Ricardo Energy and Environment– the Inventory Agency – under contract to the Science and Innovation for Climate and Energy (<abbr title="Science and Innovation for Climate and Energy">SICE</abbr>) Directorate in the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (<abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr>). Ricardo Energy and Environment is directly responsible for producing the emissions estimates for the following categories: Energy, Industrial Processes and Product Use (<abbr title="Industrial Processes and Product Use">IPPU</abbr>), and Waste. Ricardo Energy and Environment is also responsible for inventory planning, data collection, Quality Assurance (QA)/Quality Control (QC) and inventory management and archiving. Aether, a member within the consortium, is responsible for compiling emissions from railways and for the UK’s overseas territories and crown dependencies. Gluckman Consulting advises on fluorinated gas (F-gas) emissions.</p>

<p>Forestry emissions and removals in the Land-Use, Land-Use Change and Forestry (<abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr>) sector are calculated by Forest Research and the remainder of the sector is calculated and compiled by the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology (<abbr title="UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology">UKCEH</abbr>), both partners within the consortium. Agricultural sector emissions estimates are produced by Rothamsted Research, under contract to the UK Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (<abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr>).</p>

<p>Improvements to the inventory are scrutinised by the UK’s National Inventory Steering Committee (<abbr title="National Inventory Steering Committee">NISC</abbr>). The <abbr title="National Inventory Steering Committee">NISC</abbr> is made of key stakeholders to the GHGI including representatives from the suppliers above, representatives from each of the devolved governments, and representatives from key government departments including the Department for Environment, Food, and Rural Affairs, and the Department for Transport. The <abbr title="National Inventory Steering Committee">NISC</abbr> provides an oversight function and gives approval for any proposed changes.</p>

<h4 id="geographical-coverage-brbr">2.10.5 Geographical Coverage <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK inventory provides data to assess progress of the UK’s commitments under the Paris Agreement Protocol, progress towards the UK’s own Carbon Budgets and to meet commitments as a Party to the <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr>.</p>

<p>The UK’s 2030 <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr> covers territorial emissions from the England, Scotland, and Northern Ireland as well as the 3 crown dependencies, Bailiwick of Jersey, Guernsey, Isle of Man and 1 overseas territory, Gibraltar.</p>

<h3 id="mitigation-policies-and-measures">2.11 Mitigation policies and measures</h3>

<h4 id="cross-cutting-policies-and-measures-brbr">2.11.1 Cross-cutting policies and measures <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="net-zero-strategy">2.11.1.1 Net Zero Strategy</h5>

<p>The Net Zero Strategy was published in 2021 to set out how we intended to keep the UK on track for our coming carbon budgets, our ambitious Nationally Determined Contribution (<abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr>), and then set out our vision for a decarbonised economy in 2050.<sup id="fnref:120"><a href="#fn:120" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 120]</a></sup></p>

<p>In December 2024, we published the UK Government’s annual response to the 2024 Progress Report from Climate Change Committee the independent body that advises the UK on its progress to reaching net zero.<sup id="fnref:121"><a href="#fn:121" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 121]</a></sup> The government’s response recognises the challenging picture outlined by the Climate Change Committee. It also sets out the urgent action that has been taken alongside further commitments to accelerate to net zero and address the Climate Change Committee’s recommendations. We will publish an updated cross-economy plan to meet carbon budgets and <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contributions">NDCs</abbr> in due course, which will set out details of policies across all sectors of the economy.</p>

<p>Looking ahead, we will set Carbon Budget 7 by June 2026, in line with our statutory duties, for the period 2038 to 2042. This will set out the next phase of our pathway to net zero and policies to further decarbonise the UK economy.</p>

<h5 id="uk-emissions-trading-scheme">2.11.1.2 UK Emissions Trading Scheme</h5>

<p>The UK Emissions Trading Scheme (<abbr title="UK Emissions Trading Scheme">UK ETS</abbr>) is an essential part of our approach to cutting emissions and driving green investment. The scheme is run by the 4 administrations of the UK (the UK Government, Scottish Government, Welsh Government, and the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs for Northern Ireland), collectively making up the <abbr title="UK Emissions Trading Scheme">UK ETS</abbr> Authority.</p>

<p>Launched in 2021, the <abbr title="UK Emissions Trading Scheme">UK ETS</abbr> supports decarbonisation across aviation, power, and industry by setting a limit on emissions and creating a carbon price that incentivises businesses to reduce their emissions.</p>

<p>In 2022 the <abbr title="UK Emissions Trading Scheme">UK ETS</abbr> Authority consulted on aligning the scheme’s cap – the limit on emissions from the sectors covered – with our net zero and other climate targets. In 2023 we confirmed the implementation of this new tighter cap, aligning it with our net zero targets to ensure the sectors covered decarbonise at the pace required to contribute to achieving our climate goals.</p>

<h4 id="energy-brbr-1">2.11.2 Energy <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="england">2.11.2.1 England</h5>

<p>The UK Government’s energy policy through 2021-22 was to decarbonise the power sector by 2035, subject to security of supply. In November 2022, the ambition was announced to cut overall energy consumption by 15% by 2030. Energy is a devolved matter in Northern Ireland but mostly reserved in Scotland and Wales.</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>The British Energy Security Strategy<sup id="fnref:122"><a href="#fn:122" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 122]</a></sup> (2022)</strong>: set out how government intended to improve the UK’s energy security by increasing the efficiency with which we use energy, how to increase our proportion of domestically produced energy, and how to help bring down the bills of consumers. This involved measures such a zero-rating VAT on energy efficiency and clean heat technologies.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Hydrogen Strategy<sup id="fnref:123"><a href="#fn:123" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 123]</a></sup> (2021)</strong>: outlined a comprehensive roadmap for the development of the wider hydrogen economy over the 2020s and early 2030s, putting the UK at the forefront of the race to develop low carbon hydrogen. It laid the foundations for a hydrogen economy by 2030 that would support innovation and stimulate investment to scale up hydrogen technologies, while helping to achieve our Sixth Carbon Budget and net zero commitments and secure the economic opportunities of the transition. It also set out an aim to provide regular updates on hydrogen policy development, with the latest published in December 2023.<sup id="fnref:124"><a href="#fn:124" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 124]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>
<strong>North Sea Transition Deal<sup id="fnref:125"><a href="#fn:125" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 125]</a></sup> (2021)</strong>: through the North Sea Transition Deal, the offshore oil and gas industry is committed to reducing its production emissions by 10% by 2025, 25% by 2027 and 50% by 2030, against a 2018 baseline. The government continues to support the North Sea Transition Deal, including the important decarbonisation targets it set for the sector.</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="northern-ireland-executive-2">2.11.2.2 Northern Ireland Executive</h5>

<p>In 2022, the energy supply sector in Northern Ireland represented 14% of all emissions. From 1990 to 2022 the greenhouse gas emissions in the sector have reduced by 44%.</p>

<p>For the 12 month period January 2022 to December 2022, 51.0% of total electricity consumption in Northern Ireland was generated from renewable sources<sup id="fnref:126"><a href="#fn:126" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 126]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>To drive forward further action to decarbonise the energy sector, in December 2021 <abbr title="Department for Education, England">DfE</abbr> published the Northern Ireland Executive’s ‘Energy Strategy- The Path to Net Zero Energy’. Following on from which, the Climate Change Act (Northern Ireland) 2022 set a legal requirement for at least 80% of electricity consumption in Northern Ireland to be from renewable sources by 2030.</p>

<h5 id="scottish-government-2">2.11.2.3 Scottish Government</h5>

<p>The electricity sector in Scotland is the most mature sector in terms of decarbonisation, with emissions falling by 13.0 mega tonnes carbon dioxide equivalent (<abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e) between 1990 and 2022 to 1.7 mega tonnes carbon dioxide equivalent (<abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e)– an 88.1% reduction, the largest reduction of any sector.</p>

<p>In 2022, 87.9% of electricity generated in Scotland was from zero or low carbon sources (including nuclear and pumped hydro). Specifically, 71% of electricity generated in Scotland in 2022 was from renewable sources.</p>

<h5 id="welsh-government-2">2.11.2.4 Welsh Government</h5>

<p>The Welsh Government’s policy objective is to avoid the continued extraction and consumption of fossil fuels. It expects all new development to mitigate the causes of climate change in accordance with its energy hierarchy for planning, as set out in Planning Policy Wales (2018):<sup id="fnref:127"><a href="#fn:127" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 127]</a></sup></p>

<ol>
  <li>Reduce energy demand</li>
  <li>Use energy efficiently</li>
  <li>Renewable energy generation</li>
  <li>Minimise carbon impact of other energy generation</li>
  <li>Minimise extraction of carbon-intensive energy materials</li>
</ol>

<p>In the hierarchy, the extraction of minerals for the purpose of generating energy is undesirable as it is the most carbon intensive form of production. The purpose of this hierarchy is to encourage preferred generation proposals to come forward and to discourage proposals supported by the extraction of fossil fuels. In addition to Planning Policy Wales, the Welsh Government’s Coal Policy Statement (2021) is clear that it does not intend to authorise new Coal Authority mining operation licences or variations to existing licences.<sup id="fnref:128"><a href="#fn:128" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 128]</a></sup></p>

<h5 id="jersey-2">2.11.2.5 Jersey</h5>

<p>Through interconnectors to the French grid, Jersey imports most of its electricity from low carbon and certified renewable sources meaning many of the decarbonisation policies focus on electrification of on-Island heating and transport.</p>

<h5 id="guernsey-2">2.11.2.6 Guernsey</h5>

<p>Guernsey’s Energy Policy<sup id="fnref:129"><a href="#fn:129" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 129]</a></sup> sets out a target of net zero by no later than 2050 and will transition to a low carbon Island, supported by increased use of electricity to heat homes and power on-island travel. Guernsey’s Electricity Strategy<sup id="fnref:130"><a href="#fn:130" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 130]</a></sup> outlined plans to further decarbonise the electricity sector, and how increased electrification could assist in the broader energy market underpinned by additional interconnection. The Climate Change Action Plan will explore how Guernsey can achieve this target, including more broadly across the energy sector, and how feasible it is to aim to achieve net zero before 2050. In 2019, Guernsey’s government commissioned a report entitled “Future Energy Demand and Policy Considerations for Guernsey”<sup id="fnref:131"><a href="#fn:131" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 131]</a></sup>. The report forecasts a decline in total energy demand over time with an in increase in electricity demand up until 2050. The report identified the following as drivers to the predicted decline in energy and fuel demand: technological efficiencies, fuel efficiencies and the uptake of energy reduction measures such as loft insulation, hybrid vehicles, or newer more efficient gas boilers.</p>

<p>Guernsey has an interconnector, through Jersey, with France, which provides access to the European electricity grid. Additional interconnection will provide greater electricity supply security and will allow for development of on-Island renewables and potential export opportunities.</p>

<h5 id="isle-of-man-2">2.11.2.7 Isle of Man</h5>

<p>In 2019, the Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets (<abbr title="Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets">IMPACT</abbr>) Report<sup id="fnref:132"><a href="#fn:132" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 132]</a></sup> was produced. Appendices<sup id="fnref:133"><a href="#fn:133" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 133]</a></sup> 13-17 and 20 relate to energy. In 2021, the Isle of Man Future Energy Scenarios<sup id="fnref:134"><a href="#fn:134" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 134]</a></sup> report was produced, identifying potential decarbonisation routes for the Island’s electricity supply. In 2022, the Isle of Man Renewable Heating Scenarios<sup id="fnref:135"><a href="#fn:135" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 135]</a></sup> report was produced, identifying potential decarbonisation routes for the Island’s building energy needs. The Phase 1 Action Plan Progress Report<sup id="fnref:136"><a href="#fn:136" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 136]</a></sup> details progress made against the Council of Ministers’ Climate Action Plan Phase 1<sup id="fnref:137"><a href="#fn:137" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 137]</a></sup> over the period 1 April 2021-31 March 2022, including actions relating to energy. Section 1 of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027<sup id="fnref:138"><a href="#fn:138" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 138]</a></sup> sets out the Isle of Man’s current, high-level policies relating to electricity decarbonisation. In particular, it sets a target of 2030 for full decarbonisation of the national electricity supply from fossil fuels and at least 20 <abbr title="Megawatts">MW</abbr> locally generated renewable power by 2026. Manx Utilities, the Island’s publicly owned electricity company is delivering its Future Energy Delivery Strategy<sup id="fnref:139"><a href="#fn:139" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 139]</a></sup> which outlines the roadmap to the targets set out above.</p>

<h5 id="gibraltar-2">2.11.2.8 Gibraltar</h5>

<p>The Gibraltar Electricity Authority fully switched electricity generation to the North Mole Power Station in 2020. This plant runs on natural gas and represents a significant step forward for Gibraltar in terms of moving towards cleaner electricity. Although it is still a fossil fuel, it is much cleaner than the diesel oil used by the old generating stations and emissions from electricity have decreased by 37%<sup id="fnref:140"><a href="#fn:140" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 140]</a></sup> since 2015 despite the actual amount of electricity being consumed remaining fairly static.</p>

<p>In 2018 the government entered into a Solar Framework Agreement to promote the roll out of solar photovoltaic panels across the territory. In 2019 the first of these projects was deployed at New Harbours industrial park as part of a scheme to install over 3 <abbr title="Megawatts">MW</abbr> of renewable energy.</p>

<p>The Nearly Zero Energy Buildings<sup id="fnref:141"><a href="#fn:141" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 141]</a></sup> standards came into force in January 2021 which require all new buildings to meet very high standards of energy efficiency as well as to produce a minimum of 40% of their own energy from renewables.</p>

<h4 id="transport-brbr-1">2.11.3 Transport <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="england-1">2.11.3.1 England</h5>

<p>The <strong>Transport Decarbonisation Plan<sup id="fnref:142"><a href="#fn:142" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 142]</a></sup> (2021)</strong> sets out how to decarbonise the entire transport system in England, below are some of the areas that are covered:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>Technical consultation on zero emission vehicle mandate policy design<sup id="fnref:143"><a href="#fn:143" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 143]</a></sup> (2022)</strong>: Following the announcement of the UK adopting a zero emission vehicle (<abbr title="Zero Emissions Vehicle">ZEV</abbr>) mandate in the Net Zero Strategy in October 2021, the Department for Transport published a consultation seeking views on some of the design features that could be included in a car and van regulation. A summary of responses was published in 2023<sup id="fnref:144"><a href="#fn:144" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 144]</a></sup>.</li>
  <li>
    <p><strong>National Bus Strategy<sup id="fnref:145"><a href="#fn:145" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 145]</a></sup> (2021)</strong>: committed to make buses more frequent, more reliable, more comprehensive, easier to understand and use, better co-ordinated and cheaper – to increase passenger numbers and reduce congestion and carbon emissions. The National Bus Strategy also re-committed to supporting the introduction of at least 4,000 zero emission buses (<abbr title="Zero Emissions Buses">ZEBs</abbr>) and achieving a zero-emission fleet.</p>
  </li>
  <li>
<strong>Jet Zero Strategy<sup id="fnref:146"><a href="#fn:146" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 146]</a></sup> (2022)</strong>: set out its approach to achieving net zero for UK aviation by 2050. The Strategy focused on the rapid development of technologies in a way that maintains the benefits of air travel, whilst maximising the opportunities that decarbonisation brings for the UK.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Domestic Maritime Decarbonisation<sup id="fnref:147"><a href="#fn:147" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 147]</a></sup> (2022)</strong>: This consultation sought evidence on barriers and opportunities of decarbonising the maritime sector. A summary of responses was published in 2023.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Cycling and Walking Investment Strategy<sup id="fnref:148"><a href="#fn:148" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 148]</a></sup> (2022)</strong>: sets the target that half of all journeys in towns and cities will be cycled or walked by 2030. It also includes the aim to deliver a world class cycling and walking network in England by 2040.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Renewable Transport Fuel Obligation (<abbr title="Renewable Transport Fuel Obligation">RTFO</abbr>) Order<sup id="fnref:149"><a href="#fn:149" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 149]</a></sup> (2007)</strong> regulates renewable fuels used for transport. The <abbr title="Renewable Transport Fuel Obligation">RTFO</abbr> was first implemented in 2008 and was the core policy measure for meeting transport targets within the EU Renewable Energy Directive. Under the <abbr title="Renewable Transport Fuel Obligation">RTFO</abbr>, suppliers of relevant transport fuel in the UK must be able to show that a certain percentage of the fuel they supply comes from renewable and sustainable sources. Fuel suppliers that supply at least 450,000 litres of this fuel a year are obligated under the scheme.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Zero emission <abbr title="Heavy Goods Vehicle">HGV</abbr> and infrastructure demonstrator programme<sup id="fnref:150"><a href="#fn:150" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 150]</a></sup></strong>: Research and Development funding into zero emission <abbr title="Heavy Goods Vehicle">HGV</abbr> and infrastructure demonstrators will establish new hydrogen <abbr title="Heavy Goods Vehicle">HGV</abbr> refuelling sites and the deployment of hydrogen fuel cell <abbr title="Heavy Goods Vehicles">HGVs</abbr>. In addition, the Tees Valley Hydrogen Transport Hub brings together hydrogen supply (refuelling infrastructure) and demand (transport applications) with the aim of demonstrating commercial viability of hydrogen in transport. Three projects, receiving £13m funding, are using hydrogen as a fuel with a fuel cell for a range of road vehicles, and through combustion for airside support vehicles. This is being supported by new publicly accessible hydrogen refuelling stations to be built in the region.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Delivering decarbonisation through places</strong>: There is no uniform approach to decarbonisation and each place in the UK has its own role to play in helping the UK to meet its legally binding target of net zero by 2050. In 2022, through an innovation grants programme, the UK provided over £550,000 to develop early-stage innovative solutions to support the decarbonisation of local transport systems.</li>
</ul>

<p>Better data can provide new policy and operational insights, drive new products and services and ‘nudge’ people towards lower emission journeys. The department’s annual Transport and Environment statistical release draws together various data sources on transport’s environmental impact and provides guidance explaining the detail of estimating greenhouse gas emissions for different modes and journeys. Data consumers can use these data, without restrictions on use or disclosure, for journey planning applications, products and services enabling users to plan green journeys.</p>

<h5 id="northern-ireland-executive-3">2.11.3.2 Northern Ireland Executive</h5>

<p>In 2022, transport was the second largest greenhouse gas emitting sector in Northern Ireland contributing 18.1% to overall emissions. The Department for Infrastructure (<abbr title="Department for Infrastructure, Northern Ireland">DfI</abbr>) is currently developing its suite of new Transport Plans through an integrated approach with local councils Local Development Plans (<abbr title="Local Development Plans">LDPs</abbr>). This integrated approach being undertaken between <abbr title="Department for Infrastructure, Northern Ireland">DfI</abbr> and local councils provides a unique opportunity to make sure that the movement and accessibility of all forms, across all modes of transport, is considered as a key component in the development of areas at a local level. <abbr title="Department for Infrastructure, Northern Ireland">DfI</abbr> has also committed investment of over £100m in hydrogen zero emissions and electric buses to support the roll out of a public transport fleet with zero emissions from engine combustion.</p>

<p>To support the decarbonisation of transport, <abbr title="Department for Infrastructure, Northern Ireland">DfI</abbr> has also published an Action Plan for Electric Vehicle (<abbr title="Electric Vehicle">EV</abbr>) Infrastructure<sup id="fnref:151"><a href="#fn:151" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 151]</a></sup> in November 2022. The plan was developed by the Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Task-Force which was set up in December 2021 to bring together representatives from government, consumers, energy providers, industry and <abbr title="Electric Vehicle">EV</abbr> drivers to consider our <abbr title="Electric Vehicle">EV</abbr> Infrastructure requirements to deliver a fit for purpose, modern <abbr title="Electric Vehicle">EV</abbr> charging network.</p>

<h5 id="scottish-government-3">2.11.3.3 Scottish Government</h5>

<p>Transport is Scotland’s highest carbon emitting sector. The largest source of transport emissions is cars, which contribute almost 40% of transport emissions. This demonstrates the need to both transition to zero emission vehicles and reduce car use to combat climate change in a way that is consistent with our just transition principles.</p>

<p>Scottish Government and Convention of Scottish Local Authorities (<abbr title="Convention of Scottish Local Authorities">COSLA</abbr>) continue to work in partnership to produce the updated route map and it will be published in due course. The route map will set out the interventions to support the scale of behavioural change required and a timeline for implementing demand management.</p>

<p>Additionally, Scotland has one of the most comprehensive public charging networks in the UK, with over 600 public charge points, funded through public and increasingly private sector investment. Scotland has the UK’s second highest number of electric vehicle public charge points, second only to London, and has committed to enabling the delivery of approximately 24,000 additional public <abbr title="Electric Vehicle">EV</abbr> charge points by 2030.</p>

<p>Through the Older and Disabled and Young Persons Concessionary travel schemes over £370m is spent each year to provide free bus travel for over 2 million people in Scotland, including all children and young people under 22, eligible disabled people and everyone aged 60 and over.</p>

<p>Since 2020 we have invested over £150 million to put more than 800 zero emission buses and coaches on the road and install supporting charging infrastructure.</p>

<p>Our most recent £41.7 million investment in zero emission buses has leveraged 3.2 times the amount of private sector funding, moving the transition to a sustainable financial model that ends the need for continued public subsidy.</p>

<h5 id="welsh-government-3">2.11.3.4 Welsh Government</h5>

<p>The Welsh Government has committed to using the sustainable transport hierarchy when deciding on new transport infrastructure. This gives priority to walking and cycling, public transport and ultra-low emissions vehicles over other private motor vehicles.</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>Transport strategy<sup id="fnref:152"><a href="#fn:152" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 152]</a></sup> (2021)</strong>: identifies 3 priorities for the transport system
    <ul>
      <li>Bring services to people in order to reduce the need to travel</li>
      <li>Allow people and goods to move easily from door to door by accessible, sustainable and efficient transport services and infrastructure</li>
      <li>Encourage people to make the change to more sustainable transport</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>
<strong>National Transport Delivery Plan<sup id="fnref:153"><a href="#fn:153" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 153]</a></sup> (2022-27)</strong>: sets out how the Welsh Government will deliver against these priorities, by sector and by travel mode.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Electric Vehicle Charging Strategy<sup id="fnref:154"><a href="#fn:154" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 154]</a></sup> (2021)</strong>: set out its vision that by 2025, all users of electric cars and vans will be confident that they can access electric vehicle charging infrastructure when and where they need it. The associated Action Plan details the actions that will be taken to achieve this vision, grouped into 4 main outcomes:
    <ul>
      <li>Increased total charging provision</li>
      <li>A quality charging experience</li>
      <li>A sustainable approach (aligned with the decarbonisation agenda)</li>
      <li>Localised benefits</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<h5 id="jersey-3">2.11.3.5 Jersey</h5>

<p>Transport is the highest source of emissions in Jersey and has been focus of emissions reduction policies within the Carbon Neutral Roadmap<sup id="fnref:155"><a href="#fn:155" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 155]</a></sup> including incentive schemes for electric bicycles, cars and vans and the installation of charging points. Second generation biodiesel has also been subsidised within the bus and government fleet. The longer-term focus is on support for active travel and increased bus ridership.</p>

<h5 id="guernsey-3">2.11.3.6 Guernsey</h5>

<p>Guernsey’s Integrated Transport Strategy<sup id="fnref:156"><a href="#fn:156" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 156]</a></sup>, approved in 2014, sets out the strategic approach to managing the transport system on the island. Principally the Strategy takes a hierarchical approach to transport, prioritising active travel over vehicular travel, and public transport over private vehicles, which will help to reduce vehicle emissions over time.</p>

<h5 id="isle-of-man-3">2.11.3.7 Isle of Man</h5>

<p>In 2019, the Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets (<abbr title="Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets">IMPACT</abbr>) Report<sup id="fnref:157"><a href="#fn:157" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 157]</a></sup> was produced. Appendices 23-27 and 33 relate to transport<sup id="fnref:158"><a href="#fn:158" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 158]</a></sup>. The Phase 1 Action Plan Progress Report<sup id="fnref:159"><a href="#fn:159" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 159]</a></sup> details progress made against the Council of Ministers’ Climate Action Plan Phase 1<sup id="fnref:160"><a href="#fn:160" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 160]</a></sup> over the period 1 April 2021-31 March 2022, including actions relating to transport.
