Section 3 of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027<sup id="fnref:161"><a href="#fn:161" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 161]</a></sup> sets out the current, high level policies relating to transport decarbonisation. Notably, the Plan has committed to a Transport Strategy to deliver 15% sector reduction by 2027, to be underway in 2024. An independent Strategic Transport Decarbonisation Review<sup id="fnref:162"><a href="#fn:162" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 162]</a></sup> has been prepared to inform the strategy. The Climate Change Plan makes a commitment to banning first registrations of petrol and diesel cars on the Island from 2030, and hybrids from 2035.</p>

<h5 id="gibraltar-3">2.11.3.8 Gibraltar</h5>

<p>Gibraltar published its Sustainable Traffic Transport and Parking Plan in 2017. This was done after an in-depth study of the current transport network and its problems with a view to identifying solutions that encourage behavioural change and effect a modal shift towards walking, cycling and public transport.</p>

<p>Gibraltar has committed to ending the sale of internal combustion engine vehicles in line with EU targets. It also continues to promote active travel through the publication and implementation of its Active Travel Strategy<sup id="fnref:163"><a href="#fn:163" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 163]</a></sup> which seeks to make cycling and walking the natural choices for short journeys.</p>

<h4 id="industrial-processes-and-product-use-ippu-brbr">2.11.4 Industrial Processes and Product Use (<abbr title="Industrial Processes and Product Use">IPPU</abbr>) <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="england-2">2.11.4.1 England</h5>

<p>In England, the <abbr title="Industrial Processes and Product Use">IPPU</abbr> sector is being tackled through the following strategies:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>Industrial Decarbonisation Strategy<sup id="fnref:164"><a href="#fn:164" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 164]</a></sup> (2021)</strong>: Sets out a plan for decarbonising industry in line with net zero goals. The policy measures outlined in the <abbr title="Industrial Decarbonisation Strategy">IDS</abbr> were: having at least 2 Carbon Capture Usage and Storage (<abbr title="Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage">CCUS</abbr>) clusters in place by mid-2020s, which will increase to 4 by 2030, with the world’s first net zero cluster in place by 2040; creating a market for low carbon industrial products through measures designed to increase demand; leveraging Resource and Energy Efficiency (<abbr title="Resource and Energy Efficiency">REEE</abbr>) measures to reduce emissions by 11 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e per year by 2035 (including 3 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e from Iron and Steel), and updating the UK’s Emission Trading Scheme cap in place by January 2024 to send a strong market sign to the private sector to incentivise industry to take action to decarbonise.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Net Zero Strategy<sup id="fnref:165"><a href="#fn:165" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 165]</a></sup> (2021)</strong>: The industry chapter of the Net Zero Strategy sets out an indicative Carbon Budget 6 pathway for industry. This pathway and updates in the Net Zero Growth Plan (<abbr title="Net Zero Growth Plan">NZGP</abbr>) were consistent with the expectations set out in the Industrial Decarbonisation Strategy (<abbr title="Industrial Decarbonisation Strategy">IDS</abbr>), but went further in specific areas, including increased fuel switching and Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage (<abbr title="Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage">CCUS</abbr>) ambitions, and additional contributions from Resource Efficiency and Energy Efficiency (<abbr title="Resource and Energy Efficiency">REEE</abbr>) measures.</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="northern-ireland-executive-4">2.11.4.2 Northern Ireland Executive</h5>

<p>Compared to the 1990 base year, industry emissions have decreased by 3.2 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e (61.1% reduction) and now represent 9.7% of greenhouse gas emissions in Northern Ireland. This reduction is due to decreased emissions from the food and drinks industry, the chemical industry, cement production and construction industries through efficiencies in their operation and reduced usage of certain products.</p>

<p>Under the Northern Ireland Executive’s 2021 ‘Energy Strategy – The Path to Net Zero Energy’<sup id="fnref:166"><a href="#fn:166" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 166]</a></sup> a key priority was made to set out an industrial decarbonisation pathway for 2022-2030.</p>

<h5 id="scottish-government-4">2.11.4.3 Scottish Government</h5>

<p>Scotland’s industrial emissions fell from 21 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e in 1990 to 8.8 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e in 2022. This demonstrates the significant progress made by industry so far, to embrace innovative technologies and develop more efficient processes.</p>

<p>Reducing industrial emissions further is central to Scotland’s net zero commitment and our economic ambitions as outlined in our Green Industrial Strategy. Scottish Government works collaboratively with the UK Government and other devolved administrations to accelerate industrial decarbonisation across our devolved and reserved competencies, including within a joint authority for the UK Emissions Trading Scheme.</p>

<p>Effective collaboration with the UK Government is vital on issues requiring national reform and large-scale investment including <abbr title="Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage">CCUS</abbr>, electricity pricing, grid infrastructure upgrades and hydrogen business model support.</p>

<p>Operating since 2020, the Scottish Industrial Energy Transformation Fund (<abbr title="Scottish Industrial Energy Transformation Fund">SIETF</abbr>) continues to provide match funding, boosting investor confidence to progress projects that contribute to decarbonising manufacturing.</p>

<p>To support the development of further evidence-based policy proposals, Scottish Government engages closely with key industry and academic stakeholders including through the Grangemouth Future Industry Board and the Industrial Decarbonisation Research and Innovation Centre.</p>

<p>Pipeline transportation of <abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> is vital for to support the decarbonisation of industry; the Scottish Government has announced funding to accelerate a project to repurpose an existing pipeline from transportation of gas to transportation of <abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> from industrial clusters in Scotland’s central belt to Acorn, so as to ensure that this will be available at the earliest opportunity.</p>

<h5 id="welsh-government-4">2.11.4.4 Welsh Government</h5>

<p>The Welsh Government’s Manufacturing Action Plan contains an objective to “Address the climate emergency by decarbonising the manufacturing sector in Wales, underpinned by circular economy practices and processes”.<sup id="fnref:167"><a href="#fn:167" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 167]</a></sup> The Welsh Government is focussing on:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Embedding low carbon and climate resilience within its Economic Contract and expanding consideration into all other aspects of Welsh Government spend, including grants and procurement</li>
  <li>Using the Circular Economy Fund<sup id="fnref:168"><a href="#fn:168" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 168]</a></sup> as a mechanism to drive forward more recycling and less landfill, including utilisation of new technologies and processes within manufacturing</li>
  <li>Working alongside Net Zero Industry Wales, industrial clusters and hubs as they develop their emissions reduction pathways and build a solid evidence base to better understand the potential role that fuel switching and <abbr title="Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage">CCUS</abbr> can play in decarbonising manufacturing</li>
  <li>Working with Net Zero Industry Wales, the South Wales Industrial Cluster and stakeholders in North Wales, including Hynet, to understand the infrastructure necessary to decarbonise industry and maximise the benefits from relevant initiatives</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="jersey-4">2.11.4.5 Jersey</h5>

<p>Jersey does not have significant industrial processes on the island. Work continues to reduce any emissions arising from <abbr title="Fluorinated gases">F-gases</abbr>.</p>

<h5 id="guernsey-4">2.11.4.6 Guernsey</h5>

<p>Guernsey does not have a significant industrial basis, however the emissions from the industrial sector represent 10.7% of Guernsey’s emissions in 2022. This represents a 36% reduction on 1990 levels.</p>

<h5 id="isle-of-man-4">2.11.4.7 Isle of Man</h5>

<p>These sectors make up a very small proportion of the Isle of Man’s <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> inventory and so have not yet been a policy focus. Very little heavy industry occurs on the Isle of Man. The Department for Enterprise offers a range of schemes, including the Business Energy Saving Scheme<sup id="fnref:169"><a href="#fn:169" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 169]</a></sup> which supports projects to improve business energy efficiency including refrigeration and air-conditioning units. The Isle of Man ratified the Montreal Protocol and made legislation<sup id="fnref:170"><a href="#fn:170" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 170]</a></sup> relating to the use and transfer of Ozone-Depleting Substances (<abbr title="Ozone-Depleting Substances">ODS</abbr>) and <abbr title="Fluorinated gases">F-gases</abbr> in 2020.</p>

<h5 id="gibraltar-4">2.11.4.8 Gibraltar</h5>

<p>Gibraltar does not have any heavy industry therefore emissions in this sector primarily arise from the use of refrigeration gases. In this respect, efforts are focused on improving building design to limit the need for air conditioning systems.</p>

<h4 id="agriculture-brbr-1">2.11.5 Agriculture <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="england-3">2.11.5.1 England</h5>

<p>The UK set out measures to support the decarbonisation of the agricultural sector. The Plan set out emissions reductions from agriculture in England through sustainable land management practices, the uptake of innovative practices and technologies, and actions to improve the productivity and profitability of the sector. Specifically, the measures set out the potential to improve farm profitability, through increases in productivity and through opportunities for diversification on low grade land. Other measures include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>Environmental Land Management (<abbr title="Environmental Land Management">ELM</abbr>) schemes<sup id="fnref:171"><a href="#fn:171" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 171]</a></sup> (2022)</strong>: provide a powerful vehicle for achieving net zero, and wider environmental goals, while supporting our rural economy. The scheme is split into 3 parts:
    <ul>
      <li>
<strong>Sustainable Farming Incentive</strong> - this pays farmers and land managers for actions that protect and enhance our natural environment, support the sustainable production of food, and boost farm productivity and resilience.</li>
      <li>
<strong>Countryside Stewardship</strong> - this is a targeted, place-based approach that encourages sustainable farming, promotes resilience against climate change, and enhances the beauty and diversity of the countryside.</li>
      <li>
<strong>Landscape Recovery</strong> - this is for landowners and managers who want to take a large-scale, long-term approach to producing environmental and climate goods on their land. It will facilitate and fund ambitious projects through bespoke, 20+ year agreements.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>
<strong>The UK’s Agriculture Act<sup id="fnref:172"><a href="#fn:172" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 172]</a></sup> (2020)</strong>: obligates the UK Government to produce a report on food security in the UK at least every 3 years. The UK published its first United Kingdom Food Security Report 2021<sup id="fnref:173"><a href="#fn:173" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 173]</a></sup> under the Agriculture Act in December 2021.</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="northern-ireland-executive-5">2.11.5.2 Northern Ireland Executive</h5>

<p>The latest Northern Ireland Greenhouse Gas Inventory (1990-2022) reported that the agriculture sector was the largest greenhouse gas emitting sector in Northern Ireland representing 29.1% of all emissions. To drive forward action, the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (<abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr>) published the Future Agricultural Policy Decisions for Northern Ireland in March 2022<sup id="fnref:174"><a href="#fn:174" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 174]</a></sup>. Decisions that are central to this future policy include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>A Farm Sustainability Payment which recognises the need for continuation of an income support ‘safety net’</li>
  <li>A Beef Sustainability Package comprising 2 elements; Beef Carbon Reduction Scheme and Suckler Cow Scheme</li>
  <li>A Farming with Nature Package to assist farm businesses and land managers across all land types to make substantial contributions to environmental improvements and sustainability</li>
  <li>Farming for Carbon measures which encourage low carbon emission farming practices</li>
</ul>

<p>Furthermore, the Soil Nutrient Health Scheme<sup id="fnref:175"><a href="#fn:175" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 175]</a></sup> which first opened in May 2022, is a comprehensive regional soil sampling and analysis programme being funded by the department that will allow farmers to optimise crop nutrient applications, assess on-farm carbon stocks and build farm resilience through its objective to test all, or the vast majority of, the 650,000 fields used for farming in Northern Ireland to help inform their management.</p>

<h5 id="scottish-government-5">2.11.5.3 Scottish Government</h5>

<p>The Scottish Government is transforming the way we support farming and food production in Scotland to deliver our Vision for Agriculture and become a global leader in sustainable and regenerative agriculture. We want to ensure that farming across Scotland continues sustainably into the future, producing high-quality food for the nation, helping to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and delivering increased biodiversity and wider environmental benefits.</p>

<p>In 2021-22, the Scottish Government committed to bringing forward the Agriculture and Rural Communities (Scotland) Bill, which has since become an Act, to deliver that vision.</p>

<p>The National Test Programme was announced in October 2021 to provide funding for farmers and crofters to prepare their farms to meet the conditions of future agriculture policy and support.</p>

<p>Regulations came into force from 1 January 2022 to consolidate the Silage Surry and Agricultural Fuel Oil (Scotland) Regulations 2003 into The Water Environment (Controlled Activities) (Scotland) Regulations 2011. These included improved controls on the storage of slurry and digestate to reduce leakage, and a move to precision spreading methods to maximise the nutrient benefit and reduce emissions. This provides benefits to water quality, air quality, and climate change mitigation.</p>

<h5 id="welsh-government-5">2.11.5.4 Welsh Government</h5>

<p>Welsh emissions for the agriculture sector decreased to 5.6 (<abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e) in 2022, this is a -3.8% change since 2021 and -7.7% from the base year (1990).</p>

<p>The Agriculture (Wales) Act 2023 establishes Sustainable Land Management as the framework for future agriculture support.<sup id="fnref:176"><a href="#fn:176" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 176]</a></sup> The Welsh Government will introduce a new Sustainable Farming Scheme (<abbr title="Sustainable Farming Scheme">SFS</abbr>) in 2026.<sup id="fnref:177"><a href="#fn:177" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 177]</a></sup> It will provide support for farmers to respond to the climate and nature emergencies, and to produce food in a sustainable way.</p>

<p>In preparation for the <abbr title="Sustainable Farming Scheme">SFS</abbr> in 2026, the Welsh Government has introduced the Habitat Wales Scheme to increase the area of habitat land under management, along with support for Organic and Common land farmers and an extension of Farming Connect support. In addition, a new Integrated Natural Resources Scheme was launched to deliver nature-based solutions across landscapes, catchments and pan Wales. During this preparatory phase, the Welsh Government continues to support farmers and growers through a range of capital investment schemes that tackle climate change, lead to improvements in soil, air and water quality and reduce the decline in our native biodiversity.<sup id="fnref:178"><a href="#fn:178" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 178]</a></sup></p>

<h5 id="jersey-5">2.11.5.5 Jersey</h5>

<p>The Economic Framework for the Rural Environment<sup id="fnref:179"><a href="#fn:179" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 179]</a></sup> was published in 2022 and set outs emissions reduction strategies for the industry. As part of this, the revised Rural Support Scheme (<abbr title="Rural Support Scheme">RSS</abbr>) was launched in January 2023. This provides credits to industry per Integrated Farm Management Plan. Uptake of this component of the <abbr title="Rural Support Scheme">RSS</abbr> has been ahead of forecast with 80 local businesses now signed up to the scheme.</p>

<p>During the next 12 months, Jersey will continue to investigate the feasibility of farm-scale Anaerobic Digestion plants. The installation of this technology would reduce emissions from slurry and feed energy into the grid to accommodate peak demand.</p>

<h5 id="guernsey-5">2.11.5.6 Guernsey</h5>

<p>The States of Guernsey are currently reviewing their policy approach to dairy farming which is the predominant agricultural sector on the island. It is anticipated that the revised policy will be linked to payments for public goods which would include climate change mitigation and adaptation aspects.</p>

<p>As part of the development of the island’s net zero plan, consideration is being given to the potential adoption of anaerobic digestion on island.</p>

<h5 id="isle-of-man-5">2.11.5.7 Isle of Man</h5>

<p>In 2019, the Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets (<abbr title="Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets">IMPACT</abbr>) Report<sup id="fnref:180"><a href="#fn:180" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 180]</a></sup> was produced. Appendices 18 and 28 relate to agriculture. The Phase 1 Action Plan Progress Report<sup id="fnref:181"><a href="#fn:181" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 181]</a></sup> details progress made against the Council of Ministers’ Climate Action Plan Phase 1<sup id="fnref:182"><a href="#fn:182" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 182]</a></sup> over the period 1 April 2021-31 March 2022, including actions relating to agriculture. Section 4 of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027<sup id="fnref:183"><a href="#fn:183" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 183]</a></sup> sets out the Isle of Man’s current, high level climate policies relating to the agricultural sector, including a commitment to prepare an Agricultural Strategy to deliver a 15% reduction in this sector’s emissions by 2027. The Agriculture and Fisheries Grant Scheme<sup id="fnref:184"><a href="#fn:184" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 184]</a></sup> (through the Agri-Environment Scheme) provides financial incentive for several initiatives aiming to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from the sector.</p>

<h5 id="gibraltar-5">2.11.5.8 Gibraltar</h5>

<p>Gibraltar has no agricultural sector.</p>

<h4 id="land-use-land-use-change-and-forestry-lulucf-brbr">2.11.6 Land-use, Land-use Change and Forestry (<abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr>) <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="england-4">2.11.6.1 England</h5>

<p>England addresses the <abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr> sector through the following strategies and policies:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>The England Peat Action Plan<sup id="fnref:185"><a href="#fn:185" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 185]</a></sup> (2021)</strong>: set out the government’s long-term vision for managing, protecting, and restoring peatlands so that they provide a wide range of benefits to wildlife, people and the planet.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Biomass Strategy<sup id="fnref:186"><a href="#fn:186" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 186]</a></sup> (2023)</strong>: set out the results of a review of the amount of sustainable biomass available to the UK (including domestically grown perennial energy crops and short-rotation forestry), and how this resource could be best utilised across the economy to help achieve net zero.</li>
  <li>
<strong>England Trees Action Plan<sup id="fnref:187"><a href="#fn:187" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 187]</a></sup> (2021)</strong>: set out the government’s long-term, generational vision for the forestry sector to 2050. It introduced a programme of new measures to boost tree planting and establishment, improve woodland management in England and bring trees closer to people.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Nature for Climate Fund<sup id="fnref:188"><a href="#fn:188" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 188]</a></sup> (2021-present)</strong>: is the key public sector fund for tree planting and peatland restoration. The England Trees Action Plan committed the government to treble tree planting rates in England by the end of this Parliament. Its delivery is funded by the Nature for Climate Fund.</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="northern-ireland-executive-6">2.11.6.2 Northern Ireland Executive</h5>

<p>Land-use, Land-use change and Forestry (<abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr>) sector accounts for 10.1% of greenhouse gas emissions according to the latest Northern Ireland Greenhouse Gas Inventory (1990-2022), with a reduction of 20.5% from the 1990 base year to 2022.</p>

<p>To continue to drive forward emission reductions in this sector, the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (<abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr>) has taken forward the development of a Northern Ireland Peatland Strategy<sup id="fnref:189"><a href="#fn:189" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 189]</a></sup> which they consulted on during 2021. The draft strategy sets out the strategic objectives and associated targets and actions to conserve and restore peatlands in Northern Ireland.</p>

<p>Separately in March 2020 <abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr> announced a ‘Forest for Our Future’ programme which aimed to plant 9,000 hectares of new woodland by 2030 to contribute to the reduction of Northern Ireland’s net greenhouse gas emissions. Since the programme commenced, to March 2022, 876 hectares of new woodland were planted.</p>

<h5 id="scottish-government-6">2.11.6.3 Scottish Government</h5>

<p>The Scottish Government committed £250 million over 10 years to restore 250,000 hectares of degraded peatlands by 2030.</p>

<p>Peatland restoration is delivered by Peatland ACTION - a flagship partnership established by the Scottish Government with 5 public sector Delivery Partners– NatureScot (<abbr title="NatureScot">NS</abbr>), Loch Lomond and Trossachs National Park Authority (<abbr title="Loch Lomond and Trossachs National Park Authority">LLTNPA</abbr>), Scottish Water (<abbr title="Scottish Water">SW</abbr>), Cairngorms National Park Authority (<abbr title="Cairngorms National Park Authority">CNPA</abbr>) and Forestry and Land Scotland (<abbr title="Forestry and Land Scotland">FLS</abbr>).</p>

<p>In 2021-22 the total annual budget for peatland restoration was around £22 million and the Peatland ACTION partnership restored 5,370 hectares.</p>

<p>Scottish Forestry has taken measures to maximise woodland creation with the financial resources available. It will not be possible to meet the 18,000 hectares a year woodland creation target under the current budget settlement but, with additional finance generated through the Woodland Carbon Code, approximately 10,000 hectares of woodland creation may be possible in this financial year.</p>

<p>Approximately 75% of all new woodland across the UK in recent years have been in Scotland. In 2021-22, 10,480 hectares of new woodland were created out of a total of 13.890 for the UK. Scottish Forestry manages the Woodland Carbon Code on behalf of the 4 countries across the UK and is introducing greater flexibility in the Forestry Grant Scheme so that additional private finance from the carbon market can be attracted into woodland creation.</p>

<h5 id="welsh-government-6">2.11.6.4 Welsh Government</h5>

<p>The <abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr> sector in Wales provides a net sink (a removal of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere largely from the sequestration of carbon dioxide by trees) of 0.9 million tonnes of carbon dioxide (<abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub>) equivalent. The estimated size of this emissions removal has increased by 0.5% (0.005 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e) between 2021 and 2022.</p>

<p>The National Peatland Action Programme aims to restore 600-800 hectares of degraded peatland for each year of 2020-2025<sup id="fnref:190"><a href="#fn:190" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 190]</a></sup> with an ambition to increase delivery from 600ha to 1,800 per year by 2030/31<sup id="fnref:191"><a href="#fn:191" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 191]</a></sup>. 3,000ha has been restored over the first 4 years of the Programme since 2020. Its priority themes for action are:</p>

<ol>
  <li>Peatland erosion</li>
  <li>Peatland drainage</li>
  <li>Sustainable management of blanket peats</li>
  <li>Sustainable management of lowland peats</li>
  <li>The restoration of afforested peatlands</li>
  <li>The gradual restoration of our highest carbon-peatlands</li>
</ol>

<p>The Woodland Creation Grant<sup id="fnref:192"><a href="#fn:192" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 192]</a></sup> and Small Grants – Woodland Creation Scheme<sup id="fnref:193"><a href="#fn:193" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 193]</a></sup> provide financial support for the planting of trees and the installation of fencing and gates.</p>

<h5 id="jersey-6">2.11.6.5 Jersey</h5>

<p>The Carbon Neutral Roadmap<sup id="fnref:194"><a href="#fn:194" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 194]</a></sup> provides recognition that tackling the climate emergency by using nature-based solutions that also address the biodiversity crisis provides multiple benefits for our land, air and sea.</p>

<p>Jersey is supportive of regenerative land management practices and sequestration projects on-island whilst recognising our limited land area and high population density limit its potential. Support for local sinks in terrestrial or marine environment (blue carbon) will be prioritised before the purchase of off-island offsets. Any funded sequestration projects will be required to contribute to improvements in biodiversity.</p>

<h5 id="guernsey-6">2.11.6.6 Guernsey</h5>

<p>Guernsey’s Planning legislation, which comprises the Land Planning and Development (Guernsey) Law, 2005<sup id="fnref:195"><a href="#fn:195" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 195]</a></sup> and associated ordinances<sup id="fnref:196"><a href="#fn:196" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 196]</a></sup>, and the 2016 Island Development Plan<sup id="fnref:197"><a href="#fn:197" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 197]</a></sup>, along with associated planning briefs and subject plans, outlines the basis for how the island’s land is used.</p>

<p>Land use change is largely driven by pressures from development. These pressures are managed through an integrated Island Development Plan, which is based on an agreed spatial strategy for the distribution of development. Guernsey’s spatial strategy and planning policies protect the rural and natural environment from high levels of development, assist in achieving sustainable development and afford protection to important sites for biodiversity. New development is also subject to the Guernsey Building Regulations which specifically consider matters such as energy efficiency in the built environment.</p>

<p>There is no forestry industry on Guernsey.</p>

<h5 id="isle-of-man-6">2.11.6.7 Isle of Man</h5>

<p>In 2019, the Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets (<abbr title="Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets">IMPACT</abbr>) Report<sup id="fnref:198"><a href="#fn:198" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 198]</a></sup> was produced. Appendices 10A and B relate to <abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr>. The Phase 1 Action Plan Progress Report<sup id="fnref:199"><a href="#fn:199" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 199]</a></sup> details progress made against the Council of Ministers’ Climate Action Plan Phase 1<sup id="fnref:200"><a href="#fn:200" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 200]</a></sup> over the period 1 April 2021-31 March 2022, including actions relating to <abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr>. The Peatland Restoration Project<sup id="fnref:201"><a href="#fn:201" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 201]</a></sup>, commenced in 2021, aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from exposed or eroding peat, and aims to map all areas of peat on the Isle of Man and provide guidance and collaboration on the management and restoration of peatlands. The <abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr> project, completed in 2022, has led to a number of improvements in the methodology for calculating land based sources and sinks of <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> emissions. The Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027<sup id="fnref:202"><a href="#fn:202" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 202]</a></sup> commits to the production of a Land Management Framework, to deliver a 10% increase in carbon sequestration by 2027.</p>

<h5 id="gibraltar-6">2.11.6.8 Gibraltar</h5>

<p>The Gibraltar Development Plan<sup id="fnref:203"><a href="#fn:203" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 203]</a></sup> was adopted in 2009 and is intended to guide land use planning in Gibraltar for the next 10 years. The plan takes into account the competing demands on Gibraltar’s scarce land resources and provides a co-ordinated set of policies and proposals to manage future growth. A new development plan is currently being prepared.</p>

<p>Over 30% of Gibraltar’s land area is a protected area in which development is not permitted.</p>

<h4 id="waste-and-wastewater-brbr">2.11.7 Waste and wastewater <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="england-5">2.11.7.1 England</h5>

<p>England addresses waste and wastewater through the following strategies:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>Resources and Waste Strategy<sup id="fnref:204"><a href="#fn:204" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 204]</a></sup> (2018)</strong>: set out how to preserve our stock of material resources by minimising waste, promoting resource efficiency and moving towards a circular economy. It also set out the plan to become a world leader in using resources efficiently and reducing the amount of waste created as a society, in addition to the ambition to prolong the lives of the materials and goods that we use, and move society away from the inefficient, ‘linear’ economic model of ‘take, make, use, throw’.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Carbon Budget Delivery Plan<sup id="fnref:205"><a href="#fn:205" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 205]</a></sup> (2023)</strong>: set out the plan to reduce wastewater treatment emissions through improved monitoring and subsequent optimisation of operations, as well as through further improvements in modelling and data collection to improve reporting and reduce uncertainty.</li>
</ul>

<p>England tackles F-gas sector emission reductions through:</p>

<ul>
  <li>The implementation of additional phasedown steps to meet the Kigali Amendment requirement This is achieved through <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr>’s public commitment in the Carbon Budget Delivery Plan to review <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr>’s domestic F-gas Regulation.</li>
  <li>A National Health Service (<abbr title="National Health Service">NHS</abbr>) led initiative to increase incentives to prescribe inhalers not containing <abbr title="Fluorinated gases">F-gases</abbr>, as well as industry commitments to introduce propellants with lower global warming potentials in metered-dose inhalers that still do contain <abbr title="Fluorinated gases">F-gases</abbr>.</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="northern-ireland-executive-7">2.11.7.2 Northern Ireland Executive</h5>

<p>The latest Northern Ireland Greenhouse Gas Inventory (1990-2022) reported that the sector represents 3.6% of all greenhouse gas emissions in Northern Ireland with waste-water handling making up 0.6% of the total emissions. From 1990 to 2022 the emissions in the sector have reduced by 61.9%. The reduction in emissions from the waste sector (1.2 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e) is primarily due to the continued process of methane capture and oxidation systems within landfill sites. Plans are being progressed for targeted policy and legislative interventions to help tackle the remaining emissions from the sector. <abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr> is exploring the feasibility of diverting biodegradable wastes from landfill and is consulting on changes to recycling and waste management to improve the quality and quantity of what is collected and to bring business into scope of mandatory recycling.</p>

<p>Progress in this sector has been delivered though a number of plans and strategies over the past decade. The Northern Ireland Waste Management Strategy ‘Delivering Resource Efficiency’<sup id="fnref:206"><a href="#fn:206" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 206]</a></sup> was published in 2013 and set the policy framework for the management of waste in Northern Ireland to 2020. Under this Strategy Northern Ireland increased its recycling rate to over 50%. To build upon this progress a new Waste Management Strategy<sup id="fnref:207"><a href="#fn:207" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 207]</a></sup> is currently being developed by the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (<abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr>) which will seek to deliver upon that at least 70% of waste being recycled target set in the Climate Change Act (Northern Ireland) 2022 and the various recycling and landfill targets set out in the Waste and Contaminated Land (Northern Ireland) Order 1997.</p>

<p>Northern Ireland ‘Waste Prevention Programme -Stopping Waste in its tracks’ <sup id="fnref:208"><a href="#fn:208" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 208]</a></sup> which was published in 2020 set out a range of policies and actions focused on waste prevention in line with the waste hierarchy with a focus on reducing waste and supporting the principles of a circular economy. One key outcome is the continuing benefit of the carrier bag levy<sup id="fnref:209"><a href="#fn:209" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 209]</a></sup> which was introduced in 2013, with the proceeds generated being used, in the delivery of local projects which both enhance and improve the environment.</p>

<h5 id="scottish-government-7">2.11.7.3 Scottish Government</h5>

<p>Scotland has made strong progress in reducing greenhouse gas emissions from the waste management sector. In 2022, sector emissions stood at 1.6 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e, 75% lower than 1990 levels. This has been driven by a reduction in the total amount of waste going to landfill in Scotland, which has dropped by nearly half over the past decade, while over 62% of waste was recycled in 2022. In the same year Scotland met its 2025 target to reduce all waste by 15% (against 2011 levels) for the second year in a row.</p>

<h5 id="welsh-government-7">2.11.7.4 Welsh Government</h5>

<p>The latest Wales Greenhouse Gas Inventory (1990-2022) reported that the sector represents 2.8% of all greenhouse gas emissions. From 1990 to 2022 the emissions in the sector have reduced by 72%. The reduction in emissions from the waste sector is primarily due to the significant reduction in the landfilling of biodegradable waste as well as the installation of methane capture on landfill sites. There has been a significant decrease in the proportion of Local Authority collected municipal waste disposed of via landfill, falling from 42.0% in 2012-13 to 0.9% in 2023-24.</p>

<p>Beyond Recycling, the Welsh Government’s strategy for making the circular economy a reality, contains 6 core themes for keeping resources in use for as long as possible and avoiding waste:<sup id="fnref:210"><a href="#fn:210" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 210]</a></sup></p>

<ul>
  <li>Driving innovation in materials use</li>
  <li>Upscaling prevention and re-use</li>
  <li>Building on Wales’s recycling record</li>
  <li>Investing in infrastructure</li>
  <li>Enabling community and business action</li>
  <li>Aligning government levers</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="jersey-7">2.11.7.5 Jersey</h5>

<p>In Jersey, the Solid Waste Strategy<sup id="fnref:211"><a href="#fn:211" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 211]</a></sup> commits to prioritising reuse and recycling as per the waste hierarchy. Residual municipal waste is sent to an Energy Recovery Facility which generates part of our electricity. In 2022, this contributed 8% of our greenhouse gas emissions. A recent engagement campaign ‘It’s not a load of Rubbish<sup id="fnref:212"><a href="#fn:212" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 212]</a></sup>’, communicated the waste hierarchy of reduce, reuse recycle.</p>

<p>Since July 2022, the Single Use Plastics Law<sup id="fnref:213"><a href="#fn:213" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 213]</a></sup> came into force. This means Islanders no longer receive single use carrier bags with their purchases and are charged at least 70 pence per reusable bag.</p>

<p>The Construction industry generates a large proportion of waste in Jersey. Working collaboratively with the industry, we have been developing a plan to reduce inert construction waste on-island.</p>

<h5 id="guernsey-7">2.11.7.6 Guernsey</h5>

<p>Guernsey’s Waste Strategy<sup id="fnref:214"><a href="#fn:214" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 214]</a></sup> was approved in 2012 and is focused principally on waste reduction, with reuse and recycling prioritised over disposal. Waste has been diverted from landfill to processing as Refuse Derived Fuel – reducing emissions and increasing energy recovery.</p>

<p>Guernsey’s household waste Pay-As-You-Throw scheme encourages waste reduction, and leads to increased reuse/recycling, and separation of organic waste – all of which reduce emissions in terms of processing waste/recycling. Guernsey’s Waste Management Plan<sup id="fnref:215"><a href="#fn:215" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 215]</a></sup>, approved in 2018, outlines the implementation plan for the Waste Strategy and also encourages home composting of organic food waste and garden waste, which aims to reduce emissions from transporting organic waste to the green waste site, and from associated processing. Zero organic waste is sent to landfill, collected household and commercial food waste is processed off-island to an Anaerobic Digestion plant for energy recovery and PAS110 compliant digestate. This reduces emissions that would otherwise be created through landfill.</p>

<h5 id="isle-of-man-7">2.11.7.7 Isle of Man</h5>

<p>In 2019, the Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets (<abbr title="Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets">IMPACT</abbr>) Report<sup id="fnref:216"><a href="#fn:216" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 216]</a></sup> was produced. Appendices 13A, B and C relate to energy from waste. In 2004, the Island’s Energy from Waste Plant facility was completed which now processes all domestic and commercial residual waste, generating 10% of the Island’s electricity.<sup id="fnref:217"><a href="#fn:217" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 217]</a></sup> This diverts waste from landfill and has led to a significant reduction in emissions in this sector. The Phase 1 Action Plan Progress Report<sup id="fnref:218"><a href="#fn:218" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 218]</a></sup> details progress made against the Council of Ministers’ Climate Action Plan Phase 1<sup id="fnref:219"><a href="#fn:219" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 219]</a></sup> over the period 1 April 2021-31 March 2022, including actions relating to waste. Section 6 of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027<sup id="fnref:220"><a href="#fn:220" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 220]</a></sup> sets out the Isle of Man’s current, high-level policies relating to reducing emissions from waste, including a commitment to produce Waste Management and Circular Economy Strategies to deliver 15% sectoral emissions reduction by 2027.</p>

<h5 id="gibraltar-7">2.11.7.8 Gibraltar</h5>

<p>Gibraltar’s overall objective continues to be the reduction of waste wherever possible, followed by reuse and recycling, as per the principles of the waste hierarchy and the circular economy.</p>

<p>Gibraltar’s overall objective continues to be the reduction of waste wherever possible, followed by reuse and recycling, as per the principles of the waste hierarchy and the circular economy. The current kerbside recycling programme was expanded in 2012 to include paper and plastic recycling as well as cooking oil and Waste from Electrical and Electronic Equipment (<abbr title="Waste from Electrical and Electronic Equipment">WEEE</abbr>). All of Gibraltar’s waste is exported to Spain for recovery or final disposal. Current plans are focusing on the development of a Waste Management Facility in Gibraltar to maximise recovery of recyclable material prior to export. A ban on single use plastic bags<sup id="fnref:221"><a href="#fn:221" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 221]</a></sup> was introduced in 2019 along with a more comprehensive ban on single use plastic items.<sup id="fnref:222"><a href="#fn:222" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 222]</a></sup></p>

<h4 id="carbon-capture-and-storage-and-greenhouse-gas-removals-brbr">2.11.8 Carbon Capture and Storage and Greenhouse Gas Removals <br><br>
</h4>

<p>England has put in place the following strategies in regards to carbon capture and storage:</p>

<h5 id="carbon-capture-utilisation-and-storage">2.11.8.1 Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage</h5>

<p>Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage (<abbr title="Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage">CCUS</abbr>) is essential for industry to decarbonise. In the future net zero world, we will still need materials such as cement, steel, and chemicals. For many of these sectors, <abbr title="Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage">CCUS</abbr> is currently the only viable route to decarbonise at the scale required for us to meet our targets.</p>

<ul>
  <li>In November 2021, the government announced the selection of the HyNet and East Coast Cluster as the first 2 industrial <abbr title="Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage">CCUS</abbr> clusters to be deployed in the UK.</li>
  <li>In August 2022, the government announced a shortlist of 20 projects representing a range of innovative <abbr title="Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage">CCUS</abbr> technologies to be progressed to the due diligence stage for inclusion in those clusters. <abbr title="Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy">BEIS</abbr> (now <abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr>) then launched Phase-2 of the Cluster Sequencing Process to determine the projects that would make up those clusters and enter negotiations.</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="greenhouse-gas-removals">2.11.8.2 Greenhouse Gas Removals</h5>

<p>The Net Zero Strategy (2021) set out several commitments towards the ambition of deploying at least 5 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>/yr of engineered removals by 2030, potentially rising to 23 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>/yr by 2035 and 75-81 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>/yr by 2050. As outlined in the Net Zero Growth Plan and other publications, the government has taken steps to deliver on this.</p>

<p>The UK:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Commissioned research from Vivid Economics to explore policy support options for Greenhouse Gas Removal technology deployment in the UK (2019).</li>
  <li>Published a Call for Evidence based on the outputs of the Vivid Economics study, which invited views from stakeholders on whether there is a role of government in incentivising <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas Removals">GGR</abbr> development and deployment in the UK over the medium and longer-term through an effective policy and regulatory framework and, where needed, what type targeted support would be appropriate (2020).</li>
  <li>Convened a <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas Removals">GGR</abbr> monitoring, reporting and verification (<abbr title="Monitoring, Reporting and Verification">MRV</abbr>) Task and Finish Group to understand the current position on <abbr title="Monitoring, Reporting and Verification">MRV</abbr> for negative emissions, existing regulatory frameworks and standards, and the gaps that exist and work required to fill them (2021).</li>
  <li>Published a summary of responses to the Call for Evidence, which set out the government would take a portfolio approach to <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas Removals">GGR</abbr> deployment which enables the development and commercialisation of a mix a different technologies (2021).</li>
  <li>Commissioned a study from E4tech and Element Energy to explore policy mechanisms for First Of A Kind Direct Air Carbon Capture and Storage (<abbr title="Direct Air Carbon Capture and Storage">DACCS</abbr>) and other engineered Greenhouse Gas Removals (2022)</li>
  <li>Consulted on the preferred business models to incentivise early investment in GGRs, with consultations on both a technology neutral engineered <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas Removals">GGR</abbr> business model and a power <abbr title="Bioenergy with Carbon Capture and Storage">BECCS</abbr> specific model (2022).</li>
  <li>Delivered £100 million innovation funding, including through Phase 1 and Phase 2 of the Net Zero Innovation Portfolio Direct Air Capture (<abbr title="Development Assistance Committee">DAC</abbr>) and <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas Removals">GGR</abbr> Programme. This programme was announced in 2020 and is due to complete in 2025.</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="marine-and-oceans-brbr">2.11.9 Marine and oceans <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="england-6">2.11.9.1 England</h5>

<p>England has several legislation and policies in place to manage and protect the marine environment:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>UK Marine and Coastal Access Act<sup id="fnref:223"><a href="#fn:223" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 223]</a></sup> (2009)</strong>: makes provisions for the management of the marine environment, including providing for the designation of conservation zones.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Fisheries Act<sup id="fnref:224"><a href="#fn:224" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 224]</a></sup> (2020)</strong>: sets 8 objectives, including a climate change objective, that provide the basis against which the UK Administrations will manage their fisheries.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Marine Policy Statement<sup id="fnref:225"><a href="#fn:225" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 225]</a></sup> (2011)</strong>: is the UK framework used to prepare marine plans and provides the basis for making decisions that affect the marine environment. The MPS’s high-level objectives are to promote sustainable economic development, enable the UK’s move towards a low-carbon economy, ensure a sustainable marine environment and to contribute to the societal benefits of the marine area.</li>
  <li>
<strong>UK Marine Strategy<sup id="fnref:226"><a href="#fn:226" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 226]</a></sup> (2019)</strong>: sets out a vision for UK waters to achieve clean, safe, healthy, biologically diverse and productive seas, which are used sustainably. The Strategy provides a legal framework, agreed with the devolved governments, for assessing and monitoring the status of UK seas and to put in place the measures needed to achieve Good Environmental Status (<abbr title="Good Environmental Status">GES</abbr>).</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="northern-ireland-executive-8">2.11.9.2 Northern Ireland Executive</h5>

<p>The Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (<abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr>) as the Marine Plan Authority (<abbr title="Marine Protected Area, Scotland">MPA</abbr>) has a duty under the Marine and Coastal Access Act 2009 and the Marine Act Northern Ireland 2013, to prepare marine plans to cover the Northern Ireland inshore and offshore regions, which facilitate the sustainable development of Northern Ireland’s marine area. The consultation on the draft Marine Plan<sup id="fnref:227"><a href="#fn:227" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 227]</a></sup> for Northern Ireland was launched April 2018. It set out the vision for a healthy marine area which is managed sustainably for the economic, environmental and social prosperity of present and future generations. The draft Marine Plan includes policies on climate change mitigation and will provide the framework for decision making for future use of the marine area, including for offshore renewable energy. With the public consultation responses published in April 2021, <abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr> is now progressing towards adoption and publication of a Marine Plan for Northern Ireland.</p>

<p>In 2021, <abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr> commenced the development of a blue carbon action plan that sets out how natural carbon stores in marine and coastal areas will be protected and restored.</p>

<h5 id="scottish-government-8">2.11.9.3 Scottish Government</h5>

<p>The Scottish Government has set out a new Blue Economy vision for the sustainable management of Scotland’s seas, establishing long term outcomes to 2045 and including a dedicated climate outcome to support ecosystem health, improved livelihoods, economic prosperity, social inclusion and wellbeing. New actions to increase protection of the marine environment include; introducing fisheries management measures across the offshore Marine Protected Area (<abbr title="Marine Protected Area, Scotland">MPA</abbr>) network by 2025, and to consult on the inshore <abbr title="Marine Protected Area, Scotland">MPA</abbr> network during the current programme for government. and introduction of a Scottish Wild Salmon Strategy. New evidence is also being delivered through the Scottish Blue Carbon Forum, building upon actions set out in the second Scottish Climate Change Adaptation Programme<sup id="fnref:228"><a href="#fn:228" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 228]</a></sup> to address Scotland’s marine climate risks.</p>

<h5 id="welsh-government-8">2.11.9.4 Welsh Government</h5>

<p>The Welsh National Marine Plan<sup id="fnref:229"><a href="#fn:229" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 229]</a></sup> sets out the Welsh Government’s long-term vision for Welsh seas that are clean, healthy, safe, productive and biologically diverse:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Through an ecosystem approach, natural resources are sustainably managed and our seas are healthy and resilient, supporting a sustainable and thriving economy</li>
  <li>Through access to, understanding of and enjoyment of the marine environment and maritime cultural heritage, health and well-being are improving</li>
  <li>Through Blue Growth more jobs and wealth are being created and are helping coastal communities become more resilient, prosperous and equitable with a vibrant culture</li>
  <li>Through the responsible deployment of low carbon technologies, the Welsh marine area is making a strong contribution to energy security and climate change emissions targets</li>
</ul>

<p>Welsh Government is taking a spatial approach to implementing the Marine Plan, developing planning guidance and tools to provide greater spatial direction and to balance supporting renewable energy with protecting the marine environment. Sector Locational Guidance for wave and tidal stream energy<sup id="fnref:230"><a href="#fn:230" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 230]</a></sup> were published in 2022 to help understand opportunities for future sector development. In 2024, Welsh Government consulted on potential Strategic Resource Areas<sup id="fnref:231"><a href="#fn:231" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 231]</a></sup> to identify and safeguard key areas of resource for tidal stream energy. It is also working with stakeholders to develop planning guidance on opportunities for ecosystem enhancement and restoration.</p>

<h5 id="jersey-8">2.11.9.5 Jersey</h5>

<p>The Carbon Neutral Roadmap sets an ambition to promote Jersey as a centre of excellence for blue carbon sequestration. In 2022, research<sup id="fnref:232"><a href="#fn:232" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 232]</a></sup> into Jersey’s resources was published that found that Jersey’s seabed sequesters over 10,000 tonnes of carbon annually, the equivalent combined weight of the <abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> emissions produced by the Island’s agriculture and waste management sectors. Further scientific studies are underway to better understand, protect and enhance blue carbon sequestration.</p>

<p>The Jersey Marine Spatial Plan<sup id="fnref:233"><a href="#fn:233" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 233]</a></sup> has been approved. This sets out how Jersey’s territorial waters should be utilised and protected to ensure the correct balance of competing uses.</p>

<h5 id="guernsey-8">2.11.9.6 Guernsey</h5>

<p>Guernsey is in the early stages of developing a marine spatial plan, with an aim for delivery by the end of 2025. It is intended that the plan will enable renewable energy developments and potential for nature, as well as managing other uses of the marine environment. As part of this work, a Blue Carbon report will be produced in the first half of 2025 which will establish the capacity of carbon storage and sequestration in Guernsey’s waters. This will then be used to advise on the climate mitigation measures that can be undertaken within Guernsey’s marine environment.</p>

<p>The Strategy for Nature<sup id="fnref:234"><a href="#fn:234" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 234]</a></sup>, the islands national biodiversity strategy, sets out a framework to enable the long-term management of nature in Guernsey. The Strategy recognises the important role nature and nature-based solutions plays in mitigating the impacts of climate change and seeks to protect and restore habitats which play important roles in carbon sequestration and storage. It also seeks to maximise biodiversity and ensure its resilience to a changing climate.</p>

<h5 id="isle-of-man-8">2.11.9.7 Isle of Man</h5>

<p>In 2019, the Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets (<abbr title="Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets">IMPACT</abbr>) Report<sup id="fnref:235"><a href="#fn:235" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 235]</a></sup> was produced. Appendix 10C relates to blue carbon. The Phase 1 Action Plan Progress Report<sup id="fnref:236"><a href="#fn:236" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 236]</a></sup> details progress made against the Council of Ministers’ Climate Action Plan Phase 1<sup id="fnref:237"><a href="#fn:237" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 237]</a></sup> over the period 1 April 2021-31 March 2022, including actions relating to blue carbon. As of 2022 10.8% of the Isle of Man’s entire territorial sea and 51.8% of the inshore (0-3 nautical mile area) were protected.<sup id="fnref:238"><a href="#fn:238" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 238]</a></sup> Section 4 of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027<sup id="fnref:239"><a href="#fn:239" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 239]</a></sup> sets out the Isle of Man’s current, high level climate policies relating to the marine environment and fisheries sector, including a commitment to work with the fishing industry to continue to reduce the carbon footprint of trawling and dredging, increase the efficiency of fishing effort and cut fuel costs. The Manx Blue Carbon Project<sup id="fnref:240"><a href="#fn:240" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 240]</a></sup> began in 2022, working with Bangor and Swansea Universities, as well as with the UK National Oceanography Centre to research and map blue carbon stores in the Isle of Man territorial sea. The project aims to develop a comprehensive blue carbon management plan to maximise carbon sequestration and maintain and restore related biodiversity and wider ecosystem services.</p>

<h5 id="gibraltar-8">2.11.9.8 Gibraltar</h5>

<p>Under the Marine Strategy Framework Directive, Gibraltar updated the environmental assessment showing Good Environmental Status for British Gibraltar Territorial Waters (<abbr title="British Gibraltar Territorial Waters">BGTW</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:241"><a href="#fn:241" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 241]</a></sup>. In 2021 Gibraltar published an updated monitoring programme for <abbr title="British Gibraltar Territorial Waters">BGTW</abbr>. This programme is being implemented in collaboration with the University of Gibraltar. Gibraltar has legislated to increase the number of Marine Protected Areas and no-take zones, safeguarding the biodiversity and health of its waters. Gibraltar has also embarked on a project to increase biodiversity within the intertidal zone through the installation of vertipools on existing grey infrastructure.</p>

<h4 id="biodiversity-and-adaptation-brbr">2.11.10 Biodiversity and Adaptation <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="england-7">2.11.10.1 England</h5>

<p>England has delivered the following strategies to support biodiversity and tackle adaptation:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>Strategic Framework<sup id="fnref:242"><a href="#fn:242" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 242]</a></sup> (2023)</strong>: set the direction for the UK’s integrated approach to international action on nature and climate through to 2030. Its 3 overarching priorities covered: keep 1.5C alive by halving global emissions; build resilience to current and future climate impacts and; halt and reverse biodiversity loss. The framework identifies 6 global challenges to the 2030 vision and the levers available to the UK to meet those challenges. It explains the UK’s role and approach to international collaboration, drawing on our expertise, skills and leadership.</li>
  <li>
<strong>National Adaptation Plan (<abbr title="National Adaptation Programme">NAP</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:243"><a href="#fn:243" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 243]</a></sup> (2023)</strong>: sets out plans to adapt to and mitigate the risks of a warming climate on the marine environment, including to protect, restore and create blue carbon habitats and manage the risks and
opportunities to marine species, habitats, and fisheries.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Environmental Improvement Plan<sup id="fnref:244"><a href="#fn:244" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 244]</a></sup> (2023)</strong>: sets out the actions that must be taken to help restore nature, tackle environmental pollution, and increase prosperity. It states that <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> will lead a practical initiative to restore estuarine and coastal habitats (ReMeMaRe (Restoring Meadow, Marsh and Reef)), which will restore 15% of priority habitats along the English coast by 2043. Restored coastal wetlands such as saltmarsh and seagrass can sequester and store carbon.</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="northern-ireland-executive-9">2.11.10.2 Northern Ireland Executive</h5>

<p>The Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (<abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr>) has prepared the draft Northern Ireland Environmental Improvement Plan<sup id="fnref:245"><a href="#fn:245" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 245]</a></sup> (<abbr title="Environmental Improvement Plan">EIP</abbr>). The <abbr title="Environmental Improvement Plan">EIP</abbr> sets out Northern Ireland’s environmental priorities for the decades ahead and will be the basis for a coherent and effective set of interventions that can deliver real improvements in the quality of the environment in Northern Ireland. The <abbr title="Environmental Improvement Plan">EIP</abbr> will be published once it receives approval from the Northern Ireland Executive.</p>

<p>The draft <abbr title="Environmental Improvement Plan">EIP</abbr> contains a commitment for <abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr> to develop and publish a new Biodiversity Strategy<sup id="fnref:246"><a href="#fn:246" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 246]</a></sup> for Northern Ireland. In line with this commitment, <abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr>, through a co-design process, has been leading on the development of a Nature Recovery Plan for Northern Ireland based on the 23 general targets revised and agreed at the <abbr title="United Nations">UN</abbr>’s Convention on Biological Diversity (<abbr title="UN’s Convention on Biological Diversity">CBD</abbr>) meeting in December 2022 (<abbr title="The 15th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC">COP15</abbr>).</p>

<p>These targets cover the wide range of issues affecting biodiversity and, if adequately addressed, should go a long way to halt the loss of biodiversity or at least ensure many habitats and species are in a better ecological status. Target 3 of these is often viewed as the one that will have the biggest impact, if achieved. This seeks to ensure that by 2030 at least 30% of all terrestrial, inland water, and coastal and marine areas, especially areas of particular importance for biodiversity and ecosystem functions and services, are effectively conserved and managed.</p>

<p>The Nature Recovery Strategy will augment actions for promoting biodiversity in other major initiatives including the <abbr title="Environmental Improvement Plan">EIP</abbr> and the Climate Action Plan. Once published the <abbr title="Environmental Improvement Plan">EIP</abbr> and Nature Recovery Strategy will provide Northern Ireland commitments for environmental improvement to be included in the UK National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan.</p>

<h5 id="scottish-government-9">2.11.10.3 Scottish Government</h5>

<p>The Scottish Government has committed to delivering improved and enduring benefits to the natural environment through the Environment Strategy for Scotland<sup id="fnref:247"><a href="#fn:247" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 247]</a></sup>. Sitting beneath this, the Scottish Biodiversity Strategy which has now been published<sup id="fnref:248"><a href="#fn:248" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 248]</a></sup> takes into account the new post-2020 global biodiversity framework and targets for the Convention on Biological Diversity’s 2050 vision. The Scottish Biodiversity Programme<sup id="fnref:249"><a href="#fn:249" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 249]</a></sup> has been created to coordinate all activity on biodiversity including the development of a future strategic framework for biodiversity that compromises both terrestrial and marine aspects.</p>

<h5 id="welsh-government-9">2.11.10.4 Welsh Government</h5>

<p>The Nature Recovery Action Plan (2021-2022)<sup id="fnref:250"><a href="#fn:250" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 250]</a></sup> contains 5 themes for action:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Maintaining and enhancing resilient ecological networks</li>
  <li>Increasing knowledge and knowledge transfer</li>
  <li>Realising new investment and funding</li>
  <li>Upskilling and capacity for delivery</li>
  <li>Mainstreaming, governance and reporting progress</li>
</ul>

<p>Within the themes, 5 immediate priorities have been identified for further action:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Aligning the responses to the climate emergency with the biodiversity crisis</li>
  <li>Addressing the post-EU exit funding gap for agri-environment measures</li>
  <li>Providing spatial direction for targeting action for biodiversity</li>
  <li>Improving the condition of the Protected Sites Network</li>
  <li>Exploring new and sustainable funding mechanisms for biodiversity action</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="jersey-9">2.11.10.5 Jersey</h5>

<p>Priority is currently being given to protecting on-Island carbon sinks. This is being prioritised through the Island Plan<sup id="fnref:251"><a href="#fn:251" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 251]</a></sup> and our various natural area protection and enhancement programmes, such as the Jersey National Park, Ramsar sites, Biodiversity action plan, tree strategy and LEAF programme. The Climate Emergency Fund supports projects that directly address the biodiversity crisis, including those with a focus on species and habitat restoration and protection, biosecurity and the marine environment.</p>

<h5 id="guernsey-9">2.11.10.6 Guernsey</h5>

<p>In 2020, Guernsey’s government published an updated Biodiversity Strategy, entitled the ‘Strategy for Nature’. The Strategy for Nature sets a framework for Guernsey’s government, the private sector and the community to strengthen Guernsey’s response to the changes facing nature from climate change and other human made pressures. It encompasses mainstreaming biodiversity and horizon scanning for pressures on nature and increasing community awareness of nature including promoting its health and wellbeing benefits. In recognition of risks to biodiversity from climate change, the Strategy for Nature includes an objective to “Reduce pressures on nature and ensure the resilience of our natural capital and assets”. This objective will be achieved by reducing threats and pressures on our natural environment and the introduction of targeted conservation action to support priority species and habitats.</p>

<p>Guernsey’s government recognises the increased pressure of invasive non-native species (<abbr title="Invasive Non-Native Species">INNS</abbr>) in light of changing climate, and also the detrimental impact of <abbr title="Invasive Non-Native Species">INNS</abbr> on biodiversity and its resilience to the impacts of climate change. Guernsey’s <abbr title="Invasive Non-Native Species">INNS</abbr> Action Plan aims to reduce the introduction and establishment or invasive species through enhanced biosecurity and surveillance measures. The Action Plan also seeks to manage species already present, especially those which will become more invasive with the forecast changes in climate.</p>

<h5 id="isle-of-man-9">2.11.10.7 Isle of Man</h5>

<p>Ratification of numerous international conventions relating to biodiversity has been extended to the Isle of Man.<sup id="fnref:252"><a href="#fn:252" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 252]</a></sup> The Biodiversity Strategy 2015 – 2025 is in effect<sup id="fnref:253"><a href="#fn:253" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 253]</a></sup>. The Isle of Man became the world’s first entire island nation with Biosphere status in 2016.<sup id="fnref:254"><a href="#fn:254" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 254]</a></sup> In 2019, the Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets (<abbr title="Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets">IMPACT</abbr>) Report<sup id="fnref:255"><a href="#fn:255" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 255]</a></sup> was produced. Appendix 10B relates to tree planting and habitat connectivity. The Phase 1 Action Plan Progress Report<sup id="fnref:256"><a href="#fn:256" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 256]</a></sup> details progress made against the Council of Ministers’ Climate Action Plan Phase 1<sup id="fnref:257"><a href="#fn:257" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 257]</a></sup> over the period 1 April 2021-31 March 2022, including actions relating to biodiversity and adaptation. The Climate Change Act 2021<sup id="fnref:258"><a href="#fn:258" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 258]</a></sup> contains amendments to the Town and Country Planning Act 1999, setting out 6 policy areas – including “the maximisation of carbon sequestration, maintenance and restoration of ecosystems, and biodiversity net gain” to be incorporated into national planning policy by 1 January 2025. Adaptation: <a href="#section-3-11-2-7">See ‘Chapter 3, section 3.11.2.7’</a>.</p>

<h5 id="gibraltar-9">2.11.10.8 Gibraltar</h5>

<p>One of the main climate impacts that will be felt in Gibraltar is increased heat, with a forecast sharp increase in the number of hot days in a given year. Investing in the creation of new green areas within the city centre, such as the conversion of a concrete parking lot into Commonwealth Park<sup id="fnref:259"><a href="#fn:259" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 259]</a></sup> in 2014 is helping to combat the heat island effect whilst simultaneously providing new habitats and potential for increased biodiversity.</p>

<p>Gibraltar will also embark on an ambitious rewilding programme in the next 5 years. Notable species that will form part of the enhanced rewilding programme include, but are not limited to Lesser Kestrel ‘Falco naumanni’ (recently extinct as a nesting bird), Little Owl ‘Athene noctua’ and the Ocellated Lizard (‘Timon Lepidus’). The programme to artificially propagate and re-populate the endemic Gibraltar Campion (‘Silene tomentosa’) will be expanded with a new propagation facility created at Tovey Cottage Field Centre in addition to the Gibraltar Botanic Gardens. Other regionally important species will also be propagated and planted as part of a wider and ambitious habitat restoration programme within and outside the Gibraltar Nature Reserve.</p>

<h4 id="education-and-skills-brbr">2.11.11 Education and skills <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="england-8">2.11.11.1 England</h5>

<p>The education sector in the UK will play a critical role in positively responding to climate change and inspiring action on an international stage. The Department for Education is helping to create a sustainable future through education, developing the skills needed for a green economy, and supporting our sectors to reach net zero targets.</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>Strategy for Sustainability and Climate Change<sup id="fnref:260"><a href="#fn:260" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 260]</a></sup> (2022)</strong>: The department’s strategy for Sustainability and Climate Change was informed by stakeholders and young people and sets out action to 2030 on: 1) climate education; 2) green skills and careers; 3) the education estate and digital infrastructure; 4) operations and supply chains; and 5) international. The Strategy sets out initiatives including extra support for teaching about nature and climate change, a National Education Nature Park, Climate Action Award and support for education leaders to take a whole-setting approach to climate change.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Green apprenticeships</strong>: Apprenticeships in England are a core part of the government’s skills agenda, helping grow the economy by improving the skills pipeline. Apprenticeships give employees high-quality, hands-on training to start and progress in work. There are over 680 occupations with corresponding apprenticeships, from entry-level to expert. The Institute for Apprenticeships and Technical Education (<abbr title="Institute for Apprenticeships and Technical Education">IfATE</abbr>) has worked with employers to identify over 200 occupations which directly support the green economy.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Green Jobs delivery group</strong>: The Green Jobs Delivery Group was the central forum for driving forwards action on green jobs and skills across government and industry. Led by ministers and business leaders, it worked to ensure workers were supported with the transition to a green economy. Through a series of deep dives, the Green Jobs Delivery Group was identifying occupations to target key skills programmes towards green sectors and occupations.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Climate literacy across government</strong>: More generally, there now exists a training offer available to all civil servants, expanded training for Fast Streamers, and embedded climate and environment objectives within the cross-cutting policy objectives and responsibilities in the Civil Service policy profession standards.</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="northern-ireland-executive-10">2.11.11.2 Northern Ireland Executive</h5>

<p>The Department for the Economy (<abbr title="Department for Education, England">DfE</abbr>) published the Northern Ireland Executive’s energy strategy ‘The Path to Net Zero Energy<sup id="fnref:261"><a href="#fn:261" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 261]</a></sup>’ December 2021, which set out the roadmap to 2030 aiming to deliver a 56% reduction in energy-related emissions, while on the pathway to net zero by 2050. To drive the strategy forward <abbr title="Department for Education, England">DfE</abbr> will publish annual Energy Strategy Action Plans, the first of which was published January 2022<sup id="fnref:262"><a href="#fn:262" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 262]</a></sup> and set out a range of new initiatives such as a hydrogen centre of excellence and an energy skills audit leading to a Green Skills Action plan.</p>

<p>The Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (<abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr>) have been leading on the development of the Northern Ireland Executive’s Green Growth Strategy. The Strategy is the Northern Ireland Executive’s multi-decade strategy, balancing climate, environment and the economy in Northern Ireland. After extensive engagement with organisations and individuals, the draft Green Growth strategy consultation opened in October 2021<sup id="fnref:263"><a href="#fn:263" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 263]</a></sup>, with the department hosting online public consultation sessions. Responses to the consultation have been analysed and, alongside the Climate Change Act (Northern Ireland) 2022, will inform the update of the strategy.</p>

<p>Skill Up is a flexible skills programme that offers a range of free training opportunities to support upskilling and reskilling, which was launched in August 2021. Funding was initially announced by <abbr title="Department for Education, England">DfE</abbr> and the Northern Ireland Office (<abbr title="Northern Ireland Office">NIO</abbr>) for a 3-year period, to deliver up to 10,000 training places per year in accredited qualifications.</p>

<h5 id="scottish-government-10">2.11.11.3 Scottish Government</h5>

<p>Scotland’s National Strategy for Economic Transformation<sup id="fnref:264"><a href="#fn:264" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 264]</a></sup> sets out the priorities for Scotland’s economy and shows that a skilled population is fundamental to business productivity and economic prosperity. In addition, Scotland’s Purpose and Principles<sup id="fnref:265"><a href="#fn:265" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 265]</a></sup> sets out the framework for decision making for post-school education, skills and research to ensure that the system is fit for the future, delivering the best outcomes for learners, employers and public investment.</p>
