<p>Significant work is progressing to reform the Scottish education and skills system so that it is more responsive to our economic, social, and environmental needs and ambitions, and the Scottish Government will continue to invest in that system and the infrastructure that supports it, including for example, schools, colleges, universities, apprenticeships and our Innovation Centres, to enable the transition to net zero.</p>

<p>The Scottish Government’s Climate Emergency Skills Action Plan<sup id="fnref:266"><a href="#fn:266" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 266]</a></sup> (2020-2025) provided an initial framework and springboard for skills planning, development and investment across sectors of the economy known to be crucial to achieving net zero. Scotland continues to build on these strong foundations for example, through the Green Industrial Strategy<sup id="fnref:267"><a href="#fn:267" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 267]</a></sup> identifies areas of strength and opportunity for Scotland to grow globally competitive industries in the transition to net zero and outlines what government and partners will do to support stakeholders to create an enabling environment for investment and growth.In addition, Scotland’s Curriculum for Excellence incorporates an emphasis on the cross-cutting theme of Learning for Sustainability – a term that brings together sustainable development education, global citizenship and outdoor learning. A refreshed and strengthened Learning for Sustainability Action Plan was published in 2023 setting a vision (Target 2030) that by the end of this decade all 3-18 education settings will be sustainable education settings.</p>

<h5 id="welsh-government-10">2.11.11.4 Welsh Government</h5>

<p>The Curriculum for Wales, which commenced roll-out in 2022, represents the biggest change to what and how learners learn in Wales since devolution. This transformational new approach has been built by teachers and experts to prepare our learners for a changing world. One of its 4 purposes is to develop our young people as ethical, informed citizens, ready to be active citizens of Wales and the world, with building understanding of climate change and sustainability mandatory.</p>

<p>In Wales, 90% of schools across every local authority take part in the Eco-Schools programme.<sup id="fnref:268"><a href="#fn:268" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 268]</a></sup> This equates to more than 400,000 pupils – one of the highest participation rates in the world.</p>

<p>The Welsh Government funds 100% of training costs for apprentices of any age with businesses of any size. Recipients follow an approved Welsh Apprenticeship Framework such as Energy, Engineering or Construction and must be working in Wales for 51% or more of their time. There is an employer incentive to recruit disabled apprentices as well as Supported Shared Apprenticeships.</p>

<p>Green Personal Learning Accounts provide adults in employment in Wales with a fully funded option to study part-time at an Further Education (<abbr title="Further Education">FE</abbr>) college/with a training provider partner to up- and re-skill for the green economy including in energy, construction, engineering and manufacturing. Courses approved under this scheme are determined by an expert panel including employers to ensure a targeted approach to meeting industry demand for skills.</p>

<p>The Welsh Government has operated a Flexible Skills Programme (<abbr title="Flexible Skills Programme">FSP</abbr>) since 2016. The <abbr title="Flexible Skills Programme">FSP</abbr> is a training grant, available to all employers in Wales, that wish to purchase training courses to meet upskilling objectives and potentially create and fill more green jobs. The Welsh Government will contribute 50% towards the training costs. It includes specific programmes to support skills gaps in the Engineering and Manufacturing Sector as well as the development of skills to help address Net Zero challenges such as hydrogen, amongst other areas.</p>

<p>The Welsh Government’s Net Zero Skills Action Plan (2021)<sup id="fnref:269"><a href="#fn:269" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 269]</a></sup> prioritises 7 key areas of action for delivering the Welsh Government’s vision for a fairer, greener and stronger Wales:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Gain an understanding of the current skills position for each emission sector</li>
  <li>Build a shared understanding of net zero skills across Wales</li>
  <li>Grow a skilled workforce to meet our net zero commitments</li>
  <li>Strengthen the skills system</li>
  <li>Promote opportunities for early years and young people to realise their potential</li>
  <li>Cross-government and partnership approach to meet our skills commitment</li>
  <li>Just transition</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="jersey-10">2.11.11.5 Jersey</h5>

<p>A Future Economy<sup id="fnref:270"><a href="#fn:270" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 270]</a></sup> work programme has set out actions to develop a more resilient supply chain and increase skills on island. This includes the green skills necessary to decarbonise and ensure a just transition.</p>

<p>At <abbr title="The 26th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC">COP26</abbr>, the government pledged to put children first in our net zero transition. Improving climate education is vital to tackle the climate emergency. A full-time officer has been employed to improve climate education across the curriculum.</p>

<h5 id="guernsey-10">2.11.11.6 Guernsey</h5>

<p>As part of the Key Stages 1, 2 and 3 of education in Guernsey, raising awareness and learning about climate change, energy efficiency and sustainability are included in the Bailiwick of Guernsey Curriculum, published in 2017, used in Guernsey and Alderney government-maintained schools. This is achieved through subjects such as Geography and Science. Coverage is broad, focusing on, for instance: teaching and understanding how the world’s climate is changing, there being various ways to address climate change, and of the potential impacts of climate change; how sustainability is doing things in a way that ensures resources needed are not damaged or wasted and are used wisely; and about the production of carbon dioxide by human activity, the impact on the climate and greenhouse gases in the atmosphere; as well as renewable and non-renewable energy.</p>

<h5 id="isle-of-man-10">2.11.11.7 Isle of Man</h5>

<p>In 2019, the Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets (<abbr title="Isle of Man Programme for Achievement of Climate Targets">IMPACT</abbr>) Report<sup id="fnref:271"><a href="#fn:271" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 271]</a></sup> was produced. Appendix 9 relates to climate in the Manx curriculum. Legal requirements for new buildings to achieve a minimum SAP rating<sup id="fnref:272"><a href="#fn:272" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 272]</a></sup> commenced in 2020. Between 1 January 2021 and 31 December 2023 the minimum requirement was equivalent to a ‘B’ Energy Performance Certificate (<abbr title="Energy Performance Certificate">EPC</abbr>) rating in the UK, rising to the equivalent of an ‘A’ rating in January 2024. The Phase 1 Action Plan Progress Report<sup id="fnref:273"><a href="#fn:273" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 273]</a></sup> details progress made against the Council of Ministers’ Climate Action Plan Phase 1<sup id="fnref:274"><a href="#fn:274" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 274]</a></sup> over the period 1 April 2021-31 March 2022, including actions relating to education and skills. The Isle of Man Retrofit and Low Carbon Skills Analysis<sup id="fnref:275"><a href="#fn:275" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 275]</a></sup> was produced in 2022. Section 2 of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027<sup id="fnref:276"><a href="#fn:276" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 276]</a></sup> includes a commitment to upskill the construction industry in low carbon heating technologies. In schools, training with Eco Schools<sup id="fnref:277"><a href="#fn:277" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 277]</a></sup> has led to 5 schools achieving Green Flag status along with the continued roll-out of Global Teacher Training.<sup id="fnref:278"><a href="#fn:278" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 278]</a></sup></p>

<h5 id="gibraltar-10">2.11.11.8 Gibraltar</h5>

<p>Gibraltar has long had an environmental education programme, carried out collaboratively between the Department of Education and the Department of the Environment and Climate Change. This has evolved to meet the changing priorities of the education sector with a greater focus on outdoor and project based learning, with a strong environmental angle. In December 2022 Gibraltar published a Bill to amend its Education and Training Act<sup id="fnref:279"><a href="#fn:279" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 279]</a></sup> to ensure a commitment to making learning about the environment and climate justice is a fundamental principle of education policy. This revision will also bring to bear a number of commitments which will support the prioritisation of climate emergency related workstreams including a bespoke climate change curriculum framework for sustainable schools, developing climate change INSET training for educational staff and revised career advice which includes a focus on green jobs.</p>

<h4 id="sustainability-and-behaviour-change-brbr">2.11.12 Sustainability and Behaviour Change <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="england-9">2.11.12.1 England</h5>

<p>The UK is working to deliver the benefits of the net zero transition to our health, our homes and our overall prosperity. Our priority is making green choices easier, clearer and more affordable, and working with industry to remove barriers. There are numerous individual actions – some one-off and some frequent – that people can take to contribute to net zero. Choices and behaviours that impact on net zero broadly fall into 3 categories: adopting new low carbon technologies; using energy, technologies, or services more efficiently; and everyday business and consumer choices.</p>

<p>In England, there are the following strategies in place to tackle sustainability and behaviour change:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>National Food Strategy<sup id="fnref:280"><a href="#fn:280" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 280]</a></sup> (2022)</strong>: The Strategy responded to Henry Dimbleby’s independent review of the food system and set out a set of objectives to deliver “a prosperous agri-food sector”. These led to, for example, the commissioning of a review into labour shortages, establishing the Food Data Transparency Partnership, and consulting on the government Buying Standards for Food and Catering Services.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Heat and Buildings Strategy (2021)</strong>: The Strategy set out government’s overall approach to decarbonising heating, through increasing the roll out of clean heat technologies as well as the installation of energy efficiency measures. Heat pumps and heat networks were the major clean heat technologies, whilst also leaving flexibility for potential roll out of hydrogen. The strategy combined regulations to give industry certainty of technology transitions, as well as subsidies to support consumers to upgrade. These measures together built a credible path for the UK to meet its carbon budget sector effort shares for buildings.</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="northern-ireland-executive-11">2.11.12.2 Northern Ireland Executive</h5>

<p>The Department for the Economy (<abbr title="Department for Education, England">DfE</abbr>) have worked in collaboration across both the public and private sector, working with a cross-departmental steering group and a Circular Economy Coalition (an advisory panel established in 2021) to drive forward progress on the Circular Economy strategy. The Circularity Gap Report Northern Ireland, commissioned by <abbr title="Department for Education, England">DfE</abbr>, was published in June 2022 and provided a snapshot of how circular Northern Ireland currently is. The report<sup id="fnref:281"><a href="#fn:281" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 281]</a></sup> informed much of the evidence base underpinning the development of the draft Circular Economy Strategy for Northern Ireland, which is due to be published in January 2023.</p>

<h5 id="scottish-government-11">2.11.12.3 Scottish Government</h5>

<p>In May 2022 we launched 2 linked consultations, on a Circular Economy Bill and on a Circular Economy and Waste Route Map. The Bill establishes the legislative framework to support Scotland’s transition to a zero waste and circular economy, significantly increase reuse and recycling rates, and modernise and improve waste and recycling services. It is complemented by the Circular Economy and Waste Route Map, which sets out clear actions we need to take to progress a circular economy in Scotland by 2030. Together, they will help us achieve our sustainable resource and climate goals.</p>

<p>Scotland was also the first nation of the UK to implement a ban on many of the most problematic single-use plastics, with legislation coming into force in June 2022.</p>

<h5 id="welsh-government-11">2.11.12.4 Welsh Government</h5>

<p>Climate Action Wales<sup id="fnref:282"><a href="#fn:282" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 282]</a></sup> provides information and advice in relation to the following areas:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Green Home Energy Choices: Reducing energy consumption, Home upgrade choices</li>
  <li>Green Transport Choices: Driving less; taking up active travel and public transport, Electric vehicle adoption</li>
  <li>Green Food Choices: Reducing food waste, Healthier eating and sustainable food choices</li>
  <li>Green Consumption Choices: Shopping sustainably, using less, reusing, repairing and recycling</li>
</ul>

<p>The Welsh Government has updated building regulations to achieve a 37% reduction in carbon emissions for new dwellings.<sup id="fnref:283"><a href="#fn:283" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 283]</a></sup> It intends to make further changes in 2025, raising the bar to require new homes to achieve at least a 75% reduction in emissions.</p>

<p>The Welsh Housing Quality Standard exists to improve the quality of social homes.<sup id="fnref:284"><a href="#fn:284" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 284]</a></sup> Social landlords are legally obliged to meet the Standard’s requirements, including those relating to energy performance and environmental impact.</p>

<h5 id="jersey-11">2.11.12.5 Jersey</h5>

<p>Jersey’s Carbon Neutral Roadmap<sup id="fnref:285"><a href="#fn:285" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 285]</a></sup> makes a commitment to behavioural change campaigns to consider and reduce all emissions associated with Islanders’ lives. Jersey-specific carbon literacy training has been developed. Officers have worked with internal colleagues, external stakeholder through the eco active business network and ministers. As an organisation the government of Jersey has the responsibility to set an example on decarbonisation and has set itself ambitious decarbonisation targets with a focus on the government estate and fleet.</p>

<h5 id="guernsey-11">2.11.12.6 Guernsey</h5>

<p>Guernsey’s governmental strategy for transport has a focus on behavioural change with encouraging active travel as an alternative to vehicles forming a key part of the strategy. The island has a walking and cycling app to help navigate around the islands’ quiet lanes and Guernsey’s government has offered subsidies on electric bikes.</p>

<p>The island’s energy policy outlines the importance of energy efficiency measures in reducing energy related emissions and the climate change policy reaffirmed the hierarchical approaches to waste management, energy use and transport. This requires behavioural change to preserve resources and reduce emissions.</p>

<h5 id="isle-of-man-11">2.11.12.7 Isle of Man</h5>

<p>The Isle of Man became the world’s first entire island nation with Biosphere status in 2016.<sup id="fnref:286"><a href="#fn:286" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 286]</a></sup> The Climate Change Act 2021<sup id="fnref:287"><a href="#fn:287" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 287]</a></sup> includes duties for Manx public bodies, which create a statutory requirement to support sustainable development and the <abbr title="United Nations">UN</abbr> Sustainable Development goals. Each of the actions in the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027<sup id="fnref:288"><a href="#fn:288" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 288]</a></sup> is linked to one or more <abbr title="United Nations">UN</abbr> Sustainable Development Goals, and the Act requires annual progress reports to include reporting on progress toward those goals.</p>

<p>Section C of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027 sets out how the Isle of Man government intends to ‘lead by example’ in relation to climate action, this includes commitments for climate change training across the public sector and a government-wide policy review to ensure that existing practices do not restrict our ability to meet our climate goals. Section 2 of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027 includes a commitment to a public engagement campaign promoting energy efficiency (completed in 2023<sup id="fnref:289"><a href="#fn:289" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 289]</a></sup>).</p>

<h5 id="gibraltar-11">2.11.12.8 Gibraltar</h5>

<p>Gibraltar has established a field centre in the Gibraltar Nature Reserve<sup id="fnref:290"><a href="#fn:290" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 290]</a></sup> which is serving to foster a better understanding and appreciation of local biodiversity among our young people. Tovey Cottage welcomes over 600 young people each year. Gibraltar has embarked on a process of developing Carbon Literacy training for the public sector, in collaboration with the UK Carbon Literacy Project which will help individuals to understand the carbon cost of their everyday actions and ways in which they can reduce their carbon footprint. This will result in a public sector that is engaged with the climate crisis and empowered to deliver the changes needed.</p>

<p>Gibraltar is also committed to organising citizen’s assemblies on climate and nature to help raise further awareness and understanding and drive the behavioural changes needed at a societal level.</p>

<h4 id="health-and-air-brbr">2.11.13 Health and air <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="england-10">2.11.13.1 England</h5>

<p>Air pollution is the biggest environmental threat to human health. Its impacts are disproportionately felt by low-income communities, exacerbating health and social inequalities. Sources that contribute to air pollution are varied; significant sources are transport, industrial processes, agriculture and home heating – specifically household burning of solid fuels. Some actions that reduce carbon also have benefits for air quality, but this is not the case for all measures, for example biomass combustion, which can have a negative impact on air quality. Government has taken action across a range of sectors.</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>The Environment Act (2021)<sup id="fnref:291"><a href="#fn:291" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 291]</a></sup></strong>: required 2 targets for fine particulate matter (<abbr title="fine particulate matter">PM2.5</abbr>) to be set in regulation. The regulations<sup id="fnref:292"><a href="#fn:292" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 292]</a></sup> established targets for both a maximum annual mean concentration of 10 μg m-3 by 2040 and a population exposure reduction target of 35% by 2040 compared to 2018. The dual-target approach will improve public health by tackling the highest concentrations while ensuring all areas benefit from continuous improvement. It also introduced changes to the Local Air Quality Management framework<sup id="fnref:293"><a href="#fn:293" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 293]</a></sup> and improvements to the enforcement of smoke control areas<sup id="fnref:294"><a href="#fn:294" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 294]</a></sup> which limit emissions from the burning of solid fuels in homes on appliances such as stoves and fireplaces.</li>
  <li>
<strong>The UK plan for tackling roadside nitrogen dioxide (NO2) concentrations (2017)<sup id="fnref:295"><a href="#fn:295" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 295]</a></sup></strong>: legally obliged local authorities to reduce their NO2 exceedances in the shortest possible time. Four cities, Bath, Birmingham, Bradford and Portsmouth implemented Clean Air Zones amongst other measures in accordance with local plans.</li>
  <li>
<strong>The Air Quality Information Systems Review (2021)<sup id="fnref:296"><a href="#fn:296" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 296]</a></sup></strong>: established to undertake a comprehensive review of how government communicates air quality information to ensure members of the public, and vulnerable groups in particular, have what they need protect themselves and understand their impact on air quality.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Government’s response to the consultation on reducing ammonia emissions from solid urea fertilisers (2022)<sup id="fnref:297"><a href="#fn:297" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 297]</a></sup></strong>: The response indicated support for an industry-led approach that was subsequently delivered through Red Tractor farm assurance standard<sup id="fnref:298"><a href="#fn:298" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 298]</a></sup> and farm advisors.</li>
</ul>

<p>The UK Government, the Scottish Government, the Welsh Government, and the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs in Northern Ireland put in place a new regime for the development of ‘Best Available Techniques’<sup id="fnref:299"><a href="#fn:299" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 299]</a></sup> across the UK. The BAT approach ensures standards are enhanced over time by defining the techniques and technologies already in use which are the best for preventing or minimising emissions and impacts on the environment from industrial installations – this is then reflected in operator’s permits.</p>

<h5 id="northern-ireland-executive-12">2.11.13.2 Northern Ireland Executive</h5>

<p>In November 2020, the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (<abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr>) launched a consultation on a Discussion Document on a Clean Air Strategy for Northern Ireland<sup id="fnref:300"><a href="#fn:300" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 300]</a></sup>’. In June 2022, the synopsis<sup id="fnref:301"><a href="#fn:301" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 301]</a></sup> of that consultation was published by <abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr>. Work is now ongoing to develop Northern Ireland’s first Clean Air Strategy taking into account the consultation responses.</p>

<h5 id="scottish-government-12">2.11.13.3 Scottish Government</h5>

<p>The Scottish Government published its Cleaner Air for Scotland strategy<sup id="fnref:302"><a href="#fn:302" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 302]</a></sup> in 2015 setting out a series of actions for improving air quality across a wide range of policy areas. Following an independent review of the strategy in 2019<sup id="fnref:303"><a href="#fn:303" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 303]</a></sup>, which made recommendations for additional action on air pollution, a new strategy - Cleaner Air for Scotland 2: Towards a Better Place for Everyone - was published in July 2021<sup id="fnref:304"><a href="#fn:304" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 304]</a></sup>. This sets out Scotland’s air quality policy framework for the period 2021 to 2026 with a continued focus on delivery of co-benefits for air pollutant and greenhouse gas reductions.</p>

<h5 id="welsh-government-12">2.11.13.4 Welsh Government</h5>

<p>The aim of the Clean Air Plan for Wales: Healthy Air, Healthy Wales (2020) is to improve air quality and reduce the impacts of air pollution on human health, biodiversity, the natural environment and the economy.<sup id="fnref:305"><a href="#fn:305" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 305]</a></sup> The Plan sets out a 10-year pathway to achieving cleaner air is structured around 4 core themes:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>People</strong>: Protecting the health and well-being of current and future generations</li>
  <li>
<strong>Environment</strong>: Taking action to support our natural environment, ecosystems and biodiversity</li>
  <li>
<strong>Prosperity</strong>: Working with industry to reduce emissions, supporting a cleaner and more prosperous Wales</li>
  <li>
<strong>Place</strong>: Creating sustainable places through better planning, infrastructure and transport</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="jersey-12">2.11.13.5 Jersey</h5>

<p>A long-term vision for Jersey was produced in 2017 through the ‘Island Outcome Indicators’<sup id="fnref:306"><a href="#fn:306" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 306]</a></sup>. This vision includes clean air within its statement.</p>

<p>Jersey government are currently improving and relocating our air quality reference analysers (NOx, and Particulate Matter) to support our wider air quality monitoring programme and improve our ability to report data to Automatic Urban and Rural Network (<abbr title="Automatic Urban and Rural Network">AURN</abbr>) standards. Jersey is developing sensor networks in partnership with external stakeholders with the aim of providing near real-time air quality data to inform the public, influence behaviour and support sustainability workstreams.</p>

<h5 id="guernsey-12">2.11.13.6 Guernsey</h5>

<p>In 2019, the Environmental Pollution (Air Pollution) Ordinance<sup id="fnref:307"><a href="#fn:307" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 307]</a></sup> was enacted in Guernsey. This Ordinance sets local ambient air quality standards and allows greater environmental regulation of point source emitters including, but not limited to, through licensing prescribed operations, placing limits on the sulphur content of fuels and restricting burning in the open air. The limitations on burning in the open air has benefits form a climate perspective.</p>

<h5 id="isle-of-man-12">2.11.13.7 Isle of Man</h5>

<p>Actions to reduce use of fossil fuels, such as the ban on fossil fuel heating systems in new buildings, created by the Climate Change Act 2021<sup id="fnref:308"><a href="#fn:308" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 308]</a></sup> and commencing 1 January 2025, will help to improve air quality. Other health concerns related to climate change are primarily linked with adaptation. Section A of the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027<sup id="fnref:309"><a href="#fn:309" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 309]</a></sup> sets out actions relating to adaptation and resilience, including commitment to a Climate Change Risks and Opportunities Report for the Island, which is currently being prepared and will include risks to health.</p>

<p>Air quality monitoring has been increased to include NO2 and SO2 at over 60 sites around the Island, with data published monthly.<sup id="fnref:310"><a href="#fn:310" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 310]</a></sup></p>

<h5 id="gibraltar-12">2.11.13.8 Gibraltar</h5>

<p>Gibraltar has a well-established air quality monitoring network in place and results demonstrate a steady improvement in local air quality since the network started monitoring in 2005.<sup id="fnref:311"><a href="#fn:311" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 311]</a></sup></p>

<p>The switch from diesel to natural gas for the generation of electricity marked a significant improvement in levels of nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter. Efforts are now focused on reducing emissions from transport and construction.</p>

<h3 id="information-on-how-actions-policies-and-measures-are-modifying-longer-term-trends-in-ghg-emissions-and-removals">2.12 Information on how actions, policies and measures are modifying longer-term trends in <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> emissions and removals</h3>

<p>To avoid duplication, please refer to the information presented in the National Inventory Report, published on <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr>, under each sector for the estimated impact of actions, policies, and measures.</p>

<h3 id="information-on-the-assessment-of-economic-and-social-impacts-of-response-measures">2.13 Information on the assessment of economic and social impacts of response measures</h3>

<p>The government regularly assesses the impact of existing and planned policies against its emission targets, including the <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr> and Carbon Budgets. The annual Energy and Emissions Projections (<abbr title="Energy and Emissions Projections">EEP</abbr>) take account of any policies that, as of June that year, have either been implemented or those that are planned where the level of funding has been agreed and the policy design is near final.</p>

<p>Under section 10 of the Climate Change Act 2008, the UK Government must take account of economic and social circumstances when making decisions in relation to carbon budgets. In particular, section 10 of the Act requires an appraisal of the likely impact of policies on fuel poverty, the economy, and “the competitiveness of particular sectors of the economy.”</p>

<p>This information is gathered by officials and presented to the <abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr> Secretary of State on a regular basis. A summary of the economic and social impact of the policy package is also published in reports following the setting of a carbon budgets. The most recent assessment was published in the previous UK Government’s 2023 Carbon Budget Delivery Plan.<sup id="fnref:312"><a href="#fn:312" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 312]</a></sup></p>

<h3 id="summary-of-greenhouse-gas-emissions-and-removals">2.14 Summary of greenhouse gas emissions and removals</h3>

<p>Please refer to the accompanying <abbr title="Common Tabular Format">CTF</abbr> tables submitted alongside the Biennial Transparency Report.</p>

<h3 id="projections-of-greenhouse-gas-emissions-and-removals-as-applicable">2.15 Projections of greenhouse gas emissions and removals as applicable</h3>

<p>This section presents information from the most recent full update to the UK’s <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> Energy and Emissions Projections (<abbr title="Energy and Emissions Projections">EEP</abbr>) 2023 -2050, published in December 2024<sup id="fnref:313"><a href="#fn:313" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 313]</a></sup>. It includes estimates of future energy demand and GHGs in the UK up to 2050, and within this section we focus on projections up to 2040.</p>

<p>The UK’s national projections are based on a ‘With Additional Measures’ (<abbr title="With additional measures">WAM</abbr>) scenario. This takes into account policies that, as of June 2024 have either been implemented or are planned and the level of funding has been agreed and the design of the policy is near final. These projections do not present the UK’s full package of policies, as they do not include policies that have only been announced, or are in early development or being planned by the current government. They therefore are not an assessment of the UK’s delivery position against carbon budgets or the <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr>. The projections are the baseline against which new early-stage policies and proposals are assessed to monitor progress towards carbon budget targets.</p>

<p>For international reporting, the projections presented in this Biennial Transparency Report used the ‘With Existing Measures’ (<abbr title="With existing measures">WEM</abbr>) policy scenario, which excludes policies that were classed as planned at the cut-off date of June 2024. Projections in this section are for the ‘With Existing Measures’ (<abbr title="With existing measures">WEM</abbr>) scenario, unless otherwise stated.</p>

<p>The projection models incorporate information from the UK’s 1990-2022 <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> Inventory publication (published in 2022), and the historic statistics presented earlier this chapter are on the same basis.</p>

<p>Key findings show that:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Based on the <abbr title="With existing measures">WEM</abbr> scenario, the projections show that by 2030, UK emissions of the basket of the 7 greenhouse gases (GHGs) covered by the Paris Agreement would be expected to be 335 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e, approximately 479 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e below the 1990 level (59% lower); and by 2040, the projections show equivalent figures of 505 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e and 62% lower than 1990. These projections are not an assessment of the delivery position against carbon budgets: as policies and measures at an earlier stage of development are developed and implemented, the resulting emissions savings will be factored into future projections.</li>
  <li>The UK projects emissions of <abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub>, <abbr title="Methane">CH</abbr><sub>4</sub> and <abbr title="Nitrous Oxide">N</abbr><sub>2</sub>O of 61%, 66% and 60% respectively below 1990 levels by 2040.</li>
  <li>For the fluorinated GHGs, the UK projects that emissions of <abbr title="Hydrofluorocarbons">HFCs</abbr> will be 74% lower than their 1990 levels by 2040. For <abbr title="Perfluorocarbons">PFCs</abbr>, the UK projects emissions will be 90% lower, for SF<sub>6</sub> 95% lower; and for <abbr title="Nitrogen trifluoride">NF</abbr><sub>3</sub> emissions will be 42% lower than their 1990 levels by 2040.</li>
</ul>

<p>The UK is committed to meeting its 2030 <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr> target and will publish more detailed plans on delivery in due course, outlining the policies and proposals it has in place to meet the 2030 and 2035 <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contributions">NDCs</abbr> and carbon budgets up to 2037. The plan will include consideration of delivery risks and mitigations. The publication will also provide indicative implementation dates for policies and proposals; however these dates may change as proposals and policies develop over the coming years. When developing policies and proposals, the government considers alternative pathways and policy levers to meet its carbon targets.</p>

<h4 id="with-measures-projection-of-all-ghg-emissions-and-removals-and-with-additional-measures-projection-and-without-measures-projection-brbr">2.15.1 ‘With measures’ projection of all <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> emissions and removals and ‘with additional measures’ projection and ‘without measures’ projection <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The ‘with existing measures’ (<abbr title="With existing measures">WEM</abbr>) scenario includes policies that had been implemented or adopted by June 2024 but excludes planned measures. In addition, the UK provides selected data from the ‘with additional measures’ (<abbr title="With additional measures">WAM</abbr>) scenario, which includes planned measures as at the same policy cut-off date. Both projection scenarios exclude the use of credits from flexible mechanisms such as the Joint Implementation and Clean Development Mechanism (<abbr title="Clean Development Mechanism">CDM</abbr>). The UK does not produce a without measures (<abbr title="Without Measures">WOM</abbr>) scenario. Many mitigation measures were already in place when emissions projections were first produced by the UK, and there are certain policies and measures (PaMs), such as Emissions Trading Schemes (ETS), for which no past counterfactual scenario can be reliably modelled. Currently, it is not feasible to remove all these effects to produce a robust <abbr title="Without Measures">WOM</abbr> projection. However, we are exploring options that might allow us to produce a scenario that removes those policies where we can model a suitable <abbr title="Without Measures">WOM</abbr> counterfactual. We will implement this and incorporate it into future submissions as soon as we have identified a suitable methodology.</p>

<p>The figures within this National Communication include British crown dependencies and overseas territories. These territories are excluded from UK Carbon Budget’s legislation and do not appear in the <abbr title="Energy and Emissions Projections">EEP</abbr> report. According to the UK’s 1990-2022 <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> Inventory, these regions were responsible for 0.4% of total emissions in 2022. Throughout this section, the geographical scope of the presented figures includes the UK and its crown dependencies and overseas territories as denoted by the label ‘(<abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> coverage)’ unless otherwise specified.</p>

<p>Under the <abbr title="With existing measures">WEM</abbr> scenario, the UK projects <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> emissions to be around 479 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e below the 1990 level (59% lower) by 2030, and roughly 505 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>e lower by 2040. All projections include emissions from Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry (<abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr>), for consistency with Inventory Convention reporting, although the percentages are very similar if it is excluded<sup id="fnref:314"><a href="#fn:314" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 314]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>[Tables 5 and 6] show overall projections for each gas under <abbr title="With existing measures">WEM</abbr> and <abbr title="With additional measures">WAM</abbr> scenarios respectively. This shows that additional planned policies as of June 2024 are expected to mainly affect <abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> emissions, reducing them by 12 Mt more in the year 2040 than in the equivalent projection under the <abbr title="With existing measures">WEM</abbr> scenario.</p>

<h5 id="energy-1">2.15.4.1 Energy</h5>

<p>This sector includes all emissions which fall under <abbr title="Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change">IPCC</abbr> code 1. Within tables, we break this down into transport (1A3) and energy excluding 1A3. This sector includes emissions from electricity and heat production, manufacturing industries and construction (such as chemicals, iron and steel, non-ferrous metals), commercial and residential sectors. The UK projects energy emissions (excluding transport) of 65% lower than 1990 levels by 2030 and 62% lower by 2040 (see <strong>Table 10</strong>).</p>

<h5 id="methane">2.15.5.2 Methane</h5>

<p>The 2 biggest emitters of <abbr title="Methane">CH</abbr><sub>4</sub> in 2020 were agriculture and waste management. <h3 id="information-describing-the-methodology-used-to-develop-projections">2.16 Information describing the methodology used to develop projections</h3>

<h4 id="projections-methods-by-sector-brbr">2.16.1 Projections methods by sector <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK projections of emissions of <abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> and combustion-related emissions of other GHGs (<abbr title="Methane">CH</abbr><sub>4</sub> and <abbr title="Nitrous Oxide">N</abbr><sub>2</sub>O) are based on the UK’s Energy and Emissions Projections modelling suite used for its annual publication and internal analysis.</p>

<p>We produce projections of energy demand and combustion-related <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> emissions outside the power sector by applying standard statistical techniques. These project forward energy demand and emissions based on trends and relationships in past data. We adjust these projections to take account of estimated reductions in energy consumption from policies which are modelled separately using more detailed sectoral models. We then project energy-related emissions by multiplying energy demand by the relevant emissions factors<sup id="fnref:315"><a href="#fn:315" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 315]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>We produce projections of power sector generation and associated emissions by feeding our projections of electricity demand into a model of electricity supplier behaviour.</p>

<p>The following table outlines a summary of the models involved in the Energy and Emissions projections:</p>

<p id="table-22"><strong>Table 22: Modelling approaches for the projections</strong></p>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th scope="col">Model</th>
      <th scope="col">Purpose</th>
      <th scope="col">Notes</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Energy Demand Model (<abbr title="Energy Demand Model">EDM</abbr>)</th>
      <td>Projecting energy demand and associated emissions</td>
      <td>Uses bespoke econometric analysis of past energy demand by fuel and sector as published in the UK’s annual energy statistics publication – <abbr title="Digest of UK Energy Statistics">DUKES</abbr> (Digest of UK Energy Statistics). The resulting projection equations are combined with projections for drivers such as UK <abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr> growth and separately modelled policy impacts to project forward energy demand by fuel and sector. Energy demand projections are converted to emissions projections through emissions factors and calorific values.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Dynamic Dispatch Model</th>
      <td>Projecting energy supply and associated emissions</td>
      <td>This model is used to project emissions from the power sector. It takes projected electricity demand from the Energy Demand Model and provides a modelled generation mix that meets that level of demand under current power sector policies. It is a market-based model that simulates the operation of the electricity market and the investment decision of market participants. It is a profit-maximisation model incorporating the effect of UK policies which incentivise low-carbon generation through market mechanisms. Includes combined heat and power plants.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">UK <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> Inventory Non-<abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> emissions models</th>
      <td>Projecting non-combustion, non-<abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> emissions.</td>
      <td>Use emissions from the 1990-2022 <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> Inventory (GHGI) as the baseline for these emissions projections. Sectoral models are used to project forward emissions from these sources.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<p>The overall modelling approach has been consistent over time, although there have been incremental improvements to the projections which are described in the UK’s domestic <abbr title="Energy and Emissions Projections">EEP</abbr> publications<sup id="fnref:316"><a href="#fn:316" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 316]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>The principal source of past energy statistics is the Digest of UK Energy Statistics (<abbr title="Digest of UK Energy Statistics">DUKES</abbr>). The UK’s model suite projects emissions using projections for fossil fuel prices, carbon prices, economic growth, temperature and demographics. Key assumptions for projections are given in <abbr title="Common Tabular Format">CTF</abbr> Table 11.</p>

<p>The UK’s domestically published projections include variant scenarios for high and low fossil fuel price assumptions, high and low <abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr> growth rates. More detail on this is provided later in this section.</p>

<h5 id="transport-2">2.16.1.1 Transport</h5>

<p>The <abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> road transport model is an econometric response surface model integrated into the economy-wide Energy Demand Model (<abbr title="Energy Demand Model">EDM</abbr>) and calibrated against the Department for Transport’s (<abbr title="Department for Transport">DfT</abbr>’s) National Transport Model (<abbr title="National Transport Model">NTM</abbr>). The econometric model is multi-modal as it includes cars, light good vehicles (LGVs), heavy goods vehicles (<abbr title="Heavy Goods Vehicles">HGVs</abbr>), and public service vehicles (PSVs). Car demand has a link to population, and <abbr title="Heavy Goods Vehicle">HGV</abbr> demand is linked to projections for manufacturing Gross Value added (<abbr title="Gross Value Added">GVA</abbr>). Other factors which affect transport demand are the oil price, motor spirit/diesel engine share, and fuel efficiency and biofuel substitution effects.</p>

<p>Most energy efficiency improvements are policy-driven, such as by new car emissions intensity targets and complementary measures such as lower rolling resistance tyres for <abbr title="Heavy Goods Vehicles">HGVs</abbr>. Unlike for other demand sectors, impacts of policies and measures on road transport fuel demand are modelled within the <abbr title="Energy and Emissions Projections">EEP</abbr> modelling suite. Road vehicle efficiencies, motor spirit/diesel engine shares, and biofuel use under different policy scenarios are used to calculate mitigation impacts from differences in demand between scenarios.</p>

<p>Electricity demand from electric cars and LGVs is passed to the Dynamic Dispatch Model (<abbr title="Dynamic Dispatch Model">DDM</abbr>) which takes this additional demand into account when calculating power sector generation. The activity data (vehicle distances travelled) is projected using the latest <abbr title="Department for Transport">DfT</abbr> traffic forecasts.</p>

<p><abbr title="Department for Transport">DfT</abbr>’s projected traffic growth, the planned electrification of existing track, and the construction of new lines such as Crossrail and High Speed 2 underpin the rail transport model.</p>

<p>Projections for UK commercial aviation involve estimates of future UK <abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr>, consumer expenditure, population, and oil prices. The Fleet Mix Model captures efficiency improvements, for example the model assumes increasing use of biofuels. <abbr title="Department for Transport">DfT</abbr> provides more detailed information about methodology and assumptions with its aviation forecast. The modelling has extrapolated trends in the <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> Inventory to extend aviation emissions projections to <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> coverage.</p>

<p>The UK projects that national navigation will remain largely static.</p>

<h5 id="energy-supply">2.16.1.2 Energy supply</h5>

<p>The UK uses the <abbr title="Dynamic Dispatch Model">DDM</abbr> to project investment and generation in the electricity supply sector. The <abbr title="Dynamic Dispatch Model">DDM</abbr> is a market-based model that simulates the operation of the electricity market and the investment decision of the market participants in detail. It is a profit-maximisation model incorporating the effect of government policies such as Contracts for Difference which incentivise low-carbon generation through market mechanisms.</p>

<p>The <abbr title="Dynamic Dispatch Model">DDM</abbr> also models investment in the supply of heat and electricity from Combined Heat and Power plants, mostly in industry.</p>

<h5 id="industrial-and-commercial-sector-emissions">2.16.1.3 Industrial and Commercial sector emissions</h5>

<p>For emissions projections, the UK breaks manufacturing down into sectors using the Standard Industrial Classification (<abbr title="Standard Industrial Classification">SIC</abbr>). The manufacturing sectors in the <abbr title="Energy Demand Model">EDM</abbr> are:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chemicals</li>
  <li>Construction</li>
  <li>Engineering and vehicles</li>
  <li>Food, drink and tobacco</li>
  <li>Iron and steel</li>
  <li>Non-ferrous metals</li>
  <li>Non-metallic mineral products</li>
  <li>Pulp, paper and printing</li>
  <li>Textile products; and</li>
  <li>Manufacturing not elsewhere classified</li>
</ul>

<p>The UK projects Gross Value Added (<abbr title="Gross Value Added">GVA</abbr>) for each of these sectors using <abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr>, interest rates, and, in some cases, terms of trade (the relative prices of imports and exports). The UK projects total energy demand for each sector from <abbr title="Gross Value Added">GVA</abbr> and energy prices. Except for iron and steel, the model splits total energy demand into different fuels using historical fuel demands and projections of relative fuel prices. In iron and steel, the UK estimates energy demand using sector <abbr title="Gross Value Added">GVA</abbr> and the tonnages of steel produced using electricity or by the Basic Oxygen Steel (<abbr title="Basic Oxygen Steel">BOS</abbr>) process.</p>

<p>Energy demand is projected by commercial services from sector <abbr title="Gross Value Added">GVA</abbr>, and temperature based on econometric analysis of past consumption, <abbr title="Gross Value Added">GVA</abbr> and temperature.</p>

<h5 id="residential">2.16.1.4 Residential</h5>

<p>The UK projects the residential emissions from gas, oil and solid fuels use separately. The estimates depend on assumptions about the percentage of households using each fuel as their main heating source. The primary drivers of residential energy demand are household numbers, fuel prices, temperature and income.</p>

<p>Residential demand for electricity is projected using the same drivers and passed to the <abbr title="Dynamic Dispatch Model">DDM</abbr>.</p>

<h5 id="agriculture-2">2.16.1.5 Agriculture</h5>

<p>UK agriculture uses a relatively small amount of energy. Therefore, projections of its combustion emissions come from simple trend models.</p>

<p>The UK uses Food and Agricultural Policy Research Institute (<abbr title="Food and Agricultural Policy Research Institute">FAPRI</abbr>) methodology<sup id="fnref:317"><a href="#fn:317" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 317]</a></sup> to provide projections of activity, such as livestock numbers, crop production, fertiliser nitrogen use, and non-<abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> emissions to 2030. Projections for later years are held constant. The <abbr title="Food and Agricultural Policy Research Institute">FAPRI</abbr> projections come from an economic model that assumes a specific set of international prices for agricultural commodities and a path for the sterling exchange rate. Together, these factors are important determinants of the returns to farmers and hence of total agricultural production. The UK converts these <abbr title="Food and Agricultural Policy Research Institute">FAPRI</abbr> activity projections to emissions using the latest agriculture model in the UK’s <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> Inventory.</p>

<h5 id="waste-management-1">2.16.1.6 Waste management</h5>

<p>Projections of <abbr title="Methane">CH</abbr><sub>4</sub> from landfill depend on UK projections of tonnages of municipal waste going to landfill and on figures for commercial and industrial waste. Waste composition is projected from knowledge of changes to BWT processes and from projections of waste arising.</p>

<p>These projections of waste going to landfill are then run through MELMod, the landfill emissions calculation model. The MELMod model is based on the <abbr title="Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change">IPCC</abbr>’s first-order decay methodology, which the 2014 <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> Inventory report summarises. UK population projections underpin predictions of emissions of <abbr title="Methane">CH</abbr><sub>4</sub> and <abbr title="Nitrous Oxide">N</abbr><sub>2</sub>O from domestic wastewater and sewage/sludge decomposition. Industrial wastewater emissions are predicted to stay constant. BWT emissions from multiple sources are combined. Some are projected to be constant, and some are extrapolated from the latest year of historical data using sector experts’ estimates of future BWT capacity.</p>

<h5 id="industrial-processes-1">2.16.1.7 Industrial processes</h5>

<p>Manufacturing sub-sector <abbr title="Gross Value Added">GVA</abbr> projections or energy demand projections are used to project <abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> emissions from industrial processes where there is evidence of correlation. Other <abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> emissions are projected to remain constant at the last actual value from the UK’s <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> Inventory (published 2022).</p>

<p>Many methods are used for projections of non-<abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> emissions from industrial processes. Some sources use manufacturing sector GVAs while others use more detailed assumptions about future activity. Annex <abbr title="Nitrous Oxide">N</abbr> of the UK’s domestic <abbr title="Energy and Emissions Projections">EEP</abbr> publication<sup id="fnref:318"><a href="#fn:318" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 318]</a></sup> provides more information on non-<abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> emissions projection methods.</p>

<h5 id="public-sector">2.16.1.8 Public sector</h5>

<p>Sector employment levels are used as the main driver in modelling non-electricity energy demand from public services. The projections assume that the historical trend of improving energy efficiency per employee will continue. Temperature also affects public sector demand. The models break non-electricity energy demand into fuels using the same proportions as in latest historical data.</p>

<h5 id="land-use-land-use-change-and-forestry-lulucf-2">2.16.1.9 Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry (<abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr>)</h5>

<p>The Centre for Ecology and Hydrology and Forest Research model <abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr> emissions using approaches that are consistent with the current inventory methodology. They produce 4 scenarios – Baseline, Central, High and Low – for future emissions. Each makes assumptions about afforestation, wildfires, peat extraction, land use change and deforestation. They developed these scenarios with a policy maker stakeholder group and updated them in 2016 following discussions with UK devolved governments. Broadly, their central scenario is a continuation of current policies and activity rates. This is the scenario used in generating emissions projections for this report.</p>

<h4 id="estimation-of-emissions-in-crown-dependencies-and-overseas-territories-brbr">2.16.2 Estimation of emissions in crown dependencies and overseas territories <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK’s crown dependencies and overseas territories are not included in the projections which the UK produces annually to monitor progress against its own carbon budgets. The projections in this report supplement the UK annual figures with forecasts for areas that are consistent with the UK’s 1990-2022 <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> Inventory. Emissions in these territories are only a small proportion of UK emissions, making up 0.4% of the UK’s <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> coverage emissions in 2022. Two different approaches are used for projecting these territories:</p>

<ul>
  <li>For most sectors (excluding 1. Energy and memo items), emissions for crown dependencies and overseas territories are projected based on simple linear trends of the emissions in each National Communication sector based on observations from the previous 9 years;</li>
  <li>However due to the significant impact of <abbr title="Coronavirus">COVID-19</abbr> on transport sectors (particularly 1. Energy, and memo item rows), we used a different methodology. For these sectors, we projected emissions for crown dependencies and overseas territories with the same trajectory as the UK emissions for the equivalent sector.</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="strengths-of-the-projection-methodology-brbr">2.16.3 Strengths of the projection methodology <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK’s modelling methodology has the following strengths:</p>

<ul>
  <li>The initial starting point for the UK’s Energy and Emissions Projections is the latest historical data from the <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> Inventory and <abbr title="Digest of UK Energy Statistics">DUKES</abbr>. In the case of <abbr title="Energy and Emissions Projections">EEP</abbr> 2023, this was based on the UK’s <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> Inventory 1990-2022 and 2022 energy statistics (both of these with latest actuals 2022). These are well established sources of information;</li>
  <li>The main Energy Demand Model (<abbr title="Energy Demand Model">EDM</abbr>) uses econometric methods that capture long-run relationships between economic activity, energy consumption and emissions;</li>
  <li>The detailed model of electricity generation captures both short-run fuel switching and long-term investment strategies;</li>
  <li>The UK updates its projections regularly as part of the monitoring of UK national carbon budgets;</li>
  <li>Models use authoritative national and international sources for socio-economic projections;</li>
  <li>There is a rolling programme of review and update for the projection methodologies and econometric models, and modelling performance is tested by back-casting to see how well the model predicts what happened in the recent past;</li>
  <li>The projections distinguish between business as usual emissions and the emission reductions due to mitigating policies and measures; and</li>
  <li>The modelling estimates the mitigation impacts of policies using a common cross-government methodology.</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="weaknesses-of-the-projection-methodology-brbr">2.16.4 Weaknesses of the projection methodology <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK’s modelling has the following weaknesses:</p>

<ul>
  <li>The modelling generally assumes that historical relationships will continue in the future, which can fail to capture structural changes and new technologies where these fall outside the scope of included policies and measures;</li>
  <li>It hasn’t been possible to update uncertainty analysis, so uncertainty ranges quoted are still based on analysis from 2019. Similarly, analysis assumed that the drivers of uncertainty were similar to previous years;</li>
  <li>There is considerable recognised uncertainty in economic and demographic projections from external sources;</li>
  <li>The UK cannot provide separate quantified impacts for some types of policy due to modelling limitations. Policies which operate fully or partly through a price impact such as the Climate Change Levy (an environmental tax on the
energy that businesses use) cannot be quantified due to limitations with our modelling approach. These are taken into account in the modelling (through their impact on energy demand), but we do not have estimates of the individual impacts; and</li>
  <li>As with all econometric modelling, this is subject to estimation errors.</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="key-assumptions-brbr">2.16.5 Key assumptions <br><br>
</h4>

<p>A set of key assumptions about UK economic growth, demographic changes and future fuel price trajectories underpin the UK’s projections. The main sources of projected assumptions are the forecasts made by the UK’s Office for Budget Responsibility (<abbr title="Office for Budget Responsibility">OBR</abbr>) and Office for National Statistics (<abbr title="Office for National Statistics">ONS</abbr>), and supplemented by International Monetary Fund projections of world growth. Fuel prices are produced by the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (<abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr>). <abbr title="Common Tabular Format">CTF</abbr> Table 11 documents key parameters and assumptions.</p>

<p>The UK released <abbr title="Energy and Emissions Projections">EEP</abbr> 2023 -2050 in December 2024. UK <abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr> forecasts to 2023 were from the March 2024 Economic and Fiscal Outlook publication. Beyond 2023, <abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr> growth projections came from the March 2024 Long-term economic determinants forecast. The UK’s Office for National Statistics (<abbr title="Office for National Statistics">ONS</abbr>) produced 2021-based population projections in January 2024. The household projections are also from <abbr title="Office for National Statistics">ONS</abbr> and are 2018-based (but including a projection update by the Welsh Government in August 2020). <strong>Table 23</strong> shows updated socio-economic growth assumptions.</p>

<h4 id="quality-assurance-and-quality-controls-brbr">2.16.6 Quality assurance and quality controls <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Quality assurance of modelling is a high priority within UK Government, and analysis for the <abbr title="Energy and Emissions Projections">EEP</abbr> follows the <abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr> quality assurance guidelines.</p>

<p>A small group of <abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr> analysts produces the energy and emission projections, and owns, maintains and updates the Energy Demand Model (known as the <abbr title="Energy Demand Model">EDM</abbr>) which underpins the projections. The <abbr title="Energy and Emissions Projections">EEP</abbr> team liaises with other modelling teams, both inside and outside <abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr>, to quality assure and compile the data which go into the overall projections.</p>

<p>Figures relating to electricity come from iteratively solving 2 specialised models with the <abbr title="Energy Demand Model">EDM</abbr>. These are the Dynamic Dispatch Model (<abbr title="Dynamic Dispatch Model">DDM</abbr>) and the Prices and Bills Model of retail electricity prices. This cycling ensures that electricity demand is in equilibrium with prices. The co-ordinators of these models also assure projections results. Projections for non-energy non-<abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> emissions are produced by the <abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr> Science division.</p>

<p>The Centre for Ecology and Hydrology produces the UK’s <abbr title="Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry">LULUCF</abbr> projections under contract; this is overseen by the <abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr> Science and Innovation for Climate and Energy Directorate.</p>

<p><abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr> bases transport sector modelling on, and calibrates it against, the detailed models for road, rail and air used by the Department for Transport (<abbr title="Department for Transport">DfT</abbr>). These latter are in turn subject to <abbr title="Department for Transport">DfT</abbr>’s quality assurance.</p>

<p>Analytical teams in the relevant areas prepare estimates of the emissions or energy savings due to UK Government policies. Analysts prepare these policy savings estimates according to central guidance, which ensures that energy use and <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> emissions are valued consistently across UK Government.</p>

<p>Analysts send the policy savings in a standard template and the <abbr title="Energy and Emissions Projections">EEP</abbr> team checks them to look for any unaccounted overlaps and to ensure internal consistency between energy and emissions savings. The team confirms the model savings with the submitting analysts and departments. The UK updates its <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr> projections to inform progress against national carbon budgets and publishes each set of projections. The <abbr title="Energy and Emissions Projections">EEP</abbr> team improves and adapts the core Energy Demand Model incrementally, quality assuring each change to confirm validity and robustness. (The team responsible for the <abbr title="Dynamic Dispatch Model">DDM</abbr> quality assures any change relating to electricity generation). The <abbr title="Energy and Emissions Projections">EEP</abbr> team presents interim and final results to a Steering Group which oversees the process, and stakeholders review draft <abbr title="Energy and Emissions Projections">EEP</abbr> reports before publication. The UK’s independent Climate Change Committee reviews the projections after their release.</p>

<h4 id="uncertainty-brbr">2.16.7 Uncertainty <br><br>
</h4>

<p>In December 2024 the UK published annexes of data to accompany its domestic projections. These included low and high fossil fuel prices and low and high UK <abbr title="Gross Domestic Product">GDP</abbr> rates as variant scenarios and sensitivities.</p>

<h4 id="overall-uncertainty-brbr">2.16.9 Overall uncertainty <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Future values of key variables such as fossil fuel prices, the impacts of policy and demographic/economic growth cannot be known with certainty. However, these variables underpin the UK projections. Understanding the impact of this uncertainty is important in the context of the UK’s aim to reduce emissions through policy intervention, and so it is regularly investigated in <abbr title="Energy and Emissions Projections">EEP</abbr> publications. Uncertainty analysis presented here is based on the most influential drivers of energy use and emissions, previously identified through sensitivity analysis. The <abbr title="Energy and Emissions Projections">EEP</abbr> team carries out a Monte Carlo simulation to vary the values of these drivers, firstly obtaining historical distributions of input values then running the projections model on samples from these distributions.</p>

<p>The uncertainty ranges presented in this section are still derived from the uncertainty analysis from the estimates published in <abbr title="Energy and Emissions Projections">EEP</abbr> 2018, due to time constraints at the time of analysis.</p>

<p>This method underpins the 95% confidence interval estimates presented in Figure 5.3 and <strong>Table 29</strong>. The upper and lower boundaries represent the projected emissions corresponding to the lower 2.5% and upper 97.5% percentiles of the Monte Carlo simulations respectively. Although the high/low emissions projections in <strong>Figure 20</strong> show UK coverage (excluding <abbr title="crown dependencies and overseas territories">CDOTs</abbr>), they do indicate the scale of uncertainty in the projections reported in this section, as CDOT emissions were only 0.4% of the overall total in 2022.</p>

<p>This analysis excludes the electricity supply industry and possible ‘structural breaks’ in society or the economy which might significantly affect emissions. For example, societal and behavioural step changes or breakthrough technologies like improved storage could have profound impacts on the UK’s energy mix and emissions but are hard to anticipate.</p>

<p>The methodology only looks at future uncertainty and does not examine uncertainty in historical inputs or emission estimates, such as those before 2022.</p>

By 2039, the range is slightly wider with emissions projected between 23% and 29% below 2022 levels. The higher uncertainty for later years reflects the reduced confidence in modelled projections further into the future.</p>

<h4 id="projections-for-precursor-gases-brbr">2.16.10 Projections for precursor gases <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Projections for emissions from precursor gases in the UK are not included within this analysis but are produced by the National Atmospheric Emissions Inventory (<abbr title="National Atmospheric Emissions Inventory">NAEI</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:320"><a href="#fn:320" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 320]</a></sup>. The projections are produced at 5-year intervals out to 2050 and contains the pollutants regulated under the <abbr title="United Nations">UN</abbr> Gothenburg protocol.</p>

<h3 id="projections-of-key-indicators-to-determine-progress-towards-ndc">2.17 Projections of key indicators to determine progress towards <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr>
</h3>

<p>The <abbr title="With existing measures">WEM</abbr> scenario projections in this section include the impact of the UK’s implemented and adopted policies and measures at the policy cut-off point of June 2024. They are the baseline or counterfactual projection showing what the UK would expect to happen if no policies at an earlier stage of development were implemented.</p>

<p>The name, sector, <abbr title="Greenhouse Gas">GHG</abbr>(s) and activity affected, and descriptions of these policies and measures can be found in <abbr title="Common Tabular Format">CTF</abbr> Table 5. The <abbr title="With existing measures">WEM</abbr> scenario within this section does not include planned policies, but those are included within domestic reporting and are therefore shown in <abbr title="Common Tabular Format">CTF</abbr> Table 5.</p>

<p>The UK has continued to update its analysis of policies and measures expected to help meet both Nationally Determined Contributions and the targets for Carbon Budgets set under the UK Climate Change Act (2008). Over time, the UK’s projections will include newer or more recently announced policies as they progress to the impact assessment stage. Within this section, we also include the total of territorial and international aviation and shipping (<abbr title="International Aviation and Shipping">IAS</abbr>) policy savings.</p>

<p>Table 5.3.1 and Figure 5.4 show the projected impact of demand-side policies only. Power supply markets are highly interconnected, meaning it is not possible to robustly disaggregate the impacts of individual supply-side policies. We are reviewing the method for calculating savings from overall power interventions, but for now the tables in this section and in <abbr title="Common Tabular Format">CTF</abbr> Table 5 exclude the aggregated emissions savings from power supply policies.</p>

<h2 id="chapter-3">Chapter 3: Information related to climate change impacts and adaptation</h2>

<h3 id="national-circumstances-institutional-arrangements-and-legal-frameworks">3.1 National circumstances, institutional arrangements and legal frameworks</h3>

<p>The devolved governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland contribute to the UK’s overall climate objectives and have their own adaptation targets; unless stated otherwise, the information below outlines England’s approach. The devolved government has provided information on their strategies in section 3.10.</p>

<h3 id="biogeophysical-characteristics">3.2 Biogeophysical characteristics</h3>

<p>We are already seeing climate impacts across the globe, with observed increases in the frequency and intensity of heatwaves, flooding, drought and wildfires. According to the World Meteorological Organization<sup id="fnref:321"><a href="#fn:321" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 321]</a></sup>, long-term global warming is currently around 1.3°C compared to the 1850-1900 baseline, whilst in the UK, the 10 warmest years on record have all occurred since 2003<sup id="fnref:322"><a href="#fn:322" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 322]</a></sup>. Human-induced warming is increasing at around 0.25⁰C<sup id="fnref:323"><a href="#fn:323" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 323]</a></sup> per decade, leading to further increases in global and UK climate hazards into the future.</p>

<p>The latest State of the UK Climate report,<sup id="fnref:324"><a href="#fn:324" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 324]</a></sup> highlighted a year of extremes. 2022 was shown to be the warmest year in the UK series from 1884, 0.9 °C above the 1991–2020 average, and for the first time 40 °C was recorded in the UK. The period January–August 2022 was also the driest across England and Wales since 1976, with drought status declared across parts of England and all of Wales. Rising sea levels have continued to be observed in the UK and have risen by 18.5cm since 1900’s. The rate of sea level rise has also accelerated, with over 60% of the observed sea level rise (11.4cm) occurring over the past 30 years.</p>

<p>More recently, Met Office<sup id="fnref:325"><a href="#fn:325" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 325]</a></sup> observations show that 2023 was the second warmest year for the UK according to mean temperature. Both Wales and Northern Ireland experienced their warmest years on record in 2023. Changes in rainfall extremes has also begun to be observed in the UK. In 2023, the UK saw 11% more rain than average with a provisional figure of 1289.8mm falling.</p>

<h3 id="economy">3.3 Economy</h3>

<p>The economic losses from flooding in England between November 2019 and March 2020 are estimated to be about £333 million and would have been significantly larger in the absence of flood defences<sup id="fnref:326"><a href="#fn:326" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 326]</a></sup>. The ‘Monetary Valuation of Risks and Opportunities in the third Climate Change Risk Assessment(<abbr title="Third Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA3</abbr>)’<sup id="fnref:327"><a href="#fn:327" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 327]</a></sup> report found that around a quarter of the 61 climate risks and opportunities it identified each have the potential to result in economic impacts higher than £1 billion per year by 2050.</p>

<p>Disruption from climate change has the potential to reduce government revenues and increase government expenditure, reduce external performance (exports), damage infrastructure assets, increase social costs thereby increasing vulnerability for some population groups, and reduce economic growth (source: World Bank Group, 2020; Inclusive Futures, 2020). However, early adaptation action can help to reduce future costs and many adaptation actions represent good value for money. The ‘Monetary Valuation of Risks and Opportunities in <abbr title="Third Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA3</abbr>’<sup id="fnref:328"><a href="#fn:328" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 328]</a></sup> report found that, for a range of early interventions, benefit-cost ratios typically range from 2:1 to 10:1. This means that every £1 invested in these adaptation actions could result in £2 to £10 in net economic benefit.</p>

<h3 id="infrastructure">3.4 Infrastructure</h3>

<p>Recent events such as Storm Arwen in 2021 and the heatwaves of 2022 demonstrate the kinds of impacts climate risks can lead to, from power outages to buckling train tracks. The evidence suggests these impacts will get more intense and frequent under any emissions scenario to 2050.</p>

<p>To help manage climate risks to infrastructure sectors:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Ensuring that the regulatory framework is delivering adaptation outcomes</li>
  <li>Putting the necessary investment in place</li>
  <li>Engaging with infrastructure operators and regulators to improve understanding of and approaches to identifying and managing climate risk</li>
</ul>

<p>The UK has a robust system to ensure that public investment in infrastructure appropriately considers climate risk, which the <abbr title="International Monetary Fund">IMF</abbr>’s Public Investment Management Assessment<sup id="fnref:329"><a href="#fn:329" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 329]</a></sup> (<abbr title="IMF’s Public Investment Management Assessment">PIMA</abbr>) found to be relatively well-designed. The Green Book is guidance issued by <abbr title="His Majesty">HM</abbr> Treasury on how to appraise policies, programmes and projects. It also provides guidance on the design and use of monitoring and evaluation before, during and after implementation.</p>

<p>The following levers are used to manage climate risks in infrastructure.</p>

<ul>
  <li>National Infrastructure Strategy<sup id="fnref:330"><a href="#fn:330" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 330]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>UK Government Resilience Framework<sup id="fnref:331"><a href="#fn:331" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 331]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>Adaptation Reporting Power (<abbr title="Adaptation Reporting Power">ARP</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:332"><a href="#fn:332" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 332]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>Critical National Infrastructure (<abbr title="Critical National Infrastructure">CNI</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:333"><a href="#fn:333" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 333]</a></sup> policy</li>
  <li>Planning policy<sup id="fnref:334"><a href="#fn:334" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 334]</a></sup>
</li>
