  <li>Institutional framework: strengthening our understanding of climate risk to infrastructure, through the National Infrastructure Commission (<abbr title="National Infrastructure Commission">NIC</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:335"><a href="#fn:335" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 335]</a></sup>, the Infrastructure and Projects Authority’s (<abbr title="Infrastructure and Projects Authority">IPA</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:336"><a href="#fn:336" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 336]</a></sup> and the National Wealth Fund (formerly the UK Infrastructure Bank)</li>
</ul>

<p>Major public investment in infrastructure is subject to an additional level of scrutiny through the UK Government’s Infrastructure and Projects Authority, which provides an assurance function to support the successful delivery of projects within the UK Government’s Major Projects Portfolio (<abbr title="Government’s Major Projects Portfolio">GMPP</abbr>).</p>

<p>The Infrastructure and Projects Authority’s (<abbr title="Infrastructure and Projects Authority">IPA</abbr>) Gate Review process is designed to provide a realistic view on a programme and project’s ability to deliver agreed outcomes against time, cost, benefits and quality, and these Gate Reviews include tests to ensure infrastructure projects have considered climate risk and adaptation.</p>

<h4 id="global-goal-on-adaptation-gga-thematic-target-5---climate-resilient-infrastructure-brbr">3.4.1 Global Goal on Adaptation (<abbr title="Global Goal for Adaptation">GGA</abbr>) Thematic target 5 - Climate-resilient Infrastructure <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Adaptation is embedded through the planning system for major infrastructure projects. National Policy Statements (<abbr title="National Policy Statements">NPSs</abbr>) are a key part of the system for managing Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects (<abbr title="Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects">NSIPs</abbr>) and are important in ensuring that government policy is implemented effectively through the planning system. Infrastructure <abbr title="National Policy Statements">NPSs</abbr> include requirements for planning applicants to demonstrate how they have considered the risks posed by the changing climate.</p>

<p>Plans for reforms to the NSIP<sup id="fnref:337"><a href="#fn:337" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 337]</a></sup> regime that will ensure the system can support our future infrastructure needs by making the system better, faster, greener, fairer and more resilient.</p>

<p>The UK Government Resilience Framework<sup id="fnref:338"><a href="#fn:338" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 338]</a></sup>, sets out how the government will work with industry and regulators to improve the security and resilience of UK <abbr title="Critical National Infrastructure">CNI</abbr> for example by using common but flexible resilience standards across <abbr title="Critical National Infrastructure">CNI</abbr>, and by reviewing existing regulatory regimes on resilience to ensure they are fit for purpose.</p>

<h4 id="global-goal-on-adaptation-gga-thematic-target-1---water">3.4.2 Global Goal on Adaptation (<abbr title="Global Goal for Adaptation">GGA</abbr>) Thematic target 1 - Water</h4>

<p>Private investment in national infrastructure is often also subject to sector-specific regulation ensuring appropriate consideration of climate risk. This includes Water Resources Management Plans (<abbr title="Water Resources Management Plans">WRMPs</abbr>), through which water companies have a duty to set out how they will continue to supply water in their supply area over at least the next 25 years in the context of population growth and climate change. This long-term planning framework is supported by specific requirements and standards (e.g. water companies must demonstrate resilience to a 1-in-500-year drought), and by regular monitoring against company-level performance commitments on metrics like supply interruptions, leakage, and per capita consumption.</p>

<p>Most water companies have finalised their <abbr title="Water Resources Management Plans">WRMPs</abbr> with direction on how they plan to meet increasing water demands, which includes using £500 million investment to develop new infrastructure in the 2020-2025 period. The plans also include water efficiency measures such as providing water audits for businesses to consider how best to maximise their water efficiency. This will help in meeting targets to reduce leakage by 37% and non-household water use by 9% by 2038, safeguarding future water availability for businesses.</p>

<p>The Environment Agency’s latest review of draft Regional Water Resource Plans found an additional 4,860 million litres of water a day (Ml/d) will be needed in England by 2050 to meet future supply pressures: this is around a third of the water currently supplied by water undertakers. Approximately half of the 4,860 Ml/d required will need to be delivered through demand management measures.</p>

<p>We are implementing a Water Demand Target under the Environment Act 2021 to reduce use of public water supply by 20% by 2037/38. The Water Demand target is based on a trajectory for achieving household water use of 110 litres per person per day, a 50% leakage reduction from 2017/18 levels and a 15% reduction in non-household water use by 2050.</p>

<p>Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs (<abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr>) has also acknowledged recommendations made within the Baringa<sup id="fnref:339"><a href="#fn:339" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 339]</a></sup> report and will continue working with Ofwat to understand the implementation of these actions.</p>

<p>We recognise that smart metering can assist in reducing overall water consumption by enabling water companies to reduce leakage and incentivise more water efficient behaviours. Water companies have already committed to delivering a 50% reduction in leakage from 2017 to 2018 levels by 2050 and we expect Ofwat to challenge companies to deliver this and monitor progress.</p>

<p>Around 13% of households in England now have a smart water meter and this number is set to rise to 73% by 2040.</p>

<p>To help achieve our target of reducing the amount of water used per person in England per head by 20% by 2038, we have committed to working with regulators and industry on the rollout of smart meters, alongside mandatory water efficiency labelling, to enable consumers to make more water efficient choices.</p>

<p>The climate crisis is a water crisis. Despite this, the water crisis has largely gone unaddressed internationally. Through the Water Tracker for National Climate Planning<sup id="fnref:340"><a href="#fn:340" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 340]</a></sup>, supported by the <abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr>, the UK is providing partner countries with a clear pathway to design and implement coordinated and targeted climate action and meaningfully ensure the water-food-energy nexus is reflected in ambitious 1.5-aligned climate, resilience and nature plans.</p>

<h3 id="adaptive-capacity">3.5 Adaptive capacity</h3>

<h4 id="adaptation-challenges-and-gaps-and-barriers-to-adaptation-brbr">3.5.1 Adaptation challenges and gaps, and barriers to adaptation <br><br>
</h4>

<p>As well as the barriers, gaps also exist in our ability to monitor our adaptation efforts. This is due to the complexity of adaptation and the associated challenges of identifying and developing appropriate indicators. <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> has held a series of sector-specific workshops focused on the monitoring and evaluation (<abbr title="Monitoring and Evaluation">M&amp;E</abbr>) of adaptation in each sector.</p>

<p>These challenges are consistent with the findings of the Climate Change Committee (<abbr title="Climate Change Committee">CCC</abbr>) in its 2021 progress report to Parliament<sup id="fnref:341"><a href="#fn:341" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 341]</a></sup>. Adaptation process indicators (such as the number of plans adopted, or buildings retrofitted) are relatively simple to measure and so more common. Indicators that measure adaptation outcomes (such as climate-sensitive sectors of the economy being better adapted) are rarer as they are harder to measure.</p>

<h3 id="institutional-arrangements-and-governance-legal-and-policy-frameworks-and-regulations">3.6 Institutional arrangements and governance, legal and policy frameworks and regulations</h3>

<p>The UK was the first country in the world to enshrine government action on climate adaptation into law under the UK Climate Change Act (2008)<sup id="fnref:342"><a href="#fn:342" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 342]</a></sup>. The Act created a framework for strengthening UK preparedness to climate change risks. These include preparing, on a 5 yearly cycle, a UK Climate Change Risk Assessment (<abbr title="Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA</abbr>), followed by a National Adaptation Programme (<abbr title="National Adaptation Programme">NAP</abbr>), setting out actions to address the risks identified in the <abbr title="Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA</abbr>. The Climate Change Act also provides <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr>’s Secretary of State with the power, known as ‘Adaptation Reporting Power’<sup id="fnref:343"><a href="#fn:343" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 343]</a></sup> (<abbr title="Adaptation Reporting Power">ARP</abbr>) to direct infrastructure providers and public bodies to report on their preparedness for climate change; it also required <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> to publish a strategy for each round of the process. The Act established an independent Climate Change Committee (<abbr title="Climate Change Committee">CCC</abbr>) to advise government and assess adaptation progress on a biennial basis.</p>

<p>Responsibility for climate change adaptation is split between the 4 countries of the United Kingdom. National governments in Northern Ireland, Wales and Scotland are responsible for respective adaptation programmes. His Majesty’s Government (<abbr title="His Majesty’s Government">HMG</abbr>) is responsible for climate change adaptation in England and for embedding adaptation within policy areas for which it has UK-wide competence such as energy security and foreign affairs. Climate policy (both mitigation and adaptation) is devolved to the crown dependencies and overseas territories, so they are responsible for setting their adaptation policies.</p>

<p>The third National Adaptation Programme (<abbr title="The third National Adaptation Programme">NAP3</abbr>) made governance a priority over the 5-year implementation period. This included establishing a senior official Climate Resilience Steering Board to oversee strategic, cross-cutting climate adaptation and resilience issues and drive further government action to increase UK resilience to climate change.</p>

<p>In addition to the Climate Resilience Steering Board driving further government action to increase UK resilience to climate change, the UK Government will use its extensive network of overseas posts, researchers, and international relationships to identify emerging risks and escalating, where necessary, cascading risks through government’s existing risk management governance structures.</p>

<p>Addressing climate risks, requires not only an improved understanding of those risks through government action to build capability and address evidence gaps, but also coordination across and between governments through strong governance structures.</p>

<h3 id="impacts-risks-and-vulnerabilities-as-appropriate">3.7 Impacts, risks and vulnerabilities, as appropriate</h3>

<h4 id="current-and-projected-climate-trends-and-hazards-brbr">3.7.1 Current and projected climate trends and hazards <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Observations from 2022 and 2023 have aligned with general climate change trends projected for the future in the UK Climate Projections (<abbr title="UK Climate Projections">UKCP</abbr>), produced by the Met Office. <abbr title="UK Climate Projections">UKCP</abbr> projections show an increased chance of warmer, wetter winters and hotter, drier summers, along with an increase in the frequency and intensity of extremes. These increases in extremes include increase in the frequency of and intensity of hot spells in summer.</p>

<p>Hot summers and heatwaves will become more intense and longer lasting, particularly in the south-east of England. Northern Ireland and Scotland will begin to experience summers like those currently felt in the rest of the country. Summer drought conditions will occur more often in the south of the UK, like that seen in 2022. Despite overall summer drying trends in the future, projections show increases in the intensity of heavy summer rainfall events in the future, as well as increased intensity of heavy rainfall events across all seasons.</p>

<p>Sea levels are projected to rise through the 21st century and beyond for all emissions scenarios. Sea levels will rise across the UK, with greater rises in the south and east of the UK due to land movement. By end of the 21st century, sea levels in the UK may have risen by up to 1 meter.</p>

<h3 id="observed-and-potential-impacts-of-climate-change-including-sectoral-economic-social-andor-environmental-vulnerabilities">3.8 Observed and potential impacts of climate change, including sectoral, economic, social and/or environmental vulnerabilities</h3>

<h4 id="global-goal-on-adaptation-gga-process-target-1---impact-vulnerability-and-risk-assessment-brbr">3.8.1 Global Goal on Adaptation (<abbr title="Global Goal for Adaptation">GGA</abbr>) process target 1 - Impact, vulnerability and risk assessment <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK’s Third ‘Climate Change Risk Assessment (<abbr title="Third Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA3</abbr>)’<sup id="fnref:344"><a href="#fn:344" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 344]</a></sup> published in 2022, has presented strong evidence that even under low warming scenarios the UK will be subject to a range of significant and costly impacts unless further action is taken. Informed by an independent assessment undertaken by the Climate Change Committee, <abbr title="Third Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA3</abbr> identified 61 risks and opportunities to the UK from climate change, including risks to health and productivity, the built environment, businesses, the natural environment, and to public services.</p>

<p>Impacts range from a deterioration in soil health and agricultural productivity to impacts on water availability and energy generation. For example, unless we take further action, under a 2°C by 2100 warming scenario, annual damages from flooding for non-residential properties across the UK is expected to increase by 27% by 2050 and 40% by 2080. At 4°C this increases to 44% and 75% respectively.</p>

<p>Estimates represent impacts to the whole UK economy, but impacts are likely to vary significantly across localities, areas and groups.</p>

<h4 id="jersey-brbr-1">3.8.2 Jersey <br><br>
</h4>

<p>As an Island, sea level rise and associated flooding have been identified as a key risk from a changing climate.</p>

<p>There has also been a reduction is some local species, for example a 78% reduction in the brown crab since 2012 alongside an increase in some invasive species such as a 94% increase in the Asian Hornet.</p>

<h4 id="guernsey-brbr-1">3.8.3 Guernsey <br><br>
</h4>

<p>In 2012, a report (Guernsey Coastal Defences – Flood Risk Assessment Studies<sup id="fnref:345"><a href="#fn:345" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 345]</a></sup>) was published looking at the flood risk around the coastline of Guernsey. This identified that ta number of locations around the coast, particularly to the low lying lands in the north and along the west coast, are at risk from increased sea levels leading to overtopping and flooding. The States of Guernsey agreed to a prioritisation for addressing these defences, as well as additional defences to the island’s capital – St Peter Port. Further recent work as part of the development of planning policies has updated the risk levels in line with <abbr title="UK Climate Projections 2018">UKCP18</abbr> climate change predictions.</p>

<p>The island is susceptible to invasive species, with the Asian hornet having arrived over the past decade. Despite a proactive response there is an annual search for and destruction of nests.</p>

<h4 id="isle-of-man-brbr-1">3.8.4 Isle of Man <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The Isle of Man commissioned a report in 2005 to identify the potential impacts of climate change for the Isle of Man – Climate Change Scoping Study – Executive Summary<sup id="fnref:346"><a href="#fn:346" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 346]</a></sup>. This identified problems and objectives, key receptors, vulnerability thresholds and decisions making criteria, as well as carrying out a risk assessment and presenting adaptation options. It covered a wide range of sectors and identified a range of potential impacts in all areas. This will be updated with another Climate Risks and Opportunities Assessment, as required by the Climate Change Plan 2022-2027, to ensure our understanding of climate risks and vulnerabilities remains current and able to inform effective policies.</p>

<h4 id="gibraltar-brbr-1">3.8.5 Gibraltar <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Gibraltar conducted its first Climate Change Vulnerability and Risk Assessment<sup id="fnref:347"><a href="#fn:347" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 347]</a></sup> in 2022.This identified a number of key risks and vulnerabilities including energy and water supply, food importation and impacts on public health as a result of extreme heat and increase in vector borne diseases.</p>

<h3 id="approaches-methodologies-and-tools-and-associated-uncertainties-and-challenges">3.9 Approaches, methodologies and tools, and associated uncertainties and challenges</h3>

<p>A range of tools have been developed to help our partners assess climate risk and develop and deliver a policy response that affects real change.</p>

<p>These include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>The UK Climate Projections<sup id="fnref:348"><a href="#fn:348" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 348]</a></sup>, which provide up-to-date assessment of how the UK climate may change in the future, which are available at 2.2km resolution (<abbr title="UK Climate Projections 2018">UKCP18</abbr>) for local risk assessment.</li>
  <li>‘The UK Climate Resilience Programme’<sup id="fnref:349"><a href="#fn:349" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 349]</a></sup> which uses <abbr title="UK Climate Projections 2018">UKCP18</abbr> to build the evidence on climate risks, adaptation and services in the UK. It has delivered several high impact outputs to date, including climate risk indicators to support climate risk assessments and future-drainage<sup id="fnref:350"><a href="#fn:350" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 350]</a></sup>, providing estimates of changes in rainfall for use in drainage design.</li>
  <li>The ‘Green Book supplementary guidance on Accounting for the Effects of Climate Change’<sup id="fnref:351"><a href="#fn:351" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 351]</a></sup> provides guidance on how to account for climate impacts and environmental factors in policy appraisal.</li>
  <li>Ten Principles for good Adaptation’ as set out in the Climate Change Committee’s advice. These overarching principles relate to having a clear vision for a well-adapted UK and can be found in the Climate Change Committee’s third independent assessment of the UK’s climate risks<sup id="fnref:352"><a href="#fn:352" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 352]</a></sup> <sup id="fnref:353"><a href="#fn:353" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 353]</a></sup>.</li>
  <li>An ambitious Fourth Climate Change Risk Assessment (<abbr title="Fourth Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA4</abbr>) Independent Assessment for 2027. Our aims for this include:
    <ul>
      <li>Spatial considerations which distinguish risk by area, including regional and localised mapping to understand how risk varies by location.</li>
      <li>Systematic assessment of risk through sector-based, outcome-focussed groupings to better consider interdependencies.</li>
      <li>More and integrated economic analysis woven through the risk assessment.</li>
      <li>Stronger focus on adaptation action, with research driving towards resolving evidence gaps across societal and behavioural sciences.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>Since the publication of the Climate Change Committee’s Independent Assessment in 2021 we have been working at pace to mainstream adaptation to climate change in policy planning across UK Government.</p>

<h4 id="jersey-brbr-2">3.9.1 Jersey <br><br>
</h4>

<p>As a small island, sea level rise and associated coastal flooding has been assessed as a high risk. Future temperature changes and fallouts from increased instances of extreme weather including flooding are also highly likely to have an impact on Jersey’s infrastructure.</p>

<p>The Shoreline Management Plan<sup id="fnref:354"><a href="#fn:354" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 354]</a></sup> sets out how we’ll maintain and enhance our coastal defences to protect our Island over the next 100 years. The plan is updated every 10 years. The next update is due in 2030.</p>

<p>A Strategic Flood Risk Assessment<sup id="fnref:355"><a href="#fn:355" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 355]</a></sup> was commissioned as part of the evidence base to inform the preparation of the bridging Island Plan. The new Island Plan now provides an appropriate planning framework to deal with both inland and coastal flood risk.</p>

<h4 id="guernsey-brbr-2">3.9.2 Guernsey <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Guernsey government’s recently consulted on a draft ‘Local Planning Brief’<sup id="fnref:356"><a href="#fn:356" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 356]</a></sup> for the harbour areas which updated the flood projections from 2012 for the east coast using the latest UKPC18 climate change predictions. This highlighted that over the course of the next 100 year the existing harbours are likely to be inoperable due to sea levels for certain periods. This highlights the challenge facing the island as a result of climate change.</p>

<h4 id="isle-of-man-brbr-2">3.9.3 Isle of Man <br><br>
</h4>

<p>In 2024 the Isle of Man government commissioned a technical climate change risk and opportunity assessment to provide evidence for the development of an Adaptation Strategy. The climate change risk and opportunity assessment followed the principals of International Organisation of Standardisation (ISO) 14091:2021, the international standard for adaptation to climate change. An Isle of Man risk register, identifying 119 risks and 14 opportunities, has been established across 5 sectors: natural environment, health and communities, infrastructure, economy, and international dimensions. For each risk likelihood and magnitude scoring was undertaken, the risks were prioritised by their risk rating for each of the 5 sectors. Urgency scores were assigned to each of the 119 risks to indicate the need for adaptation action in 2, 5, and 10-year intervals, as well as beyond 10 years.</p>

<h4 id="gibraltar-brbr-2">3.9.4 Gibraltar <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Gibraltar’s Vulnerability and Risk Assessment (<abbr title="Gibraltar’s Vulnerability and Risk Assessment">VRA</abbr>) was conducted using a combination of desk research and stakeholder consultations to extract key information. The desk research involved analysing over 40 sources of information, including targeted studies in Gibraltar, <abbr title="Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change">IPCC</abbr> reports and studies undertaken in geographies that have a similar geographical and biophysical profile as Gibraltar (Mediterranean, urban and coastal). The consultations involved interviews and questionnaires with over 70 key stakeholders. The <abbr title="Gibraltar’s Vulnerability and Risk Assessment">VRA</abbr> is aligned with the latest definitions of terms from the <abbr title="Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change">IPCC</abbr>’s Fifth and Sixth Assessment reports which enable the assessment of climate vulnerabilities independently from hazards, focusing on sectors’ ‘propensity or predisposition to be adversely affected’. This ensures that the assessment does not incorporate uncertainties associated with climate projections.</p>

<h3 id="adaptation-priorities-and-barriers">3.10 Adaptation priorities and barriers</h3>

<h4 id="domestic-priorities-and-progress-towards-those-priorities-brbr">3.10.1 Domestic priorities and progress towards those priorities <br><br>
</h4>

<p>In 2021, Climate Change Committee published an Independent Assessment<sup id="fnref:357"><a href="#fn:357" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 357]</a></sup> of UK Climate Risk in which they identified 8 priority climate risk areas needing immediate attention over the following 2 years. These were based on the urgency of additional action, the gap in UK adaptation planning, the opportunity to integrate adaptation into forthcoming policy commitments and the need to avoid locking in poor planning.</p>

<p>The priority areas were identified as:</p>

<ol>
  <li>Risks to the viability and diversity of terrestrial and freshwater habitats and species from multiple hazards</li>
  <li>Risks to soil health from increased flooding and drought</li>
  <li>Risks to natural carbon stores and sequestration from multiple hazards, leading to increased emissions</li>
  <li>Risks to crops, livestock and commercial trees from multiple climate hazards</li>
  <li>Risks to supply of food, goods and vital services due to climate-related collapse of supply chains and distribution networks</li>
  <li>Risks to people and the economy from climate-related failure of the power system</li>
  <li>Risks to human health, wellbeing and productivity from increased exposure to heat in homes and other buildings</li>
  <li>Multiple risks to the UK from climate change impacts overseas</li>
</ol>

<p>The UK Climate Change Risk Assessment 2022<sup id="fnref:358"><a href="#fn:358" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 358]</a></sup> highlights the government’s approach to the 8 priority risk areas and outlines recent actions taken to limit these risks as well as priorities going forward.</p>

<p>For <abbr title="The third National Adaptation Programme">NAP3</abbr> and the upcoming <abbr title="Fourth Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA4</abbr> Independent Assessment, research and development of methods to monitor and evaluate adaptation actions have been prioritised. <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> is providing support to risk owning departments for monitoring and evaluating their <abbr title="The third National Adaptation Programme">NAP3</abbr> actions to better understand to what extent they are achieving their objectives and what could be done differently to inform the next <abbr title="National Adaptation Programme">NAP</abbr>, NAP4.</p>

<h3 id="adaptation-strategies-policies-plans-goals-and-actions-to-integrate-adaptation-into-national-policies-and-strategies">3.11 Adaptation strategies, policies, plans, goals and actions to integrate adaptation into national policies and strategies</h3>

<h4 id="global-goal-on-adaptation-gga-process-target-2--planning-brbr">3.11.1Global Goal on Adaptation (<abbr title="Global Goal for Adaptation">GGA</abbr>) process target 2 – Planning <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The National Planning Policy Framework (<abbr title="National Planning Policy Framework">NPPF</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:359"><a href="#fn:359" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 359]</a></sup> sets out the government’s planning policies for England and how these should be applied, guiding locally prepared plans for housing and other development. The National Planning Policy Framework was revised in response to the Levelling-up and Regeneration Bill: reforms to national planning policy consultation<sup id="fnref:360"><a href="#fn:360" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 360]</a></sup> on 19 December 2023 and sets out the government’s planning policies for England and how these are expected to be applied.</p>

<h4 id="adaptation-goals-actions-objectives-undertakings-efforts-plans-strategies-policies-priorities-programmes-and-efforts-to-build-resilience-brbr">3.11.2 Adaptation goals, actions, objectives, undertakings, efforts, plans, strategies, policies, priorities, programmes and efforts to build resilience <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="england-11">3.11.2.1 England</h5>

<p>The government’s vision for adaptation is for a country that effectively plans for and is fully adapted to the changing climate, with resilience against each of the identified climate risks. The UK Climate Change Act provides a strong foundation to enhance resilience to climate impacts, with research and evidence informing policy and organisations publishing reports on their adaptation progress through the <abbr title="Adaptation Reporting Power">ARP</abbr>.</p>

<p>Overseas, UK Government provides official development assistance funding to support communities in climate vulnerable and fragile countries to adapt and build resilience to the current and future impacts of climate change to reduce the risk of conflict. As part of the <abbr title="The 28th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC">COP28</abbr> outcome on the global goal on adaptation, we adopted the <abbr title="United Arab Emirates">UAE</abbr> Framework for Global Climate Resilience<sup id="fnref:361"><a href="#fn:361" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 361]</a></sup>, which has 7 thematic and 4 process-based targets and agreed to launch a two-year work programme on indicators related to those targets.</p>

<h5 id="northern-ireland-executive-13">3.11.2.2 Northern Ireland Executive</h5>

<p>Northern Ireland’s legal framework for climate adaptation is set out in section 60 of the Climate Change Act 2008. In line with this legal requirement the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (<abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr>) leads on the development of the Northern Ireland Climate Change Adaptation Programme (<abbr title="Northern Ireland Climate Change Adaptation Programme">NICCAP</abbr>) which sets out all departments policies and proposals in response to the latest UK Climate Change Risk assessment (<abbr title="Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA</abbr>).</p>

<p>The second Northern Ireland Climate Change Adaptation Programme (NICCAP2)<sup id="fnref:362"><a href="#fn:362" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 362]</a></sup> was published by <abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr> in September 2019 and covers the 5-year period to September 2024. The NICCAP2 is the cross-departmental response to the risks identified in the second <abbr title="Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA</abbr> which was laid in Parliament in January 2017. Work is continuing to implement the actions contained in NICCAP2.</p>

<p>The UK Climate Change Committees ‘The UK Climate Change Risk Assessment 2017 Evidence Report – summary for Northern Ireland’<sup id="fnref:363"><a href="#fn:363" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 363]</a></sup> which helped to inform the Second Climate Change Risk Assessment (CCRA2) highlighted risk areas which required more action to be taken including those associated with flood risk management.</p>

<p>In 2022, the Department for Infrastructure (<abbr title="Department for Infrastructure, Northern Ireland">DfI</abbr>) commenced construction of the Belfast Tidal Flood Alleviation Scheme<sup id="fnref:364"><a href="#fn:364" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 364]</a></sup> which aims to provide a long-term approach to tidal flood risk management over the tidal reach of the River Lagan in Belfast. The scheme, through the construction of approximately 8.5 kms of flood defences over a 2-year period, will reduce the tidal flood risk to over 1,500 properties identified as being at risk from a 1 in 200-year tidal event once completed. Under climate change projections, causing sea level rise, this number would be predicted to increase to over 3900 properties by 2080. As such the scheme has been designed to take account of the future impact of climate change as set out in the department’s ‘Technical Flood Risk Guidance in Relation to Allowances for Climate Change in Northern Ireland’<sup id="fnref:365"><a href="#fn:365" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 365]</a></sup>. The scheme design has factored the projected sea level risk to 2080 as well as allowing for future adaptability of the structures.</p>

<p>In response to risk to the coastal environment and communities <abbr title="Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, Northern Ireland">DAERA</abbr>, to support the work of the <abbr title="Northern Ireland">NI</abbr> Coastal Forum, commissioned a 3-Dimensional Coastal Survey<sup id="fnref:366"><a href="#fn:366" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 366]</a></sup> of the Northern Ireland coastline in 2020 to acquire high resolution data through the use of topographic <abbr title="Light Detection and Ranging">LiDAR</abbr>, high resolution satellite-derived bathymetry data and pilot bathymetric <abbr title="Light Detection and Ranging">LiDAR</abbr> survey.</p>

<p>In 2021 a complete airborne <abbr title="Light Detection and Ranging">LiDAR</abbr> and orthophotography survey of the Northern Ireland coastline was undertaken. This data provides a precise representation of the morphology of the coastal environment of Northern Ireland and it is intended that the surveys will be repeated to provide a robust dataset to help monitor for coastal change to be used as the evidence base to inform the future coastal policy management decisions.</p>

<h5 id="scottish-government-13">3.11.2.3 Scottish Government</h5>

<p>The Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009 sets the statutory framework for Scotland to adapt to climate change. The legislation requires Scottish ministers to set out a programme of policies and proposals (a plan) for climate change adaptation every f5 years. These plans must address risks identified in the statutory UK Climate Change Risk Assessment (<abbr title="Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA</abbr>), which is also updated every 5 years, based on independent expert advice around the evidence on current and expected future climate impacts.</p>

<p>In 2024, the Scottish Government published its third statutory adaptation plan: Scottish National Adaptation Plan 2024-2029 (SNAP3). SNAP3 describes how we will support Scots to adapt and continue to live well in Scotland’s changing climate. SNAP3 sets out a long term vision and defines Scotland’s priorities for action over the next 5 years via its 23 objectives – all of which were informed by public engagement and consultation.</p>

<p>To deliver on Scotland’s adaptation objectives, the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009 creates a legal duty across the Scottish public sector (including local authorities) to help deliver the national adaptation plan. SNAP3 includes over 200 policies focused on actions that are effective and inclusive, as part of Scotland’s just transition to net zero and climate resilience. Climate change impacts people and places in multiple ways, and communities with less capacity to adapt because of existing inequalities will need support. Scotland’s inclusive and place-based approach to adaptation is supported by the national capacity-building Adaptation Scotland programme.</p>

<p>To monitor success, SNAP3 includes a monitoring framework. This framework includes 38 data-ready indicators to track progress of the 5-year objectives and be reported to the Scottish Parliament annually; and 16 data-ready indicators to track higher level trends in resilience and longer term adaptation outcomes. The existing UK <abbr title="Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA</abbr> process provides a full and independent measure of Scotland’s overall climate resilience every 5 years; and progress of Scotland’s adaptation plans and the actions within them will continue to be independently evaluated twice within every 5-year period by the <abbr title="Climate Change Committee">CCC</abbr>.</p>

<h5 id="welsh-government-13">3.11.2.4 Welsh Government</h5>

<p>The UK Climate Change Act 2008 requires Welsh ministers to lay reports before the Senedd Cymru / Welsh Parliament on the objectives, actions and future priorities of Welsh ministers around the impacts of climate change.<sup id="fnref:367"><a href="#fn:367" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 367]</a></sup> This requirement is further strengthened by the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015, which sets out a number of overarching Well-being Goals that apply to public sector organisations in Wales.<sup id="fnref:368"><a href="#fn:368" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 368]</a></sup> Climate change is integral to all the Well-being Goals and there is specific reference to a ‘resilient Wales’, which includes resilience to the effects of climate change. Climate change is also a key element of the role of the Future Generations Commissioner for Wales and Public Service Boards (<abbr title="Public Service Boards">PSBs</abbr>) created under the Act. <abbr title="Public Service Boards">PSBs</abbr> are required to produce collaborative local well-being assessments, which must take into account the latest UK Climate Change Risk Assessment evidence. The Environment (Wales) Act 2016 also sets out further provisions in relation to climate change, including requirements for the sustainable management of natural resources as well as setting out governance arrangements for coastal and flood management.</p>

<p>Several strategic, interlinked policy developments have taken place in Wales that are helping to establish a robust strategic framework for climate change adaptation. These include publication of an updated National Development Framework, Flood and Coastal Erosion Risk Management Strategy, Water Resource Management Plans, National Peatland Action Programme, Area Statements for the management of natural resources, and development of a new Sustainable Farming Scheme which will include measures for delivering climate adaptation.</p>

<h5 id="jersey-13">3.11.2.5 Jersey</h5>

<p>The Shoreline Management Plan was agreed in January 2020. The plan aims to ensure that coastal defences continue to protect the island over the next 100 years. Sea level rise and rainfall patterns resulting from climate change were modelled to access their impacts on coastal flooding and erosion. The plan considers risks to the community, environment, and economy of Jersey. It considers the coastal defences that are in place around the Island. Policies were developed to manage the risk these present and the appropriate management policy for each unit of the coastline was agreed.</p>

<p>Climate change will increase the threat of Invasive Non-Native Species (<abbr title="Invasive Non-Native Species">INNS</abbr>). The Jersey Biological Security Framework has been set up to ensure international obligations are met and Jersey is protected from negative impacts. Components of this project include a review of current measures, establishing funding to deal with Asian Hornet threat and development of long-term management plans for Japanese Knotweed.</p>

<p>Government is working towards pulling together an overarching Adaptation Plan for the Island in the government plan period 2025-2028. The Bridging Island Plan (2022) has been informed by the Shoreline Management Plan and, as a consequence has a policy regime that seeks to direct growth to areas which are least vulnerable to the long-term impacts of climate change, including flood risk; and to ensure that new development is more resilient to the potential impacts of flooding.</p>

<h5 id="guernsey-13">3.11.2.6 Guernsey</h5>

<p>Guernsey’s Climate Change Policy outlines the importance of adaptation for the island and the need for an overarching adaptation plan. The development of the adaptation plan is due to commence in the near future. Ahead of the development of the island adaptation plan, some decisions are already being taken with the threats of climate change in mind, including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>In 2013, Guernsey’s government agreed an approach to enhancing the coastal defences to adapt to the effect of climate change. With Guernsey being a small island, with around half the island being relatively low lying, the impacts of increased sea levels are potentially significant. The regions most at risk to climate-related flooding were identified and initial options for addressing at risk areas have been provided. Implementation has started on improving the defences.</li>
  <li>From a water security perspective, Guernsey is relatively well supplied from several reservoirs, which were created by historic quarrying. There is an ongoing review of whether to continue to allocate disused quarry sites for water reserves. That review is taking into account the predicted future impacts of climate change.</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="section-3-11-2-7">3.11.2.7 Isle of Man</h5>

<p>The Isle of Man identified 3 priority issues for adaptation actions in 2015: awareness raising; public, animal and plant health; and storms and flooding. In 2020, the Department of Infrastructure formed the Flood Management Division to be responsible for all matters relating to flood risk management. National strategy documents include the National Strategy on Sea Defences, Flood and Coastal Erosion<sup id="fnref:369"><a href="#fn:369" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 369]</a></sup>. An independent review following severe flooding in the east of the Island in 2019 has also informed major works: Independent Review Final Report<sup id="fnref:370"><a href="#fn:370" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 370]</a></sup>. More information on specific projects can be found on the <abbr title="Isle of Man">IOM</abbr> Flood Hub website<sup id="fnref:371"><a href="#fn:371" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 371]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>The Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027<sup id="fnref:372"><a href="#fn:372" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 372]</a></sup> commits to the delivery of an Adaptation Strategy taking account of climate impacts across all areas of society, economy and the natural environment. This will be based on an independent Climate Risks and Opportunities Assessment (currently underway).</p>

<p>In addition, the Isle of Man Climate Change Plan 2022-2027<sup id="fnref:373"><a href="#fn:373" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 373]</a></sup> contains a commitment to add adaptation to the climate change duties for public bodies, the outcomes of which will be that adaptation becomes a statutory duty for all Manx public bodies and annual reporting on adaptation will be required.</p>

<h5 id="gibraltar-13">3.11.2.8 Gibraltar</h5>

<p>Gibraltar conducted its first Climate Change Vulnerability and Risk Assessment<sup id="fnref:374"><a href="#fn:374" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 374]</a></sup> in 2022 and is now working on developing a comprehensive Adaptation Strategy. This will focus on the priorities identified below:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>Energy</strong>: Gibraltar will increase energy diversification by accelerating investment in renewable energy and seek to identify alternative sources of energy imports. Government will also invest in energy efficiency programmes to reduce demand and promote passive approaches to cooling wherever possible.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Water</strong>: Gibraltar will work with its main water provider to ensure redundancy in back-up energy systems for desalination and investigate the use of non-brackish (but non-potable) water sources for street cleaning and irrigation.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Food</strong>: Continue diversification of food import routes and assess the impact of volatility and higher food prices on vulnerable groups.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Public Health</strong>: Assess impact of increases in extreme heat on vulnerable populations and determine ways in which these impacts could be addressed. Increase monitoring of vector borne diseases.</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="how-best-available-science-gender-perspectives-and-indigenous-traditional-and-local-knowledge-are-integrated-into-adaptation">3.12 How best available science, gender perspectives and indigenous, traditional and local knowledge are integrated into adaptation</h3>

<p>The UK Climate Projections (<abbr title="UK Climate Projections">UKCP</abbr>), produced by the Met Office on behalf of government, is a set of tools and data that show how the UK climate may change in the future. <abbr title="UK Climate Projections">UKCP</abbr> underpins the independent assessment to support the UK Climate Change Risk Assessment. The <abbr title="Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA</abbr> then informs the relevant policies and plans set out in the National Adaptation Programme (<abbr title="National Adaptation Programme">NAP</abbr>).</p>

<p>The UK is also committed to promoting equality and inclusion, including women’s empowerment and gender equality. Public authorities must fulfil responsibilities set out under the UK’s Equality Act (2010)<sup id="fnref:375"><a href="#fn:375" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 375]</a></sup> in the exercise of their functions. Through programmes such as the Protection Fund<sup id="fnref:376"><a href="#fn:376" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 376]</a></sup>, the UK supports projects that use traditional knowledge, adaptation, and historical practices to address international heritage at risk from climate change and natural disasters.</p>

<h4 id="global-goal-on-adaptation-gga-thematic-target-7---cultural-heritage-brbr">3.12.1 Global Goal on Adaptation (<abbr title="Global Goal for Adaptation">GGA</abbr>) Thematic target 7 - Cultural heritage <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Climate change impacts our cultural heritage including historic buildings, museums, heritage sites, and archives. Climate change will increase the risk of flooding to more properties and areas. Areas already prone to flooding may experience an increase in frequency and severity. Heritage assets on the coast are particularly vulnerable where severe weather and sea level rise can combine to exacerbate the impacts on already vulnerable coastlines.</p>

<p>Likewise, intangible cultural heritage, such as knowledge, traditions, and folklore will also be affected by climate change. This derives from the risk of communities and groups of people being displaced and the associated impact on their traditions and customs. Resilience to climate change can therefore protect both UK’s tangible and intangible cultural heritage, which in turn has associated benefits, including benefits to the UK’s economy through heritage-related tourism, and wider heritage-related socioeconomic benefits including contributing to wellbeing and enhancing communities’ pride in place.</p>

<p>To address climate risks to communities and the UK’s cultural heritage, the government is:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Investing billions in projects to improve the UK’s climate resilience, including, £2.4 billion until March 2026 to improve flood resilience and better protect communities across England, including from coastal erosion, safeguarding future water supplies.</li>
  <li>Providing support through the £200 million Flood and Coastal Resilience Innovation Programme (<abbr title="Flood and Coastal Resilience Innovation Programme">FCRIP</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:377"><a href="#fn:377" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 377]</a></sup>, including helping 25 local areas between 2021 and 2027 to take forward wider innovative actions that improve their resilience to flooding and coastal erosion.</li>
  <li>Refreshing Shoreline Management Plans<sup id="fnref:378"><a href="#fn:378" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 378]</a></sup> by the end of 2024 so that they remain current and relevant, using the most up to date available information.</li>
  <li>Helping UK households that are at risk of flooding to access affordable insurance through the Flood Re<sup id="fnref:379"><a href="#fn:379" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 379]</a></sup> scheme.</li>
  <li>The Department for Culture, Media and Sport and its Arm Length Bodies are working with partners to complete the actions as laid out in <abbr title="National Adaptation Programme">NAP</abbr> 3 to understand the threats, impacts and adaptation actions needed to respond to the impact of climate change on cultural heritage.</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="adaptation-actions-andor-economic-diversification-plans-leading-to-mitigation-co-benefits">3.13 Adaptation actions and/or economic diversification plans leading to mitigation co-benefits</h3>

<p>Climate adaptation is essential in achieving other climate goals, including all sectors of the UK economy reaching net zero emissions by 2050. Climate change adaptation is considered a priority for the Farming and Countryside Programme, which will support the implementation of adaptation measures through Environmental Land Management Schemes (<abbr title="Environmental Land Management Schemes">ELMs</abbr>), as referenced in section 2.15.1. <abbr title="Environmental Land Management Schemes">ELMs</abbr> will support farmers to deliver ‘public goods’ such as healthy soils, clean water and biodiversity-rich habitats. These in turn support the foundations of sustainable and resilient food production in the long term. We have worked closely with farmers, food producers and environmental experts to develop new and improved agri-environmental schemes for farmers and land managers, which encourage greater participation and incentivise collaboration and landscape scale working. We will continue to work closely with key sectors to learn from and improve these schemes over time.</p>

<h4 id="global-goal-on-adaptation-gga-thematic-target-2--climate-resilient-food-brbr">3.13.1 Global Goal on Adaptation (<abbr title="Global Goal for Adaptation">GGA</abbr>) Thematic target 2 – climate-resilient food <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The government is building the UK’s resilience to overseas climate impacts on food, as well as helping capitalise on opportunities for the UK food industry to export new products and to new markets.</p>

<p>To ensure climate-resilient food and agricultural production and supply, <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> is:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Delivering a range of measures to improve resilience and adaptation to climate change across the food supply and farming sector as set out in <abbr title="National Adaptation Programme">NAP</abbr> 3. These measures include land management practices, such as action to improve soil health and water resources and to increase tree planting on farms, along with greater investment in innovation.</li>
  <li>Developing future publicly funded research and innovation, including investments under the Farming Innovation Programme<sup id="fnref:380"><a href="#fn:380" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 380]</a></sup>, a £270m innovation programme which aims to drive up productivity and enhance environmental sustainability, enabling us to adapt to climate change more effectively, while improving levels of food security.
Continuing to support research on food supply resilience in relation to climate change and adaptation measures through the work of the Met Office’s Climate Service and Hadley Centre, and the Group on Earth Observations Global Agricultural Monitoring Initiative (<abbr title="Group on Earth Observations Global Agricultural Monitoring Initiative">GEOGLAM</abbr>) until 2025.</li>
  <li>Our supply chains are built on supply from diverse sources, domestic production (producing 62% of the food we need, by value) and imports through stable trade routes. Increasing the long-term resilience of global supply chains will help to maintain the current resilience and security of supply.</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="nature-based-solutions-to-climate-change-adaptation">3.14 Nature-based solutions to climate change adaptation</h3>

<p>The UK Prime Minister signed the Leaders’ Pledge for Nature<sup id="fnref:381"><a href="#fn:381" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 381]</a></sup> at the <abbr title="United Nations">UN</abbr> General Assembly in 2020. This Pledge has been endorsed by over 75 countries. The UK works with other countries to take forward this agenda, strengthen resilience in national economies and ecosystems, taking an integrated approach to environmental challenges and scale up nature-based solutions.</p>

<p>The National Highways Natural Flood Management Fund was established in 2020/21 to explore the benefits of using nature-based solutions to reduce flood risk as an alternative to conventional hard engineered solutions on motorway and trunk roads. Through the fund, National Highways identified a pilot project seeking to use nature-based solutions as a tool to reduce surface water flooding on motorways and trunk roads associated with the Little Don and Irwell catchments. The pilot was unique as it was a catchment partnership between National Highways, the local Rivers Trusts, and the owners of the land where the natural flood management measures would be implemented. In addition, the fund used a novel bidding platform and a natural flood management modelling tool to rank bids from landowners with proposed measures during a live auction, supported by the Rivers Trust.</p>

<p>In January 2023, Natural England launched the Green Infrastructure Framework<sup id="fnref:382"><a href="#fn:382" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 382]</a></sup> which provides voluntary principles and standards for England to help local planning authorities and developers to create or improve green and blue infrastructure at a local level, particularly where provision is poorest. The national standards in the Framework provide a consistent way to set out what good green infrastructure provision looks like. The standards are supported by evidence based practical guidance on how to plan and design good green infrastructure, as well as England-wide maps of green infrastructure overlain with socio-economic data. Well-managed green infrastructure has many advantages such as its contribution to biodiversity recovery, cleansing pollutants, absorbing noise and moderating temperatures.</p>

<h4 id="global-goal-on-adaptation-gga-thematic-target-4---ecosystems-brbr">3.14.1 Global Goal on Adaptation (<abbr title="Global Goal for Adaptation">GGA</abbr>) Thematic target 4 - Ecosystems <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Using nature-based solutions will reduce society’s vulnerability to climate risk and contribute to species recovery by providing more high-quality habitat for wildlife.</p>

<p>Measures being taken to support the adaptability and resilience of species, habitats and ecosystems to climate change impacts include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Setting out plans to increase adaptive woodland management in the updated Tree Health Resilience Strategy<sup id="fnref:383"><a href="#fn:383" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 383]</a></sup> and using use climate risk forecasts to inform net zero woodland creation policies, so that tree planting is spatially targeted to account for climate risk. This will be implemented in the post-Nature for Climate Fund forestry policies, including urban tree cover, by 2026.</li>
  <li>Developing ‘adaptation of land management to wildfire risk’ guidance by 2026 and continue to support public and private sector land managers to develop wildfire management plans.</li>
  <li>Restoring natural function and iconic water landscapes, through updated River Basin Management Plans up to 2027, to allow natural processes to re-establish and to produce the highest-quality habitats naturally, contributing to the achievement of Good Ecological Status at 75% of water bodies by 2027. Working with stakeholders to create and restore habitats and ecosystem functions, including those most at risk from climate change. This includes restoring and creating over 500,000 hectares of wildlife-rich habitat outside of Protected Sites by 2042, and restoring 75% of Protected Sites to favourable condition by 2042 – all in a manner that is suitable in the context of climate change</li>
  <li>Supporting stakeholders to use spatial prioritisation for habitat restoration and creation, informed by climate projections, such as projected hazard and land suitability mapping.</li>
  <li>Maintaining an adaptative management approach to reducing anthropogenic non-climate pressures on marine species and habitats. On Marine Protected Areas this includes delivering our new statutory target for 70% of the designated features to be in favourable condition by 2042, with the remainder in recovering condition.</li>
  <li>Restoring and creating new habitats, including through the Restoring Meadows Marsh and Reef initiative, which aims to restore at least 15% of 2 priority habitats – seagrass meadows, saltmarsh and native oyster reefs – by 2043.</li>
  <li>Improving data gathering and monitoring to support the restoration, recovery and creation of marine habitats, where relevant using effective spatial targeting, including through the marine Natural Capital and Ecosystem
Assessment programme (2022-25).</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="stakeholder-involvement-including-subnational-community-level-and-private-sector-plans-priorities-actions-and-programmes">3.15 Stakeholder involvement, including subnational, community-level and private sector plans, priorities, actions and programmes</h3>

<h4 id="public-participation-brbr">3.15.1 Public Participation <br><br>
</h4>

<p><abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr>, working with <abbr title="UK Research and Innovation">UKRI</abbr>’s Sciencewise Programme and Ipsos, ran a Public Dialogue for Climate Adaptation to understand public perceptions and attitudes towards climate adaptation in England. The dialogue explored the public’s perspectives of climate adaptation and how they think the government businesses and civil society will address the challenges of climate change.</p>

<h4 id="private-sector-brbr">3.15.2 Private sector <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Additional investment from the private sector will be required to support adaptation action over the coming decades. Indicative analysis estimates that, across all 61 risks and opportunities identified in the <abbr title="Third Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA3</abbr>, this could be as much as £10 billion per year.</p>

<p>The government has committed to support the flow of private finance into adaptation through the 2023 Green Finance Strategy<sup id="fnref:384"><a href="#fn:384" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 384]</a></sup>, it will:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Work with industry partners to improve the approach to climate resilience assessment and disclosure though developing adaptation metrics and guidance.</li>
  <li>Support private and public collaboration over the next 5 years to address barriers to investment</li>
  <li>Work with the Climate Change Committee to scope research requirements and identify adaptation investment needs and opportunities to inform the <abbr title="Fourth Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA4</abbr> Independent Assessment in 2027.</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="ownership-stakeholder-engagement-alignment-of-adaptation-actions-and-replicability-brbr">3.15.3 Ownership, stakeholder engagement, alignment of adaptation actions and replicability <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK Government has coordinated and facilitated the mainstreaming of adaptation activity through <abbr title="The third National Adaptation Programme">NAP3</abbr>. This has included establishing ownership within government for each of the 61 <abbr title="Third Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA3</abbr> risks and opportunities.</p>

<p><abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> is responsible under the Climate Change Act 2008 for coordinating the UK Government’s action on climate adaptation. <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> works closely with the Cabinet Office Resilience Directorate on the strategic cross-government coordination of climate adaptation, and with the Treasury to build climate resilience into cross-government spending decisions including through the Spending Review.</p>

<h3 id="progress-on-implementation-of-adaptation">3.16 Progress on implementation of adaptation</h3>

<h4 id="steps-taken-to-formulate-implement-publish-and-update-national-and-regional-programmes-strategies-and-measures-policy-frameworks-eg-national-adaptation-plans-and-other-relevant-information-brbr">3.16.1 Steps taken to formulate, implement, publish and update national and regional programmes, strategies and measures, policy frameworks (e.g. national adaptation plans) and other relevant information <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland submitted its first Adaptation Communication to the <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> in December 2020, setting out its plans to prepare for the impacts of climate change in the UK and to support climate change adaptation overseas. The 2020 UK Adaptation Communication covers the following:</p>

<ul>
  <li>National adaptation goals including details of NAP2 and the government’s Third Strategy for the Adaptation Reporting Power (<abbr title="Adaptation Reporting Power">ARP</abbr>).</li>
  <li>Examples of implementation of adaptation actions and implementation progress.</li>
  <li>The importance of nature-based solutions, the Adaptation Communication stresses that adaptation actions will take place across a wide range of terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems, and there is an emphasis on projects that provide multiple benefits simultaneously.</li>
</ul>

<p>An update to the UK’s Adaptation Communication in October 2021 also offered updates on progress, including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>The Climate Adaptation Summit in January 2021; under the UK <abbr title="The Group of 7">G7</abbr> Presidency, the UK launched the ‘Adaptation Action Coalition (<abbr title="Adaptation Action Coalition">AAC</abbr>)’<sup id="fnref:385"><a href="#fn:385" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 385]</a></sup> with the aim of accelerating global action on adaptation.</li>
  <li>The Foreign and Development ministers’ welcoming of the Principles for Locally Led Adaptation; the principles aim to shift the dynamic so that adaptation interventions are informed by local priorities, knowledge, and expertise.</li>
  <li>In July 2023, <abbr title="The third National Adaptation Programme">NAP3</abbr> was published by the UK Government, setting out a vision for a country that effectively plans for, and is fully adapted to, the changing climate.</li>
</ul>

<p><abbr title="The third National Adaptation Programme">NAP3</abbr> contains actions to address the risks of climate change to the natural environment, infrastructure, people and the built environment, business and industry, and international risks to the UK, as well as a chapter outlining work with local government on climate change adaptation. The <abbr title="National Adaptation Programme">NAP</abbr> sets out policies and measures to be implemented at several levels and identifies the actors responsible for their implementation. <abbr title="The third National Adaptation Programme">NAP3</abbr> is underpinned by a monitoring tool to track progress on adaptation actions, on a periodic basis.</p>

<h4 id="implementation-of-adaptation-actions-identified-in-current-and-past-adaptation-communications-including-efforts-towards-meeting-adaptation-needs-as-appropriate-brbr">3.16.2 Implementation of adaptation actions identified in current and past adaptation communications, including efforts towards meeting adaptation needs, as appropriate <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Since publication of the 2020 Adaptation Communication, <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> has continued to progress domestic action on adaptation.</p>

<p>As identified in our adaptation communications, the following actions have been Implemented:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Updating the government’s Green Book Supplementary Guidance on Accounting for the Effects of Climate Change to encourage climate change risks to be embedded in policy and programme decisions, drawing on climate evidence and assessments.</li>
  <li>Establishing new government-wide adaptation governance to provide senior-level oversight and strategic direction on the delivery of statutory duties on adaptation and resilience policy across the government.</li>
  <li>Under the UK <abbr title="The Group of 7">G7</abbr> Presidency, the Foreign and Development ministers welcomed the Principles for Locally Led Adaptation, following the UK’s endorsement of the Principles at the Climate Adaptation Summit in January 2021. The Principles for Locally Led Adaptation aim to shift the dynamic so that adaptation interventions are developed and implemented in a way that is equitable and informed by local priorities, knowledge and expertise.</li>
  <li>Investing in international disaster risk reduction: The UK contributed of £120 million to regional risk pools during the <abbr title="The Group of 7">G7</abbr> Leaders’ Summit, to support an improved response to extreme weather and climate-linked disasters.</li>
  <li>Making businesses more resilient, including implementing economy-wide, climate-related financial disclosures for businesses and investments products, which will support investment decisions to be aligned with our transition to a lower-carbon, climate resilient economy, globally.</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="how-effective-are-implemented-adaptation-measures">3.17 How effective are implemented adaptation measures</h3>

<h4 id="implementation-brbr">3.17.1 Implementation <br><br>
</h4>

<p>As set out in the UK Climate Change Act 2008, the Climate Change Committee has a duty to assess the progress in implementing the <abbr title="National Adaptation Programme">NAP</abbr>, reporting to Parliament every 2 years. The government is working closely with the Climate Change Committee to identify how best to monitor adaptation activity and assign sectoral metrics and indicators for exposure and vulnerability to risk.</p>

<p>England and devolved governments fully recognise the scale of the challenge of adapting to climate change, as set out in the <abbr title="Third Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA3</abbr> and its underlying reports.</p>

<h4 id="global-goal-on-adaptation-gga-process-target-3--implementation-brbr">3.17.2 Global Goal on Adaptation (<abbr title="Global Goal for Adaptation">GGA</abbr>) process target 3 – Implementation <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Examples of recent achievements include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> has set up new governance and an approach to actively manage the <abbr title="National Adaptation Programme">NAP</abbr> programme through regular commissions to monitor delivery against <abbr title="The third National Adaptation Programme">NAP3</abbr> commitments. Risk owning departments are responsible for developing adaptation plans and policies and evaluating the effectiveness of these throughout the <abbr title="The third National Adaptation Programme">NAP3</abbr> implementation period (2023 to 2028).</li>
  <li>Passing the landmark Environment Act 2021, which enshrines the 25 Year Environment Plan in law and includes an historic legally binding target for species abundance for 2030.</li>
  <li>Working with over 120 businesses and public bodies to support them to report on activities to strengthen their resilience to climate change. Adaptation reporting focuses on a range of critical sectors, such as rail, road, energy, water, heritage, the natural environment, and finance, as well as a pilot of reporting by local authorities.</li>
  <li>Ensuring homes are fit for the future. This includes introducing a new requirement through the Building Regulations<sup id="fnref:386"><a href="#fn:386" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 386]</a></sup> to ensure that new residential buildings are built for a warmer climate. The new requirement includes prioritisation of passive measures to address overheating, including solar gains.</li>
  <li>The UK has implemented mandatory reporting in line with recommendations of the Taskforce on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (<abbr title="Taskforce on Climate-related Financial Disclosures">TCFD</abbr>) across the economy as the core basis of Sustainability Disclosure Requirements (<abbr title="Sustainability Disclosure Requirements">SDR</abbr>). <abbr title="Taskforce on Climate-related Financial Disclosures">TCFD</abbr>-aligned reporting requires disclosure of climate related financial risk information structured around 4 thematic areas: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets.</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="coordination-activities-and-changes-in-regulations-policies-and-planning-brbr">3.17.3 Coordination activities and changes in regulations, policies and planning <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Over the 5-year <abbr title="The third National Adaptation Programme">NAP3</abbr> programme, UK Government has committed to drive coordinated action on climate adaptation, including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>As part of the ‘UK Government Resilience Framework’<sup id="fnref:387"><a href="#fn:387" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 387]</a></sup> outlined in section 1.4, the UK Government will deliver on a new strategic approach to resilience.</li>
  <li>Work to strengthen governance arrangements overseeing the implementation of <abbr title="The third National Adaptation Programme">NAP3</abbr> which better take infrastructure sector interdependencies into account, ensuring these arrangements work alongside existing governance and collaboration forums on resilience.</li>
  <li>Work with external stakeholders and member organisations to strengthen the role of the Infrastructure Operators Adaptation Forum in driving forward best practice on managing sector interdependencies including the risk of cascading failures.</li>
  <li>The government and its agencies will provide the governance structures, guidance, and plans to coordinate and align actions for nature recovery. It will explore options to establish appropriate governance arrangements so that the UK Environment Act 2021 biodiversity targets are delivered in a way that considers a changing climate</li>
  <li>‘Local Nature Recovery Strategies’<sup id="fnref:388"><a href="#fn:388" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 388]</a></sup> (<abbr title="Local Nature Recovery Strategies">LNRS</abbr>) are measures set out in the Environment Act (2021) and will support public, private and voluntary sector organisations to work together on identifying collective priorities for restoring nature and improving climate resilience</li>
  <li>The government and external partners will integrate water management by delivering catchment action plans backed up with new funding to improve all water bodies in England. This will target actions where they will deliver the greatest impact for water quality, drought and flood management, and nature recovery.</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="monitoring-and-evaluation-of-adaptation-actions-and-processes">3.18 Monitoring and evaluation of adaptation actions and processes</h3>

<h4 id="achievements-impacts-resilience-review-effectiveness-and-results-brbr">3.18.1 Achievements, impacts, resilience, review, effectiveness and results <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Effective monitoring and evaluation (<abbr title="Monitoring and Evaluation">M&amp;E</abbr>) is important for informing future decision making on adaptation. The Climate Change Committee’s Technical Report for the <abbr title="Third Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA3</abbr> Independent Assessment outlines that for many of the risks and opportunities, adaptation actions can often take a long time to take effect. In particular, the complexity of how systems respond to adaptation measures while also responding to other environmental and socio-economic pressures is not easily untangled.</p>

<p><abbr title="Monitoring and Evaluation">M&amp;E</abbr> can help assess the effectiveness of actions taken, inform resource allocation decisions and reassess goals based on their feasibility or relative importance. When developing policy responses for climate risks, policy officials will also identify accompanying process and outcome indicators. Such indicators will help us assess whether: a) actions are being delivered b) actions are efficient 8 c) progress is being made on the declared outcomes.</p>

<p>At present, gaps exist in our ability to monitor our adaptation efforts. This is due to the complexity of adaptation and the associated challenges of identifying and developing appropriate indicators. As outlined in the <abbr title="Monitoring and Evaluation">M&amp;E</abbr> annex<sup id="fnref:389"><a href="#fn:389" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 389]</a></sup> to <abbr title="The third National Adaptation Programme">NAP3</abbr>, some of the common challenges included:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Proving cause and effect for adaptation actions in a complex system with multiple drivers of change.</li>
  <li>Tracking progress to a moving target in a system with interacting and cascading climate and socioeconomic risks.</li>
  <li>The mismatch between short evaluation cycles and the time needed to effect change, especially for the natural environment.</li>
  <li>Access to high quality, affordable and trustworthy data.</li>
</ul>

<p>These challenges are consistent with the findings of the Climate Change Committee in its 2021 progress report to Parliament. Adaptation process indicators (such as the number of plans adopted, or buildings retrofitted) are relatively simple to measure. Indicators that measure adaptation outcomes (such as climate-sensitive sectors of the economy being better adapted) are rarer as they are harder to measure. Work is ongoing to identify a suite of existing and potential indicators to evaluate the success of the <abbr title="The third National Adaptation Programme">NAP3</abbr> programme. In many cases, indicators will be researched or developed as part of an action.</p>

<p>As committed to in <abbr title="The third National Adaptation Programme">NAP3</abbr>, the UK Government is developing an Monitoring Evaluation and Learning framework, expected in 2025.</p>

<h4 id="global-goal-on-adaptation-gga-process-target-4---monitoring-evaluation-and-learning-mel-brbr">3.18.2 Global Goal on Adaptation (<abbr title="Global Goal for Adaptation">GGA</abbr>) process target 4 - Monitoring, evaluation and learning (<abbr title="Monitoring, evaluation and learning">MEL</abbr>) <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Adapting to a changing climate is a dynamic problem involving complex environmental and socioeconomic systems, such as our food or energy systems.</p>

<p>Due to the complexity of this challenge, <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> is using a theory of change approach applying the logic of interventions from action to impact to developing adaptation policy. As described in the ‘Magenta Book’,<sup id="fnref:390"><a href="#fn:390" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 390]</a></sup> which sets out guidance on evaluation in government, a theory of change captures the reasoning behind how an intervention is expected to work. The main steps involved in achieving the desired outcomes will be explicitly outlined (see <strong>Figure 22</strong>). Equally importantly, policymakers will clearly define any assumptions made, the quality and strength of the evidence supporting those assumptions, and wider contextual factors. Monitoring, evaluation and learning are fundamental components of this approach and will be used to challenge the assumptions made and support continuous improvement.</p>

<p>Please see below schematic for the recommended process for developing plans to adapt to climate change. Initially, the impacts of climate change and the adaptation options available will be considered. The logical steps of the theory of change approach will then be followed to design an intervention. First, the impact desired will be clearly stated and then the necessary outcomes, outputs, activities and resources required to achieve it. Continuous feedback loops to monitor, evaluate, report and finally revise plans are needed throughout each stage.</p>

<p id="figure-22"><strong>Figure 22: Schematic of the recommended process for developing plans to adapt to climate change through a theory of change approach</strong></p>

<figure class="image embedded"><div class="img"><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67851961c6428e01318816f3/uk-biennial-2024-figure-22.svg" alt=""></div></figure>

<hr>

<p><strong>Description of figure 22</strong>:</p>

<p>Questions to consider:</p>

<ul>
  <li>What climate change impacts are expected?</li>
  <li>Will these changes threaten societal or organisational goals?</li>
  <li>What options are available to 1) reduce exposure and vulnerability to climate hazards or 2) grasp opportunities</li>
</ul>

<p>Theory of Change Process for the Adaptation Intervention:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>Impact</strong> (What it means):
    <ul>
      <li>Broader and Longer Term Effects</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>
<strong>Outcomes</strong> (What is achieved):
    <ul>
      <li>Results of the intervention</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>
<strong>Outputs</strong> (What is delivered):
    <ul>
      <li>Legislation</li>
      <li>Change in Assets or Capability</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>
<strong>Activities</strong> (What we do):
    <ul>
      <li>Analysis</li>
      <li>Engagement</li>
      <li>Programmes</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>
<strong>Input</strong> (Resources needed):
    <ul>
      <li>Investment</li>
      <li>Hours/Week</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
