</ul>

<p>(There are continuous feedback loops at each stage: Monitor, Evaluate, Report, Revise plans).</p>

<p>For each step of the theory of change define:</p>

<ul>
  <li>What assumptions have been made?</li>
  <li>What is the strength of the evidence base and how can it be improved?</li>
  <li>What wider contextual factors exist?</li>
</ul>

<hr>

<p>Monitoring, evaluation and learning fosters a culture of sharing and learning from experiences and bringing risk owning teams from across departments together into outcome-based groupings, to more easily identify synergies and interdependencies and ensure we are working together efficiently.</p>

<h4 id="approaches-and-systems-used-and-their-outputs-brbr">3.18.3 Approaches and systems used, and their outputs <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Throughout the <abbr title="The third National Adaptation Programme">NAP3</abbr> period, <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> will continue to support risk owning departments across UK Government to further develop and implement their adaptation plans.</p>

<p>The Climate Change Committee’s latest progress report in 2023 introduced a new framework which assesses 13 sectors structured around social outcomes or systems impacted by climate change, known as ‘monitoring maps’. These most notably increase the focus on tangible changes in the economy, society and the environment by identifying a set of outcomes and actions necessary to deliver climate resilience within each sector (Climate Change Committee, 2023). It also expands on the enabling conditions required to achieve the outcomes, and the role of public policy in bringing them about.</p>

<p>The Climate Change Committee (<abbr title="Climate Change Committee">CCC</abbr>) is looking to share learnings from the UK experience and to learn from others<sup id="fnref:391"><a href="#fn:391" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 391]</a></sup> about theirs. The <abbr title="Climate Change Committee">CCC</abbr> developed a set of briefings detailing the approaches, reflections and lessons learned by the <abbr title="Climate Change Committee">CCC</abbr> in 12 years of advising the UK on emissions reductions and adapting<sup id="fnref:392"><a href="#fn:392" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 392]</a></sup> to climate change.</p>

<p>England will continue to champion action to advance adaptation alongside mitigation internationally, helping to build global resilience, drive action to protect those who are most vulnerable to climate change, and learn from others as per the CCCs advice. ‘The 2030 Strategic Framework for International Climate and Nature Action<sup id="fnref:393"><a href="#fn:393" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 393]</a></sup>’ was the first strategy to integrate our approach to climate mitigation, adaptation, and other environmental policies, to maximise co-benefits and minimise trade-offs, seeking to advance global adaptation and resilience as an international priority, including through co-beneficial mitigation and nature actions.</p>

<h4 id="how-support-programmes-meet-specific-vulnerabilities-and-adaptation-needs-brbr">3.18.4 How support programmes meet specific vulnerabilities and adaptation needs <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Climate risks to the UK resulting from high temperatures, changes to air quality, and flooding can impact people’s health and wellbeing as well as on the delivery of health and social care services. These risks also impact on food safety, water quality and water supplies, and an increased likelihood of vector-borne disease in the UK. Such risks are more likely to negatively impact on some members of the population, including people with disabilities and older people. Of the UK population, 38% of disabled people are 65 and older (source: UK Disability Survey research report, June 2021). In addition, overseas climate change impacts can increase the presence of diseases within the UK.</p>

<h3 id="how-adaptation-actions-influence-other-development-goals">3.19 How adaptation actions influence other development goals</h3>

<p>Sustainable development has been considered and integrated into actions across all critical sectors identified in <abbr title="Third Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA3</abbr>, including education, health, the natural environment, and infrastructure. In addition to the actions, we are taking domestically, sustainable development is at the core of the UK’s Official Development Assistance, enabling adaptation and resilience overseas. This not only enhances the resilience of the UK to climate risk but helps support the sustainable development needs of other countries.</p>

<p>The UK’s International Climate Finance considers gender equality, disability inclusion and other sustainable development goals, with key performance indicators evaluating the success of UK International Climate Finance, including measurements of sustainable development objectives. More on this in chapter 4.</p>

<p>Adaptation and resilience of people and our natural environment contributes to many of the Sustainable Development Goals (<abbr title="Sustainable Development Goals">SDGs</abbr>). For marine ecosystems, <abbr title="Sustainable Development Goal 13 to take urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts">SDG13</abbr> and <abbr title="Sustainable Development Goal 14 to conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources for sustainable development">SDG14</abbr> on Climate Action and Life Below Water are the most relevant for ocean-climate policy, and adaptation actions contribute to the UK’s progress against the targets. The UK’s Voluntary National Review of Progress against the <abbr title="Sustainable Development Goals">SDGs</abbr><sup id="fnref:394"><a href="#fn:394" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 394]</a></sup> highlights strong progress against <abbr title="Sustainable Development Goal 14 to conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources for sustainable development">SDG14</abbr> targets. The North East Atlantic Ocean Acidification Hub has been established in the UK. The Hub will act as the European regional centre for conducting monitoring and research into ocean acidification, primarily within the Northeast Atlantic region, including the submission of data to the <abbr title="United Nations">UN</abbr> for <abbr title="Sustainable Development Goal">SDG</abbr> 14.3 on ocean acidity.</p>

<h4 id="global-goal-on-adaptation-gga-thematic-target-3--health-brbr">3.19.1 Global Goal on Adaptation (<abbr title="Global Goal for Adaptation">GGA</abbr>) Thematic target 3 – Health <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Since 2022, the climate-heath nexus has gained increasing attention, as countries recognise the importance of strengthening comprehensive policies to prevent the health impacts of climate change, building resilient and sustainable health systems, improving their ability to anticipate and implement adaptation interventions against climate-sensitive disease and health risks, bolstering climate-health information services, surveillance, early warning and response systems and a climate-ready health workforce. Subsequently, at <abbr title="The 28th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC">COP28</abbr> the UK announced the UK’s flagship Climate Resilient and Sustainable Health Systems Programme.</p>

<p>The government set out its plans to support vulnerable communities through:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<abbr title="Flood and Coastal Erosion Risk Management">FCERM</abbr> research and development projects<sup id="fnref:395"><a href="#fn:395" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 395]</a></sup>, providing a critical assessment of the links between flooding and social vulnerability, social deprivation and inequalities and in the UK.</li>
  <li>Implementing the Approved document O<sup id="fnref:396"><a href="#fn:396" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 396]</a></sup> of the Building Regulations, in June 2022, to limit excess heat and solar gains across all new residential buildings. It will use recommendations from the Housing Health and Safety Rating System review to support the effective enforcement of quality and safety standards in all tenures of residential accommodation, including standards related to excess heat by 2030.</li>
  <li>Monitoring the occurrence of vector-borne diseases (<abbr title="Vector-borne diseases">VBDs</abbr>); with the assistance of its specialised agencies, it will enhance surveillance and monitoring of overseas health risks as well as update the risk assessments of the Human Animal Infections Risk Surveillance (<abbr title="Human Animal Infections Risk Surveillance">HAIRS</abbr>) group, to provide a cross-government risk assessment defining the risk of <abbr title="Vector-borne diseases">VBDs</abbr> in the UK.</li>
  <li>Building the capacity and capability of those working in the sector and those travelling overseas to recognise cases of suspected <abbr title="Vector-borne diseases">VBDs</abbr> to increase detection of cases, limit spread and improve patient outcomes.</li>
  <li>In collaboration with its specialised agencies, making access to the Air Quality and Health Information and government Web Services available to the public and vulnerable groups.</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="cooperation-good-practices-experience-and-lessons-learned">3.20 Cooperation, good practices, experience and lessons learned</h3>

<h4 id="efforts-to-share-information-good-practices-experience-and-lessons-learned-including-as-they-relate-to-brbr">3.20.1 Efforts to share information, good practices, experience and lessons learned, including as they relate to: <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="science-planning-and-policies-relevant-to-adaptation">3.20.1.1 Science, planning and policies relevant to adaptation</h5>

<p><abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> is supporting teams to learn from each other by facilitating communities of practice, working groups and expert panels. These range across areas such as specific sector-based risks, monitoring and evaluation and economic appraisal.</p>

<p>As part of the 2024-27 Met Office Hadley Centre Climate Programme (<abbr title="Met Office Hadley Centre Climate Programme">MOHCCP</abbr>), government is working with the Met Office, academic partners and users of <abbr title="UK Climate Projections">UKCP</abbr> to develop further climate science capability to support adaptation.</p>

<p>A Climate Adaptation Research and Innovation Board (<abbr title="Climate Adaptation Research and Innovation Board">CARIB</abbr>) has been convened to ensure that adaptation research and innovation efforts are targeted to support <abbr title="The third National Adaptation Programme">NAP3</abbr> delivery over the plan period (2023-28). <abbr title="Climate Adaptation Research and Innovation Board">CARIB</abbr> brings together senior representatives from government departments, non-departmental public bodies and non-ministerial departments with major climate adaptation research and innovation (<abbr title="Research and innovation">R&amp;I</abbr>) budgets or responsibilities under <abbr title="The third National Adaptation Programme">NAP3</abbr>. This will be achieved through the development of a Climate Adaptation Research and Innovation Framework (<abbr title="Climate Adaptation Research and Innovation Framework">CARIF</abbr>) to provide strategic direction and influence spending decisions on climate adaptation across departments and UK Research and Innovation (<abbr title="UK Research and Innovation">UKRI</abbr>) programmes.</p>

<h5 id="integration-of-adaptation-actions-into-planning-at-different-levels">3.20.1.2 Integration of adaptation actions into planning at different levels</h5>

<p>The government is improving its understanding of the distributional impacts of climate change and adaptation action through research programmes for the Independent Assessment of the fourth Climate Change Risk Assessment (<abbr title="Fourth Climate Change Risk Assessment">CCRA4</abbr>) and the <abbr title="UK Research and Innovation">UKRI</abbr>-<abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> funded ‘Maximising UK Adaptation to Climate Change’<sup id="fnref:397"><a href="#fn:397" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 397]</a></sup> (<abbr title="Maximising UK Adaptation to Climate Change">MACC</abbr>) Programme.</p>

<h3 id="helping-developing-countries-to-identify-effective-adaptation-practices-needs-priorities-and-challenges-and-gaps-in-a-way-that-is-consistent-with-encouraging-good-practices">3.21 Helping developing countries to identify effective adaptation practices, needs, priorities, and challenges and gaps in a way that is consistent with encouraging good practices</h3>

<p>Since 2011, the UK has supported over 110 million people adapt to the effects of climate change. To achieve this, the UK funds a range of bilateral, regional multilateral programmes to increase adaptation action in priority sectors and assist countries with their national adaptation plans and processes.</p>

<p>This includes helping improve accessible early warning systems and preparations as well as developing the capacity to act on the risks identified and strengthening the delivery mechanisms that enable effective early action to reach those who need it most. The UK is the sole funder of the Risk-informed Early Action Partnership (<abbr title="Risk-informed Early Action Partnership">REAP</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:398"><a href="#fn:398" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 398]</a></sup>, an initiative launched in 2019 that brings together relevant actors from the development, humanitarian and climate communities on the Early Warning Early Action (<abbr title="Early Warning Early Action">EWEA</abbr>) agenda. <abbr title="Risk-informed Early Action Partnership">REAP</abbr> provides international analysis, evidence, learning, coordination, and debate, to integrate and expand a systemic shift towards acting earlier to reduce the impacts of disasters, with the target of making 1 billion people safer from disasters by 2025.</p>

<p>The UK recognises that <abbr title="Small Island Developing States">SIDS</abbr> are on the frontline of climate change and are uniquely climate and economically vulnerable. The UK’s Small Island Developing State Capacity and Resilience (<abbr title="Small Island Developing States Capacity and Resilience Programme">SIDAR</abbr>) programme, and the Sustainable Blue Economies programme, both launched in 2022, will support access to climate finance and the development of prosperous ocean-based economies.</p>

<p>The UK supports Least Developed Countries (<abbr title="Least Developed Countries">LDCs</abbr>) by:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chairing the Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems Initiative (<abbr title="Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems Initiative">CREWS</abbr>),<sup id="fnref:399"><a href="#fn:399" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 399]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>Supporting the Least Developed Countries Initiative for Effective Adaptation and Resilience (<abbr title="Least Developed Countries Initiative for Effective Adaptation and Resilience">LIFE-AR</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:400"><a href="#fn:400" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 400]</a></sup> programme since 2020.</li>
</ul>

<p>The government is also assisting in building resilience locally, the Weather and Climate Information Services (<abbr title="Weather and Climate Information Services">WISER</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:401"><a href="#fn:401" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 401]</a></sup> programme enables communities and governments to better anticipate and prepare for climate shocks and stresses, reducing their impact and protecting lives, homes and livelihoods. To date, <abbr title="Weather and Climate Information Services">WISER</abbr> has helped to avoid over £200 million worth of losses in East Africa through application of climate information and helped to improve the resilience of over 8 million people who use <abbr title="Weather and Climate Information Services">WISER</abbr> services. Additionally, <abbr title="Weather and Climate Information Services">WISER</abbr> in the Middle East and North Africa aims to deliver transformation in the generation and use of co-produced weather and climate services to support decision making at local, national, and regional levels.</p>

<h4 id="global-goal-on-adaptation-gga-thematic-target-6---livelihoods-brbr">3.21.1 Global Goal on Adaptation (<abbr title="Global Goal for Adaptation">GGA</abbr>) Thematic target 6 - Livelihoods <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK has been a leading supporter and contributor to several climate finance programmes internationally that have embedded gender inclusion within their design and combine both gender mainstreaming and gender focussed programming. For example:</p>

<p>The UK has been the leading supporter to date of the United Nations Development Programme (<abbr title="United Nations Development Programme">UNDP</abbr>)’s Climate Finance Network (<abbr title="Climate Finance Network">CFN</abbr>), which has a dedicated workstream on Gender and Social Inclusion and Climate Change Finance and supports the network’s countries in integrating gender and social inclusion into climate change planning and budgeting processes.</p>

<p>The UK has also worked to build women’s and girl’s climate resilience through investment in more inclusive core and shock-responsive social protection. Through the Better Assistance in Crisis (<abbr title="Better Assistance in Crisis">BASIC</abbr>) and Gender-responsive Social Protection (<abbr title="Gender-responsive social protection">GSP</abbr>) programmes we are providing technical assistance and expertise to support partners on how to ensure social protection systems and interventions can respond to climate risks and the differential needs of women and girls, in the <abbr title="Coronavirus">COVID-19</abbr> response and recovery.</p>

<h3 id="strengthening-scientific-research-and-knowledge-related-to-i-climate-including-research-and-systematic-observation-and-early-warning-systems-to-inform-climate-services-and-decision-making-ii-vulnerability-and-adaptation-iii-monitoring-and-evaluation">3.22 Strengthening scientific research and knowledge related to: (i) Climate, including research and systematic observation and early warning systems, to inform climate services and decision-making; (ii) Vulnerability and adaptation; (iii) Monitoring and evaluation</h3>

<p>Research and information sharing are integral to building capability. Increased awareness of climate risks will improve risk management plans and enable the public, businesses and other organisations to make more informed decisions. This is why the government is supporting and funding several innovative research programmes.</p>

<p>Under the UK’s <abbr title="The 26th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC">COP26</abbr> Presidency, we launched the Adaptation Research Alliance (<abbr title="Adaptation Research Alliance">ARA</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:402"><a href="#fn:402" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 402]</a></sup>, a global coalition of over 180 organisations across the spectrum – from research to action – from 60 economies. The <abbr title="Adaptation Research Alliance">ARA</abbr> supports action-oriented research that informs adaptation solutions and reduces risks from climate change at the scale and urgency demanded by the science. The Climate Adaptation and Resilience (<abbr title="Climate Adaptation and Resilience">CLARE</abbr>) programme<sup id="fnref:403"><a href="#fn:403" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 403]</a></sup> is a UK-Canada framework research programme on climate adaptation and resilience, aiming to enable socially inclusive and sustainable action to build resilience to climate change and natural hazards in Africa and Asia-Pacific. Bridging critical gaps between science and action, <abbr title="Climate Adaptation and Resilience">CLARE</abbr> develops new tools and supports partner governments, communities, and the private sector to use evidence and innovation to drive effective solutions to the climate challenge, whilst building the capacity of both those carrying out the research and those using the resulting evidence.</p>

<h4 id="policy-innovation-and-pilot-projects-brbr">3.22.1 Policy innovation and pilot projects <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The government has committed to support world-leading science and evidence, such as the UK Climate Projections and jointly fund a £15 million UK Research and Innovation/<abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> programme to support the research and innovation needed to deliver adaptation action.</p>

<p>As part of UK Research and Innovation’s ‘building a secure and resilient world’ and ‘building a green future’ strategic themes, the Maximising UK Adaptation to Climate Change (<abbr title="Maximising UK Adaptation to Climate Change">MACC</abbr>) programme will identify the skills, standards and data provision needed to increase adaptation capability across government and wider society.</p>

<p>The <abbr title="Maximising UK Adaptation to Climate Change">MACC</abbr> programme will build capacity, knowledge, and skills that will offer practical and scalable solutions to meet the UK’s challenges in the face of a changing climate and put the UK at the forefront of climate adaptation strategies at both the local and national level. The programme will also fund transdisciplinary research to collaborate and facilitate two-way transfer of knowledge between research, policy and other end users to drive transformation, helping the UK to adapt to climate change, focusing on 4 themes:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>theme 1</strong>: societies’ exposure and vulnerability to extreme climate hazards</li>
  <li>
<strong>theme 2</strong>: adaptation solutions</li>
  <li>
<strong>theme 3</strong>: future resilience and decision making</li>
  <li>
<strong>theme 4</strong>: enablers of adaptation</li>
</ul>

<p>UK Government investment in climate services helps to provide information for the public and businesses. Evidence from a range of studies suggests that weather and climate services, including early warning systems, can lead to economic benefit-cost ratios of around 9:1, arising from the information used to improve decision making.<sup id="fnref:404"><a href="#fn:404" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 404]</a></sup> Supported by this investment, the Met Office Hadley Centre delivers world-leading evidence on climate variability to better inform decision-making, including the UK Climate Projections. As part of the 2024-27 Met Office Hadley Centre Climate Programme (<abbr title="Met Office Hadley Centre Climate Programme">MOHCCP</abbr>), the UK Government is working with the Met Office, academic partners and users of <abbr title="UK Climate Projections">UKCP</abbr> to develop further climate science capability to support adaptation.</p>

<p>The UK is also the current chair and board member of the Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems Initiative (<abbr title="Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems Initiative">CREWS</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:405"><a href="#fn:405" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 405]</a></sup>, a specialised financing mechanism launched in 2015 that responds to the urgent need to address climate related risks and their impacts on vulnerable communities – specifically <abbr title="Least Developed Countries">LDCs</abbr> and <abbr title="Small Island Developing States">SIDS</abbr>, whilst empowering the leadership of women.</p>

<h2 id="chapter-4">Chapter 4: Information on financial, technology development and transfer and capacity-building support provided and mobilised</h2>

<h3 id="information-on-national-circumstances">4.1 Information on national circumstances</h3>

<h4 id="description-of-the-systems-used-to-track-and-report-on-support-provided-and-mobilised-brbr">4.1.1 Description of the systems used to track and report on support provided and mobilised <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK has committed to spend £11.6 billion of International Climate Finance (<abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr>) between financial years 2021/22 to 2025/26. This is new and additional climate finance support from the UK’s previous <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> commitment of £5.8 billion between 2016/17 and 2020/21. The UK spent £5.98 billion within this previous commitment period.</p>

<p>The UK aims to achieve a balance between mitigation and adaptation support through its £11.6 billion <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> commitment. We have made the following further key sub-commitments:</p>

<ul>
  <li>£1.5bn adaptation spend in 2025;</li>
  <li>At least £3bn on development solutions that protect and restore nature and biodiversity, including £1.5bn on forests, and</li>
  <li>Up to £1bn on clean energy research and demonstration programmes through the Ayrton Fund<sup id="fnref:406"><a href="#fn:406" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 406]</a></sup>.</li>
</ul>

<p>UK <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> targets strong outcomes for climate mitigation and adaptation, nature and biodiversity. We use our <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> to reduce poverty through supporting resilience and accelerating the global shift to net zero by giving developing countries access to more, better and faster finance and helping to mobilise finance from the private sector to meet climate and nature goals.</p>

<p>The UK balances our <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> spend between support for mitigation and adaptation. We invest in mitigation where there are opportunities for green-growth, where emissions are growing rapidly and in nature-rich countries that play a role as major carbon sinks to reduce future climate impacts.</p>

<p>Our <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> programmes support the most vulnerable, helping build the capacity of people and communities to adapt and become more resilient to the impacts of climate change, supporting transformation of systems, and helping countries and communities deal with impacts when they occur. There is more detail about our adaptation support for developing countries in chapter 3.</p>

<p>UK <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> supports accelerating the clean energy transition in both energy-producing and energy-consuming sectors to help countries provide access to affordable, reliable, and clean energy for all. This transition will reduce or avoid high emissions pathways, making use of innovation, different technologies, and carbon pricing and addressing social and gender barriers to clean energy access.</p>

<p>In line with the recommendations from the Dasgupta Review<sup id="fnref:407"><a href="#fn:407" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 407]</a></sup> and the commitments set out in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework<sup id="fnref:408"><a href="#fn:408" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 408]</a></sup>, we use <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> to protect, sustainably manage and restore nature, reviving natural and degraded terrestrial and marine ecosystems. We help the transition to nature positive economies by supporting governments, central banks, businesses, and financial institutions to integrate the value of nature into their decision-making.</p>

<p><abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> is part of the UK’s Official Development Assistance (<abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr>) budget. The UK met our commitment to ensure that all new bilateral UK aligned with the Paris Agreement in 2023. In addition to <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> from the <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> budget, from 2021 onwards the UK has also reported climate eligible outflows from British International Investments (<abbr title="British International Investment">BII</abbr>). The UK also puts <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> into <abbr title="British International Investment">BII</abbr>; to avoid double counting, <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> inflow amounts are deducted from climate eligible outflows for reporting.</p>

<p>The UK’s <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> is spent through these government departments: the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (<abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr>), the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (<abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr>), the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (<abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr>), and the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (<abbr title="Department for Science, Innovation and Technology">DSIT</abbr>). <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> is allocated to these departments via a wider process called a Spending Review, where budgets are allocated to departments over a set period. The most recent Spending Review completed at end of October 2024 allocated funding for UK financial years 2024/25 to 2025/26 (i.e. April 2025 to March 2026). For UK <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr>, this means budgets have been allocated to cover the full £11.6bn commitment.</p>

<p>Departments are responsible for their <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> expenditure but draw on shared guidance and methodologies where possible. An example of where methodologies are being improved is in <abbr title="Department for Science, Innovation and Technology">DSIT</abbr>. <abbr title="Department for Science, Innovation and Technology">DSIT</abbr> is developing a methodology to categorise, and attribute spend to <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> eligible projects with the view of providing a full project list with updated <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> spend during the course of 2025. The figure below outlines how <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> expenditure is identified as programmes are developed:</p>

<p id="figure-23"><strong>Figure 23: Identification of <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr></strong></p>

<hr>

<p>To measure the quality and impact of the UK’s <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr>, we aim to apply these 4 elements to all our <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> programmes:</p>

<ol>
  <li>Each programme has a <strong>Theory of Change</strong> and a logframe, with indicators and milestones for Outputs, Outcomes and Impacts.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Annual Reviews</strong><sup id="fnref:409"><a href="#fn:409" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 409]</a></sup>: Each year, each programme is scored against how well it is delivering against the Theory of Change and logframe.</li>
  <li>Across the portfolio of <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> programmes, we monitor and publish a core set of <strong>Key Performance Indicators</strong><sup id="fnref:410"><a href="#fn:410" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 410]</a></sup> measuring impact.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Evaluation and Learning</strong><sup id="fnref:411"><a href="#fn:411" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 411]</a></sup>: Many <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> programmes have independent evaluations and lessons learnt are collected and shared on a regular basis.</li>
</ol>

<p><abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> portfolio data is collected at departmental level and regularly collated at a cross-government level to support the overview of the portfolio and strategic decision making. The table below sets out when we report externally on UK <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> and data becomes publicly available.</p>

<h4 id="description-of-challenges-and-limitations-brbr">4.1.2 Description of challenges and limitations <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="impact-of-external-global-events">Impact of external global events</h5>

<p>The previous UK Government temporarily reduced the UK’s annual <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> target from 0.7% of Gross National Income (<abbr title="Gross National Income">GNI</abbr>) to 0.5%. We will remain one of the most generous donors amongst the <abbr title="The Group of 7">G7</abbr>, and our <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> offer will continue to grow in line with <abbr title="Gross National Income">GNI</abbr>. We will restore <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> spending to 0.7% of <abbr title="Gross National Income">GNI</abbr> as soon as fiscal circumstances allow. Despite these challenges we remain committed to meeting our commitments to climate finance.</p>

<h5 id="granular-data-tracking">Granular data tracking</h5>

<p>Our programme level data tables contain several hundred individual programmes. Each programme is likely to involve several delivery partners from the original recipient of UK funding right through to the recipient of support on the ground. Each stage in the delivery chain could be at a different geographical level and be mobilising other sources of finance.</p>

<p>It is therefore challenging to track <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> at a granular level. It requires capacity and capability to manage this and overall internal resources to deliver the <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> are not unlimited. It also requires data and information from external sources.</p>

<h5 id="finance-mobilised-from-technical-assistance">Finance mobilised from Technical Assistance</h5>

<p>As part of the set of Key Performance Indicators (<abbr title="Key Performance Indicators">KPIs</abbr>) developed to monitor and track outcomes and impacts from across UK <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> programmes, there are indicators for measuring private and public finance mobilised for climate action. However, these build on the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development (<abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development">OECD</abbr>) methodologies for mobilised finance, so do not capture the widest extent of finance catalysed by <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> interventions, or mobilised through technical assistance.</p>

<p>The UK welcomes the scrutiny of other organisations on our <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> to provide external assurance and identify areas of improvement. An example of this is from the Independent Commission for Aid Impact’s (<abbr title="Independent Commission for Aid Impact">ICAI</abbr>) rapid review of the <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> that was published in February 2024<sup id="fnref:419"><a href="#fn:419" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 419]</a></sup>. The government response to this report was published<sup id="fnref:420"><a href="#fn:420" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 420]</a></sup> in December 2024.</p>

<h4 id="information-on-experience-and-good-practices-to-incentivise-further-private-climate-financing-and-investment-brbr">4.1.3 Information on experience and good practices to incentivise further private climate financing and investment <br><br>
</h4>

<h5 id="incentivising-private-climate-financing">Incentivising private climate financing</h5>

<p>A key focus of the UK’s <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> is mobilising private finance to support the transition to low-carbon and climate-resilient development pathways in developing countries. Our latest cumulative <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> results show that our <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> spend has mobilised £7.8bn in private finance to support climate change. The annual amounts reported for 2021 and 2022 in our <abbr title="Common Tabular Format">CTF</abbr> tables are £2.085bn and £1.28bn.</p>

<p>The UK uses a variety of financial instruments, including grants, concessional loans, returnable loans, performance-based incentives, guarantees, and insurance, to mobilize private finance. These instruments are designed to reduce the perceived risks associated with low-carbon investments, making them more attractive to private investors. An example is the Renewable Energy Performance Platform (<abbr title="Renewable Energy Performance Platform">REPP</abbr>).</p>

<h5 id="desnzfcdo-case-study-repp">
<abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr>/<abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr> case study: <abbr title="Renewable Energy Performance Platform">REPP</abbr>
</h5>

<p><abbr title="Renewable Energy Performance Platform">REPP</abbr> provided technical and financial support to private sector developers of small-scale renewable energy projects in sub-Saharan Africa. <abbr title="Renewable Energy Performance Platform">REPP</abbr> provided tailored support and funding required in individual project finance deals to enable developers to overcome barriers to investment. These barriers include a lack of early-stage funding, costly risk mitigation instruments, underdeveloped capital markets and weak or immature policy and regulatory frameworks. To overcome these barriers, <abbr title="Renewable Energy Performance Platform">REPP</abbr> provided project development capital to support work such as feasibility studies. It also provided viability gap finance using a range of financial instruments and structures.</p>

<p>Some examples of <abbr title="Renewable Energy Performance Platform">REPP</abbr> results are a US$1m development loan to construction of Mpanda 10.2 <abbr title="Megawatts">MW</abbr> run-of-river hydropower plant in Burundi, US$1.2m mezzanine loan to Tanzania’s first ever wind farm, which began operations in July 2020, providing much-needed energy security to a growing rural population and US$2.9m to Bboxx data-driven platform that provides access to innovative products and services like plug-and-play solar home systems (<abbr title="Plug and Play solar home systems">SHS</abbr>), solar-powered water pumps and e-mobility solutions to cash-loan funding. Bboxx is making good progress in transforming the utility sector through its increased presence in West Africa.</p>

<p>The UK is also using its <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> to mobilise private finance by providing technical assistance to support regulatory reforms and build the capacity of key institutions in developing countries. This helps create a stable and predictable investment environment that encourages private sector participation in climate projects.</p>

<p>The UK funds research, development, and demonstration projects to accelerate the commercialization of innovative clean energy technologies. This includes supporting early-stage testing and scaling of new technologies and business models. Some examples of this can be seen further on in this chapter.</p>

<h5 id="supporting-policy-change">Supporting policy change</h5>

<p>The third Portfolio Evaluation of UK <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr>, Support for Policy Change<sup id="fnref:421"><a href="#fn:421" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 421]</a></sup>, found evidence that <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> had supported some aspects of policy change, and that the UK’s approach was valued by most policymakers and other donors. We welcomed the findings of this evaluation and published a Management Response<sup id="fnref:422"><a href="#fn:422" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 422]</a></sup>. Key findings were:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
<abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> works in a collaborative, non-prescriptive style in partner countries, to support the types of policy changes beneficial to climate and the environment. This collaborative approach creates a sense of ownership by partner governments which increases the likelihood of policy change occurring, and it being effective and sustainable.</li>
  <li>
<abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> has been effective in supporting changes to forestry and land-use policy in Colombia and Indonesia, and renewable energy policy in Uganda.</li>
  <li>Four types of intervention were successful in supporting policy change in national and sub-national government:</li>
</ul>

<ol>
  <li>Generating and brokering evidence to convince people to change policy</li>
  <li>Exploiting opportunities to convince a critical mass of decision makers to change</li>
  <li>Empowering others to advocate for or deliver policy change through capacity-building, and</li>
  <li>Providing resources to deliver policy change.</li>
</ol>

<ul>
  <li>Five types of intervention were successful in supporting policy change in global institutions:</li>
</ul>

<ol>
  <li>Financial leverage</li>
  <li>Creating momentum through coalitions of support</li>
  <li>Building confidence through UK expertise</li>
  <li>Leadership, and</li>
  <li>Building capability through experience</li>
</ol>

<div class="example">
  <p><strong>Case study: <abbr title="Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation">REDD+</abbr> Early Movers (<abbr title="REDD+ Early Movers Programme">REM</abbr>) Programme</strong></p>

  <p><abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr> has supported the <abbr title="REDD+ Early Movers Programme">REM</abbr> programme, which aims to reward countries or jurisdictions considered as pioneers in forest protection and climate mitigation. One of the areas the <abbr title="REDD+ Early Movers Programme">REM</abbr> programme operates in is Mato Grosso in Brazil, where the programme has delivered a project called Muxirum Quilombola. The main objectives of the Muxirum Quilombola project were to ensure communities could be empowered politically, socially, culturally and economically, with a focus on Quilombolo women and youth. Muxirum Quilombola has benefitted more than 500 Quilombola families, promoting sustainable management, environmental preservation and income generation.</p>
</div>

<div class="example">
  <p><strong>Case Study: Nationally Determined Contributions Partnership</strong></p>

  <p><abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr> has supported the <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution Partnership">NDCP</abbr> (Nationally Determined Contributions Partnership), which is a partnership of over 120 countries and almost 100 institutions, formed after the signing of the Paris Agreement, to help countries effectively implement their commitments and access finance, supporting ambitious climate action whilst enhancing sustainable development.</p>

  <p>Through the <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution Partnership">NDCP</abbr>, the UK supports developing countries to turn their <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contributions">NDCs</abbr> and other relevant climate plans into specific strategies and measures, support their implementation, as well as coordinating major climate donors to more effectively meet the needs identified.</p>

  <p>An example of the impact of the <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution Partnership">NDCP</abbr> is in Colombia. Here, the Colombian government requested the support of the <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution Partnership">NDCP</abbr> to improve the quality and ambition of their <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr>, and mobilise financial resources for <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr> investment projects. The British Embassy in Colombia was able to support this process, using their strong relationship with the Colombian government facilitated by the UK-Colombia Partnership for Sustainable Growth<sup id="fnref:423"><a href="#fn:423" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 423]</a></sup>. Five embedded advisor roles, including in-country facilitators and a climate finance advisor, were recruited by the <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution Partnership">NDCP</abbr> Support Unit, utilising funds from the UK Country Engagement Fund. These roles were dispersed across the Colombian Ministries of Environment and Sustainable Development, National Planning, Finance, and Agriculture.</p>

  <p>The support from the <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution Partnership">NDCP</abbr> helped the Colombian government to agree a revised <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr> in 2020 that included a more ambitious mitigation target of not emitting more than 169.4 <abbr title="Megatonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalents">MtCO</abbr><sub>2</sub>eq by 2030, equivalent to a 51% reduction in emissions from a revised 2030 reference scenario, as compared to a 20% reduction in their first <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr>.</p>

  <p>Thus far the Climate Finance Broker Facility (established via the <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution Partnership">NDCP</abbr> facilitator in the Colombian Ministry of National Planning) has supported 7 projects with over US$1m of funding from institutional members such as the Global Green Growth Institute (<abbr title="Global Green Growth Institute">GGGI</abbr>), the United States Agency for International Development (<abbr title="United States Agency for International Development">USAID</abbr>), the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (<abbr title="United Nations Department for Economic and Social Affairs">UNDESA</abbr>) and the World Wildlife Fund (<abbr title="World Wildlife Fund">WWF</abbr>). Coordination across these members would not be possible without <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr> Partnership support.</p>
</div>

<h4 id="efforts-taken-to-enhance-comparability-and-accuracy-of-information-reported-brbr">4.1.4 Efforts taken to enhance comparability and accuracy of information reported <br><br>
</h4>

<p>To ensure the UK’s <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> information is accurate and comparable to other sources of climate finance, we work through several mechanisms. We engage closely through the <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> transparency process, not only in reports such as this, but in the Facilitative Multilateral Consideration of Progress and through the in-donor peer review process, where we participate both as an assessee and an assessor.</p>

<p>We also work closely with the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee (<abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee">OECD-DAC</abbr>) and member countries. For example, we attend regular meetings of <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development">OECD</abbr> <abbr title="Development Assistance Committee">DAC</abbr>’s Working Party on Development Finance Statistics (<abbr title="Working Party on Development Finance Statistics">WP-STAT</abbr>) to discuss technical issues related to <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> reporting. A significant amount of recent work has been on harmonising <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development">OECD</abbr> and <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> climate finance reporting practices and aligning key guidance such as the Rio Marker handbook with the Paris Agreement.</p>

<p>The UK, through its <abbr title="The 26th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC">COP26</abbr> presidency, led on the development of the $100bn climate finance delivery plan<sup id="fnref:424"><a href="#fn:424" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 424]</a></sup> and has been closely involved in subsequent work with the <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development">OECD</abbr> and donors to publish follow up reports on progress towards the $100bn goal. The most recent of these was published in May 2024<sup id="fnref:425"><a href="#fn:425" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 425]</a></sup>, reporting that in 2022 a total of $115.9bn of climate finance was mobilised for developing countries, the first year that the $100bn goal has been exceeded.</p>

<p>The UK Government is committed to supporting the greater use of International Aid Transparency Initiative (<abbr title="International Aid Transparency Initiative">IATI</abbr>) data and other aid information across all recipient countries of <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> and works closely with other donors in country to support development outcomes.</p>

<p>The UK Government is actively engaged in efforts to fortify international aid transparency standards. This is achieved through collaboration with <abbr title="International Aid Transparency Initiative">IATI</abbr>, Civil Society Organisations, implementing partners, and other donor countries by advocating for higher aid transparency standards. The UK encourages our implementing partners to publish data on UK-funded activities in accordance with the <abbr title="International Aid Transparency Initiative">IATI</abbr> standard and provides them with the necessary guidance to do so. In line with this, information on <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> programming managed by UK Government departments is available on the <abbr title="International Aid Transparency Initiative">IATI</abbr> Datastore<sup id="fnref:426"><a href="#fn:426" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 426]</a></sup> and the UK’s Development Tracker website (<abbr title="Development Tracker">DevTracker</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:427"><a href="#fn:427" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 427]</a></sup>. Our commitment to this cause remains steadfast as we continue to work towards enhancing transparency in international aid.</p>

<p>We ensure the accuracy of our financial information by having all payments go through an internal approval process involving a programme team, a financial team and finally senior management. In the case of <abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr>, a third party provides finance services such as payment processing, meaning additional checks will be carried out. Once payments are made, they are recorded on the finance journal, which also goes through an internal checking process. <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> teams will use the journal data to record the payment in internal data systems, which in turn are used for external reporting. Data for external reporting will also be quality assured to check for accuracy. For example, the <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> programme level data was originally collated for the UK’s annual provisional <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> publication and then collated again for the UK’s final <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> publication. It has also been compiled and provided to the <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee">OECD-DAC</abbr> to support their work on reporting on progress towards $100bn.</p>

<p>For reporting mobilised finance, the UK developed a Key Performance Indicator (KPI 12)<sup id="fnref:428"><a href="#fn:428" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 428]</a></sup> for applicable <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> programmes to report against. To ensure comparability, the methodology for this KPI is aligned with <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development">OECD</abbr> <abbr title="Development Assistance Committee">DAC</abbr> methodologies for measuring the amounts mobilised from the private sector by official development finance interventions. Accuracy is ensured through a robust quality assurance process: each <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> programme reports results, these are quality assured by an analyst working closely with the programme lead. The results are then aggregated up by department and quality assured as a whole, then <abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr> results are signed off by the Head of <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> Portfolio and Strategy and the Head of International Climate and Energy Analysis. Results are then aggregated across <abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr>, <abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr> and <abbr title="Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs">Defra</abbr> and quality assured again, then assembled into an annual statistics publication and signed off again by Senior staff in each department before publication<sup id="fnref:429"><a href="#fn:429" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 429]</a></sup>.</p>

<p><abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> will continue to place a strong focus on Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (<abbr title="Monitoring, evaluation and learning">MEL</abbr>) to improve the effectiveness of our investments and those of our partners. This will be achieved through strengthening the evidence base and facilitating learning about sustainable approaches to reduce poverty and tackle climate change and environmental degradation.</p>

<p>The intended impact is to deliver transformational climate change programmes. We will build on our robust cross-government results framework and will continue to publish results annually, to allow the public to track progress against our Key Performance Indicators (<abbr title="Key Performance Indicators">KPIs</abbr>).</p>

<p>All <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> programmes are required to collect and report on relevant <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> <abbr title="Key Performance Indicators">KPIs</abbr>, disaggregated by gender, age, and disability where possible, alongside other programme-specific indicators. Where the UK co-funds a programme with other donors, only ‘UK-attributed’ <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> results are included, in proportion to the UK’s donor share.</p>

<p>For each key performance indicator, results are added together across all relevant programmes and over time, to give cumulative results across the whole <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> portfolio. We use <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> <abbr title="Key Performance Indicators">KPIs</abbr> alongside a broad range of evidence to evaluate the success of our <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> programmes and inform funding decisions to maximise value for money and the successful delivery of our strategic climate, nature and sustainable development objectives. We will continue to review the <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> <abbr title="Key Performance Indicators">KPIs</abbr> and the way we use them to inform our decision-making, to ensure that we are achieving climate, and nature impacts in line with our priorities and the needs of developing countries.</p>
