For the current phase of delivery, <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> analysts are working across government to update our approach to portfolio monitoring and evaluation, building on lessons learnt from <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> to date.</p>

<h3 id="information-on-institutional-arrangements-for-the-provision-of-technology-development-and-transfer-and-capacity-building-support">4.2 Information on institutional arrangements for the provision of technology development and transfer and capacity-building support</h3>

<p>The UK Government departments responsible for delivering our <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> commitment work together in several ways for the provision of technology development and transfer and capacity building support. There is more detail on technology development and transfer later in this chapter. Drawing on each department’s expertise, <abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr>, <abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr> and <abbr title="Department for Science, Innovation and Technology">DSIT</abbr> work together on the Ayrton Fund. <abbr title="Department for Science, Innovation and Technology">DSIT</abbr> have key research organisations such as UK Research and Innovation (<abbr title="UK Research and Innovation">UKRI</abbr>) as some of their arms-lengths bodies and deliver many of their <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> projects through UK universities. <abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr> draw on their overseas network and use this to ensure support can be country specific. Whilst <abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr> are responsible for much of the domestic policy on areas such as energy transition and draw on this expertise in a developing country context.</p>

<p>This complementary approach across departments is also used for the provision of capacity building support. We have used some case studies below to demonstrate this.</p>

<div class="example">
  <p><strong>Case study: <abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr> overseas network engagement with UK-based teams</strong></p>

  <p><abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr> has a large network of individuals with significant skills and experience in international delivery of <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> programmes. <abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr>’s people, presence, instruments and systems allow us to deliver catalytic global leadership, multilateral and private sector leverage, and significant direct, real-world, bilateral results and impact. The <abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr> has a strong Climate and Environment Cadre based overseas and in the UK. Additional Cadres such as the Food and Agriculture and Urban and Infrastructure are deeply engaged in delivery of our international climate finance. Programme Managers are a key element of the strong expertise that exists across <abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr> for <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> delivery, overseeing spend and tracking results and will work closely with advisors.</p>
</div>

<div class="example">
  <p><strong>Case study: Sustainable Cooling and Cold Chain Solutions (<abbr title="Sustainable Cooling and Cold Chain Solutions programme">SCCCS</abbr>) programme</strong></p>

  <p>Sustainable Cooling and Cold Chain Solutions (<abbr title="Sustainable Cooling and Cold Chain Solutions programme">SCCCS</abbr>) works with United Nations Environment Programme (<abbr title="United Nations Environment Programme">UNEP</abbr>) in partnership with the University of Birmingham to influence the uptake of cooling and cold-chains solutions across Africa and India. <abbr title="Sustainable Cooling and Cold Chain Solutions programme">SCCCS</abbr> uses a ‘hub and spoke’ model; setting up regional hubs and developing <abbr title="Specialised Outreach and Knowledge Establishments">SPOKES</abbr> (Specialised Outreach and Knowledge Establishments) to share research, innovation and knowledge on cooling and cold-chains for both food and vaccine supply chains. There are additional workstreams supporting the development of modelling, policies and tools that implement global best practice and provide technical assistance for policy makers. Since its establishment in 2019 the programme has influenced the uptake of cooling and cold-chains solutions in 51 developing countries and supported over 1,600 people to adapt to the effects of climate change by improving food and vaccine preservation.</p>
</div>

<div class="example">
  <p><strong>Case study: <abbr title="UK Partnering for Accelerated Climate Transitions">UK PACT</abbr></strong></p>

  <p>UK Partnering for Accelerated Climate Transitions (<abbr title="UK Partnering for Accelerated Climate Transitions">UK PACT</abbr>) supports <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr>-eligible countries with high mitigation potential to increase their climate ambitions and implement that ambition more rapidly, more effectively, and more equitably. <abbr title="UK Partnering for Accelerated Climate Transitions">UK PACT</abbr> is jointly funded and governed by the <abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr> and <abbr title="Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, previously knows as Business, Energy &amp; Industrial Strategy (BEIS)">DESNZ</abbr>.</p>

  <p>Key features of <abbr title="UK Partnering for Accelerated Climate Transitions">UK PACT</abbr> are that it aims to respond explicitly to partner government demand for capacity building interventions, and that it shares UK expertise (for example in areas such as climate legislation, green finance, and smart energy). <abbr title="UK Partnering for Accelerated Climate Transitions">UK PACT</abbr> operates through a ‘hybrid’ model of dedicated programme funded teams of <abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr> Officials based overseas providing local context to programme strategy and implementation in-country, and UK based officials providing global programme strategy and delivery.</p>

  <p>Between April 2021 and March 2022, <abbr title="UK Partnering for Accelerated Climate Transitions">UK PACT</abbr> delivered 114 mitigation technical assistance projects across 16 partner countries.</p>

  <p>30 skill-shares and 7 secondments were delivered, with 6,265 people receiving training, with training beneficiaries rating the trainings as 4.5/5 in terms of usefulness.</p>

  <p>The programme delivered full scale country programmes in Colombia, Mexico, South Africa, China, and extensions were agreed to extend 44 projects from the first funding rounds to provide multi-year delivery.</p>
</div>

<div class="example">
  <p><strong>Case study: Small Island Developing States Capacity and Resilience Programme (<abbr title="Small Island Developing States Capacity and Resilience Programme">SIDAR</abbr>)</strong></p>

  <p>Announced at <abbr title="The 26th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC">COP26</abbr> in Glasgow, the <abbr title="Small Island Developing States Capacity and Resilience Programme">SIDAR</abbr> programme aims to raise £40m over 5 years to <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr>-eligible Small Island Developing States (<abbr title="Small Island Developing States">SIDS</abbr>) to increase capacity and improve international funding and policy frameworks. This will enable <abbr title="Small Island Developing States">SIDS</abbr> governments to better access and utilise climate finance available to them.</p>

  <p>The <abbr title="Small Island Developing States Capacity and Resilience Programme">SIDAR</abbr> programme has delivered some important outcomes. These include:</p>

  <ul>
    <li>Supporting the Resilient and Sustainable Islands initiative (<abbr title="Resilient and Sustainable Islands Initiative">RESI</abbr>) to launch the Resilient monthly podcast series;</li>
    <li>Hosting the first public engagement and high-level technical discussions on the <abbr title="United Nations">UN</abbr>’s Multidimensional Vulnerability Index (<abbr title="Multidimensional Vulnerability Index">MVI</abbr>);</li>
    <li>Putting in place 2 regional agreements supporting the Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre and Global Green Growth Institute in the Pacific;</li>
    <li>Supporting 2 events that considered how to address financing and economic issues facing <abbr title="Small Island Developing States">SIDS</abbr>, and;</li>
    <li>Taking forward a new partnership for sustainability and resilience through <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development">OECD</abbr> Development Assistance Committee and the Alliance of Small Island States (<abbr title="Alliance of Small Island States">AOSIS</abbr>) Taskforce<sup id="fnref:430"><a href="#fn:430" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 430]</a></sup>.</li>
  </ul>
</div>

<h3 id="underlying-assumptions-definitions-and-methodologies">4.3 Underlying assumptions, definitions and methodologies</h3>

<p>The UK’s climate finance reporting methodology is set out below:</p>

<h4 id="reporting-year-brbr">4.3.1 Reporting Year <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Calendar year. We have reported spend for 2021 and 2022 in our data tables referenced in section 3. The £11.6bn <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> commitment starts in the UK fiscal year 21/22, which runs from April to March. So, 2021 calendar year figures will include some spend from the previous <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> commitment.</p>

<h4 id="exchange-rate-brbr">4.3.2 Exchange Rate <br><br>
</h4>

<p>We report in pound sterling and convert to United States dollars using the <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development">OECD</abbr> annual exchange rate<sup id="fnref:431"><a href="#fn:431" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 431]</a></sup> for the relevant year.</p>

<h4 id="funding-status-brbr">4.3.3 Funding Status <br><br>
</h4>

<p>We use the ‘committed’ status for our reported spend. This reflects that the money has been accounted as spent from government budgets and the figures we report are the same as how we are tracking the budget internally. We do not report political pledges that have not yet been followed up with actual funding being provided. For some programmes, such as our contributions to multilateral funds, we use a funding instrument called a Promissory Note. This commits a level of funding to the named recipient of the note, who is then able to request cash drawdowns from the note, which the government (as the note issuer) provides. For accounting purposes (and therefore our reporting methodology) we report the spend at the point the Promissory Note is formally issued and not the subsequent cash drawdowns.</p>

<h4 id="channel-brbr">4.3.4 Channel <br><br>
</h4>

<p>We report the channel as multilateral for those funds and core contributions to organisations already pre-named on the multilateral tab<sup id="fnref:432"><a href="#fn:432" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 432]</a></sup> In addition if we have reported the spend as multilateral for our wider <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> reporting to the <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee">OECD-DAC</abbr>, we will also use this channel.</p>

<p>All other spend will be reported under the bilateral channel. We will use the multi-bilateral channel for specific programmes via multilateral organisations. We don’t use the regional channel.</p>

<h4 id="funding-source-brbr">4.3.5 Funding Source <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Most of our reported climate finance comes from the UK’s <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> budget. The only exception are climate eligible outflows from the British International Investments (see section 1.1 for further information).</p>

<h4 id="financial-instrument-brbr">4.3.6 Financial Instrument <br><br>
</h4>

<p>We report most of our spend as grant as this finance is provided with no requirement for return of funds back to us (except where funding is unused once a programme has finished or in cases where funding has been misused). We do report some spend as equity as this relates to programmes where we invest in vehicles that will purchase assets where we have a legal right to returns made on these assets. There is also a programme that uses a combination of grant and equity finance.</p>

<h4 id="concessional-finance-brbr">4.3.7 Concessional finance <br><br>
</h4>

<p>As most of our climate finance comes from the UK’s <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> budget it must comply with the <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee">OECD-DAC</abbr> rules on <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> eligibility as well as spending requirements set out in the UK’s International Development Act<sup id="fnref:433"><a href="#fn:433" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 433]</a></sup>. We use <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee">OECD-DAC</abbr> PSI (Private Sector Instrument) rules for our equity spend which includes assessments both as the institutional level (the entity that receives our funding) and at the instrument level (the downstream investment made by that entity) to ensure the finance is concessional and the value reported reflects the development effort made. Returns from these instruments that come back to UK Government count as negative <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> and will count against <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> targets unless re-spent.</p>

<h4 id="type-of-support-brbr">4.3.8 Type of support <br><br>
</h4>

<p>We assess whether our support is mitigation or adaptation as part of the overall process set out in figure 1, where we use the <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development">OECD</abbr> Rio Marker guidance. We only report spend as cross-cutting where we are not able to split the amounts for example subscription payments to the <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr>.</p>

<h4 id="sectorsub-sector-brbr">4.3.9 Sector/sub-sector <br><br>
</h4>

<p>For the sector classification, we assess the programme to see which of the drop-down sectors is the best fit (Energy, Transport, Industry, Agriculture, Forestry, Water and Sanitation, Cross-Cutting or Other). We will use ‘Other’ where the other main sector choices don’t seem a good match and will include a more specific sector, typically this will be the sub-sector choice.</p>

<p>For sub-sector classification we report the same <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee">OECD-DAC</abbr> 5-digit sector code as used for the same programme when reporting the spend to the <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee">OECD-DAC</abbr>.</p>

<h4 id="capacity-building-andor-technology-development-and-transfer-objectives-brbr">4.3.10 Capacity building and/or technology development and transfer objectives <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Many of the programmes we support with our <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> will be contributing to these objectives. For example, capacity building and other types of technical assistance are often an essential element to ensuring the other objectives of the programme can be achieved. In our reporting we select a set of examples that showcase how our <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> is supporting these objectives rather than attempting to report every programme that is contributing.</p>

<p>We use our knowledge of the programme to identify which programmes to tag and will draw on other sources of information e.g. the summary description of the programme on <abbr title="Development Tracker">DevTracker</abbr> (see footnote 4) or if the programme (for tagging as capacity building) has been marked with the ‘Free-Standing Technical Co-operation’ marker under our <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee">OECD-DAC</abbr> reporting.</p>

<p>We’ve recently developed an additional 4 Key Performance Indicators to monitor <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> technical assistance programmes – covering countries supported, individuals and organisations supported, climate policies informed, and emissions reduced or avoided supported by <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> technical assistance<sup id="fnref:434"><a href="#fn:434" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 434]</a></sup>.</p>

<h4 id="climate-specific-support-brbr">4.3.11 Climate specific support <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Please see figure 1 for an overview of the process used to identify if our programmes are climate specific and the level of climate finance we should report. Again, the Rio Marker guidance is used to support this assessment.</p>

<h4 id="avoiding-double-counting-brbr">4.3.12 Avoiding double counting <br><br>
</h4>

<p>We report our climate finance spend at the point the money leaves government; this means we do not double count contributions made by other donors. For example, our contribution to a multi-donor trust fund such as the Green Climate Fund (<abbr title="Green Climate Fund">GCF</abbr>) is done when we make contributions to the <abbr title="Green Climate Fund">GCF</abbr> itself rather than when the <abbr title="Green Climate Fund">GCF</abbr> makes downstream payments into specific projects, at which point all the donor contributions will be mixed increasing the risk of double-counting.</p>

<p>For private finance reporting, where possible we use project level information to make sure that there is no double-counting. The data we report to the <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development">OECD</abbr> is also used in their climate finance provided and mobilised report, after the <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development">OECD</abbr> has done additional checks to make sure there’s no double-counting across donors. By using the <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development">OECD</abbr> <abbr title="Development Assistance Committee">DAC</abbr> methodologies for measuring the amounts mobilised from the private sector by official development finance interventions we are minimising the likelihood of double counting occurring.</p>

<p>We don’t use <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> to purchase carbon credits for compliance with our own domestic climate targets, so we avoid double-counting in this type of support under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.</p>

<p>Unless we are the sole funder or there is clear country specific agreement associated with our funding, we don’t attribute our spend to specific individual countries. If a programme is benefitting multiple countries (and the selection is specific enough to mean that a less granular geographic level e.g. global or regional is not more appropriate) then we will list those countries for that programme reporting line in our data tables under section 3. But we won’t report a specific spend amount per country.</p>

<p>As covered under section 1.1 we avoid double counting the climate finance spend through <abbr title="British International Investment">BII</abbr> by deducting the <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> inflow amount from the climate eligible outflows we report.</p>

<h4 id="private-finance-brbr">4.3.13 Private finance <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Funding is only classified as ‘mobilised private climate finance’ if it meets 3 definitional tests:</p>

<p>Private finance test: Is the finance provided by a private organisation?</p>

<p>Finance is classified as public or private based on the type of organisation providing the finance. In general, organisations are defined as public if they are government agencies, or if governments own more than 50% of equity/shares in an organisation with multiple shareholders (for example, a bank with both public and private shareholders). In all other cases, they are classified as private organisations.</p>

<p>In some cases, this ownership-based approach may not accurately reflect the character of financial transactions made by organisations that are publicly owned but operate according to market-oriented commercial or private principles. In these cases, programmes may classify reporting based on who exercises control of investment decisions or based on the principles used to make investment decisions.</p>

<p>Climate finance test: Is the finance intended for climate change adaptation or mitigation purposes?</p>

<p>Finance is categorised as climate finance if the purpose of the project/programme includes support to meet climate change mitigation and/or adaptation goals, based on <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development">OECD</abbr> Statistical Reporting Directives. Climate financing is not determined based on whether the source of the finance is nominally drawn from a climate change fund/window/etc.</p>

<p>If finance also provides support to other (non-climate) goals, only the portion of the funding directed towards climate goals is counted as climate finance.</p>

<p>Mobilised finance test: Has the finance been mobilised by the <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr>, i.e. is it additional and causally linked to <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> funding or support?</p>

<p>Mobilised finance is funding from another actor that has been directed to an objective, project or programme that would otherwise not have benefitted from these funds and is a direct result of the original mobilising actor’s efforts.</p>

<p>This doesn’t include finance that would have occurred anyway without the initial <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr>. This definition requires funds to be additional, in that they would not otherwise have been allocated to a climate objective or activity, and that the <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> programme can identify a causal link between its funding or actions and the mobilised finance.
Mobilised resources need to be estimated based on boundaries to define the scope and account for the total private finance that could be associated with different public interventions. We aim to establish these boundaries at project-level, according to different instruments:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Project-level boundaries for grants, loans and syndicated loans. In these cases, mobilised financing might include upfront project level financing (i.e. resources committed to the project from the private sector at the time of project approval) or subsequent financing following UK investment (i.e. resources mobilised after the project has been operating, such as when commercial banks or venture capital funds finance a project part-designed or financed by the UK Government).</li>
  <li>For other types of financial instruments, such as guarantees and Collective Investment Vehicles, the precise boundaries will vary according to the level and quality of available data, as well as causality considerations based on conservative approaches.</li>
  <li>We follow the guidance in the <abbr title="Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development">OECD</abbr> <abbr title="Development Assistance Committee">DAC</abbr> methodologies on reporting for specific instruments, including on setting appropriate boundaries at the instrument level.</li>
</ul>

<p>Mobilised private finance is reported based on the year in which the finance is legally committed by the organisation/actor. To note in our private finance mobilised data set submitted as part of this <abbr title="Biennial Transparency Report">BTR</abbr> - The amount mobilised reported by the UK represents the private finance mobilised that can be attributed to the UK within the given year only (i.e. 2022 only) whilst the amount of resources used to mobilise the support represents the total UK commitment to the programme and not the amount committed in the given year. This means the 2 figures cannot be directly compared across programmes as the amount mobilised is an in-year value whilst the amount of resources is a cumulative figure.</p>

<h4 id="ensuring-support-addresses-needs-and-priorities-of-developing-countries-brbr">4.3.14 Ensuring support addresses needs and priorities of developing countries <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK uses a variety of approaches to ensure that its climate finance support is addressing the needs and priorities of developing countries. The UK’s work on aligning all <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> with the Paris Agreement includes a requirement that the spend must be aligned, and where possible elevate, to countries <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr>’s and adaptation plans. Individual programme business cases (which are publicly available via the <abbr title="Development Tracker">DevTracker</abbr> website) will set out in more detail how this requirement is being met.</p>

<p>The UK provides support for programmes that developing countries can bid into, where the application and assessment process will require that the funding proposals are aligned with a country’s climate action plans. For example, the Mitigation Action Facility<sup id="fnref:435"><a href="#fn:435" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 435]</a></sup> or the Green Climate Fund<sup id="fnref:436"><a href="#fn:436" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 436]</a></sup> where a funding proposal must be supported by a letter from the recipient country government.</p>

<p>The UK also supports programmes that facilitate wider access to climate finance for countries climate action plans. These include the UK setting up the Taskforce on Access to Climate Finance and supporting programmes such as the <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr> Partnership<sup id="fnref:437"><a href="#fn:437" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 437]</a></sup> and the Climate Finance Accelerator<sup id="fnref:438"><a href="#fn:438" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 438]</a></sup>.</p>

<h4 id="how-support-is-in-line-with-the-long-term-goals-of-the-paris-agreement-brbr">4.3.15 How support is in line with the long-term goals of the Paris Agreement <br><br>
</h4>

<p>As referenced elsewhere in this chapter, the UK has committed to align its bilateral <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> spend with the Paris Agreement and delivered on this from 2023. The UK will continue to engage with our multilateral partners to ensure our multilateral <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> can also be aligned. The UK is implementing this commitment by:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Undertaking climate risk assessments for <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> programming</li>
  <li>Using carbon pricing in <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> programme appraisals</li>
  <li>Ensuring <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> programming is line with the UK Government’s fossil fuel policy<sup id="fnref:439"><a href="#fn:439" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 439]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>Ensuring that <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr> programming is aligned to, and where possible elevate, countries <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contributions">NDCs</abbr> and adaptation plans.</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="new-and-additional-finance-brbr">4.3.16 New and additional finance <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK determines that its climate finance is new and additional as our £11.6bn commitment is completely new climate finance from our previous £5.8bn commitment. Also, the finance reported under section 3 has not been reported in previous <abbr title="United Nationals Framework Convention on Climate Change">UNFCCC</abbr> biennial reports.</p>

<h4 id="how-the-information-provided-represents-a-progression-from-previous-levels-of-finance-under-the-paris-agreement-brbr">4.3.17 How the information provided represents a progression from previous levels of finance under the Paris Agreement <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK’s current 5 year £11.6bn <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> commitment is a doubling of its previous 5-year commitment of £5.8bn. Within the £11.6bn, the UK has a target to spend £1.5bn on adaptation in 2025, which is a doubling of the adaptation the UK spent in 2019.</p>

<p>There will be annual fluctuations in the UK’s level of climate finance based on the budget allocations made in the Spending Review process and these in turn can be impacted by in-year pressures (see section 4.2 for examples of these). But the overall volumes of climate finance the UK is providing are increasing.</p>

<h4 id="multilateral-finance-brbr">4.3.18 Multilateral finance <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK uses a combination of in-flow and outflow approaches to determine the level of multilateral finance reported. Where the UK has deemed that a multilateral is providing 100% climate finance e.g. Climate Investment Funds, then our full in-flow contribution is reported as climate specific. Where a multilateral fund or programme is deemed as providing less than 100% climate finance e.g. Global Environment Facility, then the UK splits the level of its inflow contribution as general and climate specific. The assessment on the level of climate finance is estimated by the scope of the fund/programmes activities to determine what amount is climate specific.</p>

<p>For the years covered under this <abbr title="Biennial Transparency Report">BTR</abbr> report (2021 and 2022) the UK is not reporting as climate finance its core contributions to multilateral banks e.g. World Bank. However as set out in the UK’s written ministerial statement (see footnote 7) in future years, the methodology will change and climate specific shares from multilateral bank core contributions will be reported.</p>

<h3 id="information-on-financial-support-provided-and-mobilized-under-article-9-of-the-paris-agreement">4.4 Information on financial support provided and mobilized under Article 9 of the Paris Agreement</h3>

<h4 id="united-kingdom-brbr">4.4.1 United Kingdom <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK has included the relevant information and data in the climate finance reporting tables.</p>

<h4 id="jersey-brbr-3">4.4.2 Jersey <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Jersey Overseas Aid (<abbr title="Jersey Overseas Aid">JOA</abbr>) is the Island’s independent, publicly funded relief and development agency. Its annual budget is distributed through development and humanitarian funding streams. <abbr title="Jersey Overseas Aid">JOA</abbr> allocates its funding through bilateral partnerships with pre-approved international non-governmental organisations (<abbr title="Non-Governmental Organisations">NGOs</abbr>), multilateral organisations and <abbr title="United Nations">UN</abbr> Agencies.</p>

<p>Between 2018-2022, <abbr title="Jersey Overseas Aid">JOA</abbr> streamlined its development programme – operating in 6 countries across 3 thematic areas: Dairy for Development, Financial Inclusion and Conservation Livelihoods. Each of the themes contain cross-cutting components that indirectly contribute to Article 9 of the Paris Agreement. In particular, the Conservation, Lives and Livelihoods portfolio contributes to climate resilience and conservation efforts with a strategic focus on ‘the link between human development and environmental protection.</p>

<p>In addition, <abbr title="Jersey Overseas Aid">JOA</abbr>’s humanitarian funding stream includes direct response to the effects of climate change globally.</p>

<h4 id="guernsey-brbr-3">4.4.3 Guernsey <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The Guernsey Overseas Aid and Development Commission (<abbr title="Gurnsey Overseas Aid &amp; Development Commission">GOA&amp;DC</abbr>) is part of the Guernsey government and is mandated to distribute funds for aid and development overseas by making contributions to charity programmes and to disaster and emergency relief. The <abbr title="Gurnsey Overseas Aid &amp; Development Commission">GOA&amp;DC</abbr> does not provide bilateral funding. Its overall budget for 2022 was £3.225 million. This increased to £4.397million by 2024. The majority of its budget is spent on 4 workstreams. The Single Year Project Grant Aid Awards are grants of up to £55,000 (£50,000 in 2022) each for projects being undertaken by charities registered in the United Kingdom, Guernsey or Jersey. Many of these projects, but not all, relate to or include elements that help to mitigate the impact of climate change. The 2022 Budget for this workstream was £2.354 million. The Multi Year Project Grant Aid Awards are similar to the above except they are grants of up to £165,000 (£150,000 in 2022) each for projects over a 3 year period. In addition, the <abbr title="Gurnsey Overseas Aid &amp; Development Commission">GOA&amp;DC</abbr> considers Multi Year Awards which demonstrate a particular focus on mitigating the impact of climate change or ‘reaching the further first’ (e.g. on the grounds of disability, ethnicity, displacement, etc.). The 2022 Budget for this workstream was £300,000. The third main workstream is Disaster and Emergency Relied Awards. Applications are welcomed from Charities already known to the Commission, or donations are made to the Disasters Emergency Committee (<abbr title="Disasters Emergency Committee">DEC</abbr>) Live Appeals. These often are for climate related emergencies. The 2022 Budget for this workstream was £360,000. The final main workstream is Community Partnerships which encourages Guernsey community groups to raise funds for international development through this match funding scheme. The 2022 Budget for this workstream was £125,000.</p>

<p>The Table only shows Awards made in 2021 and 2022 which fully or partially relate to mitigating climate change.</p>

<h4 id="isle-of-man-brbr-3">4.4.4 Isle of Man <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The Isle of Man International Development annual budget is distributed via 5 funding streams, which in 2018 – 2019 included an increase of £100,000, raising the budget from £2.4 million to £2.5 million. Emergency funding is reserved for the Disasters Emergency Committee (<abbr title="Disasters Emergency Committee">DEC</abbr>) Live Appeals, which is allocated where necessary and focused on specific disaster situations, including climate related emergencies such as flooding and cyclones. The largest funding stream, International Development Partnerships, is a 2-year funding cycle worth £1.2 million per year and which is open to application by charities registered in the UK or Isle of Man. Since 2020 and remaining for 2024-2026, Climate Change is 1 of 2 designated themes for this funding stream, inviting applications for projects specifically tackling the causes and impacts of climate change globally. More locally, the Small Grants funding stream is open only to Isle of Man registered charities for up to £100,000 each per funding round, to carry out an International Development project of their design. This stream similarly welcomes applications which address the effects of climate change. All Isle of Man government funding streams are open to application by registered organisations except for Disaster and Emergency Relief, which is allocated to be mobilised at short notice.</p>

<p>*Exchange rate calculated using historical exchange rates on the given payment date from Exchange Rates website<sup id="fnref:440"><a href="#fn:440" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 440]</a></sup>.</p>

<p>Please see [annex 1]: Support provided by crown dependencies.</p>

<h3 id="information-on-support-for-technology-development-and-transfer-provided-under-article-10-of-the-paris-agreement">4.5 Information on support for technology development and transfer provided under Article 10 of the Paris Agreement</h3>

<h4 id="strategies-employed-to-support-technology-development-and-transfer-including-case-studies-brbr">4.5.1 Strategies employed to support technology development and transfer, including case studies <br><br>
</h4>

<p>UK development assistance is actively supporting the development of new and improved technologies and business models which help tackle climate change, while also reaching the poorest; providing life changing services, creating green jobs, building resilience and boosting local and national economies.</p>

<ul>
  <li>The UK uses international climate finance (<abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr>) and other levers to support technology-driven innovation that will help developing countries decarbonise high-emission sectors and move towards clean energy systems.</li>
  <li>The UK is committed to a comprehensive, long-term and co-ordinated UK capability-building offer on clean energy access and transition for emerging and developing countries, enhancing their implementation of nationally determined contributions (<abbr title="Nationally Determined Contributions">NDCs</abbr>).</li>
  <li>This includes accelerating and scaling up the transition to clean and affordable technology in sectors such as energy and mobility, working through programmes and partnerships, such as the <abbr title="The 26th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC">COP26</abbr> Breakthrough Agenda, the Energy Transition Council, and others, as well as investing and working with partners to increase global funding for decarbonisation through multilateral initiatives such as the international Climate Investment Funds, Mitigation Action Facility, <abbr title="Energy Sector Management Assistance Programme">ESMAP</abbr>, and the global <abbr title="Nationally Determined Contribution">NDC</abbr> Partnership.</li>
  <li>The Ayrton Fund<sup id="fnref:441"><a href="#fn:441" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 441]</a></sup> is a UK International Climate Finance (<abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr>) commitment of up to £1 billion on clean energy innovation. It is part of the wider £11.6 billion of <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> and provides Official Development Assistance (<abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr>) for the Research, Development, and Demonstration (<abbr title="Research, Development and Demonstration">RD&amp;D</abbr>) of innovative, clean energy technologies and business models for developing countries over the 5-year period between April 2021 and March 2026.</li>
  <li>The Ayrton Fund focuses on a series of high priority Ayrton Challenge technology areas, which are critical but off-track for delivery of <abbr title="United Nations">UN</abbr> Sustainable Development Goals 7 and 13, and where the UK is well-placed to support. These include areas such as energy storage, next generation solar, sustainable cooling, clean hydrogen, smart energy systems and more.</li>
  <li>By the end of Year 3 of the Ayrton Fund (FY 23/24), UK innovation-focused <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> reached 27m people in developing countries with improved access to clean energy, leveraged over <strong>£1.8 billion</strong> in private and public finance, reduced <strong>4.1m</strong> tonnes of <abbr title="Carbon Dioxide">CO</abbr><sub>2</sub> (equivalent to the annual carbon footprint of over 700,000 people in the UK<sup id="fnref:442"><a href="#fn:442" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 442]</a></sup>), and created and supported 169,000 green jobs.</li>
  <li>Under the Breakthrough Agenda<sup id="fnref:443"><a href="#fn:443" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 443]</a></sup> launched by World Leaders at <abbr title="The 26th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC">COP26</abbr>, we are building coalitions, partnerships and platforms with the ambition that developing countries have ready access to aggregated, coordinated and impactful assistance in each sector of the economy.</li>
</ul>

<div class="example">
  <p><strong>Case Studies</strong></p>

  <ul>
    <li>UK support to the Energy Sector Management Assistance Programme (<abbr title="Energy Sector Management Assistance Programme">ESMAP</abbr>) assists low and middle-income countries to reduce poverty and boost growth through environmentally sustainable energy solutions. They work to accelerate the energy transition required to achieve <abbr title="United Nations">UN</abbr> Sustainable Development Goal 7 to ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable, and modern energy for all.</li>
    <li>The <abbr title="Energy Sector Management Assistance Programme">ESMAP</abbr>-IFC Offshore Wind Development Program supported by the UK enables sharing of expertise for countries developing their own offshore wind roadmaps. It received the Collaboration Award at the Global Offshore Wind Awards 2023, recognising the Program’s efforts to accelerate deployment of offshore wind in emerging markets.</li>
    <li>A further example is, SunCulture, a Nairobi-based solar irrigation start-up supported by the <abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr> and partners since 2018, has recently raised investment from British International Investments and also $27m<sup id="fnref:444"><a href="#fn:444" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 444]</a></sup> in Series B funding including from the Private Infrastructure Development Group (PIDG) to expand delivery of its ‘pay-as-you-pump’ solar water pumping equipment which has already reached more than 40,000 farmers in East Africa, tripling typical yields and actually reducing overall water use with more efficient irrigation approaches – boosting livelihoods and helping people adapt to more variable rainfall.</li>
  </ul>
</div>

<h4 id="support-provided-at-different-stages-of-the-technology-cycle-brbr">4.5.2 Support provided at different stages of the technology cycle <br><br>
</h4>

<p>For example, the Ayrton Fund covers a range of UK <abbr title="Official Development Assistance">ODA</abbr>-funded clean energy Research, Development and Demonstration (<abbr title="Research, Development and Demonstration">RD&amp;D</abbr>) support, focused on delivering real change across 3 interconnected themes which describe the whole energy system and its applications, and link with the 3 pillars of supply, demand, and delivery, while supporting the Global Net Zero agenda. The diagram below illustrates the key types of intervention made by programmes across the Ayrton portfolio.</p>

<h4 id="foundational-research-and-training-brbr">4.5.3 Foundational Research and Training <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK’s Ayrton Fund, has been developing targeted research, knowledge, and information products on a range of topics (e.g. clean energy access<sup id="fnref:445"><a href="#fn:445" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 445]</a></sup>, energy system models<sup id="fnref:446"><a href="#fn:446" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 446]</a></sup>, low carbon development<sup id="fnref:447"><a href="#fn:447" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 447]</a></sup>, modern cooking<sup id="fnref:448"><a href="#fn:448" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 448]</a></sup>, efficient appliances<sup id="fnref:449"><a href="#fn:449" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 449]</a></sup>, etc.); targeted training, job placements and internships<sup id="fnref:450"><a href="#fn:450" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 450]</a></sup> in clean energy businesses; new clean energy master’s courses and modules<sup id="fnref:451"><a href="#fn:451" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 451]</a></sup> in developing country universities; UK Chevening clean energy access scholarships<sup id="fnref:452"><a href="#fn:452" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 452]</a></sup> for southern scholars; and research partnerships with local clean energy access institutions and organisations in the South. Ayrton Fund activities under this intervention have benefited 67 countries in Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and the Indo-Pacific. For example, the UK’s Clean Climate Growth (<abbr title="Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth">CCG</abbr>) programme’s tools and training supported the development of Uganda’s Energy Transition Plan<sup id="fnref:453"><a href="#fn:453" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 453]</a></sup> (<abbr title="Uganda’s Energy Transition Plan">ETP</abbr>). The <abbr title="Uganda’s Energy Transition Plan">ETP</abbr> sets Uganda’s pathway to achieve universal access to modern energy and sustainably power the country’s economic transformation. The <abbr title="Uganda’s Energy Transition Plan">ETP</abbr> was developed by Uganda’s Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development, with support from the International Energy Agency (<abbr title="International Energy Agency">IEA</abbr>) in partnership with <abbr title="Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth">CCG</abbr>. <abbr title="Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth">CCG</abbr> provided training to Ugandan government officials in the use of <abbr title="Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth">CCG</abbr> open-source modelling tools and supported them in the creation of energy systems models. The resulting analysis provided an input in the development of the <abbr title="Uganda’s Energy Transition Plan">ETP</abbr>.</p>

<h4 id="open-calls-brbr">4.5.4 Open Calls <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK is stimulating a pipeline of new ideas and innovations in clean energy technologies and business models that have the potential to be commercialised and scaled-up in developing countries, particularly through UK-international joint ventures. The UK is achieving this by supporting open funding competitions through Energy Catalyst, which is funded through the Transforming Energy Access (<abbr title="Transforming Energy Access">TEA</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:454"><a href="#fn:454" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 454]</a></sup> platform and the Global Challenges Research Fund (<abbr title="Global Challenges Research Fund">GCRF</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:455"><a href="#fn:455" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 455]</a></sup> and has provided financial and technical support to over 90 UK-led <abbr title="Research and development">R&amp;D</abbr> projects in Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and the Indo-Pacific, across the full spectrum of Ayrton thematic challenges. There have also been a series of Open Calls focused on the <abbr title="Research and development">R&amp;D</abbr> of productive use appliances (PREO)<sup id="fnref:456"><a href="#fn:456" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 456]</a></sup>, efficient appliances suited to off-grid contexts (LEIA)<sup id="fnref:457"><a href="#fn:457" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 457]</a></sup>, mobile-based technologies (GSMA Fund)<sup id="fnref:458"><a href="#fn:458" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 458]</a></sup>, and energy innovations in humanitarian contexts (Humanitarian Grand Challenge Fund)<sup id="fnref:459"><a href="#fn:459" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 459]</a></sup>.</p>

<h4 id="technology-accelerators-brbr">4.5.5 Technology Accelerators <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK has conducted a series of funding calls by the Modern Energy Cooking Services (<abbr title="Modern Energy Cooking Services">MECS</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:460"><a href="#fn:460" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 460]</a></sup> programme focused on solving modern cooking challenges (including around supply chains, integration with mini-grids, alternative cooking fuels etc.) and via the Cross Boundary Mini-Grids Innovation Lab<sup id="fnref:461"><a href="#fn:461" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 461]</a></sup> which convenes mini-grid developers around priority prototypes testing new business model innovations for mini-grids. This intervention type should see significant growth with the start of new projects funded through the flagship Zero Emissions Generator<sup id="fnref:462"><a href="#fn:462" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 462]</a></sup> (<abbr title="Zero Emissions Generator">ZE-Gen</abbr>) initiative, and Next Generation Solar projects funded through a new partnership between the <abbr title="Transforming Energy Access">TEA</abbr><sup id="fnref:463"><a href="#fn:463" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 463]</a></sup> platform and the Sunrise Network<sup id="fnref:464"><a href="#fn:464" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 464]</a></sup>.</p>

<h4 id="venture-building-brbr">4.5.6 Venture-building <br><br>
</h4>

<p>We are providing financial and technical support to innovative start-ups, and small and medium sized businesses (<abbr title="Small and medium sized businesses">SMEs</abbr>) to scale-up their clean energy offers in developing countries, mostly in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, through stategic partnerships with organisations like the Shell Foundation<sup id="fnref:465"><a href="#fn:465" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 465]</a></sup>, Acumen<sup id="fnref:466"><a href="#fn:466" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 466]</a></sup>, GSMA<sup id="fnref:467"><a href="#fn:467" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 467]</a></sup>, the Global Innovation Fund<sup id="fnref:468"><a href="#fn:468" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 468]</a></sup>, and the World Bank<sup id="fnref:469"><a href="#fn:469" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 469]</a></sup>.</p>

<h4 id="market-building-brbr">4.5.7 Market-building <br><br>
</h4>

<p>The UK has supported a range of market-enabling intitutions, market-supporting digital platforms, and specialist funds working mainly in Sub-Saharan Africa. Developments in the last year include the Shell Foundation-led Market Institutions Facility<sup id="fnref:470"><a href="#fn:470" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 470]</a></sup>, Mirova’s Gigaton Fund<sup id="fnref:471"><a href="#fn:471" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 471]</a></sup>, Odyssey’s Results Based Finance platform<sup id="fnref:472"><a href="#fn:472" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 472]</a></sup>, the Carbon Value Exchange<sup id="fnref:473"><a href="#fn:473" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 473]</a></sup> (<abbr title="Carbon Value Exchange">CaVex</abbr>), the ongoing work of the Global Distributors Collective<sup id="fnref:474"><a href="#fn:474" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 474]</a></sup>, and action across several Crowfunding Platforms<sup id="fnref:475"><a href="#fn:475" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 475]</a></sup>.</p>

<h4 id="country-demonstrators-brbr">4.5.8 Country Demonstrators <br><br>
</h4>

<p>At <abbr title="The 28th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC">COP28</abbr>, the UK announced its intention to develop a <strong>Climate Innovation Pull Facility (<abbr title="Climate Innovation Pull Facility">CIPF</abbr>)</strong> providing up to £185 million to pull-up innovative climate mitigation solutions in developing countries, to the point at which they help shape local markets and are ready for large scale deployment in those contexts. In turn, this will help accelerate global climate action in line with the Paris Agreement, and progress on the Sustainable Development Goals.</p>

<p>In November 2023, a <strong>£40m scale-up of the Transforming Energy Access (<abbr title="Transforming Energy Access">TEA</abbr>) platform</strong> was included in the UK announcement<sup id="fnref:476"><a href="#fn:476" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 476]</a></sup> at <abbr title="The 28th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC">COP28</abbr> in Dubai, to facilitate clean energy demonstrators funded by <abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr> Country Posts and to scale-up work on sustainable cooling and energy efficiency. So far, new demonstrators have been agreed in Tanzania, the Pacific and Indonesia, with additional demonstrators currently in design in Zambia, Somalia, and Rwanda, showing strong uptake on the new mechanism.</p>

<p>This financial year 2023/24, <strong>£9.1m was awarded to 16 innovation projects via Energy Catalyst Round 10</strong><sup id="fnref:477"><a href="#fn:477" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 477]</a></sup>, that started from April 2024, and to improve clean energy access in 11 countries in Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and the Indo-Pacific (including Fiji, Papua New Guinea, and Indonesia). This is part of a broader UK Government investment of £40.3m in 67 innovation projects to be funded by the <abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr> and the UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. It includes 4 projects funded by the Tanzania British High Commission via the new <abbr title="Transforming Energy Access">TEA</abbr> demonstrator offer.</p>

<p>In November 2023, a <strong>£15m scale-up of the UK’s Modern Energy Cooking Services (<abbr title="Modern Energy Cooking Services">MECS</abbr>) programme</strong> was included in the UK’s Ayrton Fund announcement<sup id="fnref:478"><a href="#fn:478" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 478]</a></sup> at <abbr title="The 28th Conference of Parties at UNFCCC">COP28</abbr> in Dubai, to facilitate clean energy demonstrators funded by <abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr> Country Posts. So far, new demonstrators have been agreed in Tanzania and Uganda to scale-up and demonstrate eCooking from April 2024.</p>

<h4 id="support-for-the-development-and-enhancement-of-endogenous-capacities-and-technologies-of-developing-country-parties-brbr">4.5.9 Support for the development and enhancement of endogenous capacities and technologies of developing country Parties <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Through the UK’s Ayrton Fund programming, the UK has been supporting the endogenous capacities of developing countries:</p>

<p><strong>The UK’s Clean Climate Growth (<abbr title="Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth">CCG</abbr>) Fund launched a new partnership with the International Energy Agency (<abbr title="International Energy Agency">IEA</abbr>)</strong> on their Affordable and Sustainable Energy System for Sub-Saharan Africa programme<sup id="fnref:479"><a href="#fn:479" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 479]</a></sup>, which provides support to selected countries to improve their data management and long-term planning to facilitate development of low-carbon energy systems. <abbr title="Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth">CCG</abbr> will provide training in its modelling tools to government officials in target countries such as Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda, Uganda, Zambia, etc.</p>

<p><strong>BRILHO Mozambique</strong>: is a country programme that catalyses private sector investment and innovation, and government support in Mozambique, to increase energy access through supply of household solar, mini-grids and improved cooking solutions.</p>

<ul>
  <li>The programme has provided technical support to the government of Mozambique in drafting the regulatory framework for off-grid areas, making Mozambique a more attractive market for investors in the renewable energy sector.</li>
  <li>In 2023/24, BRILHO held workshops<sup id="fnref:480"><a href="#fn:480" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 480]</a></sup> with government and industry representatives in the areas of leadership, gender equality and social inclusion, and women’s empowerment. These sought to strengthen the capacity of institutions in the energy sector to create a gender-sensitive, inclusive, and conducive environment for the implementation of business models that tackle the needs of vulnerable people and increase the representation of women in the energy sector value chain.</li>
</ul>

<p>UK support to <strong>Mission Efficiency</strong> funded the development of 3 innovation roadmaps under the Ayrton Fund’s Industrial Decarbonisation challenge in Brazil, Kenya, and Vietnam. It also funded a publicly accessible toolkit<sup id="fnref:481"><a href="#fn:481" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 481]</a></sup> that facilitates more integrated support on energy efficiency by identifying priority sectors by country and leveraging existing tools from partner programs and platforms, as well as other leading institutions around the world.</p>

<h4 id="efforts-to-encourage-private-sector-activities-related-to-technology-development-and-transfer-and-how-such-efforts-support-developing-country-parties-brbr">4.5.10 Efforts to encourage private sector activities related to technology development and transfer and how such efforts support developing country Parties <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Our <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> programmes are having a global impact, as set out in our published annual International Climate Finance (<abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr>) results<sup id="fnref:482"><a href="#fn:482" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 482]</a></sup>. Since 2011 UK <abbr title="International Climate Finance">ICF</abbr> has leveraged £7.8 billion of private finance for climate change. Examples of UK efforts to encourage private sector activity through Ayrton Fund programming:</p>

<h5 id="transforming-energy-access-tea-platform">4.5.10.1 Transforming Energy Access (<abbr title="Transforming Energy Access">TEA</abbr>) platform</h5>

<ul>
  <li>Between 2016 and 2024, the £265m <abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr> Transforming Energy Access<sup id="fnref:483"><a href="#fn:483" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 483]</a></sup> (<abbr title="Transforming Energy Access">TEA</abbr>) platform, which invests in early-stage testing and scale-up of new clean energy technologies and business models for developing countries, leveraged £1.5 billion in additional investment into clean energy research, innovation and scale-up from both public and private sources.</li>
  <li>
<abbr title="Transforming Energy Access">TEA</abbr>-supported innovators have gone on to raise significant investment capital, including for example Sheffield-based Mobile Power<sup id="fnref:484"><a href="#fn:484" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 484]</a></sup> who developed an innovative battery swapping and distribution system in use in Sierra Leone, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Liberia, Uganda, Zambia, Gambia and Nigeria and have raised over £5m in follow on investment. Mobile Power have rented their portable batteries over 16 million times to date and have 55,000 active customers who use these batteries to power electric motorbikes, for phone charging, lightening, and for powering small DC appliances such as TVs and fans.</li>
  <li>Another example of a <abbr title="Transforming Energy Access">TEA</abbr>-supported innovator is Wales-based SureChill<sup id="fnref:485"><a href="#fn:485" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 485]</a></sup> who developed a unique cooling technology approved by the World Health Organisation that ensures a refrigerator remains perfectly cool during any power outage, and who raised over £7 million in follow on investment. SureChill refrigerators are used in several countries in Sub-Saharan Africa including Kenya, Senegal, Nigeria, Zambia, and Mali.</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="africa-clean-energy-programme-ace">4.5.10.2 Africa Clean Energy Programme (<abbr title="Africa Clean Energy Programme">ACE</abbr>)</h5>

<ul>
  <li>
<strong>The Africa Clean Energy Programme (<abbr title="Africa Clean Energy Programme">ACE</abbr>)</strong> is a regional programme including a Challenge Fund supporting start-ups or expansion of household solar energy businesses in 9 countries in Sub-Saharan Africa and supporting the deployment of mini grids through the African Development Bank.</li>
  <li>During the Ayrton Fund period, the programme leveraged £2.8 million in private finance in support of programme activities and is estimated to have provided 0.67 <abbr title="Megawatts">MW</abbr> of installed off-grid clean energy capacity.</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="global-facility-to-decarbonise-transport-gfdt">4.5.10.3 Global Facility to Decarbonise Transport (<abbr title="Global Facility to Decarbonise Transport">GFDT</abbr>)</h5>

<ul>
  <li>The <strong><abbr title="Global Facility to Decarbonise Transport">GFDT</abbr></strong> is a new, first of its kind World Bank Trust Fund<sup id="fnref:486"><a href="#fn:486" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 486]</a></sup> that provides financial and technical assistance to support transport decarbonisation in low and middle-income countries. Its mission is to accelerate innovation and investment in climate-smart mobility solutions, with the goal of achieving net zero in the global transport sector by 2050. GFTD funding and project preparation helps move big transport decarbonisation projects that otherwise would not go forward. In doing so, the Fund empowers low and middle-income countries to build transport systems that not only reduce emissions, but are also safe, modern, inclusive, and resilient.</li>
  <li>Three <abbr title="Global Facility to Decarbonise Transport">GFDT</abbr> innovation-focused projects have been badged as Ayrton to date, including in India (developing a new business model to help unlock commercial financing at scale for e-buses, e-motorcycles and electric 3-wheelers).</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="efforts-to-accelerate-encourage-and-enable-innovation-including-research-development-and-deployment-efforts-and-collaborative-approaches-to-research-and-development-brbr">4.5.11 Efforts to accelerate, encourage and enable innovation, including research, development and deployment efforts, and collaborative approaches to research and development <br><br>
</h4>

<p>Examples of Ayrton Fund activities accelerating innovation include:</p>

<h5 id="international-science-partnership-fund-ispf">4.5.11.1 International Science Partnership Fund (<abbr title="International Science Partnership Fund">ISPF</abbr>)</h5>

<ul>
  <li>International Science Partnership Fund (<abbr title="International Science Partnership Fund">ISPF</abbr>)<sup id="fnref:487"><a href="#fn:487" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 487]</a></sup> will facilitate participation of world-class UK academic researchers and their international partners in cutting-edge research. This is an existing fund that supports world-class research in cutting-edge science and innovation to tackle the major themes of our time: Planet, Health, Tech, and Talent.</li>
  <li>Under the theme of ‘Resilient Planet’, <abbr title="International Science Partnership Fund">ISPF</abbr> will give researchers and innovators access to global talent, large-scale facilities, research ecosystems and markets to swiftly move forward ideas to greater maturity, applicability, and commercialisation.</li>
  <li>The programme will build on <abbr title="Department for Science, Innovation and Technology">DSIT</abbr>’s small portfolio of energy research and ensure a strong strategic direction of the work and coherence with other government departments. It will comprise a combination of scaling-up of existing activities, such as Innovate UK’s Energy Catalyst and EPSRC’s energy access projects, and new thematic projects in areas such as solar/biofuels, whole systems, heating/refrigeration, sustainable transport, and industrial energy.</li>
  <li>The fund launched in December 2022 with an initial £119 million. A further £218 million was announced in November 2023 for research and innovation partnerships with low and middle-income countries to support sustainable development.</li>
  <li>Research partnerships that bring together multiple countries and both university and private sector expertise, produce game-changing technologies, innovations and evidence, benefiting hundreds of millions of people in lower-income countries. The UK’s International Science Partnerships Fund is an example of how we can foster prosperity by solving shared global research and innovation challenges. Genuine partnerships are essential to achieve the ambitions set out in the UK’s Science and Technology Framework and the International Technology Strategy.</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Transforming Energy Access (<abbr title="Transforming Energy Access">TEA</abbr>) platform</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li>The £265m <abbr title="Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office">FCDO</abbr> Transforming Energy Access<sup id="fnref:488"><a href="#fn:488" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 488]</a></sup> (<abbr title="Transforming Energy Access">TEA</abbr>) platform funds the research, development and demonstration of new clean energy technologies and business models for developing countries.</li>
  <li>Between 2016 and 2024, through effective partnerships and collaborative approaches with the private sector, academia, <abbr title="Non-Governmental Organisations">NGOs</abbr> and international organisations, <abbr title="Transforming Energy Access">TEA</abbr> has stimulated UK-led research and development of <strong>662 new clean energy technologies and business models</strong> in areas such as energy storage<sup id="fnref:489"><a href="#fn:489" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 489]</a></sup>, sustainable cooling, electric pressure cookers, remote network management, energy access crowdfunding<sup id="fnref:490"><a href="#fn:490" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 490]</a></sup>, improving clean energy access for <strong>27 million people</strong> in developing countries (including 13 million women).</li>
  <li>It has also <strong>leveraged £1.5 billion</strong> of additional investment into clean energy technology research, innovation and scale-up from both private and public sources; created and supported <strong>125,000 sustainable long-term jobs</strong> (including 27,000 jobs for women); supported <strong>759 young Africans</strong> with job placements and <strong>1,135 managers</strong> with specialist training in clean energy access businesses; and led to the <strong>avoidance of 2.7 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions</strong>.</li>
</ul>

<h5 id="clean-energy-innovation-facility-ceif">4.5.12 Clean Energy Innovation Facility (<abbr title="Clean Energy Innovation Facility">CEIF</abbr>)</h5>

<ul>
  <li>The <abbr title="Clean Energy Innovation Facility">CEIF</abbr> 1.0 programme, under the umbrella <abbr title="Clean Energy Innovation Facility">CEIF</abbr> platform, aims to accelerate the commercialisation of innovative clean energy technologies in developing countries along key themes such as industrial decarbonisation, sustainable cooling, smart energy, and energy storage. A programme extension of up to £55m (<abbr title="Clean Energy Innovation Facility">CEIF</abbr> 2.0) has been approved and started in March 2024. The <abbr title="Clean Energy Innovation Facility">CEIF</abbr> 2.0 programme will focus on piloting and demonstrating innovative technologies across 3 key themes - industrial decarbonisation, sustainable cooling, and smart energy.</li>
  <li>Up to 2023/24, <abbr title="Clean Energy Innovation Facility">CEIF</abbr> 1.0 supported 55 sustainable cooling technologies with 62 pilots in Colombia, Mexico, Nigeria, Kenya, Rwanda, India, and Bangladesh. The pilots focused on key themes, namely cooling in cities, cold chains, temperature-controlled logistics, space cooling, and cooling-as-a-service (<abbr title="Cooling-as-a-service">CaaS</abbr>) business models. Alongside this, the International Finance Corporation (IFC) - delivery partner for <abbr title="Clean Energy Innovation Facility">CEIF</abbr> - launched the India Cooling Innovation Lab<sup id="fnref:491"><a href="#fn:491" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 491]</a></sup> in December 2023 bringing together technology innovators and local companies to pilot innovative smart energy technologies.</li>
  <li>Under the Industrial Decarbonisation theme, in 2023 <abbr title="Clean Energy Innovation Facility">CEIF</abbr> supported 17 ongoing projects in Morocco, Mexico, Dominican Republic, Colombia, Türkiye, Pakistan, India, Vietnam, Bangladesh, as well as regional activities in East Asia and Pacific and those with a global reach. Under the Smart Energy theme, <abbr title="Clean Energy Innovation Facility">CEIF</abbr> redefined the fund based on lessons learnt over the past 4 years and planned a strong pipeline of projects showcasing the impact of these changes.</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="knowledge-generated-brbr">4.5.13 Knowledge generated <br><br>
</h4>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>The <strong>UK’s Climate Compatible Growth (<abbr title="Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth">CCG</abbr>)</strong> programme has produced knowledge products which are being used in teaching and research within 7 universities or research institutes in Low and Middle-Income Countries.</p>
  </li>
  <li>Further to attending <abbr title="Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth">CCG</abbr> training courses, academics within these 7 universities are either teaching <abbr title="Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth">CCG</abbr> tools in their courses or using <abbr title="Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth">CCG</abbr> tools in their research. Examples include: at Strathmore University<sup id="fnref:492"><a href="#fn:492" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 492]</a></sup> in Nairobi, Kenya, the <abbr title="Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth">CCG</abbr> energy systems modelling tool OSeMOSYS<sup id="fnref:493"><a href="#fn:493" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 493]</a></sup> is being taught as part of the Masters of Science in Sustainable Energy Transitions; at the Addis Ababa Institute of Technology for Research Advancement<sup id="fnref:494"><a href="#fn:494" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 494]</a></sup> <abbr title="Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth">CCG</abbr> tools are being used to assess the potential impact of climate change on hydropower supply in Ethiopia; at Makerere University<sup id="fnref:495"><a href="#fn:495" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 495]</a></sup> in Kampala, Uganda <abbr title="Clean Climate Growth or Climate Compatible Growth">CCG</abbr> tools including Model for Analysis of the Energy Demand (<abbr title="Model for Analysis of the Energy Demand">MAED</abbr>) and OSeMOSYS<sup id="fnref:496"><a href="#fn:496" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 496]</a></sup> are being taught in the ‘Master of Energy Economics and Governance’ course.</li>
  <li>
<strong>The Accelerating Smart Power and Renewable Energy in India (<abbr title="Accelerating Smart Power and Renewable Energy in India">ASPIRE</abbr>)</strong> seeks to leverage carbon financing to provide market-driven solar-powered induction cooking solutions to target households in India that are below the poverty line and use firewood as their primary cooking fuel. In 2023/24, the programme facilitated 17 strategic engagements between Indian and UK organisations, disseminated 50 technical study reports enriching knowledge exchange, and empowered 1,800 senior level stakeholders through capacity building workshops.</li>
</ul>
